title: ROBO BRIDGE MCP
pitch: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more!
about_excerpt: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more! Like Comment Story Updates Main Overview, with robot arm, and train on the final built bridge Built Simple Wall Building Bridge Building Rubiks Cube Pushing the "MORE BRICKS" button Building a Checkerboard Bridge Hologram View Train testing the bridge Train testing the bridge 2 Inspiration I loved building with lego for years, and wanted to see what it would look like if a robot could build with bricks in an interactive simulation. Thought this was a bit ambitious, it is buggy in areas, but hopefulyl it shows what future interactive games could look like with WebMCP. What it does ROBO BRIDGE MCP is a browser-based robotics simulator built around a robot arm and a shared construction environment. Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the workspace, plan structures, control the robot, place bricks, request more materials and react to changes made by you in the scene. There are over 31 native WebMCP tools available for controlling the robot, planning, placing the bricks, and modifying the environment. When testing it out, ask your agent to explore the tools, and iterate with it to build different structures. I was suprised when i asked it for a checkerboard pattern and rubiks cube that it nailed it! How I built it The simulator runs entirely in the browser using Three.js in a static website with no server-side processing. A shared build area, inventory and revision state are used by both the Human and the AI agent. You decide what to build, and the agent plans on how to build it and which tools to use. The WebMCP tools are used to trigger code that drives the robot movement to place bricks. I tried to get the agents to do the full robot joint commands and it took too long, so it essentially controls the TCP and gripper of the robot, and inverse kinematics handles the rest to position the robot joints within its workspace. Challenges The hardest part was getting the robot arm to build structures AND adapt if the user would place a brick in the middle of its plan. I also had to make the interaction fast enough for a natural live demonstration while keeping placement validation deterministic. So a real robot arm wouldnt move that quickly, but you can play around with the speed settings in the menu. (Note some larger builds may take a while, even with 1 second brick pick-and-place cycle time, the planning and number of bricks will greatly increase the time the build takes) What I learned WebMCP is awesome! This live demo game opens up a lot of possibilities. Hopefully i can get it to build larger buildings, streets and towns later on. You could also potentially control a real robot arm through the browser. Or even its own dedicated web game, where people can connect their agents to it to build cool stuff. title: SwiftXR
pitch: From prompt to 3D: WebMCP-powered creation inside SwiftXR.
about_excerpt: From prompt to 3D: WebMCP-powered creation inside SwiftXR. Like Comment Story Updates Codex controlling SwiftXR Inspiration For a long time, building 3D, AR, or VR web experiences meant hiring developers, stitching tools together, and spending more than most small businesses could afford. SwiftXR was built to change that by making immersive web experiences something creators and e-commerce teams can build themselves. The editor already has AI features to speed things up. But when we saw the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to take it one step further: what if someone could open SwiftXR and ask an external AI agent — like ChatGPT — to actually work in the editor with them? Not by guessing at the page, but by calling real SwiftXR editor tools. What it does SwiftXR MCP adds WebMCP tools to the SwiftXR editor so AI agents can work inside the user's authenticated browser session. A user can describe what they want, and the agent can: Create and set up a scene Add 3D assets, media, and interactions Move, rotate, and scale objects Adjust lighting, backgrounds, and camera behavior Preview changes in the editor Publish the finished experience to the web The editor UI stays open the whole time. The user can watch what the agent changes, undo it, or jump in and adjust things manually. How we built it We exposed SwiftXR editor actions as structured WebMCP tools. Instead of an agent scraping the page or sending screenshots back and forth, it receives a clear list of available operations and calls them directly. The flow is straightforward: User prompt → AI agent → WebMCP tool call → SwiftXR editor action → published experience Each tool has a defined input, so agent actions stay predictable. For example: { "tool": "add_3d_asset", "input": { "sceneId": "scene_123", "assetUrl": "https://example.com/chair.glb", "name": "Chair" } } Because the tools run in the live SwiftXR session, changes show up immediately in the editor. Challenges we ran into Choosing tool boundaries that were useful to agents without exposing every internal editor detail Making sure agent actions mapped cleanly to visible editor state Handling actions that needed confirmation, like publishing or deleting content Keeping the normal no-code experience intact while adding agent support on top Accomplishments that we're proud of Making SwiftXR editor actions available as structured WebMCP tools Building a workflow where agents and users can work on the same live editor session Avoiding fragile DOM scraping in favor of reliable, schema-based tool calls Turning a natural-language prompt into a published 3D, AR, or VR experience What we learned Agents are much better at editing apps when the app tells them what it can do Structured tool calls beat page scraping for anything complex, especially an editor Keeping the human in the loop matters: people want to see and control what the agent changes The hard part was deciding which editor actions to expose, and at what level of detail What's next for SwiftXR Expand the toolset to cover more editor features, templates, and asset workflows Add richer permissions and confirmation flows for sensitive actions Improve multi-step agent workflows for larger projects Explore analytics so creators can see how published experiences perform Keep making immersive web creation faster, cheaper, and more accessible through AI Built With 3d ai-agent editor-tools mcp no-code swiftxr three.js webmcp xr Try it out swiftxr.io Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Hammed Arowosegbe shoile abdulazeez Like Share this project: Updates Hammed Arowosegbe started this project — Sep 03, 2026 11:03 AM EDT

title: Port Authority
pitch: A browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect.
about_excerpt: A browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it# PORT AUTHORITY The harbor master for WebMCP. No agent docks on vibes. Port Authority is a browser-only workbench for documenting and auditing the tool contracts a page exposes through WebMCP. It turns the page’s agent-facing surface into something a developer can inspect, redline, approve, and export. An agent may inspect contracts, run deterministic checks, stage one bounded revision, and preview documentation. It cannot approve its own proposal. Only the visible human controls can grant clearance, return a revision, or reset the manifest. Live application: port-authority-webmcp-preview-0904a.mjohnson1307.workers.dev The working loop ARRIVE → INSPECT → REDLINE → CLEAR → EXPORT The accepted registry starts at revision 1 with six deterministic findings. One is a deliberate, concrete contradiction in the documented propose_contract_revision example: - baseRevision: "1" + baseRevision: 1 The schema requires an integer, but the seeded example supplies a string. The golden path is real application state, not a scripted mock: The agent lists the five registered tools. The agent audits the accepted manifest and receives six findings. The agent inspects propose_contract_revision and confirms INVALID_EXAMPLE from declared contract data. The agent stages the smallest allowed revision: the same example array with only baseRevision changed from "1" to 1 . The accepted registry remains unchanged while the revision waits in DRY DOCK . A human reviews the exact payload and selects GRANT CLEARANCE — Accept this exact revision or RETURN TO SHIPPER — Reject without changing registry . After clearance, the accepted revision becomes 2, the audit count becomes five, and INVALID_EXAMPLE disappears. SHIP’S PAPERS opens four synchronized projections of the accepted registry. Demo prompt Audit the loaded Port Authority manifest. List the WebMCP tools, run the deterministic contract inspection, and inspect propose_contract_revision. If the declared data confirms that its example uses a string where baseRevision requires an integer, stage the smallest bounded revision that changes "1" to 1. Do not infer runtime behavior and do not grant your own clearance. After the human grants clearance: Reinspect the cleared manifest, report the remaining finding count, and open the four accepted artifact projections. Confirm whether the repaired example now matches its declared schema. To reset the demo, select RESET LOCAL CATALOG and confirm the browser-local reset. Reloading the page also starts a new in-memory session. Five registered berths WebMCP tool What it may do list_tool_contracts List the five accepted contracts, revisions, annotations, side-effect classes, and finding counts. get_tool_contract Inspect one exact accepted contract and visibly select it in the workbench. audit_tool_contracts Run deterministic checks over declared contract data and populate CUSTOMS INSPECTION . propose_contract_revision Validate and stage one fixed-name, allowlisted metadata revision for human review. It cannot accept it. preview_contract_bundle Open four projections generated from the currently accepted registry. The tool names are fixed. Revision patches reject unknown fields, stale base revisions, invalid schemas, empty changes, and attempts to rename executable tools atomically. One accepted source src/contracts/registry.ts is the canonical contract registry. That one accepted source drives: top-level document.modelContext.registerTool() metadata; the visible HARBOR MAP and registration explorer; deterministic audit findings; staged before/after revisions; registration metadata; the canonical JSON manifest; the Markdown reference; and the OpenAPI 3.1 documentation chart. Output schemas, examples, recovery guidance, lifecycle states, prerequisites, privacy notes, and side-effect classifications are Port Authority documentation extensions. They are not presented as native registerTool() fields. The OpenAPI artifact is documentation only. Synthetic paths carry explicit x-webmcp-* , x-documentation-projection: true , and x-network-endpoint: false markers. It creates no HTTP routes or network endpoints. What the audit proves Port Authority checks only facts supported by the accepted contract data, including: missing, malformed, or vague contract fields; missing, open, or internally inconsistent input schemas; examples that do not validate against their declared schemas; conflicts between read-only annotations and declared side effects; missing untrusted-content hints for developer or external output; missing recovery guidance; duplicate tool names; and disagreements between the accepted registry and generated projections. It does not prove runtime behavior, actual side effects, privacy, security, or semantic truth. Those remain developer-review responsibilities. Browser and trust boundary Browser-only React application. No backend, database, account, authentication, remote API, analytics, telemetry, or cloud persistence. No arbitrary code execution. No model call or external service is used by the deterministic audit. Agents may inspect, audit, stage, and preview. Only visible human controls may accept, reject, or reset. WebMCP is progressive enhancement. The visible workbench remains usable when document.modelContext is unavailable. Runtime registration is imperative on the top-level document.modelContext ; there is no WebMCP polyfill or dependency on introspection APIs. Run locally Node.js 22 or newer and npm are recommended. git clone https://github.com/villagealchemist/permission-slip-webmcp.git cd permission-slip-webmcp npm ci npm run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1 Open the local URL printed by Vite in a WebMCP-capable browser to exercise the five page tools. Other browsers receive the complete visual workbench. Verify npm run docs:contracts npm run typecheck npm run lint npm run test npm run build The current suite covers schema boundaries, atomic revision rejection, stable audit findings, runtime output contracts, WebMCP registration, human-only acceptance, and artifact projection consistency. Static documentation generation writes these accepted-registry files under docs/generated/ : webmcp-contracts.json webmcp-reference.md openapi.json The in-page SHIP’S PAPERS workbench additionally exposes live registration metadata, so the browser presents four accepted projections. Project map src/contracts/ canonical registry, audit rules, revision boundary, projections src/workbench/ shared browser-local state and human-only decisions src/webmcp/ validation, fixed tool bindings, registration lifecycle src/contract-explorer/ visible Port Authority workbench scripts/ deterministic documentation generator docs/ architecture, privacy, and WebMCP notes The implementation walkthrough is in DEMO.md . Architectural and trust-boundary details are in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md , docs/WEBMCP.md , and docs/PRIVACY_MODEL.md . License MIT © 2026 Village Alchemist Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Port Authority Built With cloudflare-workers css3 html5 javascript json-schema mcp openapi-3.1 react react-testing-library typedoc typescript vite vitest webmcp wrangler Try it out port-authority-webmcp-preview-0904a.mjohnson1307.workers.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived, designed, built, tested, documented, and released Port Authority as a solo project, using ChatGPT and Codex as AI collaborators. I developed its WebMCP contract registry, five registered tools, deterministic audit engine, bounded revision workflow, human-only approval boundary, artifact projections, interface, automated tests, and Cloudflare deployment.  inspiration

 How We Built It 
 

 
 Built the frontend and backend using modern web technologies (HTML5/JavaScript) deployed seamlessly on Vercel. 
 Implemented WebMCP developer tools and schemas to expose key accounting endpoints safely to client-side AI agents. 
 Configured custom routing and real-time ledger validation to ensure balanced double-entry accounting records.

title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: NexusCanvas
pitch: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke.
about_excerpt: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke. Like Comment Story Updates The host doesn't prompt, so the page does Open it in ChatGPT and just ask Every call, args, result, duration Tools appear when the human selects a component The canvas compiles to real YAML The WebMCP surface, listed live Poisson arrivals, bounded queues, true p50/p95/p99 The agent drew this in a single tool call The human broke it, the agent found it The page grades the design, the model can't argue with it The human edits the same state the agent reads Postgres at 110%, 3% errors, p95 1609 ms Inspiration Every time I asked an AI to design a system, I got a picture. It would produce a tidy Mermaid diagram, tell me the design "scales well," and move on. But the diagram was a dead artifact the moment it appeared. If I changed my mind, the conversation and the diagram drifted apart. And the model had no way to check its own claim, it asserted that the architecture held up, because asserting is all a language model can do about a system it cannot run. WebMCP changes what is possible, because the page stops being a canvas the model draws on and becomes a participant. The page can hold the state. The page can do arithmetic the model cannot fake. And critically, I can reach into that same state with a mouse while the agent is working. So I built the thing I actually wanted: a whiteboard that pushes back. The agent proposes an architecture, the browser computes whether it survives contact with load, and when I break something by hand, the agent has to notice. What it does NexusCanvas is a system-architecture canvas that ChatGPT operates directly through 14 base WebMCP tools plus 3 contextual ones. It runs entirely client-side, meaning no backend, no API keys, no account. The agent can build a whole system in one apply_blueprint call, audit it, model load against it, inject outages, and compile it to Docker Compose. But the point is not that the agent draws. The point is what the page does back: It computes what the model cannot fake. An audit engine finds single points of failure, missing caches, insecure protocols and orphaned queues, and returns a letter grade. Two independent load engines report utilisation, error rate and latency percentiles. A Compose generator emits real YAML from the graph. It reads my edits. I take Redis offline by hand in the Inspector. The agent calls get_architecture , sees the outage nobody told it about, reruns the same load, and reports that Postgres went from 36% to 125% utilisation as reads that were being absorbed by the cache fall through to the database. It asks before destroying anything. The host I tested never prompts on destructiveHint , so the page prompts instead, the tool call blocks on a real modal and the agent waits for my click. Clicking Cancel returns a declined result the agent reports honestly. The demo arc is a design review: the agent builds a 17-component e-commerce system, the audit grades it D (51) , we fix it together to A (94) , and then I break the cache to prove the improvement was real. How I built it Static React 18 + TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for shared state, Dagre for layout. Deterministic TypeScript engines for everything that produces a number. Deployed as static files. I wrote the specification before the code, a blueprint, numbered requirements with acceptance criteria, and a tool contract document fixing every tool's description, JSON Schema, annotations and example result. Tool descriptions were then copied into the implementation verbatim , because a tool description is a prompt: it is the only thing the model on the other side reads before deciding whether to call you. The closed-form capacity model walks the graph in topological order, excluding back-edges. For each component, $$C_i = \text{capacityRps}_i \times \text{replicas}_i \times s_i, \qquad s_i = \begin{cases} 0.5 & \text{degraded} \ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ $$u_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{C_i}, \qquad \text{served}_i = \min(\lambda_i, C_i), \qquad \text{dropped}_i = \lambda_i - \text{served}_i$$ Routers split their served traffic by normalised edge weight; services fan out $\text{served} i \times w {ij}$ per edge, so a weight of $0.2$ reads as a 20% cache-miss rate. Latency stretches as a component saturates, capped so the number stays finite: $$\ell_i(u) = \begin{cases} \ell_i & u < 0.5 \[4pt] \dfrac{\ell_i}{1 - \min(u,\,0.9)} & u \geq 0.5 \end{cases}$$ The discrete-event simulator exists because the closed-form model cannot show cascades. It runs a simulated clock over a binary min-heap event queue with Poisson arrivals, exponential interarrival times drawn as $\Delta t = -\ln(U)/\lambda$ , plus per-component concurrency limits, bounded queues, hop timeouts, bounded retries, and upstream workers held while awaiting downstream calls, so connection-pool exhaustion emerges instead of being asserted. It reports true $p_{50}$, $p_{95}$ and $p_{99}$ from completed-request samples. Randomness is seeded by an FNV-1a hash of the graph and scenario, driving a mulberry32 generator threaded explicitly through the run. Same graph, same seed, bit-identical output, which is what makes it testable, and what makes the agent's claims reproducible. 57 tests cover the engines, tool input validation, the WebMCP adapter against host stand-ins, and the demo sequence. Challenges we ran into I did not know what ChatGPT's browser actually did. So before writing a line of app code, I shipped a probe page registering seven deliberately awkward tools and ran it inside the ChatGPT desktop app. It answered questions no specification could: the host exposes document.modelContext but not navigator.modelContext , it accepts content-array results, it picks up tools registered seconds after load, and it waits on a pending promise. That one hour saved the project. The host has no unregisterTool . Calling it throws a TypeError . My whole contextual-tool design assumed tools could appear and disappear with UI state. Rather than pretend, the adapter keeps one stable dispatcher per registration and marks it dormant when its context is gone, excluded from active counts and from get_architecture , and returning a guarded {ok: false, error, hint} if the retained callback is invoked anyway. The Tools panel shows dormant rows honestly instead of claiming a removal that did not happen. My audit was confidently wrong. The first run graded the reference architecture F , flagging the load balancer, API gateway and message queue as single points of failure, all of which ran multiple replicas. A structural chokepoint is not a SPOF if it is replicated. Adding a replicas == 1 precondition took one line and turned an audit a judge would distrust into one that survives scrutiny. Killing the cache made the database less busy. The model routed reads catalog → redis → postgres at a 20% miss rate, so marking Redis down removed 80% of the database's load, the exact opposite of what a cache outage does. The fix is a rule the spec had never stated: a downed cache drops nothing and forwards 100% of its inbound traffic downstream. Postgres went from 110% to 217%, and the demo's most important beat became true. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page disagrees with the model, and the page is right. That is the whole thesis, and it holds: the agent cannot talk its way past an audit grade or a utilisation figure it did not compute. Two independent engines, a one-pass closed-form model and a seeded discrete-event simulator, reach compatible conclusions about the same graph from completely different mathematics. And the honesty of the submission itself. Where the host's behaviour is unverified, the documentation says so rather than rounding up. Where the engines are comparisons under stated assumptions rather than predictions of production, the UI says that too. What we learned A tool description is a prompt. Adding six words to add_component , noting that stateful types default to one replica, was the difference between the agent adding a redundant cache and adding a new single point of failure on camera. Tool granularity decides whether the demo is watchable. Fine-grained tools mean forty round-trips to draw one system. One coarse apply_blueprint call draws it in a single beat. Registration lifecycle is a product concern, not plumbing. Tools that linger after their UI is gone are tools the agent will call when they cannot work. Determinism is a feature, not an implementation detail. It is what lets a person re-run what the agent claimed and get the same answer. A cost estimator, and it is the feature I most want. Right now the page tells you whether a design survives load. It should also tell you what that design costs , because in practice the argument about an architecture is never purely about correctness. title: The Line List
pitch: An agent-native manufacturing copilot that turns a product idea into a manufacturer-ready plan, finds the right partners, and prepares outreach through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native manufacturing copilot that turns a product idea into a manufacturer-ready plan, finds the right partners, and prepares outreach through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent-Native Document Collaboration Package Design Comparing Manufactories Outreach Inspiration I started The Line List because my girlfriend sells banana bread, and we started asking a simple question: what would it actually take to get her product manufactured and into stores? The answer was way more confusing than it should be. Manufacturer websites are inconsistent, important details are hard to find, and new founders usually do not even know what questions they should be asking. I wanted to make that process feel less overwhelming. The Line List originally started as a public directory of food and beverage manufacturers. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built a new sourcing workspace that lets a founder and their AI agent work through the process together. What it does A founder can describe what they want to make in plain language. Their agent then creates a living product brief and helps them work through the decisions that actually matter, such as product format, production volume, shelf life, packaging, and where they want to sell. The founder can review everything visually in the browser, explore a packaging direction in 3D, and see which information was confirmed, suggested, or still unknown. Once the product is ready for research, the agent can find manufacturer possibilities and explain why each one appeared. The Line List does not pretend that missing information is a match. Supported details include sources and review dates, while unknowns and possible conflicts remain visible. The agent can also prepare manufacturer-specific introduction drafts, but it cannot contact anyone on its own. The founder selects the manufacturers, reviews the exact information being shared, approves the message, and separately confirms when they are ready to send it. How I built it I built the experience with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Prisma, Three.js, and WebMCP. The website exposes structured tools that let the agent create and update the same product workspace the founder sees on the page. The tools cover workspace creation, product updates, packaging previews, manufacturer matching, PDF export, outreach preparation, and readiness checks. The important part was making WebMCP feel like part of the product instead of attaching a chatbot to the side of the website. The person handles visual decisions and final approvals, while the agent handles the repetitive research, organization, and drafting work. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was managing shared state between the person, the agent, and the website without letting them overwrite each other. I had to keep confirmed founder statements separate from agent suggestions, preserve unknown information, make mutations safe to retry, and ensure that manufacturer requirements could not be silently weakened just to produce more results. Packaging was another challenge. I wanted the agent to do more than recommend a package in text. It needed to open the actual 3D workbench so the founder could see the direction, make changes, and approve the exact version that would become part of the manufacturing brief. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud of the broader-search approval flow. If no manufacturer publicly proves every required capability, the agent cannot quietly relax the search. The founder sees the exact before-and-after criteria, reviews what will change, and decides whether to continue. Even after broadening, unsupported details stay marked as unknown. I am also proud that the experience goes beyond a basic WebMCP demo. It creates a persistent workspace, connects agent actions to visible interface changes, includes a real packaging workbench, produces evidence-backed manufacturer possibilities, and keeps the founder in control of anything external. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the website and agent each handle the parts they are best at. The agent is good at turning a messy idea into structured information, researching options, and preparing work. The browser is better for comparing results, reviewing visual changes, understanding what will be shared, and making final decisions. Building around that relationship made the experience feel much more useful than either a normal form or a standalone chatbot. What's next for The Line List Next, I want to improve the packaging models, expand the manufacturer data, and let founders manage multiple products and manufacturer conversations from one account. The larger goal is to make launching a physical product feel less like navigating an industry built for insiders. A founder should be able to start with an idea, understand what they need, find the right production partners, and move forward without guessing through every step. title: MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab
pitch: Your approval changes what the agent can do.
about_excerpt: Your approval changes what the agent can do. Like Comment Story Updates APPLY ABSENT — The agent can inspect and propose, but no mutating tool exists before player approval. APPLY ADDED — Visible player approval creates one single-use tool bound to the exact reviewed plan. EXACT APPLY → UNDO ADDED — Apply removes itself after one use and exact undo takes its place. MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab Your approval changes what the agent can do. Live app: https://second-player-lab.asterai.chatgpt.site/ Source and MIT license: https://github.com/mcpilotandmore/mcpilot-adaptive-play-lab at v1.0.0 Demo video: https://youtu.be/etHmptvGNvc (119 seconds) What we built Most accessibility menus ask players to solve the problem before they can use the solution. A player leaves the action, guesses which settings might help, and changes several controls. MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab turns that guesswork into one short, reversible experiment. The player completes a 20-second fixed course. A browser agent reads device-local measurements such as accuracy, collisions, pauses, movement balance, and response time. It proposes the smallest supported change while explaining what it intends to preserve. The player reviews the exact values and approves or declines them. If approved, the agent applies only that reviewed plan. The player repeats the same course and answers a simple question: better, about the same, worse, or skip. The app then reports every available change, calls out regressions, and keeps an exact undo available. The agent never plays, approves, or answers the experience check-in for the person. An optional OpenAI Realtime voice guide can explain that division of labor out loud. The player explicitly starts the microphone, sees live captions, and can ask what the current step means. The guide receives only a bounded summary of visible page state, has no tools, and cannot change the lab; it automatically disconnects after two minutes. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP The information needed for this interaction exists inside the open game page: the completed trial, current settings, selected needs, supported adjustment limits, proposal state, player approval, and undo snapshot. An assistant looking at screenshots would have to infer that state and hope it remained current. WebMCP lets the page expose those facts as small, structured tools tied to the live session. More importantly, it lets the page change which tools exist as the player makes decisions. Before approval, the agent can inspect the game, read the trial measurements, discover supported adaptations, and propose a plan—but there is no apply tool. When the player clicks Approve exact plan , apply_approved_tune registers for that proposal. It accepts only the approved ID and values; after use, it disappears and exact undo becomes available. The same rule protects the result. After the second trial, compare_play_trials remains unavailable until the player answers or explicitly skips the on-screen check-in. There is no WebMCP tool for submitting that answer. This is not a webpage with a permanent automation API attached. The player's visible choices determine what the agent is technically capable of doing next. How it creates a better experience Instead of trying eight settings blindly, the player gets one explainable proposal from the completed trial. Nothing changes silently. The values stay visible, the second run uses the same course, and the saved snapshot can restore every setting. The app also refuses to turn a flattering number into a success story. A higher score is not enough if collisions, response time, or the player's own experience became worse. Better can support an objectively strong result but cannot create one. About the same prevents a clear-improvement verdict. Worse vetoes success. Skip allows an objective comparison but not a player-benefit claim. Post-video live validation This final played pair was completed after the published 1:59 demo and is documented in the repository; the video demonstrates the permission-gated workflow, not these exact trial IDs or this exact outcome. The same player tested One-hand-left controls and reduced motion through In-app browser WebMCP: inspect, read signals, propose, visible approval, exact apply, then exact undo. , while preserving The player still steers, collects signals, and avoids visible hazards on the same timed course. . Baseline: trial-ebaf831f-a54c-4359-99a8-69253269ad4f Adapted trial: trial-b6cf2c66-4577-4153-bc9d-d07eb733c6ae Player check-in: Worse for me Score: 1750 → 1750 (0) Accuracy: 100% → 100% (0 pt) Collision rate: 0/10s → 0/10s (0/10s) Median collect time: 2307 ms → 2970 ms (+663 ms) Verdict: needs another iteration Player observation: The player selected Worse for me through the visible player check-in after the adapted trial. Accuracy: 100% to 100% (0 pt). The run did not produce enough qualifying gains to clear the product's success policy, so the page calls for another iteration. What people and agents can now do together The agent reads several measurements, checks supported ranges, constructs a valid configuration, keeps both trials tied to the same course and approved plan, and presents every tradeoff. The person keeps the decisions only they can make: playing the game, approving a change, and reporting how the result felt. That division is the point. A recommendation-only assistant has no page-defined, session-bound way to inspect, apply, verify, and undo this experiment. A fully autonomous agent should not grant itself permission or decide whether a change helped someone. With WebMCP, neither side impersonates the other. This is designed to reduce the guesswork involved in trying an alternative control or presentation setup. For game developers, it demonstrates a reusable permission pattern whose deterministic game state stays local. Optional voice is a separate explanation layer: microphone audio and a bounded page-state summary go to OpenAI only while the player is connected. How we implemented WebMCP MCPilot Adaptive Interactive Play Lab uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and the imperative WebMCP API. Six base tools handle inspection, signal reading, adaptation discovery, proposal creation, clearly labeled sample data, and preset export. Apply, compare, and undo register only when application state permits them. A server-only OpenAI Realtime WebRTC route powers the optional captioned guide with no tools and no access to game mutations. Strict schemas reject extra properties, and application code checks every supported range again. IDs and saved settings keep both runs connected, while the UI and WebMCP tools pass through the same validation rules. The exact application source is commit cb7f19545b1c22bb32003435a5655459ea2945c9 , deployed as Sites version 21. Its deterministic behavior is covered by 101 product tests. Gameplay telemetry, settings, approvals, and comparisons remain device-local; there is no account system, backend MCP server, or database. Optional voice streams microphone audio and a bounded page-state summary only while connected, and the standard API key remains server-side. The result is a working human-agent loop built around a simple rule: the agent can help the game listen, but the player remains in control. Built With api openai react realtime sites typescript vinext vite webmcp Try it out second-player-lab.asterai.chatgpt.site github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Built the end-to-end product: game design, WebMCP capability lifecycle, player-gated approval and comparison, OpenAI Realtime voice guide, verification, deployment, and demo production. The agent calls three real web MCP tools. Inspect reads live state. Signals returns the completed run with its source and limits. title: Mausam
pitch: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Mausam turns Mumbai’s live weather evidence into agent-ready, actionable forecasts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Interactive map close-up - Zoomed view of the MMR map with rainfall intensity scale Desktop landing view - Mausam header with live status and the Mumbai rainfall intelligence map Mobile layout - Mausam on a phone-sized viewport, showing header and map Full product page - End-to-end scroll of the Mausam site, from hero through map and supporting sections MMR rainfall map - Full Mumbai Metropolitan Region choropleth with locality labels and intensity legend Mausam Mausam (pronounced "mow-sum") is the Hindi word for weather or season. I chose the name because this project grew out of Mumbai's unpredictable monsoon. In Hindi, people often ask, "Mausam kaisa hai?" , or "How is the weather?" My project tries to answer the more useful version of that question: What changed? Where is the rain moving? Does Borivali face the same risk as the rest of Mumbai? Is this worth interrupting someone for? Inspiration Mumbai's weather rarely behaves like a simple forecast. During the monsoon, the sky can change within minutes. One suburb may get intense rain while another stays almost dry. A forecast that says "rain in Mumbai" may be technically correct and still be useless to someone deciding whether to leave home. That gap inspired Mausam. It watches several sources, compares new evidence with the last report, and sends an update only when something has changed. I started with one question: Can I build a weather service that remains alert without becoming noisy? What it does Mausam produces two complementary weather reports for Mumbai: A near-term nowcast covering approximately the next three to six hours. A five-day outlook comparing GFS and ECMWF forecast models. The primary nowcast combines: IMD PPI-Z and SRI radar frames; Windy rain-accumulation imagery; short-range GFS and ECMWF frames; readings from Borivali and Kandivali East; scraped rain statistics; local weather-station observations; and the previous report’s state. It evaluates Borivali separately from the wider Mumbai Metropolitan Region because rainfall can vary significantly across the city. The five-day pipeline compares GFS and ECMWF at five forecast horizons: $$ 2\ \text{models} \times 5\ \text{horizons} = 10\ \text{forecast frames} $$ Mausam delivers the result through email, Discord, a local alert banner, and an Astro website. It also chooses when to check again. Dangerous conditions get a faster follow-up; stable conditions can wait. The website also exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_weather_nowcast get_weather_outlook get_forecast_reasoning A compatible browser agent can call these tools to read the forecast as structured data instead of scraping the page. How I built it I built Mausam over five months with Bun and TypeScript. Each month solved a problem that appeared once the previous version started running in real conditions. April: Building the evidence pipeline The first version downloaded radar images and stored them in S3-compatible object storage. I wrote utilities to find the latest image, convert it to a compact JPEG, compare it with the previous frame, upload new evidence, and safely remove old objects. That led to the rule at the center of the project: $$ \text{Analyse} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if evidence changed} \ 1, & \text{during the morning guarantee} \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ Weather sources often publish the same frame more than once. Analysing every copy would waste multimodal model calls and send repetitive notifications. Mausam compares the image bytes first. A morning exception still guarantees one baseline report each day. Once that worked, I connected the images to a multimodal weather agent. I added rain observations, local station data, saved summaries, email delivery, Telegram alerts, and BullMQ scheduling around it. By the end of April, Mausam had evolved from an image-processing script into a continuously scheduled weather service. May: Making scheduling dependable In May, I focused on the less exciting part that decides whether an automated service survives: failure handling. The pipeline schedules another attempt when a source fails or an image has not changed. Active-hour checks stop jobs from running at unsuitable times, while severity-based delays revisit urgent conditions sooner. This was when scheduling became part of the weather decision rather than a fixed cron interval. June: Adding rendered maps and Discord Some weather sources do not provide a direct image. Windy renders its accumulation map inside a web application. I added Puppeteer to open the page, wait for the weather layer, take a controlled screenshot, and pass it through the same pipeline as a downloaded image. A shared ingestion helper means the rest of the application does not need to know where an image came from. Discord replaced Telegram as the technical reporting channel. A separate gRPC integration handles delivery, so communication failures stay outside the weather analysis process. I also added Uptime Kuma heartbeats and automatic startup jobs so Mausam could run unattended. July: Expanding from hours to days The original system only answered, "What happens over the next few hours?" In July, I added a second pipeline to answer, "What could the next five days look like?" It finds the newest usable GFS and ECMWF runs, resolves changing Tropical Tidbits image URLs, and collects frames at approximately (+24), (+48), (+72), (+96), and (+120) hours. All ten images are staged before analysis. If one required frame cannot be prepared, the incomplete set is removed instead of mixing different or partial model runs. Running the system exposed another problem: a retry could repeat actions that had already succeeded. I strengthened the workflow with: Zod-validated configuration and model output; Redis-backed previous-report state; decision caching using evidence-derived run identifiers; delivery locks and completion markers; follow-up-job deduplication; and separation between queue construction and process side effects. The model interprets uncertain weather evidence. Regular application code controls persistence, delivery, retries, and scheduling. This boundary keeps free-form model behavior away from side effects. August: Building the web experience In August, I started retaining the two newest frames from each primary source. A pair of images shows basic movement and development that one snapshot cannot. I also compressed primary evidence to reduce multimodal input cost. The estimated image-token load fell from roughly 50,000 tokens in the earlier high-frame case to around 7,500: $$ 1-\frac{7{,}500}{50{,}000} =0.85 =85\% $$ I extended the agents with structured website fields and Zod validation. Using bun:sqlite , I persist nowcasts and outlooks for an Astro and React frontend. The stored data includes separate Borivali and Mumbai/MMR alert levels, headlines, rain probability, peak timing, confidence, station observations, source summaries, daily outlook cards, model comparisons, and detailed reasoning. The website presents the current alert, local conditions, five-day forecast, source summaries, model comparison, and reasoning. I also integrated an interactive Mumbai Metropolitan Region map. It connects report data to localities and visualizes alert severity, rain intensity, forecast movement, and differences across the region. The last addition was WebMCP. When a browser exposes document.modelContext , the React application registers three focused, read-only weather tools. Each returns bounded structured data and labels the result as AI guidance. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the complete website, making agent interaction a progressive enhancement rather than a dependency. The full path now looks like this: $$ \text{Weather sources} \rightarrow \text{Evidence pipeline} \rightarrow \text{Structured reasoning} \rightarrow \text{Reliable delivery} \rightarrow \text{Web experience} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP interaction} $$ Challenges I ran into Inconsistent weather sources Some sources provide files. Others need browser rendering. Forecast URLs change with model initialization times, and station or rain-statistics endpoints can fail on their own. I wrote source-specific resolvers behind one ingestion interface. A missing required radar frame stops the run. An optional source can fail without taking the whole forecast down, and Mausam uses retained evidence where appropriate. Detecting real changes A newly published file does not always contain new weather. Running the agent on identical frames would consume resources and wear out the person receiving alerts. Exact byte comparison is predictable, but it has a trade-off: an encoding change can look new to the system even when the two images look identical to a person. Preventing duplicate alerts A run may successfully send an email and then fail while posting to Discord. Retry

title: Voivent MV Studio
pitch: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools.
about_excerpt: Agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP with 38 browser-native tools. Like Comment Story Updates Procedural 3D Forest with multilingual lyric glow and multitrack scene timeline. Audio-reactive 3D orbital rings and procedural lighting pulsing to the beat. Inspiration While modern text-to-video AI generators can produce visually striking clips, they present a fundamental workflow bottleneck for creators: once a video is rendered into flat pixels, making precise micro-adjustments—such as rotating a camera angle by 5 degrees, nudging lyric timing by half a second, or reusing customized 3D assets across scenes—becomes nearly impossible without regenerating everything from scratch. We realized true creative collaboration requires structural, parametric control. By exposing a procedural 3D scene graph, multitrack timeline, and audio signals directly to AI agents via WebMCP, creators and agents can co-direct, iteratively polish details, and reuse assets non-destructively through natural conversation. WebMCP unlocks unique, interactive creative workflows that take browser-based music video production to the next level. What it does Voivent MV Studio is an agent-native 3D music video production suite powered by WebMCP. 38 Browser-Native WebMCP Tools : Autonomous agents (such as ChatGPT) inspect studio capabilities, build 3D voxel worlds, split timeline chapters, translate & synchronize lyrics, and trigger video exports. Visual Self-Inspection ( get_mv_preview ) : The agent captures real-time canvas snapshots to visually evaluate lighting, composition, and text safe-zones, autonomously refining parameters without human intervention. Procedural 3D World Engine : Real-time voxel terrain generation, orbital landmarks, dynamic lighting, atmospheric fog, and cinematic cameras rendered directly in the browser via Three.js, WebGPU, and WebGL. Multitrack Timeline & Lyric Sync : Non-destructive multi-scene splitting (intro, verses, chorus, drops, narrative chapters, or time-of-day transitions), multilingual lyric translation with syllable-precise timing alignment, and audio-reactive beat pulses. In-Browser 1080p MP4 Export : Full hardware-accelerated video rendering inside the client browser via WebCodecs and MediaBunny. How we built it WebMCP Layer : Built 38 structured tools registered on document.modelContext spanning 3D scene graphs, timeline actions, audio stems, and diagnostics. Frontend & 3D : React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js with WebGPU/WebGL acceleration. Client-Side AI & Audio : Web Audio API beat detection, and on-device AI source separation running locally via ONNX Runtime Web. Cloud Infrastructure : Cloudflare Workers for edge hosting, R2 storage for streaming AI model assets, and Cloudflare Workers AI (Whisper) for optional vocal transcription. Challenges we ran into Designing a tightly coupled visual feedback loop where the AI agent can iteratively validate its own 3D scene compositions via Base64 canvas snapshots. Orchestrating non-destructive multitrack timeline operations while maintaining seamless audio-video synchronization across multi-scene splits. Achieving fast 1080p MP4 video rendering entirely inside standard web browsers using WebCodecs and MediaBunny without offloading video encoding to backend servers. Accomplishments that we're proud of Fully operational suite of 38 WebMCP tools operating reliably with ChatGPT and autonomous browser agents. Autonomous multi-scene direction: splitting music tracks into distinct narrative scenes and musical chapters with dynamic camera paths and audio-reactive pulses. Heavy computing in the browser: running real-time 3D graphics, local ONNX stem inference, and 1080p video muxing directly on the user's device without requiring expensive GPU rendering servers. What we learned WebMCP proves that the open web can host rich, stateful, and non-destructive creative ecosystems for AI agents. Instead of treating AI as an isolated prompt-in/pixel-out generator, WebMCP unlocks an unprecedented paradigm: humans and agents building, inspecting, and iteratively polishing unique 3D interactive experiences together. What's next for Voivent MV Studio Native DAW Integration : Bridging Voivent MV Studio with our standalone digital audio workstation (Voivent DAW), allowing creators to stream multitrack audio and lyric maps directly into the WebMCP environment. Intuitive "Co-Pilot" Real-Time Jamming : Deepening the collaborative experience where creators and AI agents run side-by-side—intuitively directing 3D lighting, camera cuts, and visual shaders in real-time. Multi-Agent WebMCP Sessions : Enabling multiple specialized agents (e.g., dedicated lighting, camera, and typography agents) to coordinate simultaneously through WebMCP tool calls. Built With cloudflare-workers onnx-runtime-web react three.js typescript vite web-audio-api webcodecs webgl webgpu webmcp Try it out studio.voivent.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Built as a solo creator pair-programming alongside my AI coding partner! Designed the 3D studio, timeline, and all 38 WebMCP tools. Building with WebMCP sparked endless new creative ideas, and I'm super excited to keep pushing the evolution of human-agent co-creation on the web! title: Looop
pitch: Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
about_excerpt:
Looop brings teams together to plan, collaborate and resolve issues in one place, with WebMCP-enabled AI agents that can manage events for you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Group chats are often the main go-to for communication when planning for events and projects. However, the actual plan and flow of logistics often end up buried under jokes, photographs, and various digresses from conversation. As such, this results in confusion and frustration with messages like "Did anyone see my message about xxx?" or "At what stage are we for this plan?" or "Sorry, what are my responsibilities for today again?". 
This is where WebMCP fits the use case well. By allowing AI agents to interact directly with structured web interfaces, WebMCP can help agents read the latest plan, understand assigned responsibilities, and take actions on the board without relying on noisy chat history. This creates a shared and structured source of truth that both people and AI agents can easily understand and act upon. 

 What it does 

 Looop gives every event (wedding party, offsite, household chore chart) one shared board, which includes tasks grouped by urgency, flagged issues for attention, day-by-day timeline and a computed event health score. The core actions on the board such as creating and editing tasks, flagging and resolving issues, are exposed as MCP tools. Users can simply ask their agent "What tasks are still open on the wedding board?" or "Add an urgent task for the caterer" or "Flag that the venue has not confirmed headcount". The agent can even act as a collaborator, proposing concrete next steps for a stuck task or open issue , as well as starter tasks for event based on its title and description , and providing a concise summary of the event history . 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is hosted on Vercel and backend on Render. The frontend of Looop was built with React and Typescript on the frontend, Tailwind for UI styling. It has a Go backend on Chi with MongoDB for storage. The WebMCP layer lives on the frontend with document.modelContext.registerTool() covering full CRUD on events, its tasks and issues plus status actions like complete_task and resolve_issue and multiple tools that let the agent write suggestions and catch the user up on the event progress. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The gap between UI implementation and connecting with the rest of the pipeline also turned out to be a challenge. The frontend was first built against mock data which expedited the design process, but the process of wiring every page to the backend surfaced a long list of real bugs. These included route prefixes that did not match between frontend and backend, and a field name mismatch that silently dropped task notes. This also affected the WebMCP testing in ChatGPT's in-app browser, since the underlying API calls had to work reliably before I could register tools that depended on them during execution. I also learnt to budget more time for WebMCP edge cases, such as incomplete requests and ambiguous inputs, rather than focusing only on the ideal tool flow. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the full loop working with an agent in ChatGPT's browser calling a real tool, hitting the hosted Go backend and writing to the database, and having that change show up on the board was the largest accomplishment. I was happy for not just settling for CRUD as the whole product and registering tools such as get_event_summary computing a genuine health score instead of just listing rows, and suggest_task_completion/suggest_issue_resolution letting the agent contribute reasoning to the board, not just data entry was also one of the main goals achieved. 

 What we learned 

 The main concept here was implementing MCP hands-on to create a functional project and learning the concept from scratch. One of the biggest concepts learnt was the difference between MCP and WebMCP, particularly that WebMCP tools are registered directly on the frontend through the browser rather than being exposed from a backend MCP server. 
A lot of learning also came from testing the tools repeatedly and handling edge cases. I had to check that every tool was callable, that fields and routes matched correctly across the codebases and that incomplete requests were handled gracefully. For example, creating a task without an assignee meant deciding how the tool should respond or whether it could fall back to the current user, while ambiguous member names required additional resolution. Thus, I learnt that thorough testing is essential when building agent-facing tools. 

 What's next for Looop 

 In the near future, Looop could move towards real authentication and user accounts , replacing the current localStorage-based placeholder identity with secure accounts that persist across devices. We also see potential in richer integrations , connecting Looop with calendars and other tools that people already use for event planning, making it easier to keep everything in sync without having to switch between different platforms. Based on user feedback, more WebMCP tools could be registered on Looop to efficiently serve real-world purposes for collaborative event planning.

 What it does

 Customer intent

 The goal is to help customers move from naturally describing what they want to finding relevant products in the actual Shopify store. 

 How we built it 

 We built the project by integrating WebMCP into the existing GodreryTone Jewellery Shopify storefront and exposing specialized tools for different parts of the shopping journey.

 It also incorporates: 

 
 Market-aware product availability

 Pricing considerations

 Direct routing to Shopify product pages 
 

 The project was developed around the principle that:

 Challenges we ran into

 Another challenge was ensuring that the AI experience does not make assumptions on behalf of the customer, particularly when regional alternatives, availability, pricing, or shipping need to be considered. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that the project moved beyond a theoretical WebMCP implementation and was applied to a real Shopify jewellery storefront with real products and real commerce considerations .

 We learned the importance of understanding the underlying: 

 
 Business rules 
 Product availability 
 Regional differences 
 Currency 
 Pricing 
 Shipping 
 Customer control 
 

 before an agent can provide a genuinely useful recommendation. 

 Most importantly, I learned how WebMCP can turn existing web functionality into structured capabilities that an AI agent can use to help customers interact with a real business.

title: Gym & Tonic
pitch: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours.
about_excerpt: Gym & Tonic turns “I should work out” into a week you can actually live. ChatGPT coaches, your plan stays private, and every decision remains yours. Like Comment Story Updates Today: A daily dashboard with one next action, workout recovery, walking minutes, and private habit check-ins. Progress: A calm view of completed workouts, minutes, walking, habits, history, and optional weight trends. Planner 1: See your weekly status, progress, and next useful action at a glance. Planner 2: Start, resume, view, or add a short workout based on what your day needs. Coach Suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Coach suggesting for schedule changes via WebMCP Planner 3: Plan fourteen morning and evening sessions without overwriting your existing workouts. Planner 4: Review progress, insights, meals, templates, calendar export, and coach proposals. Workout: A focused guided workout with exercise cues, illustrations, optional timers, and explicit finish control. Meals: Searchable meal ideas with dietary filters, preparation times, ingredients, substitutions, and favourites. Settings: Personalize goals, training preferences, habits, alerts, weight tracking, analytics, and data controls. Inspiration I built Gym & Tonic because “I should probably work out” is one of the most popular fitness plans in the world, and one of the least effective. Most fitness apps give you endless exercises, complicated programs, and enough numbers. I wanted to build something that helps people turn good intentions into a realistic week they can actually follow. What it does Gym & Tonic is a local-first fitness planner for people starting or returning to exercise. It helps users plan weekly sessions, follow guided workouts, use optional timers, reflect after training, track consistency, discover practical meal ideas, and see what their next useful action is. The WebMCP integration lets ChatGPT act as a coach that understands the live training plan. It can check the week, identify gaps, suggest sessions, fill empty slots, and propose swaps. The important part is that the coach does not get to quietly rearrange someone’s life. Every change becomes a proposal that the user can approve or reject. How I built it I built Gym & Tonic with Astro, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind, and WebMCP. The application is local-first, so plans, completions, reflections, and workout progress stay in the browser. There are no accounts, no backend, and no mysterious fitness spreadsheet being sent into the cloud. I used Fraunces and Inter to give the interface an editorial feel, then added guided workout screens, progress views, accessible navigation, responsive layouts, exercise illustrations, local persistence, offline support, and privacy-conscious analytics. The agent tools are registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Read actions can inspect the plan, while write actions are staged for approval through one proposal pipeline. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was not generating a workout. The internet has generated enough workouts to keep humanity busy until the sun explodes. The real challenge was handling the small but important states: pending proposals, rejected changes, active workouts, timers after reload, completed sessions, optional reflections, local storage migrations, mobile navigation, and the difference between “planned” and “actually completed.” I also had to make sure an AI coach could be helpful without becoming an unsupervised personal trainer with admin privileges. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am proud that Gym & Tonic feels like a complete product rather than just a workout generator. A user can arrive with no plan, choose a manageable starting point, place a session, open a guided workout, complete it, reflect, and see that progress represented immediately. I am also proud of the trust model. The coach can do the planning legwork, but the user remains in control of every meaningful change. The project is open source, local-first, responsive, accessible, and designed to work for people who are building consistency rather than chasing perfection. What I learned I learned that good AI product design is often about restraint. It is easy to make an agent that can change things. It is much harder to make one that explains what it wants to do, waits for approval, and respects the user’s ownership of the result. I also learned that the most important product state is often not “success” or “failure.” Sometimes it is simply “you started, and that counts.” What's next for Gym & Tonic Next, I would like to add printable training diaries, installable PWA support, deeper exercise guidance, richer progress storytelling, and more ways for the coach to explain why it is making a suggestion. I would also like to explore a mode where the coach can defend a rejected proposal with evidence from the user’s plan, without becoming annoying enough to be muted immediately. For now, Gym & Tonic is focused on one useful promise: helping people make a plan, follow through, and come back next week. title: HABITAT/NULL
pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together.
