title: TagTitan Listing Studio
pitch: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable.
about_excerpt: A listing studio for print-on-demand sellers where the agent presses the same buttons you do, in the same grid, with every action visible and overridable. Like Comment Story Updates The grid, and the activity log that stamps every action as agent or human. Inspiration A print-on-demand seller with forty designs does the same chore forty times, multiplied by every marketplace they sell on. Etsy allows a 140 character title and 13 tags. Amazon Merch allows 60 characters, no price claims, and two bullets. Redbubble wants 15 tags of up to 30 characters each. The work is not creative. It is compliance, and it eats a day. Handing it to an AI has always meant choosing between two bad options. Either the agent described what to write and the seller pasted forty listings by hand, or the seller handed an opaque tool their credentials and hoped. One is dictation. The other is abdication. Neither is collaboration. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP changes the shape of the problem, because the tools live on the page the seller is already looking at. The studio is a grid. Designs down the side, marketplaces across the top, one listing per square. It publishes twelve tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Ask the agent to fill the grid and the squares fill in front of you. Every field stays editable. Every action, yours or the agent's, lands in the same activity log stamped with who did it. The design rule the whole project follows is that a tool is never a private back door . Each one is a thin wrapper over an action that a button in the interface also calls. One store, one set of mutations, one log. buttons (app.js) ---+ +---> studio.js ---> live TagTitan API tools (webmcp.js) --+ | +---> one grid, one activity log That symmetry is what makes the collaboration legible. The agent cannot do anything the seller cannot see, undo, or do themselves. How it creates a better user experience The seller never leaves the page, never pastes anything, and never loses sight of what was done on their behalf. They can interrupt at any square. A batch that would have been forty context switches becomes one instruction and a grid they supervise. It also degrades honestly. With no agent connected the studio is a complete tool you can drive by hand, and the header states plainly which mode you are in. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Supervised bulk work. "Take all four designs, do Etsy and Redbubble, premium voice." The agent calls the same actions the buttons call, and the seller watches each square resolve, fixing anything wrong in place. A critique loop against a real scorer. The agent calls grade_listing , reads back a 0 to 100 score broken into title, tags, description and readability with concrete fixes, then calls update_listing to apply one. It checks its own work against the same grader the seller sees. Marketplace rules as shared context. list_marketplaces returns live character and tag limits for 18 marketplaces, so the agent reasons about real constraints instead of guessing. Correction without restarting. "The Etsy title is too generic, make it about cottagecore." One field changes. Nothing else regenerates and no context is lost. Knowing when to stop and ask. account_status reports remaining quota, so before a large batch the agent can tell the seller to sign in rather than burning what is left. How we built it The front end is deliberately plain: no build step, no framework, no dependencies. studio.js holds all state and every mutation. app.js renders it and wires the buttons. webmcp.js registers the tools. The last two are peers, and neither can reach past the store. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "generate_listings", description: "Write full listings for products across the selected marketplaces...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { /* ... */ } }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); Every execute is wrapped so a thrown error becomes a readable tool error rather than a crash, and each call writes to the shared activity log before returning. The listing engine behind it is the live TagTitan API, a shipped commercial product, so the output is what real sellers actually publish rather than demo filler. The twelve tools Tool What it does read_studio Full state: products, marketplaces, listing status, scores account_status Whether the seller is signed in and how much quota remains list_marketplaces 18 marketplaces with live title, tag and content limits add_product Add a design as a new row remove_product Drop a row and its listings set_marketplaces Choose which marketplaces are columns set_tone Set the brand voice for everything generated after suggest_keywords Real buyer search phrases for a seed term generate_listings Write listings across the grid grade_listing Score a listing 0 to 100 and return fixes update_listing Rewrite one field of one listing export_csv Every finished listing as bulk-upload CSV Challenges we ran into The API restricts CORS to an allowlist. Calling it from a new origin returned 400 with no allow header. Rather than widen the allowlist we proxy /api server-side, so the browser only ever makes same-origin requests and the backend needed no change at all. That also let the session cookie ride along without any SameSite juggling. The free tier allows one listing per browser, in total. Cookie tracked, and it silently truncates a multi-marketplace request to a single marketplace. Anyone opening the site cold got one square filled and then a wall, which made the whole studio look broken. Adding sign-in fixed it, and signed in the API writes every marketplace in a single call. The backend sleeps. It runs on a free instance that takes about 23 seconds to wake. A judge whose first click hangs that long assumes the project is broken, so a scheduled function now pings it every ten minutes. What we learned The interesting constraint in WebMCP is not what the agent can do. It is what the human can still see. It would have been easier to give the agent a fast private path to the API and let the UI catch up afterwards. Everything good about this project came from refusing that and making both paths identical. What's next Unifying the studio session with the main TagTitan app, image-driven listings so a design can be dropped straight in, and pushing finished rows to marketplace APIs directly instead of exporting CSV. title: BingeWatcher
pitch: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours
about_excerpt: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I watch a lot of movies and TV shows. A LOT. My biggest pet peeve is figuring out what to watch next. Using an LLM for inspiration can be helpful, but it usually requires a lot of unnecessary back and forth. Even after all that, I sometimes end up not liking any of its recommendations. I wanted a way to discover movies and shows with an agent while staying in control, actively making choices and telling it what interests me and what doesn’t. I also wanted an immersive visual experience where I could explore a title, watch its trailer, check where it is streaming, and save it to my watchlist. Then I wanted to take it one step further: planning entire weekends around everything I wanted to bingewatch. When I explored WebMCP, I realized that I could now collaborate with an agent instead of delegating the whole task to it. I could stay in complete control while letting an agent do the grunt work for me. That’s how I came up with BingeWatcher . What it does BingeWatcher is a movie and TV discovery app built for people and their WebMCP agents to use together. You can explore trending titles, search for something specific, combine filters such as genre, language, release year, runtime, and streaming provider, and open detailed pages containing trailers, recommendations, ratings, seasons, episodes, and streaming availability. Titles can be saved to a personal watchlist or added to an ordered lineup for a movie night, themed marathon, or entire weekend. The most important part is how those lineups evolve. An agent can create and maintain a lineup, but the person remains in control. You can: Lock a title that must stay Mark another as Not for me and (optionally) explain why Reorder the lineup yourself Change its preferences Ask the agent to rebuild only the remaining picks The agent works around those decisions instead of replacing them. BingeWatcher also tracks movie-level and episode-level progress, supports lightweight reactions, and keeps a history of changes made to each lineup. Everything remains fully usable without an agent. How I built it I built BingeWatcher as a single application using Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Bun . Movie and TV metadata comes from TMDB , including search results, posters, genres, recommendations, trailers, seasons, episodes, ratings, and regional watch providers. I also integrated the Streaming Availability API for direct provider links where available. The app uses SQLite for persistent data. Anonymous visitors receive a secure, HTTP-only browser session, so their watchlist, progress, reactions, and lineups remain available when they return. Lineups also have separate secure edit/resume links and read-only sharing links. I exposed the application through WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The tools cover discovery, title details, recommendations, watchlists, progress, reactions, and complete lineup management. Most importantly, the WebMCP tools do not operate on a separate agent-only system. They call the same backend operations used by the human interface, which means both sides share the same data, validation rules, locks, vetoes, and revision checks. Agent actions such as searching, opening a watchlist, or creating a lineup also navigate and update the visible interface. The production application runs in a Docker container on Render with SQLite stored on a persistent disk. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was deciding how much control the agent should have. Letting an agent replace an entire lineup would have been easy, but it would also make human decisions feel temporary. I had to design the system so that locks, vetoes, ordering, preferences, and concurrent edits were treated as durable constraints. Supporting movies, complete TV series, and individual seasons inside the same lineup introduced another layer of complexity. Progress also needed different behavior: movies are tracked at the title level, while TV progress is tracked by episode so that season and series completion can be derived correctly. Another challenge was making WebMCP actions feel visible. A tool technically succeeding in the background was not enough. If an agent searched for a title or opened a newly created lineup, the interface needed to visibly follow that action so the person could immediately inspect and continue the work. External media APIs introduced their own complications. Search and discovery are separate operations in TMDB, so combining text searches with detailed filters required carefully joining and validating the available metadata. Streaming data also varies by region and provider. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I’m most proud that BingeWatcher feels like a complete product even when no agent is connected. In my opinion, that's how products are meant to be in the age of agent <-> human collaboration. The human interface is a beautiful (if I may say so myself) website designed to deliver a premium discovery and planning experience to its target audience: cinephiles and TV buffs. It includes rich discovery, detailed title and season pages, ordered lineups, watchlists, progress tracking, reactions, drag-and-drop reordering, trailers, preferences, history, secure sharing, and much more. At the same time, the agent can work across nearly the entire product through WebMCP. It can discover titles, understand live lineup state, respect locked picks and vetoes, make precise changes, validate the result, and leave the final decisions to the person. I’m also proud of the core collaboration loop: an agent can build a lineup, a person can lock one pick, reject another, change the order, and ask the agent to rebuild only what remains. That interaction captures what I wanted BingeWatcher to be- AI agents helping someone express their taste instead of replacing it. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is how WebMCP, once standardized and widely adopted, can become the go-to way for websites to enable human <-> agent collaboration. This is where I believe all software will converge over the coming years. The best experience came from making the normal application excellent first, then giving the agent access to the same meaningful actions. WebMCP became much more useful when its tools represented real product capabilities rather than isolated technical endpoints. I also learned how important tool descriptions and schemas are. They do more than document an API. They establish the boundaries of the collaboration. A clear description can tell an agent when to stop, what it may change, and which human decisions it must preserve. All the while keepig context bloat to a minimum. Finally, I learned that visible state matters. People trust an agent more when they can see what it opened, what it changed, and what it deliberately left alone. What’s next for BingeWatcher The next step is permanent accounts for people who want cross-device access, using email magic links, Google, or passkeys while preserving the anonymous-first experience. I would also move production persistence to a network database before supporting multiple application instances, add real-time collaborative editing, and continue improving personalized discovery using watch history, reactions, watchlists, and explicit preferences. I also want to add multiplayer (more humans) lineups and watchlists for planning movie nights and weekends with friends. Longer term, I want BingeWatcher to become a shared home for planning more kinds of entertainment, with richer group planning, better provider-aware recommendations, and perhaps even support for books. title: Aligna
pitch: A human-governed operating system that uses WebMCP to let AI understand projects, surface blockers, review commitments and recommend where attention should go next.
about_excerpt:
A human-governed operating system that uses WebMCP to let AI understand projects, surface blockers, review commitments and recommend where attention should go next.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Aligna began as a practical response to a problem I kept encountering while managing several very different projects with AI: the information existed, but understanding what actually deserved attention still required repeatedly reconstructing context. 

 The original Aligna system became a human-facing governance layer for projects, commitments, blockers and priorities. The WebMCP Challenge raised a more interesting question: what if an AI agent did not have to interpret that system indirectly through a visual interface? 

 WebMCP provided the missing bridge. 

 What it does 

 The challenge build turns Aligna into an agent-readable operating system while keeping the human in control. 

 It exposes five read-only WebMCP capabilities: 

 
 Understand Aligna 
 Review a project 
 Identify blockers 
 Review upcoming commitments 
 Recommend the next area of attention 
 

 This allows an AI agent to interrogate the same structured operating state presented to the human, rather than trying to infer meaning from pixels, page structure or an unstructured conversation. 

 The result is a simple division of responsibility: Aligna holds the governed state, WebMCP exposes deliberate capabilities, the agent reasons over them, and the human retains authority. 

 How we built it 

 Aligna existed before the challenge as a personal life and project-management system. For the WebMCP Challenge, I created a separate public-safe competition build using fictional demonstration data and added the WebMCP interaction layer. 

 The competition work included defining and implementing the five WebMCP capabilities, creating the fictional public dataset, adapting the dashboard for a judge-facing demonstration, deploying the live application, publishing the open-source repository, and verifying the capabilities against the deployed build. 

 The WebMCP surface is deliberately read-only. The agent can understand, review and recommend, but it cannot silently alter canonical project state or assume human approval authority. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was not simply exposing data. It was deciding what an agent should be allowed to know and do . 

 A useful agent interface needs more structure than giving an AI unrestricted access to an application. Each capability therefore has a defined purpose and boundary. 

 A second challenge was demonstrating a real operating concept without exposing the private information contained in the operational Aligna system. The public competition build consequently uses entirely fictional, public-safe tracker data while preserving the structure and behaviour needed to demonstrate the concept. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We turned an existing human-facing operating system into a working agent-readable application without giving the agent unrestricted authority. 

 The final build exposes five deliberate WebMCP capabilities, runs against a deployed public-safe dataset, and demonstrates those capabilities through a live application and open-source repository. 

 Just as importantly, the public competition build was designed as a separate, fictional-data environment so private operational Aligna data would not be exposed publicly. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changed how I think about application interfaces. 

 A dashboard can serve a human extremely well while remaining awkward for an AI agent. Giving the agent structured capabilities alongside the human interface creates a much cleaner model: humans and agents can interact with the same underlying system through interfaces designed for each of them. 

 That opens up possibilities well beyond Aligna. Any structured operational application could potentially expose a carefully governed agent interface without surrendering control of the underlying system. 

 What's next for Aligna 

 The next step is to explore governed write workflows in which an agent can propose changes while explicit human approval remains the authority boundary. 

 Longer term, Aligna could become an agent-native governance layer across multiple projects and workflows: not an autonomous system making decisions for the user, but a structured environment that helps humans and AI work from the same operational truth.

about_excerpt: forge repo-specific skills from the open web, with your agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most of what we learn still lives in places built for humans, not agents: podcasts, blog posts, talks, documentation, and newsletters. They’re full of useful techniques, but they aren’t skills an agent can pick up and apply to a specific codebase. fondof gives that knowledge a second life. Give it a source URL, a stated need, or up to four sources, and it turns the underlying ideas into a concise, repo-specific skill—with attribution intact. We also wanted to explore what an agent-native web actually feels like. With WebMCP, fondof exposes its capabilities directly to agents, so a user can stay in a conversation and say: “Find me a skill on React performance and forge one from this talk for my repo.” What it does fondof turns knowledge into agent-ready skills: Extract — pulls actionable ideas from articles, YouTube, docs, or free-text needs. Fit — matches those ideas to a target repo’s stack, conventions, and paths. Forge — creates a short, copyable skill for Cursor, Claude, Kiro, or any agent. Hand off — copies Markdown or creates a shareable /s/{hash} link. Attribute — preserves source attribution and optionally anchors provenance on Monad. It exposes three WebMCP tools: search_skills — search the public skill pool. get_skill — retrieve a skill by hash. compose_skill — forge a skill from URLs or a stated need. Humans decide what they want; agents handle the extraction, discovery, composition, and formatting. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 16, Framer Motion, Tailwind, deployed on Netlify. API: Cloudflare Worker + Hono, with Durable Objects for coordination, KV for sessions, and Workers AI for LLM + embeddings. Ingestion: Firecrawl / Readability for articles and docs, YouTube transcripts, plus a local fallback for offline needs. Search & fit: Exa for semantic discovery, plus /api/skills?q= for searching the public skill pool by topic, repo, stack, or source. Blockchain: SkillPool on Monad testnet for optional public provenance. Agent layer: webmcp-provider.tsx registers the three tools; /.well-known/webmcp and Permissions-Policy enable discovery. Monorepo: pnpm workspaces across web , api , core , cli , contracts , and shared . We also dogfooded the build process in Kiro with a spec-first trail mapping directly to the shipped code. Challenges we ran into Multi-source composition: Combining up to four sources requires deduplication, merging, progress tracking, and partial-failure handling without losing the whole batch. Agent UX: WebMCP tools need to tell an agent not just what they do, but when to use them, what inputs they need, and how to recover from failures. Attribution without friction: We wanted every skill traceable to its sources without requiring wallets or sign-in for the happy path. Honest failures: Instead of silently swallowing bad URLs, the Studio surfaces ingest errors and compose_skill returns structured source_failures . Accomplishments that we're proud of A real, deployed WebMCP implementation with three working tools, a /.well-known/webmcp manifest, and the correct permissions configuration. Multi-source skill composition across up to four URLs, with per-source progress and failure reporting. A public skill pool with search, source-domain pages, and shareable skill pages. Agent discovery, retrieval, and creation as one continuous workflow. Honest degradation when ingestion fails, fallbacks are used, or the chain is unavailable. Open source and tested: MIT licensed, with 209 passing tests and a live Cloudflare Worker. What we learned The browser can be the integration layer. WebMCP lets the site expose its capabilities directly to agents, without requiring a custom MCP server or separate API key. Search is essential for agent-native apps. If an agent can’t find an existing skill, it will re-forge what already exists. Attribution can become a network primitive. Sources produce skills, skills get reused and re-forged, and outcomes can eventually feed back into the pool. Humans + agents work best as a loop: the human decides, the agent discovers and composes, and the human stays in control. What's next for fondof Creator analytics so authors can see which content became skills and where those skills were used. Knowledge clusters to turn the skill pool into a map of related sources, ideas, and re-forges. Outcome verification using PRs, screenshots, and repo deltas to measure real-world usefulness. Agent-to-agent challenges for contesting and re-forging skills with transparent evidence. A lightweight reward layer for creators and high-quality forgers, tied to usage and verified outcomes.  ScAInce Draw 

 As a physics student, I've learned that the right diagram can often make a difficult problem immediately understandable. While sketching a figure on paper takes only a few seconds, creating the same diagram digitally is surprisingly time-consuming. Unlike mathematical equations, which are straightforward to typeset (thank goodness we have LaTeX), diagrams are a completely different story. I've spent dozens (maybe hundreds) of hours tweaking figures just to make it look right. 

 With the rise of AI, I became curious whether it could automate this process. The results were initially disappointing. At first there was no even harness for generating diagrams, and even when equipped with general-purpose coding tools, AI struggled to produce accurate diagrams -even for simple block diagrams, let alone figures describing physics problems. 

 This led me to an important observation: diagram creation is an ideal human-in-the-loop task . AI can dramatically accelerate the drafting process, but the final validation should remain with the human, who ultimately decides whether the figure correctly represents the intended concept. 

 This idea became ScAInce Draw . 

 What is ScAInce Draw? 

 ScAInce Draw is a graphical application for creating mathematical and physics diagrams, which covers geometry, mechanics, optics, circuits. 

 The application is equipped with WebMCP , exposing a rich set of tools that allow AI agents to construct diagrams programmatically while performing numerous validations. These validations help prevent common issues such as overlapping elements, inconsistent layouts, and incorrect object placement. 

 Beyond the WebMCP itself, ScAInce Draw also includes a dedicated Skill . As demonstrated throughout this year, MCPs are significantly more effective when paired with a skill. 

 Human–AI Workflow 

 ScAInce Draw supports two complementary workflows: 

 
 Human → AI 

 
 The user quickly sketches the diagram. 
 The AI refines it into a clean, pixel-perfect figure. 
 
 AI → Human 

 
 The AI generates the initial diagram from a natural-language description. 
 The user validates the result and applies the final adjustments. 
 
 

 Current Status 

 ScAInce Draw is still an early-stage prototype, but it already demonstrates the potential of combining WebMCP with a domain-specific graphical application. 

 The application is still relatively simple, but it already contains a substantial amount of validation logic. In my testing, it consistently generates accurate diagrams from well-crafted prompts (e.g. from elementary mechanics problem statements). 

 There is still considerable room for improvement, particularly in refining the generated layouts and validations. However, my experiments consistently show that integrating WebMCP significantly improves both the quality and the speed of AI-generated scientific diagrams (as an alternative to simply asking ChatGPT to click around the browser and figure out what it can do) 

 Ultimately, ScAInce Draw demonstrates that meaningful diagram generation is not simply a drawing problem - it is a collaborative workflow where AI accelerates creation while humans provide the final validation and scientific judgment.

title: Previz
pitch: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame.
about_excerpt: Direct your vision. Let AI choreograph every frame. Like Comment Story Updates Project Story About the project Previz is a browser-based 3D blocking and camera previsualization tool built for human–agent collaboration. Directors can stage characters, animate cameras, mark important positions, and describe creative goals in natural language. A WebMCP-enabled agent can then inspect the complete scene, propose a shot plan, calculate precise trajectories, validate them, and update the visible project. Inspiration Film previsualization tools are powerful, but turning an idea like “follow the character, hide the second performer, then reveal both in one continuous shot” into animation often requires manually editing hundreds of positions, rotations, and keyframes. We wanted to explore a more natural workflow: the human directs while the agent handles calculation. Instead of controlling the interface through fragile mouse coordinates, the agent receives structured access to the same scene the director sees. WebMCP made that relationship possible. What it does Previz provides a browser-based workspace for: Adding and positioning characters and cameras in a 3D scene Creating character and camera keyframes on a timeline Previewing the selected camera in real time Adding world-space and camera-space annotations Importing scene geometry and changing its visualization style Saving, importing, and autosaving project data Exporting camera previews as video Exposing the project to agents through WebMCP The accompanying previz-director Codex skill turns directorial intent into validated character blocking and camera motion. It reads the scene, discusses a creative plan with the user, calculates trajectories, checks continuity and safety, and writes the approved result back into the editor. How we built it The interactive editor uses Three.js and WebGL for the scene, characters, camera frustums, lighting, imported geometry, transform controls, and real-time camera previews. The timeline and editing interface are implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The application is packaged with React, Vinext, Vite, and Cloudflare’s runtime tooling so it can run locally or as a hosted web application. WebMCP is implemented through two tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : read_state returns the complete project and its current revision. write_state accepts a complete project and an expected revision, validates the data, updates the editor, creates an undo snapshot, and autosaves the result. Both tools use JSON Schema. Revision checking prevents an agent from overwriting newer human edits. We also created the previz-director skill, which defines a two-stage workflow: Read the scene and agree on the directorial plan. Calculate, validate, and execute the approved character and camera trajectories. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was connecting creative language to exact 3D motion. A request can be visually clear to a director while leaving many mathematical details unspecified: timing, path shape, camera distance, target transitions, angle continuity, and collision clearance. Camera movement introduced additional problems. Smooth positions do not guarantee smooth framing, and direct look-at calculations can cause sudden rotations during close passes or near-vertical shots. We needed to consider speed, acceleration, angular motion, occlusion, and composition together. Another challenge was safe human–agent collaboration. The agent may spend time calculating a scene while the user continues editing it. Revision-based writes ensure that stale calculations cannot silently replace newer work. Finally, we had to keep the visual editor responsive while rendering multiple views, imported geometry, shadows, annotations, playback, and video exports. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Previz does not treat WebMCP as a remote-control layer. The agent works with meaningful project concepts—characters, cameras, annotations, frames, and trajectories—instead of imitating clicks and drags. Other accomplishments include: Transactional, revision-protected project updates Immediate synchronization between agent writes and the visible editor Per-frame trajectory support for precisely calculated movement A reusable directing skill that separates creative approval from execution World-space and camera-space annotation workflows Browser-based video preview and export Automated coverage across 62 application tests A completely browser-based workflow with no traditional 3D application required What we learned We learned that the strongest agent experiences divide responsibility clearly. Humans are best at narrative intent, taste, rhythm, and deciding what an audience should feel. Agents are valuable when a creative decision expands into hundreds of dependent calculations and consistency checks. We also learned that structured state is much more reliable than visual automation. Giving the agent a small, well-described tool surface produced safer and more understandable behavior than exposing every interface control individually. Most importantly, planning and execution need a clear boundary. Having the agent present its interpretation before writing the scene keeps the user in control and prevents technically valid motion from becoming the wrong creative choice. What's next for Previz Next, we want to add: Adjustable focal length and camera sensor controls Look-at and subject-tracking constraints Editable easing and motion curves Motion paths and onion-skin visualization Keyframe copy and paste More detailed collision and occlusion diagnostics glTF and USD camera export Multi-user and multi-agent collaboration Additional WebMCP tools for targeted, incremental scene operations A reusable library of blocking and cinematography patterns Our long-term goal is to make Previz a shared creative surface where people direct ideas and agents turn those ideas into precise, editable cinematic motion. title: Teachback
pitch: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people.
about_excerpt: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A person sets the reusable boundary by comparing source and proposal, then tightening the permitted arrival time. Human approval gates the commit. Only the exact approved run can be applied, with expiry, digest, version, and replay checks. The agent drafts; the website keeps control. A WebMCP-capable agent turns the record into reusable operations and wording. Recorded work becomes structured evidence. Teachback preserves saved operations, exact diffs, and evidence IDs—not clicks. Preparation is not execution. WebMCP returns exact proposed changes while the reservation remains unchanged. The website refuses work outside the published boundary and returns the compensation case to a person. Teachback is a WebMCP app that converts one handled case into a reusable, approval-first workflow, so agents can suggest actions while humans keep control of execution. What Teachback does Teachback explores a practical question: how can a team reuse an experienced person's response without treating one successful case as unlimited permission? The demo uses synthetic hotel reservations. A staff member handles Aiko's late arrival in the normal website and saves four operations: the arrival update, a meal box, a guest message, and a shift handoff. Teachback records semantic commands, exact before-and-after values, and evidence IDs—not click coordinates. A WebMCP-capable agent reads that record and authors its own playbook draft. It must identify supported operations, replace Aiko's name and time with permitted case fields, preserve the recorded wording, and propose an arrival boundary. The website checks the proposal against the actual evidence. A person then compares source and reusable wording, tightens the cutoff, and publishes the reviewed version. Publication is deliberately not a WebMCP tool. For Emma, the agent reads the published version and current case data, then asks Teachback to prepare a run. The website evaluates deterministic safeguards and produces the exact diff. Nothing changes until a person reviews that proposal and selects Approve and apply in the website. The agent can read the committed result afterward, but it has no approval or application tool. When the same playbook is tried on Noah's compensation request, the website returns PLAYBOOK_NOT_APPLICABLE and sends the case back to a person. Why WebMCP is the right interface The difficult part is not clicking hotel fields. It is turning concrete work into a proposed reusable structure, then carrying that structure into a new case without blurring who decides. A generic page reader sees labels and pixels; WebMCP exposes the concepts that matter: demonstrations, evidence-backed drafts, published versions, cases, and prepared runs. This creates a clean division of responsibility: the person demonstrates work, edits boundaries, publishes, and applies; the agent interprets the recording, drafts reusable wording, and prepares a case-specific proposal; the website validates evidence, enforces fixed safeguards, calculates exact changes, and refuses work outside the published boundary. The result is an explicit handoff between interpretation and authorization. An agent can help with the genuinely ambiguous part—drafting from evidence—without receiving a generic mutation API or the authority to approve its own output. How WebMCP is implemented The TypeScript/React application registers seven typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(): teachback_get_demonstration teachback_create_draft teachback_update_draft teachback_list_playbooks teachback_list_cases teachback_prepare_run teachback_get_run Tool input is schema-checked and size-limited. Draft steps must cite recorded evidence, reproduce the final saved operations, and parameterize source-specific names, dates, IDs, and times. Published playbooks are immutable versions. Preparing a run binds it to the case version and published-content digest. Human approval is bound to the exact run digest, expires after five minutes, and can be used once. Request IDs make mutating WebMCP calls idempotent, while compact receipts and session limits prevent unbounded browser storage growth. The audit trail separates Human, Agent, and Website decisions. Prototype scope Teachback is a client-side prototype with eight synthetic reservations and four supported operation types. It demonstrates recording, proposal validation, human publication, exact-diff approval, deterministic refusal, and audit semantics. It is not connected to a real hotel system and does not claim production authentication, authorization, multi-user storage, arbitrary browser automation, or autonomous batch execution. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Paradox
pitch: A testing tool for WebMCP apps — find the race a human and an AI agent ship together, and prove the fix against every explored future.
about_excerpt: A testing tool for WebMCP apps — find the race a human and an AI agent ship together, and prove the fix against every explored future. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The counterexample in focus: $2,399 reviewed, $23,999 changed, $23,999 committed — invariant violated, 9 steps minimized to 3. The landing at the moment the race commits — the only color that ever enters the universe. Explore Futures: 36 schedules, 27 violating futures, the shortest failure ready to focus. Verify: the exact counterexample replayed — BLOCKED, STATE_CHANGED, 0 surviving counterexamples. Ledger: inspect_expense binds a review token to $2,399 · v7 — two live WebMCP tools on the rail. The human edits to $23,999 · v8; the unsafe tool approves it against the v7 review — the recorded race. Inspiration Software used to have one operator at a time. WebMCP gives the same live application two: a human using the interface and an AI agent invoking structured tools. Each path can look correct in isolation while their interleaving is unsafe — the agent inspects one version of an object, the human changes it, and the agent then commits an action based on a state that is no longer true. This is not an agent-quality problem: in our recorded race the agent behaves exactly as instructed. It is an application-contract problem, so the repair belongs in the tool contract. Playwright tests your pages; agent evals test your prompts. Nobody was testing the states created when both operators act on the same application at the same time. So we built the testing tool for that. What it does Paradox is a testing tool for WebMCP apps. It records semantic operations from a real WebMCP application, explores every valid human-agent interleaving of those operations, evaluates every reached state against business invariants, and returns the shortest replayable counterexample. Then it proves the fix: a constrained semantic version guard on the tool contract, verified by replaying the exact counterexample (blocked with STATE_CHANGED ) and re-exploring the complete bounded model. The recorded race, live on the site (nothing prerecorded or hardcoded): The agent calls inspect_expense and reviews expense 481 at $2,399, version 7 . The human edits the amount to $23,999, version 8 . The agent calls approve_reviewed_expense with the review token it already holds. The intentionally unsafe implementation approves $23,999 · v8 against a v7 review. Paradox explores all 36 schedules , merges 11 equivalent branches, and finds 27 counterexample futures ; the shortest minimizes 9 machine steps to 3 essential operations . The version guard is applied to the tool contract; the exact counterexample replays as blocked — STATE_CHANGED ; guarded re-exploration reaches 0 surviving counterexamples (36 schedules / 34 states). WebMCP leverage Every agent operation runs through real tools registered on document.modelContext (with a navigator.modelContext fallback) — nothing is simulated in the UI. The capability surface is dynamic and state-scoped: 2 tools on the ledger, 3 during exploration, 4 at the finding ; stale tools retire through an AbortController, and toolchange keeps the on-page capability rail truthful to the actual registry. Tool results carry guide fields, so the tools themselves steer an agent (or a judge) through record → explore → repair → verify. Spec conformance details we sweated: execute callbacks return plain values (the host serializes), inputs are zod-validated, readOnlyHint annotations are accurate, and a Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) header gates the surface. Verified live end-to-end in the ChatGPT in-app browser — including an improvised amount ($1,337) proving every number is computed, not canned. How we built it The engine is deterministic TypeScript — no LLM decides what is safe. Bounded breadth-first exploration over micro-step interleavings, canonical state hashing with equivalent-branch merging (multiplicity preserved), invariant evaluation at terminal states, operation-level counterexample minimization, exact replay, and re-exploration for repair verification. The app is Next.js (App Router) with Zustand; the landing is a physics-true relativistic black hole in WebGPU whose only color enters when the race commits its violation — and drains back out as the guard eliminates every dangerous future. The SDK ships the complete tester ( bun add github:Joe-Simo/paradox-webmcp ), including a fully automatic tier: record one line per operation (actor, reads, writes) and analyzeRecording synthesizes the model, explores every interleaving, and reports every stale-belief commit; verifyRecordingRepair proves the guarded fix. A cross-validation test expresses the expense race purely through the public SDK API and reproduces the lab engine's published numbers exactly — two independent implementations agreeing. Challenges we ran into Making tool callbacks read live state (not stale React closures); rotating tool surfaces without leaking stale capabilities (AbortController lifecycles with rollback on partial registration failure); keeping every displayed number traceable to engine data; and building an adversarial review loop — 22 review agents across nine dimensions verified every claim against the code, the spec, and the live deployment before submission. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real ChatGPT clean-room pass on the production site: the full golden path through live WebMCP tools, surfaces rotating 2 → 3 → 4, the race reproduced and blocked with STATE_CHANGED on a non-scripted amount. Strict TypeScript, 24 unit tests, 5 Playwright e2e (including accessibility), and a 2:00 4K60 demo rendered entirely from the live product. What we learned The agent is never the culprit — the tool contract is. The shippable pattern that falls out of Paradox is simple: WebMCP write-tools should carry the version their belief was formed on and reject stale commits with STATE_CHANGED . That one contract change turns an intermittent, unreproducible race report into a deterministic, provable fix. What's next for Paradox The expense scenario is a reference implementation of a category, not the category itself: the identical race ships in carts, bookings, refunds, approvals, and permissions the moment an agent and a human share live state. Next: richer automatic hazard classes beyond stale-commit, broader invariant libraries, and CI integration so every WebMCP app can explore its futures before its users do. Honesty notes Exploration is bounded and reports incompleteness honestly; zero findings means none survived the explored model — not universal correctness. The demonstrated repair is a constrained semantic version guard, not arbitrary source synthesis. Try it (2 minutes) Live: https://www.paradoxwebmcp.com · Docs: https://www.paradoxwebmcp.com/docs · Source: https://github.com/Joe-Simo/paradox-webmcp — testing instructions for a WebMCP-capable browser are in the README. title: THREAD
pitch: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish.
about_excerpt: THREAD is a shared execution graph where humans and AI agents negotiate, simulate, and safely apply plans that can actually finish. Like Comment Story Updates THREAD turns project planning into a negotiated contract: agents propose with evidence, and only humans approve. Agents can inspect, simulate, and recommend—but only a human can approve and atomically apply a plan. A live dependency graph keeps tasks, risks, constraints, critical paths, forecasts, and agent actions in one shared state. Compare Safest, Fastest, and Highest-impact proposals with exact graph changes, constraint checks, and seeded forecasts. Every approved change records its actor, reason, and evidence in the decision ledger, with full rollback available. 1. Forty-six WebMCP tools expose strict, debuggable state, backed by Cloudflare D1 persistence and browser-local recovery. Inspiration Most project-management tools tell you what needs to be done, but not whether the plan can actually succeed. A checklist might show 20 unfinished tasks while hiding the facts that only five determine the deadline, one uncertain task could delay everything, and the total plan has almost no chance of finishing with the available time and budget. AI assistants can suggest improvements, but those suggestions often remain trapped in a chat instead of becoming safe, visible changes to the real plan. I built THREAD to give humans and AI agents the same structured reality: one dependency graph, one planning engine, one simulation model, and one persistent workspace. What it does THREAD turns a goal into a living execution graph. Each task can contain: Dependencies Status and priority Minimum, expected, and maximum duration Confidence Cost Description and graph position A workspace also tracks deadlines, budgets, resources, hard constraints, risks, milestones, and available capacity. From this information, THREAD can: Calculate the critical path Identify slack, conflicts, and bottlenecks Show which tasks block the most downstream work Run reproducible Monte Carlo simulations Estimate finish probability, median completion time, P80, P95, and cost exposure Identify the risks and tasks driving schedule variance Compare immutable what-if scenarios Apply, replan, optimize, or roll back structured changes Record human, agent, system, and persistence activity The seeded demonstration models the work required to submit THREAD itself. It includes 14 tasks, 21 dependencies, three hard constraints, quantified risks, limited capacity, and a fixed budget. Its baseline simulation shows that a plan can appear reasonable while still having only about a 71% chance of finishing. Users can test alternatives such as cutting nonessential work, recruiting help, or adding more features. Every scenario runs through the same seeded engine, making comparisons reproducible rather than arbitrary. Human-agent collaboration THREAD is not a chatbot placed beside a task board. Through WebMCP, a compatible agent can directly understand and operate the project’s structured state. The live application currently exposes 38 native tools covering: Workspace, task, dependency, constraint, risk, resource, timeline, and activity retrieval Task, milestone, dependency, risk, resource, constraint, and scenario creation Task updates, completion, prioritization, movement, and risk resolution Critical-path analysis, conflict detection, bottleneck discovery, simulation, and feasibility calculation High-level plan application, optimization, replanning, scenario comparison, and rollback These tools use strict schemas and stable identifiers. Invalid relationships—including self-dependencies, duplicates, missing tasks, and dependency cycles—are rejected before they can corrupt the graph. Human actions and agent actions use the same domain services. When an agent changes a task, the human sees that change in the graph. When the human changes a constraint, the agent reads the updated value. The activity stream shows who performed each action, making agent participation visible and reversible. How I built it I designed THREAD around a shared application layer instead of implementing separate logic for the interface and WebMCP. The visual interface, planning engine, persistence system, and WebMCP tools all operate on the same workspace model. This prevents the agent-facing representation from drifting away from what the user sees. The planning engine performs deterministic critical-path calculations across the dependency graph. The simulation engine then evaluates task-duration ranges, confidence, costs, capacity, dependencies, and quantified risks across seeded iterations. Using a fixed seed means that the same plan produces the same result. That reproducibility is important when a human and agent are comparing alternatives: an improvement should come from the plan changing, not from random noise. Workspace state is persisted with Cloudflare D1, with browser-local recovery available when remote persistence cannot be reached. A dedicated WebMCP debugger displays the complete registered surface and can test read tools, mutation tools, malformed inputs, state synchronization, and reset behavior. The public demo requires no signup or API key, allowing judges to load a complete workspace immediately. Challenges The hardest challenge was keeping the human interface and agent interface synchronized. It would have been easier to create a collection of WebMCP wrappers that returned demonstration data. Instead, each tool needed to call the same validated services as the visible application and produce a real state change. Graph correctness was another challenge. Dependency editing must prevent cycles while continuously recalculating task timing, slack, and the critical path. Simulation also required care. A percentage is not useful if it cannot be explained or reproduced, so THREAD reports percentile estimates, cost ranges, failure sources, and variance drivers alongside the headline probability. Finally, I had to make a complex planning model understandable. The graph, inspector, risk panels, feasibility score, scenario cards, simulation results, and activity history all needed to reveal depth without overwhelming a first-time user. What I learned I learned that WebMCP becomes most valuable when it exposes capabilities that are difficult and unreliable to perform through visual clicking alone. An agent can retrieve an entire dependency graph, identify bottlenecks, simulate the plan, and apply a validated set of operations through structured tools. Meanwhile, the human retains the interface best suited to judgment: a visual graph, transparent comparisons, and an inspectable history. The strongest human-agent experiences do not hide the agent or replace the human. They give each participant the right interface while keeping both grounded in the same state. What I am proud of I am most proud that THREAD is more than a technical WebMCP demonstration. It is a functioning planning product with: A complete visual workspace Real dependency and risk modeling Reproducible simulation Persistent shared state A substantial native WebMCP surface Human and agent activity tracking Scenario isolation and rollback A dedicated verification console A judge-ready, no-signup demo What is next The next step is deeper plan negotiation: allowing agents to prepare several simulated proposals while humans lock non-negotiable constraints, compare visual graph differences, answer structured tradeoff questions, and approve the final plan. The long-term vision is for THREAD to become an execution environment where humans and agents do not merely discuss goals—they build, test, negotiate, and maintain a plan that has a measurable chance of succeeding. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate
pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests.
about_excerpt: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Shown, ran, refused: one attack caught by the mandate Devpost submission — ROAST (WebMCP Challenge, filled 30 Aug 2026) Name: ROAST · break WebMCP consent, then fix it with a mandate Pitch: A coffee shop an AI agent can use, and misuse. Three attacks fool WebMCP consent dialogues; a human mandate - intent, authority, effect - refuses them before any dialogue can lie. Live demo + tests. Thumbnail: data/webmcp-challenge/roast-devpost-thumb.png Demo: https://crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ Essay: https://crowley.nl/blog/webmcp-consent-theater.html Built with: javascript, webmcp, mcp, html5, css3, elevenlabs, github-actions, security Project Story (pasted into "About the project") Inspiration I first heard about WebMCP on Greg Isenberg's YouTube channel, where the conversation was all possibility: agents driving websites through your own browser, no scraping, no brittle automation. I love MCP, so I started reading the proposal properly. What struck me was the gap: the security story was thin. WebMCP's best trick is that the agent inherits your logged-in session - and that same trick is the loaded gun. So I asked the obvious questions. How does consent actually work here? What could go wrong? And when it goes wrong, what would stop it going wrong again? What it does ROAST is a fake coffee shop an AI agent can drive through WebMCP - and misuse. It plays four acts: No consent - the agent acts silently on your session Naive consent - a dialogue shows the tool's friendly description; feels safe Poisoned consent - the same dialogue, with three real attacks underneath: label mismatch, tool substitution, and a hidden-instruction manifest. You approve a coffee; your shipping address changes, your account closes The mandate - the proposal. You grant bounded authority up front: two coffees, $30, never my address, ask before paying. Every call is checked against the executed tool and the hidden chain, before any dialogue renders The model is Intent → Authority → Effect . Inside the mandate the agent just works - no prompt fatigue. Outside it, the call is refused before a dialogue exists to be fooled. At the boundary (paying), it escalates to the human. Once. A built-in test rig asserts all nine cases - three attacks, six legitimate paths - live on the page. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, no framework, one funnel: every tool call (simulated or real) resolves through request → resolvePlan → mandate check → consent gate → execute → log . The attacks are pure functions that warp the mapping between what is shown and what runs - which makes them honest test cases, not theatre. Tools register for real via navigator.modelContext where the browser supports it; a deterministic sim harness plays the same pipeline everywhere else. The instrumentation panel shows intent, consent, and effect side by side - the technical truth lives "below the waterline" of the UI. Challenges we ran into The honest one: the mandate check runs inside the page, and the page is the attacker. We state this in the UI rather than hide it. In a real deployment the mandate belongs in the browser or the agent - the layer a site cannot rewrite. ROAST prototypes it in the page because the page is what a demo controls. That is the proposal to the spec, not a shipped fix. The other challenge was UX density: showing an attack, a refusal, and the raw call log without drowning the visitor - solved with plain-English verdicts above the waterline and the technical log beneath it. What we learned The consent moment is the whole human-agent interface, and a dialogue that renders a human-authored description is a dialogue that can lie. Better warnings do not fix this; bounded authority does. Checking the executed call against a standing mandate defeats all three attacks with one invariant: an effect may only execute when it matches both the declared tool and the human's current mandate. What's next for ROAST Take the mandate out of the page: a browser-level or agent-level authority layer for WebMCP, mandates expressed in the user's own words and parsed to scopes, and fingerprinted tool manifests so substitution is detectable across the boundary. The write-up and the argument live at crowley.nl/webmcp-challenge/ . Built With css3 html vanilla-javascript-(native-es-modules) Try it out crowley.nl crowley.nl Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo entry. I'm a design leader, not a career developer: I did the research into WebMCP's consent gaps, designed the four-act demo and the mandate model (intent, authority, effect), wrote the attack scenarios and the copy, and built it with Claude Code as my pair - reviewing and directing every step. The security argument, the interaction design, and the video are mine. title: ZShop Agent Cart
pitch: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart.
about_excerpt: A shared shopping workspace where humans set intent and WebMCP agents search, compare, and safely build the cart. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopping agents are often forced to infer intent from pixels, scrape inconsistent product cards, and guess whether an action is safe. ZShop Agent Cart explores a better contract: the storefront exposes precise capabilities while the shopper keeps a visible, shared workspace and remains in control of consequential choices. What it does ZShop registers five WebMCP tools directly from the live storefront: set_shopping_goal makes the shopper's brief visible to both human and agent. search_products searches the live catalog and returns compact, comparable facts. inspect_product reads current price, stock, fulfilment, description, and option requirements. view_cart reads the authenticated shopper's selected items and total. add_product_to_cart adds simple products through the existing signed-in session. The on-page companion shows the shared goal and a live activity trail, so the human can see what the agent is doing without leaving the shopping experience. Products with variants are deliberately not guessed: the tool returns a product URL and asks the shopper to select options. Checkout remains human-controlled. Why WebMCP is the right fit Commerce mixes fast-changing facts, authenticated state, and actions with different risk levels. WebMCP lets the site describe each capability with a narrow JSON schema and behavioral annotations instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer the UI. The result is faster and more reliable than click automation, while preserving the storefront's own validation, authentication, and cart rules. Before this extension, a shopper could browse ZShop and an agent could separately offer generic advice. Now they can work in the same live catalog and session: the person states intent and handles preference-heavy decisions; the agent retrieves current facts, narrows choices, and performs bounded cart work; both share visible context. How we built it The Nuxt 4 client plugin detects document.modelContext , then registers typed tools with registerTool . Each tool has a constrained input schema, clear descriptions, and read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints. Tool handlers call the same production catalog and cart APIs as the storefront and reuse the existing auth token. A Vue composable keeps the shared goal and recent action log reactive in the companion UI. Focused Vitest coverage validates product normalization and rejects malformed search terms and numeric inputs. A CDP-based WebMCP host test injects the browser API, verifies all five registrations, executes the goal and live catalog search tools, and confirms that the human-visible companion updates. Challenges The central design challenge was choosing boundaries, not simply exposing every UI action. Product options cannot be selected safely from incomplete intent, and checkout has financial consequences, so neither is automated. Another challenge was keeping the experience useful outside a WebMCP-enabled browser; the storefront still works normally and the companion explains when agent capabilities are unavailable. Accomplishments Five working WebMCP tools backed by a live multilingual catalog. Shared human-agent context visible in the existing storefront. Authenticated cart access without a second agent-specific account system. Explicit safety boundaries for variants and checkout. Reproducible tests, public source, MIT license, and dated challenge-period commits. What we learned Agent-native UX is strongest when structured capabilities and visible human feedback are designed together. Schemas make actions reliable; the companion makes them understandable. The most important tool behavior can also be a refusal to guess. What's next Next we would add preference memory approved by the shopper, side-by-side comparison cards generated from tool results, and a confirmation protocol for reversible versus consequential actions. We would also localize tool descriptions alongside ZShop's Chinese, English, Thai, and Traditional Chinese interface.
