title: BuildParty
pitch: A shared space for humans and agents to collaborate together. Create your own party, invite your friends, lets agents update in real time the page content and let your feedbacks directly.
about_excerpt: A shared space for humans and agents to collaborate together. Create your own party, invite your friends, lets agents update in real time the page content and let your feedbacks directly. Like Comment Story Updates BuildParty, a space for humans and agents Collaborate with your teammates with no context drift Build adaptive learning notebook, for self-learning or with a friend Fine-tuning of webmcp tools with deterministic evaluations Refine agent plans in a dedicated UI on the go! Inspiration Agents are now really good at generating HTML/CSS/JS artifacts to help convey understanding to users by visualizing content. There are already services that enable agents to easily host static pages, but these lack interactivity. At the same time, agents are mainly used by one user only, and there isn't that much of a multiplayer mode. When collaborating with coworkers or friends, we have to manually send artifacts/plans, gather feedback, and potentially go through multiple sessions and iterations to reach the final desired state. Multiple agents can work toward the same goal, but in complete isolation. My goal was to try to use a super simple platform to enable a new kind of multiplayer agents × humans collaboration. What it does BuildParty allows anyone to create a party. It is completely their own, and agents can automatically connect to it using WebMCP tools. Each party is initially empty, but any connected agent can add and modify “artifacts”, which are self-contained HTML/CSS/JS components. The owner can share the link so that other users can join on any device, connect their agents, and see changes in real time. Users can interactively add comments and suggestions directly on the page for all agents to see. The page is fully synced, and each change is saved as a revision. The owner can roll back to a previous revision at any time. At the end, the owner can finalize the party, closing any further modifications and compacting all artifacts together into a single HTML page ready to download. Each block supports persistent state so that interactive elements such as text areas, buttons, etc. can work. The flow is very simple for agents: read a specific block, modify it or add a new one, and read comments. This can be used for a range of different use cases: collaborative planning before starting a long implementation, ephemeral agent observability dashboards to see specific progress, and more. How we built it This was built using webmcp for tools, custom-made evaluation with WebMCP-bench using daytona cloud sandboxes, electric for sync and PostgreSQL for the underlying db. Challenges we ran into Evaluating WebMCP capabilities is very hard because, on top of the current agent context, we add a new dimension: the website state. Even if my basic evaluations worked, when manually testing I often ran into cases where the agent could not efficiently figure out which tool to call or in which order. To fix this, I built a small WebMCP evaluation framework based on a finite state machine: each state encodes a website state fixture and the available tools, while transitions to other states define specific tool calls. From this FSM specification, I can automatically implement tool discovery and give agents information about the available flow of tool calls. I also defined an evaluation bench with a set of tasks that consist of an initial state, a target end state with a sequence of expected tool calls, and an initial prompt. With this, I was able to fine-tune tool descriptions and improve the agent's understanding of how to use the website context efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of Everything works, and I'm already using it for some use cases! What we learned I learned a lot about what is possible with WebMCP and how to reason about it. I believe that, at some point, we could somehow ditch frontend frameworks as we know them and start with only a state flow/state machine representation of the app, then enable UI components “on demand” that automatically adapt to the user's preferences and needs. This would also be awesome for accessibility, as we could automatically derive not only visual frontends but other frontend formats as well. What's next for BuildParty If there's some interest, I would like to rework the whole artifact engine to make it more robust to agent changes and enable different formats such as Markdown editors, code blocks with interpreters (Jupyter Notebook style), and embedded databases. I would also like to improve the human side with a more precise feedback system, chatbox, authentication, etc. Built With codex electric postgresql webmcp Try it out buildparty.app github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jules D Like Share this project: Updates Jules D started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:17 PM EDT

title: The Website That Speaks AI
pitch: Turning a real Italian business website into an agent-ready experience with WebMCP, so AI can understand its services, reason about customer needs, and safely prepare real-world actions.
about_excerpt: Turning a real Italian business website into an agent-ready experience with WebMCP, so AI can understand its services, reason about customer needs, and safely prepare real-world actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most business websites today are designed entirely for humans. A customer opens a website, navigates through pages, reads about services, tries to understand whether the company can solve a specific problem, finds the contact page, and finally submits a request. But the way people use the web is beginning to change. Increasingly, a user may simply ask an AI: “My security door is stuck in Ceprano. Find someone who can help me and help me contact them.” This project explores what happens when a real business website is ready for that interaction. Our core idea is simple: The web already has an interface for humans. We created a layer for AI agents. And that led us to a second idea: Maybe we do not need to teach agents how to use every website. We can teach websites how to speak to agents. Instead of forcing an AI to reconstruct the meaning of a business by navigating pages, interpreting the DOM and guessing how the website works, the website itself can expose its business knowledge, services, rules, constraints and available actions directly to compatible agents. Website knowledge → Agent understanding → Reasoning → Human confirmation → Safe action What we built We integrated WebMCP into the live website of Show Room La Finestra , a real Italian business operating in windows, doors, security doors, sunshades, aluminium systems, technical assistance and custom metalwork. This is not a simulated storefront or a website created specifically for the challenge. It is a real production Joomla website that existed before the challenge and continues to serve real customers normally. We added an Agent Interface Layer alongside the existing human interface. Through WebMCP, a compatible AI can discover structured business knowledge and capabilities directly from the website and use them to understand the business, reason about a customer's request and, when appropriate, prepare a safe action. The implementation exposes structured capabilities such as: business information; available services; detailed service knowledge; contact options; contact request preparation; confirmation-gated submission. For example, a customer can ask an AI for help with a blocked security door. The AI can: discover the WebMCP capabilities exposed by the website; understand which business service is relevant; determine what information is needed from the customer; prepare a structured contact request; show the complete request to the user; ask for explicit confirmation; only after confirmation, proceed with the existing website contact workflow. The AI therefore does not need to blindly navigate pages and guess what the company does. The website can explain itself. Another important design choice is that WebMCP is intentionally not exposed globally across every page of the website . Different pages have different purposes, so they can expose different agent contexts. A homepage can explain the business and its services. A service page can expose service-specific knowledge, rules and constraints. A contact page can expose contact options and controlled actions. A page with nothing useful for an agent can expose nothing at all. The website does not need one large AI interface. Every page can become its own AI interface when it makes sense. Why WebMCP WebMCP creates a new interface between websites and AI. Traditional websites expose visual interfaces optimized for humans. AI systems can attempt to interpret those interfaces, but important business meaning may be distributed across navigation structures, text, forms and application logic. WebMCP allows the website to expose that meaning explicitly. For a local business, this can mean exposing: who the business is; what services it provides; where it operates; service-specific knowledge; business rules and constraints; what information an action requires; which actions are available; when human confirmation is required. The result is not about replacing the website. It is about giving the same business two interfaces: one for humans and one for AI. One website. Two interfaces: Humans + AI. We also wanted to explore WebMCP without introducing unnecessary infrastructure. This implementation does not require a separate MCP server for the agent to discover, configure or connect to. The WebMCP capabilities live directly on the existing website and are exposed through document.modelContext when a compatible client visits a page where the integration is enabled. The agent does not connect to an MCP server somewhere else. It visits the website — and the website speaks for itself. Safety and human control A key design decision was that discovering and preparing an action should not automatically execute it. For potentially consequential actions such as sending a customer request, the system follows a human-confirmation pattern: discover → understand → collect → prepare → review → confirm → act The AI can do the work required to understand the request, collect the required information and prepare the interaction, but the user remains in control of the final action. Preparation and execution are deliberately separated. A prepared contact request contains the exact information that would be submitted. The agent must show that information to the user. The request cannot be submitted unless explicit confirmation is provided. Preparation does not equal execution. The website also exposes bounded business knowledge. The agent should not invent prices, availability, timing, warranties or other information that the business has not provided. When something requires confirmation from the company, the agent must treat it as unknown rather than inventing an answer. How we built it The existing production website runs on Joomla + Gantry 5 . Rather than rebuilding the website around WebMCP, we added an agent-facing layer to the architecture that was already working. The integration is loaded through a small deferred JavaScript loader on the pages where agent capabilities are needed. That layer registers WebMCP tools through: document.modelContext The current implementation exposes six structured tools: get_business_info list_services get_service_details get_contact_options prepare_contact_request submit_contact_request The existing Joomla website continues to serve human visitors normally. No Joomla Core modification was required. No database modification was required. No external LLM API was required. No new AI backend was required. No separate MCP server was required. The WebMCP layer works as progressive enhancement . If WebMCP is unavailable in the browser, the normal website continues to work unchanged. If WebMCP is available, the same website gains an additional structured interface for compatible agents. We also reused the existing Joomla contact workflow rather than creating a parallel contact system. After explicit user confirmation, the WebMCP layer can use the website's existing same-origin Joomla form and its current validation and CSRF protection. This allowed us to explore an important question: Can an existing real-world business website become agent-ready without replacing the systems that already work? Our implementation demonstrates that it can. Challenges The biggest challenge was not simply exposing tools. It was deciding what an AI should be allowed to understand and do . Real businesses contain ambiguity. Services overlap. Customer requests can be incomplete. Location can matter. Information can change. An AI should not invent business capabilities, prices or availability. And an action should not happen simply because the AI is technically capable of performing it. We therefore focused on: clear business semantics; bounded capabilities; explicit rules and constraints; page-specific context; safe failure behavior; human confirmation before consequential actions. Another challenge was deciding how much context should be exposed to an agent. A simple approach would have been to expose the same large set of tools and information everywhere. Instead, we chose a page-scoped architecture . Different pages can expose only the knowledge and capabilities that make sense in that context. This keeps the agent context smaller, more relevant and easier to control. Another important challenge was integrating this new agent-facing layer without disrupting the existing production Joomla website. The goal was not to create a WebMCP demonstration website. The goal was to make an existing website WebMCP-capable while preserving the website that customers already use. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not only about browser automation. It can change the relationship between a website and an AI. Instead of asking: “How can an AI learn to use this website?” we can ask: “How can this website cle

title: Nightstand — a health diary you run by voice
pitch: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend.
about_excerpt: A local-first health diary you run by voice. On WebMCP, every on-screen action is also an agent tool so people who can't type keep their records hands-free. Zero backend. Like Comment Story Updates The home screen — everything you do here, your agent can do by voice. 19 of 19. Entries it logs show "logged by your agent." Track medications by voice or on screen — the same tool either way. Schedules are versioned so past adherence stays truthful. Ask your agent to prepare a doctor summary — symptom trends, adherence, as-needed doses — downloadable as a real, selectable-text PDF. Inspiration The person I built this for has rheumatoid arthritis. Pain and stiffness in the hands make filling in a form miserable — and it's a disease that asks for a log every single day , for a consultation that happens once every three months, when nobody remembers the details. The people who most need to keep a health diary are often the ones who can least type one. So the diary shouldn't be typed. It should be spoken. WebMCP's own explainer names this exact motivation: it can "enable agents to assist users of accessibility technology." I wanted to take that literally — expose an entire app as agent tools, so someone who cannot comfortably type can run all of it hands-free by voice. What it does Nightstand is a local-first health diary you operate by talking to your AI agent. Speaking, hands-free, you can: Log naturally — "My knee hurts, about a seven, and I took my methotrexate" becomes two records from one sentence, with a single confirmation. Correct and undo by voice — "Actually, make it a five." "No, undo that." When you can't retype, the repair path is the product. Adjust the interface by voice — make the text bigger, jump to a section, raise contrast. Prepare a doctor's summary — "Prepare a summary for my doctor" reveals a printable report (symptom trend, medication adherence, as-needed doses), and one large 56 px button downloads it as a real, selectable-text PDF — generated in the browser, no backend. The whole flow is co-browsing : the person watches the screen while the agent acts, so every step is visible and reversible. How I built it WebMCP is the center of the project, not a wrapper around it. True parity, not a hand-typed number. Every capability is declared once — id, tool name, description, zod schema, handler — and from that one declaration come the on-screen control and the WebMCP tool, the published inputSchema , the runtime validation, and the TypeScript types. The "19 of 19" badge reads the registry, and a test compares the on-screen actions against the tools in both directions, so the number cannot drift. Three trust layers — 5 read-only answer tools, plus act and transact tools that change state. Because Nightstand is a co-browsing journey with a human present, it safely spans all three, with undo and explicit confirmations as the guardrails . An untrusted-input boundary. Tool arguments are produced by a language model, so every handler validates them with zod at the edge; past that point the data is typed and trusted, and invalid arguments return a readable error instead of writing a bad number into a medical record. One write path , so undo covers every write — spoken or tapped. You refer to things by name, never by id : the agent is never handed an identifier it can't hand back. Stack: Next.js (static output: 'export' ), React 19, TypeScript (strict), Tailwind 4, zod, idb over IndexedDB, pdf-lib (zero-dependency, lazy-loaded), Vitest. Zero backend — no API routes, server actions, or middleware — and zero outbound requests after load. The privacy promise holds because the repository has nowhere to hide anything. Challenges I ran into Printing is dead in the ChatGPT app's embedded browser. window.print() and Ctrl+P simply don't work there. I pivoted the doctor summary to a client-side PDF download that works both in a full browser and in the app. A page-initiated voice download loses user activation in that embedded browser and is stopped by the browser's policy — proven, not a bug I could fix. So the summary is a button : the agent prepares it by voice, and the person taps one large target. Timezone-correct clinical math. Adherence and local-day logic had to survive DST and non-UTC offsets, or a number handed to a doctor could be wrong. Pinned timezone test fixtures caught real bugs. Honest domain limits. The schedule model understands daily times, not weekly ones, so a weekly DMARD like methotrexate is logged as as-needed rather than scored — the app says so instead of reporting a wrong number. Which agents actually call the tools? I found that ChatGPT's Chrome extension drives the DOM instead of calling the WebMCP tools — while the judged surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled) genuinely consume them. Verifying that shaped where the demo lives. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Capability parity that's real, not claimed — enforced by a test that gates every commit. Privacy by architecture — verified zero outbound requests three different ways. Accessibility as the reason the app exists — WCAG 2.2 AA, 56 px targets, a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 . Independently validated by Google Chrome Labs' official webmcp-evals harness: 11/11 tool calls pass against the live deployment — real WebMCP calls, not DOM automation. What I learned WebMCP's value for accessibility isn't enabling voice — a DOM-driving agent can operate a site too. It's making agent operation reliable, safe, correct, and portable for something as sensitive as medical records: a typed contract with validation and undo, a smaller data footprint than screen-scraping, and one tool surface that works for any agent — in-browser or headless. And a design rule I'll keep: never hand the agent an identifier it cannot hand back. What's next Weekly and complex medication cadence, so DMARDs are scored for adherence. More entry types and languages. A caregiver mode: the same tool surface, operated by a headless agent someone sets up for a person who can't. title: Guild
pitch: The multiplayer visual workspace where humans and local AI teammates plan, design, and build software together on one shared canvas.
about_excerpt: The multiplayer visual workspace where humans and local AI teammates plan, design, and build software together on one shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Building software with AI still feels surprisingly fragmented. A product brief may live in a document, architecture in a diagram, tasks in an issue tracker, designs in another tool, and implementation evidence inside pull requests. AI assistants usually operate in separate chat windows with incomplete context. Humans spend time copying information between tools, resolving conflicting output, and figuring out what changed. We asked a simple question: What if humans and AI teammates could build a software project together inside the same visible workspace? That idea became Guild . Guild is inspired by the flexibility of Whimsical, the multiplayer presence of Figma, the structured execution of Linear, and the capabilities of modern coding agents. The difference is that AI is not hidden behind a chat sidebar. AI Workers appear as actual project collaborators with defined roles, owned workspace regions, live progress, visible results, and accountable changes. WebMCP was essential to this vision. Traditional browser agents have to interpret pages from pixels, DOM elements, and button labels. That approach is fragile and gives the agent very little understanding of the product’s actual domain. With WebMCP, Guild can expose structured operations such as: Search the project canvas Read semantic relationships Create or update project artifacts Launch a team of AI Workers Monitor active Jobs Add precisely anchored feedback Publish immutable design revisions Record implementation evidence Stop, retry, or undo work Guild is therefore not merely a web application that an agent can operate. It is a shared collaboration environment intentionally designed for people and agents to use together. What it does Guild is a multiplayer visual workspace where humans and locally running AI Workers build the same software project on one shared infinite canvas . Instead of separating product thinking, architecture, design, implementation planning, feedback, and AI execution across disconnected applications, Guild keeps everything in one persistent project context. One shared infinite canvas Every Guild project has one multiplayer canvas with three creation modes. Diagram mode Diagram mode supports: Product requirements Brainstorming User journeys User flows System architecture Database architecture API relationships AI and agent architecture Decisions and impact maps Task mode Task mode supports: Engineering tasks Implementation plans Bugs Reviews Testing Launch checklists Project status Task cards can contain Markdown descriptions, checklists, status, priority, labels, assignees, links, and semantic relationships. Wireframe mode Wireframe mode supports: Product screens Web and mobile interfaces Interface states User flows Low-fidelity prototypes Design annotations These modes share the same canvas rather than creating separate diagram, task, and design applications. Fifteen neutral canvas object types Guild uses a small set of flexible visual primitives: Shape Sticky note Text Mind-map node Table Icon Image Link Section Annotation Drawing Task Stack Wireframe frame Wireframe component Semantic metadata gives these objects their project meaning. A shape can represent a service, database, API, requirement, decision, or AI system without requiring a separate renderer for every software concept. Objects can be connected with relationships including: contains informs requires implements represents supports depends_on calls reads_from writes_to emits triggers verified_by affects blocks supersedes This produces a visual software-project graph rather than a collection of unrelated cards. Multiplayer collaboration Multiple people can work in the same workspace in real time. Guild synchronizes: Cursor position Canvas viewport Current selection Editing state Comments Canvas changes Worker progress Runner availability Project activity Every human, WebMCP, and Worker action is attributed in the activity history. AI Workers with real responsibilities An AI teammate in Guild is called a Worker . Each Worker is configured through a Role Profile containing: Name and handle Project responsibility Instructions Local execution engine Owned canvas section Visual identity Available capabilities For example, a Guild team could include: Product Lead Product Designer Systems Architect Research Engineer Backend Engineer Frontend Engineer Security and Evaluation Lead A user can save these Role Profiles as a team and launch them together with one project brief. Team Runs and Jobs When the user selects Run Team , Guild deterministically creates one Job for each selected Role Profile. Every Job receives: The same high-level brief Role-specific instructions Full bounded read context An owned section An atomically reserved canvas region Optional dependencies A short-lived assignment capability Workers can understand the broader project, but they can modify only the objects and regions assigned to them. Guild does not use a hidden planning model to decide which Workers should run. The user-selected team and its configuration determine the Job fan-out. Visible parallel work Workers do not disappear into background chat sessions. Guild shows: Which Worker is active Whether it uses Codex or Claude Code What it is currently doing Which canvas section it owns Which object it is working on Whether its Job is queued, running, blocked, failed, or completed What artifacts and comments it produced If no compatible local Runner is available, the Job remains durably queued and the interface truthfully displays Waiting for Runner . Canvas-native feedback and revision Humans can annotate work directly on the Guild canvas or inside a hosted design preview. Feedback may be attached to: An entire workspace A section A specific canvas object A precise point on a design A selected rectangle on a design An immutable screen revision Annotations remain drafts until the user opens Review & Send . Guild groups the feedback by the responsible Worker and creates at most one revision Job per target Worker. Every exact anchor is preserved, including the design revision, route, viewport, scroll position, point, or rectangle. Immutable design revisions Design Workers can publish hosted previews as immutable revisions. Guild stores: Design-set identity Deployment identity Preview origin Screen names and routes Desktop and mobile viewports Related canvas objects Capture status Revision history Human approval decisions Users can inspect a design inside Guild, compare revisions side by side or with a slider, request changes, and approve a specific immutable revision. Implementation evidence External implementation work can be reported back into Guild as bounded evidence: Repository Branch Commit Pull request Changed files Checks Preview deployment Related canvas objects Provenance Guild carefully distinguishes a reported claim from independently verified information. A reachable link may be labeled Link verified , but Guild does not falsely claim that it executed a test or inspected a commit when it did not. Reversible execution Human actions, WebMCP calls, and Worker changes pass through the same command service. Each accepted operation creates an attributable Change Set . Team Runs can be undone with conflict awareness, preserving unrelated human edits made afterward. Jobs can also be stopped or retried. Stale Worker attempts are fenced so they cannot continue writing after cancellation or reassignment. Guild's 25 WebMCP tools Guild exposes 25 structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . These tools operate on the real application state. They are not mocked endpoints or a separate agent-only database. Each tool has: A clear natural-language description A structured input schema Runtime validation Authentication and workspace authorization Abort support Audited execution Machine-readable results The same domain rules used by the human interface Workspace discovery and understanding 1. list_workspaces Lists the Guild workspaces available to the signed-in user. This gives the browser agent an explicit starting point instead of forcing it to infer workspace names from navigation elements. 2. get_workspace_context Reads bounded live project context, including: Workspace metadata Canvas objects Semantic relationships Role Profiles Saved teams Team Runs Runner state Placement guidance Color guidance The response is intentionally bounded so an agent can understand the project without loading an unbounded canvas. 3. search_canvas Searches visible content and semantic metadata inside one workspace. An agent can find requirements, designs, decisions, implementation tasks, evidence, services, risks, or any other project artifact. video_transcript_excerpt: Hi, this is a demo video for Guild, which is an AI workspace where you and your AI agents can work together in one visual infinite canvas. The project stays visible instead of getting lost across different tabs. Now, let us see this in action. I've opened a new Guild workspace for Cinemaverse. Now, we are building Cinemaverse, which turns a screenplay into a researched filming location and production requirements in this tab. I have assembled six agents, and each one owns a different part of the board. Guild shows when an agent is queued, working, publishing, blocked, or ready for review. One Cloud Code agent handles the design, and five Codec agents are handling the rest of the product, as you can see on the board. As each agent finishes its work, its work appears inside its own area in the canvas. I can move across the completed regions and review each result in context. The agent panel shows who is active, while the canvas shows what the agent has actually produced. Now, how are these are getting updated? So, Guild gives these agents 25 relevant CP tools. They can read the project, search the canvas, create and update objects, connect artifacts, report progress, start teams, and publish revisions through a shared interface. Each of the component is readable on the canvas, and I can open it for more detail. Here, the front-end results expands into structured markdown with its implementation plan and tests. The design agent has now published six product screens into its own canvas region. So, I can review the complete design without even leaving Guild. Feedback also happens directly on the canvas. Here, I want a specific area and I ask the Claude agent to design as per my request. Once I have added the comments and when I'm finished, Guild groups the comments with the responsible agent. I can add one overall note and send revision packets to each of the agent to make the required agent required changes as I want. The follow-up then starts in the local agents I'm already signed into. Codex updates the architecture and the revised result appears inside the scene in the canvas region. The Claude agent has returned the revised design with clear hierarchy, stronger contrast, and the visual direction I requested. I can question the result, request changes, verify the sources, and see the agent update the canvas in real time. Now, finally, Guild brings the canvas, agent orchestration, live progress, contextual feedback, versions, approval history, and undo in one workspace. The agents can work in parallel while the project stays visible and the final decision stays with me. So, this is Guild and I hope you like it.

title: Local Buzz
pitch: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time.
about_excerpt: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time. Like Comment Story Updates The agent does not click through the UI. Local Buzz exposes structured WebMCP tools, and the results appear directly in the same interface. Local Buzz combines a live city interface with WebMCP so a person and their AI agent can plan together. The human brings taste. The agent handles complexity. Local Buzz provides the live city. WebMCP enables one shared experience. Inspiration “What should we do tonight?” sounds simple, but the answer is scattered across event sites, venues, ticketing platforms, local calendars, social media, and word of mouth. AI can already recommend events or generate itineraries, but chat is a poor interface for exploring a city. A map is better for geography. A timeline is better for sequence. Visual browsing is better for taste. That led to a different question: What if a person and their personal AI agent could explore and shape a night together, inside the same live web experience? What it does Local Buzz turns your city into a shared real-time workspace for a person and their AI agent (starting with Stockholm and San Francisco). Local Buzz knows the city: what is happening, where, when, how much it costs, and what is currently available. The user's agent can bring something Local Buzz does not need to collect: context about the user. Together they can: discover relevant happenings surface candidates directly on the city map stage an evening on a visual timeline let the human lock, reject, or change individual choices let the agent read those changes and adapt around them repair an existing night when something becomes unavailable The important idea is that Local Buzz is not an AI itinerary generator. It is a shared model of a night that stays alive. It answers the age old question: where can I go have fun right now? Why WebMCP The human and the agent need different interfaces into the same application. The human works visually through maps, cards, timelines, locks, and direct manipulation. The agent works through structured WebMCP tools for searching happenings, showing candidates, reading the current plan, staging changes, locking stops, and repairing the plan. Both operate on the same underlying application state. For example, when a human locks a stop in the interface, the agent sees that constraint the next time it reads the plan. If another event becomes unavailable, the agent repairs only the affected portion instead of throwing the entire itinerary away and starting over. This is the interaction we wanted to explore with WebMCP: Agent acts → interface changes → human intervenes → agent understands the intervention → reality changes → agent repairs the shared state → human approves. How we built it Local Buzz is built as a proof-of-concept web application using the Modeless design system. The application has one shared domain model that powers both the human interface and its WebMCP tools. Human actions and agent actions call the same underlying application functions rather than maintaining separate UI and agent state. For the challenge prototype, we focus on Stockholm and San Francisco and use a small normalized set of real local event and venue data. Local Buzz adds derived metadata where useful for planning. A last-minute event availability change used in the demo is intentionally simulated so the repair behavior can be demonstrated deterministically and is clearly labeled as such. What we learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is that websites can be designed from the beginning for two collaborators with different strengths. The human brings taste, intuition, and judgment. The agent handles search, constraints, timing, and complexity. The website provides the live domain state they collaborate around. What I've been exploring is the surface area of how much a web app can be adapted for the end user based on agentic interactions. In some ways, it starts to become reminiscent of push, or streaming, data if the agent is making a lot of updates. I believe there's a lot of use cases for WebMCP around real-time data. title: NWA Growth Signal
pitch: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page.
about_excerpt: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page. Like Comment Story Updates Four real WebMCP calls completed in one visible workflow: search, list changes, inspect, and stage. The brief remains human-review-required. One parcel, two filings: VAR26-0397 Withdrawn and RZ26-00511 Recommended, kept distinct with their official sources. A three-filing brief staged for human review. Nothing is published or sent. The signal desk: the same dated municipal record for people and browser agents. Inspiration An agenda-wording-only heuristic could determine just 3 of 23 real planning outcomes, and 2 of those 3 were wrong: the wording implied approval for requests that were actually tabled. This week, Rogers changed an existing 8/18/26 outcome row in place from Tabled to 9/1 to Recommended to City Council , with no separate September 1 row. That is the kind of quiet procedural change that can burn land and development teams, lenders and title professionals, local journalists, and public-interest planners in Northwest Arkansas. Municipal records are public, but the procedural truth is scattered across agendas, minutes, outcome tables, hearing pages, and companion filings. One parcel can have several filings with different statuses. NWA Growth Signal gives a person and a browser agent a dated, filing-level planning evidence desk for Bentonville and Rogers, Arkansas. Adjacent products serve related jobs. CivicPlus provides agenda and meeting management. Regrid provides a parcel and property map. PermitFlow provides permitting workflow. NWA Growth Signal focuses on the evidence handoff between a researcher and an agent as official planning records change. What it does Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? The research task has four distinct steps, each with a clear contract. search_planning_cases filters 5 verified records by municipality, procedural status, residential relevance, and pending government action. list_status_changes returns the filings whose verified status moved since the previous check, with the official source on both dates. inspect_case_record returns one filing-level record with its context and official sources. stage_source_backed_brief places 1 to 5 selected records into the visible briefing workspace. The agent receives typed results from the same dated data the person sees instead of inferring status from page wording or clicking by coordinates. How does it create a better experience? One prompt can drive the whole flow: “Find residential Bentonville and Rogers cases still awaiting procedural action. List which filings changed status since the previous verification, inspect their official evidence, and stage a three-item brief without representing any recommendation as final approval.” The fixed demo script takes 10 direct human control activations or 4 agent tool calls. Each real handler call adds an on-page receipt, so the person can see search, list changes, inspect, and stage start and then succeed or fail in order. What can people and agents now do together? The person states the research intent and keeps editorial judgment. The agent searches, inspects the filing-level evidence, and stages the brief. The person can check every selected filing and source before using it. The staging tool cannot publish, send, or persist a brief, and only a human control can record review. How did we implement WebMCP? The page registers all 4 tools atomically with document.modelContext.registerTool after the record set loads and supports AbortSignal . Handler inputs are validated. The 3 read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Search, inspection, staging, the ordinary browser interface, and the receipt row all use the same deterministic record operations, so the agent and person work from one application state. Every filing also carries a status_history : its August 25 and September 2 statuses, the official source checked on each date, and a note where the record moved or went silent. The tools return it through their existing outputs, and the page shows the same line beside each filing, so an agent inspecting RZ26-00419 sees Tabled on August 25 and Recommended on September 2 with the same outcome-table URL for both, not a single current label. A fourth tool, list_status_changes , landed after the first demo video was recorded; the current video shows it in the same run. It reads that same status_history and returns the filings whose verified status moved between the previous check and the current one: RZ26-00419 (Tabled to Recommended) and RZ26-00511 (Scheduled to Recommended), each with the official source checked on both dates. With changed_only set to false it also lists the six unchanged filings and their notes, such as FP26-0005 absent from the reissued agenda. It is read-only, registered atomically with the other three, and writes the same on-page receipt: 2 filings changed since 2026-08-25. What changed during the challenge The project was created during the challenge. Its first commit was 85c27f7 on August 26, 2026. In the 8 days since the first snapshot, the official record moved 4 times across just 5 tracked records: Rogers RZ26-00511 , Poplar Street Paired Homes at 408 E. Poplar, moved from Scheduled to a 9/1/26 outcome of Recommended to City Council . Its companion filing on the same parcel, VAR26-0397 , still reads Withdrawn by applicant . The split-filing result is now Withdrawn plus Recommended, and council action is still pending. Rogers RZ26-00419 , 209 W. Locust, changed inside the same 8/18/26 row. On August 25 it read Tabled to 9/1 ; on September 2 it reads Recommended to City Council . The table publishes no separate September 1 row. Bentonville FP26-0005 , Brier Hill Phase II final plat, appeared on the September 1 agenda published August 25 as CivicClerk file 9108 . The city reissued that agenda as file 9133 without the filing. The current CivicClerk event record now points to agenda file 9143 ; the tracked filing contents are unchanged, and FP26-0005 remains omitted. No reason, outcome, or new date is published, so the product keeps the filing visible with its last published status and states what changed. Rogers RZ26-00345 , 6253 S. Mt Hebron Rd, disappeared from the outcome table. No City Council action appears in the official sources reviewed, so the product retains the last recorded status, Recommended, and says the row is gone. Bentonville RZ26-0041 , FP26-0003 , and FP26-0004 were heard September 1 according to the agenda. Minutes are not yet published, so the product represents no outcome for them. We also tested the approach on a held-out historical study: 23 real Rogers requests, 26 procedural events, 6 meetings in 2025, and 12 official agenda and minutes documents. NWA Growth Signal preserved 26/26 exact statuses through both inspection and staging. Expected source pairs were present in 26/26 record-wide outputs. All 23/23 same-meeting agenda and minutes pairs were present, and 3 multi-meeting lifecycles stayed intact. The request wording left 20 of 23 outcomes unknowable; as the opening example shows, it also gave the wrong answer for 2 of the 3 outcomes it appeared to reveal. How we built it NWA Growth Signal is a dependency-free static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript site deployed on Cloudflare Pages. A dated JSON snapshot holds the editorial sample. Shared JavaScript owns deterministic filtering, record inspection, brief staging, freshness checks, and receipts. The WebMCP adapter and the ordinary browser interface call those same operations. The release has 99 passing dependency-free tests, a deterministic benchmark, and a fail-closed freshness gate. The current video and public main both reflect the 99-test release. The team used Codex and Claude Code for implementation, review, testing, and submission work; Hyperagent for municipal research and editorial work; and Google Gemini for the approved demo narration. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was preserving truth at the filing level while the official record kept moving. A parcel summary would hide the difference between a withdrawn variance and a rezoning recommended to City Council. We carried each filing, status, source, and date through the data, tools, interface, benchmark, and demo. The other hard boundary was useful agent action without an unsafe side effect. Staging had to be visible and valuable while leaving review and any later use of the brief with the person. One browser request that searches, inspects, and stages a source-backed brief, with a live receipt for every handler call. 99 passing tests, all 4 tools exercised, input validation, atomic registration, cancellation support, and a fail-closed freshness gate. title: Tokuchu
pitch: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents
about_excerpt: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Six years ago, I cofounded a cafe where much of our revenue has come from bulk orders for events. Event organizers often request customizations, from dietary restrictions to names printed on party favours. But the specifications for these customizations can be difficult to collect. Organizers may not yet know exactly who is attending, what each guest needs, or which details a vendor requires. That uncertainty creates a lot of manual back and forth. An intermediate source of truth gives agents somewhere to coordinate this information. I built Tokuchu to explore how WebMCP could connect an event’s attendee information with the requirements of a personalized purchase. What it does Tokuchu is a WebMCP-native application that helps your agent manage event participants and their needs. Its sister website, Customworks, is a Shopify storefront with WebMCP tools for configuring personalized merchandise and preparing a checkout. An organizer can ask ChatGPT’s browser to create an event and add attendees, then browse Customworks for a suitable gift. The store supplies the product’s customization requirements, which the agent brings back to Tokuchu. Tokuchu reconciles those requirements with attendee information and relevant shared event details. It identifies missing answers and validates the resulting values against the store’s constraints. After approval, the agent can prepare one personalized item per complete attendee, leave incomplete attendees pending, and save the checkout in Tokuchu. The organizer completes payment through Shopify. Tokuchu also supports scoped vendor access to fulfillment information, so a vendor can report an issue without receiving unrelated attendee data. How we built it I built Tokuchu with Next.js and TypeScript, with PostgreSQL persistence and deployment on Render. Its event, attendee, and vendor pages expose WebMCP tools appropriate to each page’s role. On Customworks, I added merchant tools to the Shopify storefront. get_customization returns a product’s required fields, constraints, and variants. add_customized_to_cart accepts the configured items and creates a separate personalized cart line for each included attendee. Tokuchu stores the product contract alongside the event’s records. Its validation and reconciliation logic produces a fulfillment manifest, and approvals reference a specific revision of that information. The main website entry uses ChatGPT’s browser. Tokuchu also has an interface that people and browser agents can manipulate, including an in-app chatbox that invokes its managed workflow. The final demo shows an agent entering prompts into that chatbox. A separate local Stagehand runner provides another way to exercise the cross-site WebMCP flow. Challenges we ran into It took time to configure the WebMCP tools and page instructions so ChatGPT could reliably discover and use them. Testing different scenarios also revealed edge cases that the data model did not yet account for, particularly when attendee information was incomplete or needed to be mapped to a product’s requirements. Working through those cases meant checking both what the agent understood and how Tokuchu recorded the resulting information. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of building two live websites that work together to turn attendee information into personalized orders. Setting up Customworks also gave me practical experience with agentic e-commerce, including how product customization connects to Shopify’s cart and checkout. The store is configured to support real orders once test mode is turned off. An agent can prepare much of the personalized order through the browser, with the organizer reviewing the checkout before payment. That brings the project closer to the kind of ordering workflow I would want to use at our own cafe. What we learned I learned how much the initial setup of a website matters for agents. The page metadata and instructions directed toward them need to be clear and available when they first arrive, so they can understand what the site offers and how to navigate it. Making those entry points easy to discover can be just as impactful as refining the individual tools. A useful capability becomes much easier to work with when the agent can find it and understand when to use it. What's next for Tokuchu I’d love to continue experimenting with storefronts that provide useful information for agents to process, and explore how their requirements can inform what an event organizer asks attendees. I’d also like to develop an iteration of Tokuchu that helps us process orders at our own cafe, using what I’ve learned here to reduce the back and forth around bulk orders and customizations. title: EOL Desk
pitch: Upcoming OSS end-of-life dates — one public page for humans and WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt:
Upcoming OSS end-of-life dates — one public page for humans and WebMCP agents.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 EOL Desk is a calendar of upcoming end-of-life and support-cutoff dates for popular open-source libraries and frameworks. Those facts are already structured (name, version line, date, successor, source). A human needs a scannable board; an agent needs typed actions — not a screenshot of a table and not a private MCP server the human cannot see. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The page is the product and the tool host. On load we register list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , and suggest_upgrade_path via document.modelContext.registerTool . ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled discovers the same dataset the UI renders. No login wall, no second API for agents. 

 Better user experience 

 Without WebMCP, a maintainer either hunts vendor blogs and changelogs by hand, or lets an agent scrape HTML and hope the date is still in the DOM. Both drift. EOL Desk is one board for humans and agents: scan upcoming cutoffs, open a row, or call typed tools for JSON. One source of truth. 

 People and agents together 

 Before, asking what dies in 90 days meant the model guessed from training data or scraped pages. Now a person keeps the board honest while ChatGPT or Chrome WebMCP calls list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , and suggest_upgrade_path on the same page. Shared structured facts, no scrape. 

 How we built it 

 Greenfield public page on Cloudflare Pages/Workers. On load we feature-detect document.modelContext (fallback navigator.modelContext ) and register three tools with the Imperative API against the same dataset as the table: list_upcoming_eols , get_eol_detail , suggest_upgrade_path . Tested with the ChatGPT in-app browser and Chrome 149+ chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 

 Judge access: none needed, public page. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 A 48-hour build window. Getting a public GitHub repo up under an existing RonnyKane account. Sorting out the difference between a Devpost portfolio project and actually attaching it to the hackathon. And the fact that WebMCP only works for judges in the ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with the testing flag enabled. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 Shipped a public live URL, an MIT-licensed repo, and a sub-3-minute demo with all three tools registered on the page. 

 What I learned 

 The product is the page as the tool host. Humans and agents need one source of truth, not a scrape. 

 What's next for EOL Desk 

 Keep the calendar current and the tools stable through judging (Sep 4-21).

title: Airlock
pitch: A private, in-browser data workbench: your CSV is parsed, queried and summarised entirely inside the tab; the agent calls WebMCP tools and gets only the answers.
about_excerpt: A private, in-browser data workbench: your CSV is parsed, queried and summarised entirely inside the tab; the agent calls WebMCP tools and gets only the answers. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone repeats the same warning — "don't paste your bank statement into a chatbot" — and yet AI is genuinely good at exactly that kind of analysis. The blocker was never capability; it's that every normal path (upload the file, paste the rows, sync to a server) copies your raw records out of your hands before any analysis happens. WebMCP hinted at a different shape entirely: what if the agent could call tools that run inside the page and receive only the answers? I wanted to find out whether a hosted AI could analyse something as sensitive as a year of personal spending — or a payslip — without ever receiving it. What it does Airlock is a private, in-browser data workbench. You load a CSV with date , description , category and amount columns and it's parsed and analysed entirely inside your browser tab. The page registers seven WebMCP tools — describe_dataset , sum_by_category , filter_rows , monthly_trend , find_anomalies , top_expenses , clear_highlights — and an agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) calls them and gets back only aggregates. Ask "what am I spending most on?" or "is anything unusual?" and it answers with real numbers, while the rows it's reasoning about are highlighted in your own table for you to read. On the bundled synthetic year of spending — 965 transactions across 12 categories — it isolates the four genuinely unusual charges by per-category z-score. Open DevTools during the conversation and the network panel stays empty. How I built it Plain TypeScript and Vite, papaparse for CSV, no backend — a backend would undercut the whole premise. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , each reading from a module-level store so handlers never close over stale state. The load-bearing design decision is privacy mode : it ships on by default, so the row-returning tools answer with counts, totals and category names instead of row contents, describe_dataset even withholds the file name, and only the human can lower the gate — no tool is registered to change it, because a consent gate the agent can open by itself isn't one. It also re-arms to on every time a new file is loaded, so a fresh, more sensitive file never inherits a previous "off." Challenges I ran into The sharpest one was a flaw in my own premise, caught mid-build: "the file stays in the tab" only rules out an upload — anything a tool returns reaches the model anyway. That redesigned the entire project around drawing the privacy boundary at the answer , not the file. Others: proving it to a real external agent rather than self-invocation, which I did by driving the live tools through Chrome's experimental WebMCP CDP domain, the same path a real MCP client takes; a WebMCP quirk where a thrown error reaches the agent as a generic failure, so I return errors as values to keep the recovery hints; and a consent footgun where turning privacy off then loading a new file left it exposed — fixed by the re-arm-on-load behaviour above. What I learned WebMCP's real novelty isn't "tools on a web page" — it's that computation happens where the data lives , which is what makes it possible to keep the raw data and still get the analysis. I also learned that privacy is about control, not lockout : a default-safe, human-controlled, reversible gate is a far better model than all-or-nothing. And that a WebMCP project is only truly proven when an external agent drives it — so the boundary is enforced in the tool layer and unit-tested directly (27 tests), not just asserted in the UI. What's next for Airlock Tightening the consent model further: auto-reverting privacy after a single disclosed answer, scoping disclosure to only the highlighted rows, and a k-anonymity guard on the aggregate tools to close query-composition reconstruction by an adversarial agent. And input breadth — PDF and image ingestion via pdf.js and in-browser WASM OCR, kept strictly client-side so the guarantee that nothing leaves the tab still holds. title: FlightDeck
pitch: A live TestFlight directory built for people and AI agents with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A live TestFlight directory built for people and AI agents with WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Public TestFlight programs are surprisingly difficult to discover. There are many interesting beta apps, but the links are scattered across repositories, forums, social posts, and individual developer pages. For users, finding something relevant often means manually scanning long lists and opening links one by one. At the same time, independent developers need testers, but getting a public TestFlight link in front of the right people is difficult. FlightDeck started from a simple idea: what if a TestFlight directory could work not only for people browsing manually, but also for AI agents helping users discover software? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of forcing an agent to inspect a page, understand its layout, and simulate clicks, the website can expose structured tools that describe exactly what the agent can do. That creates value on both sides: users can ask an AI assistant to find interesting beta apps, while developers gain another discovery channel for their public TestFlight programs. What it does FlightDeck is a live directory of public TestFlight programs across iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, and visionOS. People can use the site normally to: search by app name filter by platform filter by availability see whether a beta is accepting testers, full, closed, or removed open the real TestFlight join link AI agents can access the same catalog through six WebMCP tools: search_testflight_apps get_testflight_app list_testflight_platforms get_catalog_stats filter_visible_catalog prepare_testflight_join This allows an agent to handle requests such as: “Find macOS betas that are accepting testers.” “Show me available visionOS projects.” “Find this app and give me its TestFlight link.” One important part of the project is that the agent and human interfaces are connected. For example, when an agent uses filter_visible_catalog , the page itself updates to show the same filtered results. The user can immediately see what the agent found. FlightDeck currently tracks roughly 1,000 real public TestFlight programs and automatically refreshes its data. How we built it FlightDeck is intentionally lightweight. The frontend is built with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and is hosted on GitHub Pages. The TestFlight catalog is synchronized from the open-source pluwen/awesome-testflight-link dataset. A GitHub Actions workflow periodically downloads the latest data, transforms it into the local catalog format, validates the generated files, and deploys the updated site. WebMCP is implemented using imperative tool registration with: document.modelContext.registerTool() Each tool has a defined input schema, structured output, and explicit validation. The six tools share the same underlying catalog used by the visible interface, so the human-facing website and the agent-facing tools never operate on separate datasets. We also added strict argument validation. Invalid platform names, unsupported availability values, invalid limits, missing IDs, and unexpected fields return structured INVALID_ARGUMENT errors rather than being silently accepted. The WebMCP implementation was tested in Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled and with the WebMCP Model Context Tool Inspector. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was understanding what makes a WebMCP integration genuinely useful rather than simply exposing arbitrary functions. The first version of the project accidentally registered seven tools instead of six. A declarative WebMCP tool was being generated automatically from HTML attributes on the search form in addition to the six imperative tools. That duplicate tool could change the page state, but its WebMCP call did not complete correctly. It was a particularly useful failure because the site appeared to work visually while the agent-facing contract was broken. We removed the declarative duplicate and kept a single, explicit implementation for each capability. Another challenge was validation. Early versions were too permissive. For example, an invalid limit could be silently clamped and an unknown platform could simply return zero results. That is acceptable for some user interfaces, but poor behavior for an agent tool because it hides errors from the caller. We changed the tools to reject invalid arguments explicitly and return structured errors. Keeping UI state and agent state synchronized was another important design problem. We wanted agents to do more than query hidden data. Some actions should also be visible to the person using the page, so tools such as filter_visible_catalog update the actual interface. Accomplishments that we're proud of The most important accomplishment is that FlightDeck is not a mock demo. It operates on real public TestFlight data. The published site currently contains roughly 1,000 beta programs and automatically refreshes from the upstream source. We are also proud that the site remains fully useful without AI. WebMCP is an additional capability rather than a requirement. A person can visit FlightDeck and use it like a normal website, while an agent can interact with the same application through structured tools. The final implementation exposes exactly six WebMCP tools, with no duplicate declarative tools and no console errors. We also built automated tests that verify tool registration, schemas, argument validation, error handling, and protection against unintended UI mutations on invalid requests. The full project is open source, automatically deployed, and accessible through a public live URL. What we learned The biggest lesson was that making a website agent-friendly is not the same thing as giving an agent access to the DOM. A good agent interface needs clear capabilities, predictable contracts, explicit validation, and structured results. WebMCP also changes how we think about website UX. Traditionally, the website is the interface. With WebMCP, the website can have two interfaces at the same time: one designed for people and another designed for agents. They do not have to be independent. In FlightDeck, the most interesting interactions happen when both interfaces cooperate. We also learned that strict validation matters much more for agent-facing tools than it may initially appear. Silent normalization can make an agent believe a request succeeded when it actually changed meaning. Finally, we learned that relatively simple web applications can become significantly more useful to AI systems without requiring a backend, an external API, or a large framework. What's next for FlightDeck The next step is improving discovery beyond exact app-name search. We want agents to be able to help users find projects based on intent, such as: “Find experimental productivity apps.” “Show me unusual macOS utilities.” “Find new visionOS projects worth testing.” That will require richer metadata such as categories, developer information, descriptions, and potentially App Store metadata where available. Another direction is better support for developers who are looking for testers. FlightDeck could provide a simple submission workflow for developers to add or update their public beta programs. We also want to improve catalog freshness and make availability changes easier to detect. Longer term, FlightDeck could become a two-sided discovery layer between people looking for interesting experimental software and developers looking for engaged testers, with AI agents acting as the bridge between them. title: Roomwright
pitch: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A browser room planner an AI furnishes from your words, placing, checking, and fixing the layout through the page's WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In September 2024 I moved to a new country, into an empty apartment I'd only seen in photos. A year later, almost to the week, I moved again. Different place, same problem. Both times it went like this: you stand in the middle of a bare room with a phone full of furniture tabs and no real sense of scale, you order things that don't quite fit, and you spend evenings pushing an imaginary couch around in your head. It isn't just me. Every fall a wave of people do exactly this: new students, new arrivals, first apartments, furnishing a room they can only picture in fragments. What you want in that moment is simple: what do I need, how would it look, what will it cost, and once it's all in, is there any floor left to stand on? That's a planning problem, and planning is exactly what an agent should be good at. But a chatbot can only describe your room back to you. It can't move anything in it. WebMCP changes that: a page can hand its own capabilities to an agent as tools. So I built the page worth handing over. What it does Roomwright is a 3D room planner that runs entirely in the browser. You draw a room, set the doors and windows, and place furniture from a catalogue of parametric pieces. Every item has real dimensions and required clearances. Orbit it, drop to a floor plan, resize or recolor anything, and it keeps a running shopping list with a total. Every one of those actions is exposed to an agent as a WebMCP tool . There are 19 of them. So instead of clicking, you can say: "Studio apartment, 4.6 by 7 metres, door on the south wall, two windows on the east. Bed against the back wall, a sofa splitting off the living area, a small dining set by the window." The agent reads the tools the page offers and builds the whole thing: resizing the room, cutting the openings, furnishing three zones, running the planner's own clearance checks, catching its own overlaps, and fixing them. Then you take over: "turn the sofa toward the TV, lose that chair." Same room, same undo history, you and the agent trading turns on one canvas. How WebMCP powers it The key decision: the UI and the agent mutate the exact same state. There's a single store, and a button click and a tool call go through the same action. So undo/redo, autosave, shareable-URL persistence, and live layout validation all just work for the agent. There is no agent-specific code path for any of them. Tools register against document.modelContext using the spec's AbortSignal lifecycle, in four groups: Read : get_room , list_catalog , get_shopping_list Build : add_item (resolves a product by id, name, or fragment, so the agent never has to guess), create_custom_item , duplicate_item (with an east-west / north-south mirror so "a chair on each side" is actually symmetric), remove_item Arrange and check : move_item , rotate_item , resize_item , set_variant , set_room_dimensions , set_opening , remove_opening , suggest_spot (grids the room and returns candidate positions), check_layout (overlaps, blocked doors/windows, clearance failures, walkways under 0.75 m, narrowest gap) Show : select_item (highlights a piece, opens its inspector), set_view , reset_layout suggest_spot and check_layout matter most. They give the agent a feedback loop, not just setters. It places, checks, notices a conflict, and re-plans, visibly, in the activity log. How I built it React 19 + TypeScript + Vite React Three Fiber + drei + @react-three/postprocessing for synthetic image-based lighting (no HDRI file), real shadow-mapped shadows, screen-space AO, and a restrained post pass Parametric furniture : every piece is authored geometry keyed on its kind, not a glTF download, so the bundle stays small and every dimension is real Zustand for the single shared store, Tailwind CSS v4 for the UI Device-aware quality tiers (High / Medium / Low, auto-detected from the GPU string and core count, with a live framerate monitor that steps down) so it runs on a laptop, not just a workstation Deployed on GitHub Pages Challenges The spec is still moving. Early references used navigator.modelContext ; the current spec uses document.modelContext and has no unregisterTool . You unregister by aborting an AbortSignal . I probe both and use the signal lifecycle, with a short retry in case the host injects the API after first paint. Shared post-processing broke drei's ContactShadows. EffectComposer sets gl.autoClear = false , and ContactShadows relies on autoClear to wipe its render target, so moving a piece smeared shadow trails across the floor. Fixed by dropping ContactShadows for a directional shadow map plus per-frame screen-space AO. The agent kept guessing product ids. It saw sofa-halden and tried coffee-milo (the real id is table-milo ). Fuzzy resolution plus returning the full catalogue on a miss fixed it in one step. Symmetry. duplicate_item offset copies by a fixed diagonal, so "a lounge chair on each side" never mirrored. Added a real mirror across the room's centre line, and floor lamps now auto-aim at the room centre so a mirrored pair points the right way. Testing WebMCP is hard today. Only ChatGPT's desktop in-app browser exposes document.modelContext (plus Chrome 149 behind a flag), and it's gated by account type. What I learned The leverage in WebMCP isn't the tool calls. It's the shared state . The moment the agent and the human mutate the same model, everything the app already does (undo, validation, persistence) becomes something the agent does too, for free. Design the state model well and the agent integration is almost nothing. And tool descriptions are the API. Fuzzy product resolution, mirror options, and full-catalogue errors did more for reliability than any prompting. The agent behaves well when the tools let it. What's next Real glTF furniture and user uploads, photo-assisted room capture, L-shaped and multi-room layouts, a path-traced render mode. And a retailer-facing version: drop these tools onto product pages, and every shopping agent can lay out a real room instead of guessing. title: Chalkboard
pitch: Teach students with your agents on Chalkboard: a collaborative infinite canvas where 23 WebMCP tools let your AI co-teacher draw, write, highlight and react live as you teach together.
about_excerpt:
Teach students with your agents on Chalkboard: a collaborative infinite canvas where 23 WebMCP tools let your AI co-teacher draw, write, highlight and react live as you teach together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 A real classroom isn't a lecture; a board everyone can point at. 

 Online, that feeling disappears. A teacher talks, students watch. The board is gone. 

 We built Chalkboard to bring it back: a shared infinite canvas where a teacher and students draw, write and react together, live. 

 Then we wondered, what if a third participant could join? Not a chatbot on the side, but a classmate who can use the board. 

 Teach students with your agents. 

 What It Does 

 Create a room, share the link, and everyone sees the same chalkboard. When someone draws a line, it appears for everyone. When someone sends a ❤️, it floats across the screen. 

 Now invite your agent. 

 Say: “Teach the Pythagorean theorem.” 

 Your agent doesn't just reply in text. It opens the same room as you, picks up the chalk, writes $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, draws the triangle, labels the sides, and highlights the proof stroke by stroke, while students watch. 

 It’s not controlling a copy of the classroom. It’s in the classroom. 

 Why WebMCP 

 We could have built a separate API for every agent action one for drawing, one for writing, one for reacting. Instead we let the website speak for itself. 

 With WebMCP , Chalkboard simply says: here are the things I can do: draw, write, highlight, react, raise a hand, manage the room. 

 The browser exposes those capabilities at navigator.modelContext . The agent discovers them and calls them like any other tool. No custom wiring, no shadow app. 
 Your Agent → WebMCP → Chalkboard → Everyone's Board
 
 The agent doesn't need to know how our canvas works. It just knows what the classroom allows. 

 How We Built It 

 Chalkboard is a web app: a canvas for drawing, Socket.IO for real-time sync, and LiveKit for voice. 

 We wrapped every classroom action — drawing a stroke, writing text, sending a reaction as a simple tool. The browser gathers those tools and offers them through WebMCP, the new web standard for agents. 

 When an agent joins a room, it joins like any student over a websocket. It listens to the room, remembers what's on the board, and when asked to teach, it chooses tools and emits the same events your browser does. A reaction tool even opens the emoji picker and picks one, so you see the interaction, not just the result. 

 If a viewer asks the agent to do something only an editor can do, the agent politely refuses it borrows your permissions, not its own. 

 What We Learned 

 The moment an agent can act instead of just answer , everything changes. A lesson feels real when you watch it being made. 

 We also learned that the web doesn't need a separate world for AI. If a site can tell an agent what it can do, the site itself becomes the interface. 

 Challenges 

 Making a remote agent feel present was hard. It had to join the same room, see the same board, and act through the same browser tools, without lag, without breaking the live sync, and without giving it more power than the student who invited it. 

 Getting browsers, real-time sync and WebMCP to agree was the puzzle. Solving it meant the agent is no longer outside the classroom looking in. It's sitting at the desk next to you. 

 What's Next 

 We started with drawing. Next is understanding an agent that watches the board, notices a mistake, circles it, and offers a hint. A classroom that is collaborative and agent-accessible by default. 

 Chalkboard is our small experiment in that future: where you don't build a separate app for your agent — you just bring it to class.

pitch: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw.
about_excerpt: A trip finder with real, slow fare searches and a Cancel button that actually cancels - timers clear, nothing lands after, and the agent knows exactly what it never saw. Like Comment Story Updates The trip finder: destinations, budget, and dates Tool console: get_brief tool called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: long-running tools accept execute(args, {signal}) and are genuinely abortable - a cancelled search stops mid-flight, not just in the UI. Inspiration "Somewhere warm under ₹40,000 for four days from Bengaluru" is a complete brief to a friend and an impossible query to a travel site, which wants a destination first, then makes you wait through a slow search per place - with no way to say "that's enough, I've seen what I need." What it does Jhola exposes catalogue, fare search, stay availability, and hold as tools. The agent runs one slow search across twelve destinations while results land one card at a time; the moment the traveller has seen enough, they press Cancel and the search stops honestly - timers cleared, nothing lands afterward, the agent told exactly what was found and what was never searched. A cancelled search returns a first-class partial report, never an error. Booking is irreversible, so there's no book tool at all - Book is a human-only button; holding is reversible, so hold_itinerary is a tool. How we built it execute(args, { signal }) , honoured all the way through: search_fares and check_stays advance through staged timers that obey the AbortSignal Chrome hands every tool call. One AbortController per call, shared by all four ways a call can end - the in-flight strip's own Cancel, the tool console's Cancel, the cancel_call tool, or the caller's own signal - and the activity log always says which one fired. Challenges we ran into Building runtime fallbacks for when Chrome's real cancellation bridge has gaps: if a Cancel click doesn't visibly end the in-flight record within 250ms, the console aborts the call directly and says so; if executeTool() 's own promise doesn't resolve with the string the call actually produced, the console reads it off the call's own record instead - both proven against a simulated broken bridge, not just the happy path. And, like its sibling apps, a self-abort race in hold_itinerary 's dynamic registration, found and fixed with the same deferred-abort pattern. Accomplishments that we're proud of A cancel that is actually honest - a stopped search names exactly what it never searched, instead of pretending it finished or silently discarding the question. What we learned Real cancellation UX needs a fallback story, not just a happy-path signal - a judge's browser, a flaky bridge, or a headless test environment can all diverge from the ideal case, and the app has to stay honest in every one.
