title: ExceptionOSMCP
pitch: The agent-operable command center for resolving business exceptions safely.
about_excerpt: The agent-operable command center for resolving business exceptions safely. Like Comment Story Updates ExceptionOS Inspiration Operational teams spend hours resolving supplier delays and other business exceptions by moving between dashboards, spreadsheets, policies, and approval systems. AI agents can help, but traditional websites only expose interfaces designed for humans. Agents must interpret visual elements, guess which buttons to press, and operate without clear authority boundaries. We built ExceptionOS to explore a different model: operational software that exposes structured capabilities directly to agents while keeping humans in control of material decisions. What it does ExceptionOS is an agent-operable operations command center centered on a realistic supplier disruption. Pacific Components has reported that a battery-module purchase order will arrive nine days late. The disruption threatens a production order, a customer delivery, and $84,000 in revenue. Through WebMCP, an agent can: Retrieve the structured exception. Trace affected production and customer orders. Read its spending and approval policy. Search for qualified alternative suppliers. Compare recovery strategies. Simulate a resolution without changing business records. Request human approval when the plan exceeds its authority. Execute the approved supplier change. Verify that the customer commitment is protected. Produce an auditable evidence ledger. The recommended recovery plan changes the supplier to Northstar Cells for an additional $3,400, protecting the delivery date and $84,000 in revenue. Because the agent’s autonomous spending limit is $2,000, ExceptionOS blocks execution until a human explicitly approves the plan. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP ExceptionOS is not a conventional dashboard with an AI chatbot added to it. WebMCP is the application’s structured agent interface. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to interpret cards, tables, buttons, and changing application state visually. With WebMCP, it receives purpose-built tools with typed inputs, structured results, safety annotations, and clearly defined authority boundaries. The experience demonstrates a complete operational workflow: Observe → Investigate → Compare → Simulate → Ask → Act → Verify WebMCP makes the workflow faster and more reliable while letting the application control what the agent can read, simulate, and change. How it improves the user experience Humans no longer have to manually collect information from multiple screens, calculate the consequences of each option, or reconstruct what an agent did. The agent handles structured investigation and comparison. The human concentrates on the decision that requires judgment and authority. ExceptionOS also keeps the user informed through a live agent-activity panel. Every tool invocation visibly updates the interface, making the agent’s work understandable rather than invisible. After execution, the evidence ledger records the complete human-agent decision trail for accountability and review. What humans and agents can do together Before WebMCP, operational applications were largely human-operated, while agents had to approximate human interaction through screenshots and browser automation. ExceptionOS enables a safer partnership: The agent investigates structured operational data. The agent compares and simulates recovery plans. The application enforces organizational policy. The human approves consequential actions. The agent executes only within that approval. The system independently verifies the outcome. Both parties receive an auditable evidence trail. This combines machine speed with human authority. How we implemented WebMCP The browser application registers ten tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_exception get_impacted_orders get_policy search_alternative_suppliers compare_recovery_options simulate_resolution request_approval execute_resolution verify_resolution get_evidence_ledger These tools invoke the same stateful application logic used by the visible interface. Agent activity therefore changes the application in real time. ExceptionOS also exposes the same capabilities through a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint at /mcp. It supports initialization, tool discovery, tool calls, structured results, and safety annotations. Read and simulation operations are marked read-only. execute_resolution is marked destructive and requires explicit human confirmation plus an approver name. Calls without approval are rejected. How we built it Suggested “Built With” tags: WebMCP Model Context Protocol TypeScript React Next.js JSON-RPC Streamable HTTP ChatGPT GitHub Challenges we ran into The central challenge was designing tools that represented operational capabilities rather than simply exposing UI controls. We separated the workflow into read, plan, act, and verify capabilities. We also needed to ensure the agent could investigate and simulate freely without gaining unrestricted execution authority. The approval boundary became a core part of the architecture: requesting approval does not grant approval, and execution is rejected unless explicit human authorization is supplied. Another challenge was making agent activity visible enough for users to understand. We addressed this with synchronized interface state, a live tool-call feed, execution status, and an evidence ledger. Accomplishments that we're proud of Implemented ten meaningful WebMCP tools. Created a complete, stateful agent workflow rather than isolated tool demonstrations. Added a genuine human approval boundary. Blocked unapproved destructive operations. Made every agent action visible in the user interface. Added post-execution verification and an auditable evidence ledger. Exposed the capabilities through both browser WebMCP and remote MCP. Produced a polished, deterministic scenario that judges can understand quickly. What we learned Agent-native websites require more than tool discovery. They require carefully designed authority, observability, verification, and evidence. We also learned that the best division of responsibility is not to make agents omnipotent. Agents are strongest at structured investigation and comparison, while humans should retain control over consequential decisions. WebMCP provides the bridge between those roles. What's next for ExceptionOSMCP ExceptionOS could expand to additional operational exceptions, including inventory shortages, logistics disruptions, quality incidents, invoice discrepancies, and customer-delivery risks. Future versions could connect to real ERP, procurement, logistics, and policy systems. The same authority model could support role-based approval limits, multi-stage approvals, organization-specific policies, and cryptographically signed evidence records. The broader vision is an agent-operable layer for enterprise software in which every action is structured, policy-aware, observable, and verifiable. title: Blast Radius

about_excerpt:
See the full blast radius — and let your AI agent see it with you, live.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Supply-chain compromises like the 2018 event-stream incident don't just hit one package — they reach thousands of services through dependencies nobody on the team has ever read. Security review of this kind is exactly the task an AI agent should help with: precise, structured, and fast. But almost every "AI + your app" integration today means the agent works blind, guessing through a UI, while the human has no idea what it's doing until it's done. WebMCP flips that: the agent calls exact tools you define, and — if you build it right — the human can watch it happen. We wanted to see what supply-chain security review looks like when a human and an agent are looking at the exact same screen at the exact same time. 

 What it does 

 BlastRadius is a real-time supply-chain blast-radius visualizer with two tools exposed via WebMCP. An agent can call trace_blast_radius on any package name, and instead of the result disappearing into a JSON blob only the agent sees, the dashboard's graph, stats, and attack-path breadcrumb update live in front of the human watching. An agent can also call flag_dependency_for_review to flag a suspicious package with a reason and severity — which surfaces instantly as a card in a "Flagged for Review" panel on the human's screen, ready for their judgment call. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is React with a dark, terminal-style dashboard: a search bar, a stats row (packages affected, services exposed, persistence multiplier, maintainer risk), a force-directed dependency graph, and the flagged-review panel. The WebMCP layer is two tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() at the app's entry point. Neither tool just returns data — each dispatches a browser CustomEvent that the dashboard listens for and reacts to visibly, which is the core design decision: agent action becomes human-visible UI change, not a silent side channel. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 We started by wrapping an already-built dashboard's live Express/HydraDB backend with WebMCP tools — a stronger, more "production" story on paper. Under real deadline pressure, that backend deployment broke (missing environment configuration on a fresh Vercel project), and debugging it live was eating the little time we had left. Rather than gamble the whole submission on fixing infrastructure blind, we rebuilt the core experience as a fully self-contained client-side app with realistic mock data — same UI, same WebMCP tools, same live-update behavior, zero external dependencies to fail at the worst possible time. That decision is the actual story of this build: knowing when to cut a dependency rather than lose the demo entirely. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the live-update pattern actually working — an agent calling a tool and a human watching the dashboard change in real time, not a delay, not a refresh — on a tight clock. And recognizing under pressure that a working, honest, self-contained demo beats a broken "more impressive" one; that's a real engineering call, not just a technical one. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest one: agent-native features live or die on what the human sees, not what the agent gets back. A tool that returns clean JSON but changes nothing on screen is invisible collaboration — which isn't collaboration at all. We also relearned, the hard way, that infrastructure dependencies (env vars, database connections, multi-service deploys) are the first thing to break under time pressure, and that having a fallback path matters as much as the primary build. 

 What's next for BlastRadius 

 Reconnecting the WebMCP layer to the real HydraDB-backed backend now that the deploy issue is understood, so the tools operate on live 10k-package data instead of mock data. Beyond that: more collaborative tools where the agent doesn't just report findings but proposes actions (e.g., "pin this dependency," "open a rollback PR") that the human approves directly from the flagged-review panel — moving from "agent reports, human decides" toward a true shared workspace.

title: GridTwin
pitch: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where AI explores deterministic energy scenarios while humans retain final authority. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Planning context — synthetic baseline, approved criteria, and seven WebMCP tools ready. Visible exploration — genuine tool calls create and compare three deterministic scenarios. Outage proof — grid at 0 kW while the battery serves all eight critical hours. Human authority — the agent shortlists; only the planner approves. Decision brief — the approved plan becomes a transparent, print-ready recommendation. GridTwin One-line Summary GridTwin is a WebMCP civic microgrid sandbox where an AI agent visibly explores deterministic energy scenarios while the human retains authority over constraints, final plan selection, and export. Problem Climate and resilience officers at small councils and housing associations often need to choose one indicative solar-and-battery configuration before they can pursue a grant or commission a professional feasibility study. The decision spans budget, emissions, and outage resilience, but existing energy tools are usually designed for specialists and generic AI interfaces can hide what an agent changed or why it recommended an option. That is a poor fit for a consequential early-stage decision. A useful agent must make the decision space easier to navigate without obscuring assumptions, silently relaxing constraints, or taking final authority from the person accountable for the outcome. Solution GridTwin turns the fictional Riverside Estate into a shared, visible planning workspace. The human approves a £400,000 capital budget, a 40% emissions-reduction target, eight hours of critical-load coverage, and a resilience-first priority order. A real browser agent then uses seven page-defined WebMCP tools to read the baseline, run bounded solar-and-battery scenarios, compare transparent metrics, diagnose infeasibility, and shortlist a feasible candidate. Every scenario uses the same deterministic hourly dispatch model. Every tool action appears in the activity rail and visibly changes scenario cards, comparisons, or report state. Infeasible candidates show every violation in natural units. Agent advice remains reversible. Only the human can approve criteria, select the final plan, or open the browser print flow. The signature result is the fixed 18:00–02:00 outage: grid contribution falls to zero, the balanced 275 kWp solar / 500 kWh battery plan supplies critical load for all eight hours, and the final action belongs to the human approving the plan. Why This Matters GridTwin demonstrates a WebMCP pattern for consequential human-agent work—not just an energy calculator. Before WebMCP, a generic assistant could describe possible configurations, but it could not reliably operate the same visible, structured planning state as the human or leave an auditable trail of each action. With WebMCP, the agent can navigate a non-trivial decision space through narrow tools while the application remains the source of truth for calculations, feasibility, lifecycle state, and authority. The result is a better user experience because the human sees the work happen, can inspect assumptions and violations at the point of use, and retains explicit control over every consequential transition. The civic-energy example makes that collaboration concrete: abstract capacities become continued critical services during an outage. GridTwin does not claim to produce an engineering design. It helps a real target user make a transparent decision about what deserves professional evaluation next. How We Used AI GridTwin contains no embedded chatbot and calls no model API. AI enters through an external agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser, which discovers and invokes the page-defined WebMCP tools. The agent can: read the synthetic Riverside Estate baseline and fixed assumptions; stage constraint suggestions for human review without applying them; choose bounded solar and battery inputs and run real deterministic scenarios; compare two or three current scenarios without an opaque score; diagnose the nearest candidate when every option is infeasible; create a reversible shortlist for a feasible plan; and prepare an immutable decision-brief preview after human approval. The agent cannot approve constraints, approve or reconsider a plan, reset the comparison, print, download, or publish. Those actions have no WebMCP schema. After human approval, advisory mutations are frozen until the human explicitly reconsiders the decision. All authoritative metrics come from GridTwin's pure client-side model, not from model-generated arithmetic. WebMCP makes the agent's structured actions visible, testable, and subordinate to the application's lifecycle rules. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary development agent across the 30-hour solo build. It helped turn the initial idea into the scope, PRD, technical specification, and sequenced checklist; implemented the deterministic dispatch engine, reserve policy, lifecycle reducer, persistence, WebMCP adapter, civic interface, outage visual, and A4 report; added regression and browser tests; diagnosed integration failures; rehearsed the real in-app-browser workflow; deployed to Vercel; and prepared the handoff documentation. The builder actively directed the work rather than accepting a generated solution wholesale. Three mandatory review pauses produced concrete corrections, including refresh-safe activity identity, stricter restored-state validation, full post-approval agent freeze, HTTPS in-app-browser verification, and a settled chart capture. The builder also rejected an embedded-chat fallback, an opaque composite score, hidden constraint relaxation, and dramatic but dishonest tariff assumptions. That collaboration mirrors GridTwin itself: Codex explored and implemented within an explicit plan, while the human reviewed the consequential product, authority, credibility, and scope decisions. Key Features Exactly seven direct WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . One shared deterministic engine for every bounded solar/battery combination—no optimizer, randomness, precomputed scenario cards, or special-case balanced branch. Visible tool activity, a fixed 600 ms abortable pending interval, atomic scenario commits, and safe interruption handling. Versioned human-approved constraints with current/stale scenario lineage. Direct cost, emissions, reserve, resilience, feasibility, and natural-unit violation metrics with no composite score. Transparent all-infeasible diagnosis and staged—but never automatic—constraint suggestions. Distinct reversible agent shortlist and direct human-approved selection. Signature 18:00–02:00 outage view with grid at 0 kW and eight uninterrupted critical hours for the balanced plan. Immutable A4 decision-brief snapshot and human-controlled Print → Save as PDF flow. Session refresh recovery that restores committed work but never converts partial operations into completed results. Persistent synthetic-data, model-version, constraint-version, and indicative-planning caveats. Architecture GridTwin is a static React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed on Vercel. Human UI or WebMCP callback ↓ shared validated command boundary ↓ pure deterministic domain calculation ↓ complete atomic reducer transition ↓ session snapshot and visible workspace/report src/domain/ : fixed synthetic inputs, validation, hourly dispatch, convergence, annualization, outage stress test, feasibility, and non-composite nearest ordering. It imports no React or browser code. src/state/ : context/reducer, versioned lifecycle, authority gates, interruption recovery, and sessionStorage compatibility. src/webmcp/ : seven JSON schemas, direct imperative registration, all-or-nothing discovery, cleanup, cancellation, readiness, and stable result envelopes. src/components/ : purpose-built civic planning interface, Recharts analysis, and a small fixed-node energy-flow SVG. Report path: an immutable snapshot of matching approved state; no recalculation, automatic download, or publication. The annual operating estimate and outage stress test share one dispatch function but remain separate calculation paths. Battery state converges across repeated representative days, a noon-to-outage reserve policy applies consistently, and the outage test clones the actual prepared 18:00 state. pitch: The web adapts. You don’t have to. With WebMCP, your agent and participating websites plan an evening around your access needs.
about_excerpt: The web adapts. You don’t have to. With WebMCP, your agent and participating websites plan an evening around your access needs. Like Comment Story Updates A calm cinema view. Two seats together, with Alex at the aisle. The person can change and confirm the choice. Dinner before the film: three pictured dishes, including a favorite. Ingredient exclusions and kitchen questions stay visible. Inspiration “Plan a movie night for us next week. Dinner first would be lovely.” It is a small request, but the websites involved can ask a lot of someone: bright screens, moving content, crowded controls, a seat map to navigate and a menu to check. Having to explain your access needs again at each step adds more work. I wanted to show a different kind of assistance. An agent should be able to use preferences you have chosen to share, make the page easier for you to use and stay alongside you when you make a decision. What it does The demo follows Alex and Lea, a fictional couple with shared example preferences. Alex has a migraine today and wants his familiar calm view. He prefers an aisle seat beside Lea. She has explicitly shared peanut and avocado allergies. The cinema switches to dark, low-glare, still visuals. The agent finds a 20:15 showing next Friday and two seats with Alex at the aisle. Alex asks to move one row back; the pair moves together, keeping that arrangement. He reviews and confirms the demo tickets himself. Dinner comes next. An 18:00 table leaves time for a 90-minute meal, a short walk and arrival before the film. Three pictured dishes replace a long list, including Alex’s favorite mushroom risotto. Ingredient exclusions remain visible, and uncertain kitchen information stays a question. Alex can inspect the full menu, change the proposal and confirm the table. Why WebMCP Personal context becomes useful when an agent can act on the page. WebMCP exposes what each site supports: display changes, rendered measurements, available seats, dinner calculations and menu information. The agent can also ask the restaurant to show a smaller selection in its own interface. Each site owns its design and booking rules. The agent makes supported requests; the person sees the result. A display receipt carries only functional preferences between the venues. Names, diagnoses, allergies and booking details are kept out of that receipt. Final booking confirmation stays with the person. How I built it React, TypeScript and Vite power two participating venues. Their tools use document.modelContext.registerTool , with validated inputs and shared handlers for the visible interface and agent calls. The hosted version has separate cinema and restaurant pages on one HTTPS origin. The home experience is a labelled preset walkthrough. A real external agent can read the supplied example context and call the native tools directly. Both paths have been tested on the deployed site; the repository includes reproducible inputs and results. What I learned The most useful moment is a small correction: “one row further back.” Assistance should preserve what matters while making that change easy. I also learned to separate a supported preference from a promise: calm visuals are not a treatment, and matching recipe ingredients is not an allergy-safety guarantee. This is a working prototype for participating sites, with synthetic bookings and no production memory service. Validation with disabled participants is still ahead. The next step is learning which adaptations help people complete their own tasks. Built during the challenge The adaptive contract, participating websites, native tools, tests and demo were built during the submission period. The repository began on September 1, 2026. Existing building blocks include React, TypeScript, Vite, Fontsource, Vitest, Playwright and axe-core. Code and generated demo artwork are MIT licensed; fonts retain their own license notices. title: La Bàn - Career Guidance for Vietnamese AI Transition webmcp
pitch: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library...
about_excerpt: La Bàn turns a career-guidance website into an in-browser MCP server: the AI agent a Vietnamese worker already trusts reads our verified occupation database and research library... Like 1 Comment Story Updates A screen demo of chatGpt in-app Note: the app is hosted on Render's free tier, so the server spins down after 15 minutes of inactivity - the first request may take up to a minute while it wakes up. Once warm, everything responds quickly. Inspiration The ILO estimates generative AI could impact more than 20% of jobs in Vietnam — and nearly 80 million workers across ASEAN are in occupations likely to be affected. Millions of them are asking the same question: "Will AI take my job - and what should I learn?" The answers they get online are generic, and when LLMs write them, the citations are sometimes fabricated. We measured it: across 12 Vietnamese worker personas, a single-prompt baseline produced 2 fabricated citations out of 26 - fluent, confident, and unverifiable. For decisions this life-altering, that's disqualifying. La Bàn (Vietnamese for The Compass ) already existed as a career-guidance platform with a curated Vietnam occupation database and research library. The WebMCP Challenge gave us the missing piece: instead of being a destination the worker visits once, the site could become the evidence engine behind every agent conversation about their career. Existing tools are either static career sites (no agent) or chatbots (no verifiable data, no persistence, no human gate) — La Bàn brings the three together: the page supplies the evidence, the agent reasons over it, and the human holds the pen. What it does La Bàn is an in-browser MCP server . Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser (or Chrome with the WebMCP flag) and your agent immediately gets 12 tools in three layers: Evidence (client-side, works with zero API keys): lookup_occupation reads a curated Vietnam resilience database with MOLISA/O*NET codes and task-level automation exposure; search_research returns verifiable sources from WEF, ILO, the World Bank and more. Analysis : analyze_career_transition runs a verified multi-agent pipeline (Profiler → Evidence Gatherer → Analyst → Verifier) where only what the tools return can be cited , and every citation is checked against the corpus. Workspace (writes): save_career_plan , add_milestone , update_milestone_progress , share_plan_to_community - every single write opens an approval modal inside the page . A rejection means the agent asks what to change; it never retries blindly. The human and the agent share one page. What used to be tab-switching between a chatbot and a static website — with nothing saved or tracked — becomes a single conversation: the agent looks up the occupation, pulls the research, scores the risk, and drafts an editable 90-day plan; the human edits it in a modal before it's saved, both track progress across sessions, and an Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real time. Writes never happen without explicit human approval. How we built it Progressive enhancement : tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema inputs and readOnlyHint annotations. In a normal browser the app runs unchanged; in an agent's browser it becomes a workspace. The honesty layer : when an occupation isn't in the database (a watch repairer, for example), lookup_occupation says so - and the agent falls back to research evidence instead of inventing a resilience score. Verification-first pipeline : the Verifier checks schema, guardrails and every citation; on failure, the analyst repairs its own output. Ablation showed the interesting part: tools alone changed nothing on grounding - the verifier loop is what eliminated fabrication (91.7% → 100% grounding, 2 → 0 hallucinated citations, 12/12 valid schemas). Stack : React 19 + Express + Gemini (multi-agent pipeline), localStorage workspace persistence, deployed on Render's free tier. 119 unit tests cover the agents, verification and every WebMCP handler. Challenges we ran into requestUserInteraction is not universally supported. During rehearsal on the real ChatGPT in-app browser, the Codex WebMCP shim exposed the API but threw on every call, breaking all workspace writes. The fix: treat the wrapper as best-effort with a try/catch fallback to the in-page modal - the human gate stays intact in every runtime. Free-tier reality. Our analysis endpoint was "timing out" in ChatGPT - but measured directly it returns a full verified result in ~16 seconds warm. The real culprit was Render's spin-down after 15 idle minutes. Cold start, not code. Teaching an agent to say "I don't know." The database covers 10 occupations. Designing tools whose no-match response is genuinely useful - and watching ChatGPT relay that honesty instead of hallucinating - was the most satisfying moment of the project. Accomplishments & what we learned A baseline with measurable fabrication became a demo where the agent refuses to invent data in front of a live audience. Writing WebMCP tools is really API design for a new kind of user - the tool descriptions we wrote read like prompts, and the agent followed them ("call this FIRST", "cite these instead of guessing"). Retrieval alone doesn't stop fabrication. Verification that can send work back does. Try it: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask "I'm an accountant in Hanoi, will AI replace me?" - then say "Save me a 90-day plan to become a data analyst" and approve it in the page. title: Studymesh
pitch: A study board where you and an AI agent work together — add tasks, set alarms, build quizzes, and track progress, all through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A study board where you and an AI agent work together — add tasks, set alarms, build quizzes, and track progress, all through WebMCP.

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story

 Dashboard — streak, XP, and agent activity, shared live between user and the AI. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Focus timer — start it yourself, or ask the agent to start one for you. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live progress charts — task completion and subject breakdown, updated in real time. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Alarms — set by user or by the agent in plain English, with a real popup and sound. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Dashboard — streak, XP, and agent activity, shared live between user and the AI. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Focus timer — start it yourself, or ask the agent to start one for you. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Live progress charts — task completion and subject breakdown, updated in real time. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Alarms — set by user or by the agent in plain English, with a real popup and sound. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Dashboard — streak, XP, and agent activity, shared live between user and the AI. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI study tools are just a chatbot bolted onto the side of an app — the agent talks, but you still do all the clicking. WebMCP made a different kind of tool possible: one where an agent doesn't just describe what to do, it actually does it, on the same board a student is already looking at. StudyMesh grew from that idea — a study workspace where a human and an AI agent share one board and are equally capable of acting on it. 

 What it does 

 StudyMesh is a study workspace with a task board, alarms, flashcards, a quiz zone, a focus timer, and a live progress dashboard. Every one of those actions — adding a task, setting an alarm, building a quiz, starting a focus session — can be done by clicking in the UI, or by asking an AI agent in plain English. Both paths hit the exact same backend logic, so there's one shared source of truth no matter who acts on it. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — WebMCP tools have to run client-side since document.modelContext is a browser API. Seven tools are registered on document.modelContext in mcp.js : add_study_task, reschedule_tasks, set_alarm, generate_flashcards, generate_quiz, start_focus_session, and track_progress. Each tool's execute function calls the same REST endpoints the human-facing UI calls, backed by a Python FastAPI server that holds the shared state. Quiz and flashcard content comes from a curated knowledge base of real facts for common syllabus topics (Physics, Chemistry, Biology, History, CS, Math), not generic filler text. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making sure an agent action and a human click were truly indistinguishable in effect took some care — every WebMCP tool had to route through the same backend function as its UI counterpart, with no separate "shortcut" path for agents. Getting alarms to fire reliably (with a browser notification, an in-app popup, and a sound) without a native OS scheduler was another one — solved by computing the trigger time server-side and having the client poll and confirm the fire exactly once. 

 What we learned 

 Building this made it clear that the real value of WebMCP isn't a chatbot with extra steps — it's giving an agent the same tools a human already has, on the same page, so the two can genuinely hand off work to each other mid-task without anything breaking. 

 What's next for StudyMesh 

 Persisting state in a real database instead of in-memory, expanding the curated content library to more subjects, and adding collaborative study boards where multiple students and their agents share one workspace.

title: RiffSmith
pitch: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Write riffs with an agent: the whole editor is 15 WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Tools: the 15 tools with their real descriptions, styled like the app. Import modal: a messy hand-written tab pasted in, with the section headers, chug runs, 5h7, dead notes and slides. Mountain King in E standard mid-playback with the rig open, model showing RiffSmith Distorted. Imported result: that tab as a song with sections, repeat marks, a 3/4 bar, and the amp selected. Showcase: the Guitar Showcase's 16th-note riff section with the playhead on it. Inspiration I play guitar in a metal band, and like every guitarist I have a folder of half-finished riffs living in text files. Tab editors make those playable, but writing metal in one is slow, mechanical work: sixteenth-note chug runs, odd meters, repeats, and sections you have to loop a dozen times to know if they're any good. That's exactly the kind of structured, iterative writing an AI agent is good at, and yet an agent looking at a tab editor sees a grid of identical cells it can only click one at a time, with no idea what a cell means, whether a write landed, or what any of it sounds like. WebMCP was the missing piece. Instead of teaching an agent to screen-read a grid, give it the editor's own verbs. RiffSmith is the tab editor where every feature is a tool, and the human and the agent write in the same document at the same time. What it does RiffSmith is a browser tab editor for guitar and bass, tuned for metal. It imports and exports ASCII tab, including messy hand-written tabs with dense chug runs, section headers, and repeat marks. It handles per-bar time signatures from 2/4 to 12/8, grids from quarters to 16th triplets, and loops any section while you keep editing. Playback runs through a sampled guitar engine with persistent per-string voices: palm-muted chugs, hammer-ons, pull-offs, taps, slides, bends, vibrato, tremolo picking, pinch harmonics, dead notes, and chord strums, built from real direct-input recordings with open licenses. The signal goes through a real Neural Amp Modeler capture running as WebAssembly inside an AudioWorklet (the bundled one is a capture I trained on my own rig), or a built-in amp chain. A performance layer adds what a hand does: tension glide on every pick, pick position, one-sided fretting-hand vibrato, finger-shaped bends, pick scrape, wound-string slide squeak, fret clank, and micro-timing. Bass tunings get a real bass and their own amp. Every one of those capabilities is exposed to agents as one of 15 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : songs, bars, notation, imports, the rig, and playback. An agent can create a song, write a four-bar riff in one atomic call, set the amp tighter with all downstrokes and double tracking, play it, and read back the tab to verify its own work, while the human watches it land in the grid and edits any note it wrote. How I built it Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and the Web Audio API, deployed as a static site on Vercel. There is no backend; songs live in localStorage and sample banks and amp captures in IndexedDB. The WebMCP layer follows one rule, parity: every tool runs through the same state operations the UI uses, so there's no agent-only document or hidden mode. Tool returns are built for verification, with write_notes echoing the affected bars back as ASCII tab and get_song returning the full rendering. Notation is validated before any write, and a rejected token comes back with the complete notation guide so the agent can self-correct. Writes take a batch that is validated in full and applied atomically. Calls go through a serialized queue and mutations wait for React to commit before the next call runs, which gives read-after-write consistency for chains like create-then-read. Tools register at module evaluation, before React mounts, so an agent's first page snapshot already has the complete set, and a console shim at window.__webmcp is always available for testing. The audio engine is a lookahead scheduler placing events on the audio clock, driving a sampler with continuous per-string voices, plus an experimental physical string model written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (no bindgen, about 21 KB) that runs in its own AudioWorklet. Sound comes from the Guitar-TECHS dataset (CC BY 4.0), FreePats (CC0), and Karoryfer's bass (CC0), chosen string-aware so a note plays from the string it's tabbed on. Every sound decision was measured before it shipped: offline renders through the real engine, pitch tracking, banded spectra, transient detectors, and level profiles around transitions. The pure scheduling and import layers have 31 unit tests. Challenges I ran into Pitch shifting is time stretching. Web Audio's detune folds into playback rate, so every pitched sample also stretches its pick transient. That was the source of a lot of "synthy". The fix was a set of real-recording handovers: held bends, slides, hammer-ons and pull-offs crossfade into a recording of the target pitch, energy-matched and decay-matched. The "pick" in every hammer-on. Legato kept sounding picked no matter what we did to the crossfade. The real bug was that the envelope was being re-read about 130 ms early and reset upward on every legato event. Tracking the envelope analytically from our own schedule fixed it in one afternoon after days of chasing filters. A dead string in the dataset. The low E string of the Guitar-TECHS guitar had almost no upper partials, about 28 dB below the same pitches on the A string, and that's the string every metal riff lives on. We regenerated its partials from the recorded fundamentals, fitted to the A string's spectrum. The first pass came out 145 cents flat because the files are 48 kHz and the script assumed 44.1. A pitch check caught it. Licensing. The best-sounding amp capture we found is not redistributable, and the rules require the submission to be fully open. The answer was to train a capture of my own rig and ship it with the repo under MIT, so the hosted demo and the repository are identical. Bare tools aren't usable tools. The first version of the tools worked and agents still failed with them: silent write errors, snapshot pipelines that missed late-registered tools, create-then-read races. Most of the WebMCP work was making the tools honest and verifiable, not making them exist. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A human and an agent editing the same riff at the same time, audibly, with no export step and no agent mode. The agent writes a riff, I click a cell it wrote and change one note while the loop keeps running, and it builds a variation on my edit. That was the whole point and it works. The engine went from a sampler to something a guitarist listens to and says "that's pretty great": real-recording legato landings, one-sided vibrato, finger-shaped bends, a fully synthesized pinch harmonic that screams through the amp, a bass with its own amp, a slide squeak that follows the speed of the slide, and a physical string model in Rust running in the browser. Every tool is verifiable by the agent that called it, and the whole thing runs as a static page with no server. What I learned Agents need feedback loops more than they need features. The tools that mattered most were the ones that echo the result of a write back as tab, return the notation guide with a rejection, and guarantee that a read after a write sees the write. Registering tools before the framework mounts matters because snapshot pipelines are unforgiving about timing. On the audio side, measure before you listen. Almost every "it sounds synthy" turned out to have a specific, measurable cause (input level into the capture, a compressor that shouldn't have been there, a stretched transient, an envelope step) rather than a vibe, and an offline render harness found each of them faster than ears could. And a real guitarist's ear is the final test. Several things that measured fine still got sent back. What's next for RiffSmith Chord and multi-string helpers in write_notes so agents can write power chords and octaves in fewer lines. Drum and bass companion tracks on the same scheduler. Render-to-WAV. MIDI and Guitar Pro export. A clean-channel capture and a bass capture to sit next to the distorted one. A wider low-tuned sample bank recorded on my own guitar, since no open dataset covers Drop B. And publishing the WebMCP bridge pattern (serialized queue, commit waiting, early registration, console shim) as a small standalone package so other editors can adopt it. title: PaperSpace
pitch: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Break free from linear PDF reading. PaperSpace gives people and AI agents a shared spatial desk to navigate evidence, gather related pages, and present research through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI tools treat a research paper as a file to summarize or a block of text to retrieve from. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What becomes possible when a person and an agent share a paper's text and its spatial reading environment inside the browser? Reading a paper is rarely linear. A reader moves between related work, methods, equations, figures, experiments, and appendices while building a mental map of where each idea lives. Conventional PDF viewers collapse that map into one page at a time. Chat interfaces collapse it even further into excerpts detached from their visual source. PaperSpace preserves that spatial memory. Every page of every imported PDF is unfolded onto a borderless two-dimensional desk. Pages remain live, selectable PDF surfaces, but they can also be moved, grouped, searched, compared, and revisited as part of a persistent visual workspace. The browser is essential to this interaction. It owns the PDFs the person explicitly selected, the rendered pages, the local text index, the page geometry, the current camera, and the workspace the person is looking at. WebMCP gives an agent direct access to that authorized, browser-local state, keeping the person and the agent aligned on one live workspace. We built PaperSpace for the WebMCP Challenge as a focused, open-source, single-person tool centered on reading, understanding, and presenting research papers. PaperSpace is a shared spatial instrument where the person controls the source material and the agent helps organize attention inside the same visible world. What it does PaperSpace is a local-first spatial desk for research papers. When a person imports a PDF, PaperSpace unfolds every page from left to right and top to bottom using each page's real aspect ratio. Every page becomes an independently movable and resizable live sheet with selectable text. The complete paper stays visible as a spatial place with its reading order intact. PaperSpace extracts text and normalized page geometry locally with PDF.js. Each page becomes searchable as soon as its index is ready. A reusable inspect_workspace briefing reports exact coverage and compact sampled page excerpts, so an agent can prepare once and then read the broadest useful contiguous range in one call, including the whole paper when full context matters. Through WebMCP, the agent can search the available corpus, batch-read paper text, locate an exact passage, and guide the shared camera to that region. The camera first pulls back to establish spatial context, travels across the desk, and then lands with the source itself centered in a calm view with generous breathing room. The app exposes nine WebMCP tools: inspect_workspace returns reusable readiness, compact paper briefs, every page's world geometry, visual artifacts, sequences, and camera state. search_papers progressively searches indexed pages and returns page-level matches with normalized source regions plus exact coverage. read_paper_pages reads one contiguous range or a whole indexed paper in one call, with optional block geometry and an explicit caller-selected character cap. focus_region guides the camera to a search match or an explicit PDF region. arrange_papers reflows pages into reading-order grids and arranges complete paper groups. snapshot_paper_region places a source-linked raster crop from an exact PDF region. place_plot creates a safe declarative line plot from finite numeric data. place_image validates and places PNG, JPEG, and WebP visuals. present_sequence creates a captioned sequence of semantic paper regions and visual artifacts. PaperSpace also gives the agent an explicit delivery contract. When PaperSpace is available, substantive introductions, explanations, reviews, comparisons, and answers grounded across multiple paper regions are delivered through present_sequence . Chat provides concise supporting context, while a single grounded passage can use focus_region and simple localized Q&A remains lightweight. The sequence interaction is the heart of the product. Suppose one experiment is explained across related work, methods, and results on three distant pages. The agent can build a three-frame sequence with a caption for each view. When presentation begins, PaperSpace temporarily draws those original pages together beside their paper in first-appearance order. Quiet numbered source slots preserve the paper's topology throughout the presentation. The same original page can support several region frames through one staged page. Visual artifacts stay in their existing world positions. Exiting the sequence restores every moved page—including its position, size, and layer—and returns the camera to its exact entry state. Keeping a sequence saves its semantic frames; replaying it organizes pages again from their current positions and restores them again afterward. This enables requests such as: “Find where this experiment is motivated, defined, and evaluated, then organize those pages for me.” “Focus on the ablation equation and keep the surrounding paragraph in view.” “Read the method and results, plot the reported trend, and place it beside the source page.” “Present the three views in sequence and explain what changes between them.” Everything happens on the same desk the person can inspect and manipulate. Agent actions produce visible feedback, and temporary organization is transactionally isolated from the person's saved layout. Spatial mutation tools perform an atomic visual preflight inside the app. Standard calls place plots, images, source crops, and arrangements in clear areas. An agent can use force: true for an intentional dense layout, while media, schema, source-target, and security validation remain active. How we built it PaperSpace is a pure frontend SvelteKit and TypeScript application compiled as a static site for Cloudflare Pages. Browser storage and browser-authorized files provide the complete runtime state. The application is organized around four client-side layers: Svelte components render the infinite desk, unfolded PDF sheets, artifacts, search interface, frame editor, and presentation chrome. A single reactive workspace model owns paper metadata, per-page geometry, the camera, artifacts, semantic sequences, and all person- and agent-triggered state transitions. PDF.js renders pages and extracts text plus normalized block geometry in a same-origin Web Worker. IndexedDB stores validated workspace metadata, browser-authorized PDF copies, raster images, and saved semantic frames. The workspace schema stores a stable paper identity and page number for every PDF page, while position, size, and layer remain mutable world properties. PDF inspection records each page's true dimensions. A deterministic row-major layout uses a bounded column count to keep long papers spatially legible, and complete paper bounds are used to prevent different imports from overlapping. Every page has a DOM sheet so its identity remains stable in the world. PaperSpace activates detailed PDF canvas and text rendering near the viewport and above a useful zoom threshold, keeping long unfolded papers responsive. PDF rasterization uses a two-tier residency system. Every successfully rendered page retains a 288-pixel-wide aspect-preserving preview, while an LRU applies a 48-million-pixel budget to unpinned high-resolution page canvases. Pages in the strict viewport, the current focus target, and the active sequence frame are pinned and may temporarily exceed that budget. A compact preview preserves visual continuity as high-resolution canvases move through the working set. Raster canvases and selectable text layers have independent lifecycles, and a double-canvas pipeline swaps each completed bitmap into view atomically. Region targeting uses top-left normalized coordinates. The same semantic region can therefore be mapped through a page's current world geometry after the page has been moved or resized. Camera motion is handled by a cancellable controller with pull-back, travel, and landing keyframes, smooth center interpolation, logarithmic zoom interpolation, distance-aware timing, responsive caption-safe insets, and an immediate path for prefers-reduced-motion . Presentation staging is transactional. PaperSpace validates every frame before changing state, deduplicates source pages by first appearance, snapshots their exact geometry and the entry camera, stages the original pages, and exposes their source slots. Presentation mode pauses page manipulation, while persistence serializes the source geometry and entry camera to keep the durable desk unchanged. WebMCP is registered directly through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP adapter is intentionally thin: every tool calls the same workspace
video_title: paperspace webmcp demo
video_transcript_excerpt: This is PaperSpace, a browser-native research workspace that exposes its live reading desk to AI agents through WebMCP. The paper is our test. Can an agent turn one request into visible, grounded interaction? The user asks Codex, "Introduce this paper using PaperSpace." PaperSpace is open beside the conversation in the built-in browser. WebMCP lets that page expose its own capabilities to the agent. So, the answer appears as visible interaction on the shared desk with chat providing concise guidance. When the page opens, Codex discovers the tools declared by the site. It calls inspect workspace once for a compact desk briefing, reads the index paper in one broad request, then calls present sequence with semantic page regions and captions. The browser-local workspace connects the agent directly to the active reading context. PaperSpace keeps every PDF page live on a borderless two-dimensional desk. Page identity and order remain visible while positions can change. Browser authorization keeps the PDF, extracted text, layout, and saved sequences together in local workspace storage. For a grounded introduction, present sequence gathers the relevant original pages, preserves their source slots, and adds a caption to every view. Here, Codex moves from the paper's motivation to its method, to the evidence with every explanation anchored to the original pages. If the user asks about a precise figure or equation, focus region targets normalized coordinates on the live page. The camera pulls back, travels across the desk, and lands with the requested region centered in a readable view. The person can redirect the motion at any time. Every command participates in one shared reversible state. The person sees each change in the browser, can move pages or stop a flight, and can keep or exit a sequence. On exit, Paper space restores the exact page geometry and the previous camera. That is the Web MCP loop. Codex understands the request, the browser exposes the tools, and Paper space becomes the shared interface. It is a pure SvelteKit front end, persisted in IndexDB, and deployable to Cloudflare Pages. The browser itself is the integration layer.

title: DataSweep Pro — agent-human data cleaning on WebMCP
pitch: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible.
about_excerpt: An AI agent and a person clean the same spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools. Every change is previewed on real tables, approved by a human, attributed, and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "AI cleans your data" demo we'd seen had the same shape: a chat box, a spinner, and a table that changed. You never saw what the model was about to do, you couldn't check its arithmetic, and if it was wrong you started over. WebMCP changes what's possible there. If a page can publish real tools on document.modelContext , an agent doesn't need to guess at your UI — it calls the same functions your buttons call. That reframes the problem. The interesting question stops being "can a model clean a spreadsheet" and becomes "what has to be true before you'd let one write to your data?" Our answer: it has to show you what it measured, ask before it writes, record who did it, and let you undo it. So we built the execution environment for that, rather than another chat wrapper. What it does DataSweep Pro is a data cleaning studio where an agent and a person work on the same messy spreadsheet through the same 15 WebMCP tools . Load a CSV. Eight analyzers run concurrently and find what's actually wrong — mixed date formats, duplicates, currency strings that won't sum, whitespace that breaks joins, outliers, and rows the parser silently dropped. Each finding carries the measurement behind it and a suggested fix. An agent can do the same thing through the same tools. The load-bearing property: There is no separate "agent path" that could behave differently from the buttons. Everything runs locally. Your file is parsed and queried by DuckDB compiled to WebAssembly, in the tab. External communication — a model API, a desktop MCP client, a GitHub pull request — is opt-in and separately gated. How we built it Four layers, each testable without the one above it. Arrows point one way only: the domain layer knows nothing about tools, and the engine knows nothing about MCP. The WebMCP surface. 15 tools registered via @mcp-b/global . Each is one ToolDefinition — name, description, JSON Schema, annotations, execute — and that single object serves three consumers: WebMCP registration, the in-app Tool Inspector, and the agent loop. That's what guarantees the schema a reviewer inspects is the schema an agent is offered. Bridgeable to Claude Desktop with @mcp-b/webmcp-local-relay . The approval gate. A mutating tool called without a confirmation_token runs the transformation against scratch tables, measures exactly what changed, drops the scratch tables, and returns a token. Your data hasn't moved. The token is bound to a fingerprint of the exact arguments, single-use, and expiring — so an agent can't preview something harmless and reuse the token for something else. Enforced once in middleware, not per tool. A mutating tool declared without a preview() throws at construction rather than silently skipping the gate. Prompt injection. A spreadsheet cell is attacker-controlled text. Cell content leaves every tool inside a fence carrying a per-call random nonce, so injected text can't forge the closing tag and escape into the instruction region. Pattern detection also runs, but it's treated as advisory — the structural defence is what holds for payloads no rule matches. Testing. 380 tests. The integration and security-eval suites run real DuckDB-Wasm through its Node bindings, not a mock, because the interesting bugs live in the SQL. title: Forge
pitch: Imagine and build shared 3D worlds with ChatGPT, agents and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Imagine and build shared 3D worlds with ChatGPT, agents and WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Welcome to Forge Molty Our favourite logo Home sweet home Inspiration Building a 3D world is fun, but it can take hours of planning and placing blocks. We wanted to make creating a world as simple as walking to a location and describing what you imagine. Forge started with one question: What if you could point somewhere and ask your agent to build there with whatever you imagined? Instead of replacing the player, the agent works alongside them. The player decides where to go, what to create, and how it should feel. ChatGPT and your agent helps turn that vision into something real. How we built it Hosted on ChatGPT Sites + Render Built on top of Voxelize What it does Forge is a browser-based voxel world that multiple players can build through conversation. Multiple players can explore the world, look at a clearing, and say, "Build a lobster here." ChatGPT and your agent understands the location, designs the structure, and builds it directly in the world. The players can then continue the conversation: Replace the wooden roof with glass. Build a wall around this area. Make the lobster taller. Each request changes the same live world, allowing the players and your agent to build and refine ideas together. 1. Why is your use case a strong fit for WebMCP? Before WebMCP, an agent could suggest what to build, but it could not understand where the player was standing, what they were looking at, or what existed nearby. Building in 3D depends on this spatial context. WebMCP connects your agent to the live world, giving it the context and actions needed to understand what the player means by "build it here" and turn their idea into something they can immediately see and explore. 2. How does it create a better user experience? Players do not need to enter coordinates, learn a complex editor, or place every block manually. They can explore naturally, point at a location, and describe what they want. Your agent handles the design and construction while the player stays focused on the creative idea. 3. What can people and agents do together that was difficult or impossible before? The player's movement and attention become part of the conversation. The player chooses where to build and provides the creative direction. ChatGPT and your agent understands the surrounding world, plans the structure, and places hundreds of blocks. Together, they can create and refine a world through simple conversation. 4. How did you implement WebMCP? I registered two WebMCP tools in Forge. get_player_context gives your agent the player's position, target, and nearby terrain. build_structure applies your agent's building instructions to the live world. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was helping ChatGPT and the agent understand words like "here" and "there." We needed to give it enough information about the player's location and surroundings without overwhelming it. We also had to make sure that completed buildings appeared correctly, remained responsive during construction, and stayed in the world after a reload. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a complete experience where multiple players can point at a location, ask ChatGPT to build something, and watch it appear. What we learned We learned that agents are most helpful when they understand what the person is currently doing. Players are good at imagination, exploration, and deciding what feels right. Agents are good at planning and carrying out repetitive work. Forge brings those strengths together. What's next for Forge Next, we want multiple people and their agents to build in the same persistent world. We also want players to point at existing creations and ask Forge to expand, repair, restyle, or remove them. Our goal is to make creating digital worlds accessible to players and agents who can describe what they imagine. title: Say to Match
pitch: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have a young child. That fact colors how I read every AI-and-jobs headline these days — not the "AI helps you do more" stories, but the ones asking who's still employable once it doesn't need us the same way. I can probably navigate whatever labor market shows up in the next few decades — but what about him, and the much larger group of people who aren't glued to AI news, aren't early adopters, and won't have a head start? If there's an idea that makes that future a little better, it's worth more shared broadly than kept to myself. The second thread: most of what I see about AI's impact on work focuses on how power users squeeze more out of it. But the thing that actually feels novel about general-purpose AI isn't that it helps the technically fluent go faster — it's that it can meet people with no technical fluency exactly where they are. That's a strength no prior wave of software had. I wanted a concrete example of that strength doing real work, not just a slide. I'm sure other people have had a version of this thought before me — I'm not claiming the idea is original. What changed is the timing: WebMCP makes "any web page can be a real market participant" something you can actually build this month, not something that requires a platform to bless it first. So this submission is less "look what I made" and more "here's a working example of what I think this technology is for — someone should be pointing this direction." What it does Say to Match (StM) turns any static web page into a participant in an open task market with one script tag. A page that needs something declares a Job in plain natural language. A page that can provide something declares a Skill — whether the provider behind it is an AI agent or a human professional. Both are exposed as real document.modelContext WebMCP tools. A Broker , backed by an LLM, discovers these tools across independent origins, matches Jobs to Skills, orchestrates the handoff between two pages that have never heard of each other, verifies the delivered work against the original requirement, and releases payment from escrow it held in trust. No platform account, no onboarding, no API key required to participate — just a script tag and a sentence anyone can write. Concretely, a Job doesn't have to be a coding task: a small NGO transcribing a budget PDF into a CSV, a gig worker offering to survey Tokyo cafés with just a phone, a small business owner asking a licensed accountant to spot-check AI-transcribed receipts, or a social app team asking an 18–24-year-old for an honest first-time onboarding reaction. None of it requires knowing what WebMCP or JSON Schema even are. How we built it The WebMCP layer is real, not simulated. document.modelContext tools are actually registered on two genuinely independent origins (Requester and Worker), with a same-surface polyfill so it runs even without the experimental browser flag enabled. The multi-origin story is real too. The Broker's agent drives an actual headless Chromium instance via Playwright, opens the Requester and Worker as separate pages, and calls document.modelContext. callTool(...) inside each page's own context — proving this isn't one app quietly answering its own API calls. Verification is tiered and real. Tier 1 runs the submitted work against an actual sandboxed regression test. Tier 2 is an LLM-as-Judge (DeepSeek via OpenRouter) that reviews the deliverable against the original job text — and explicitly screens for prompt-injection attempts from either side, since the requester's job description and the worker's deliverable are both untrusted text from the judge's point of view. The trust design is documented, not hand-waved. docs/PROTOCOL.md maps StM's Job/Match/Settlement objects onto Google's AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) Mandate pattern instead of reinventing signed-authorization primitives, and works through an adversarial catalogue — specific dishonest moves the Requester, the Worker, or the Broker itself could attempt — each one explicitly labeled as already defended in this PoC, designed but not implemented, or an honestly unsolved open problem. It's actually deployed , not just runnable locally: three genuinely separate origins running on Cloud Run, built from the same container image, with GitHub Actions publishing the image automatically on push. Worth being upfront about: the code, the deployment, and this write-up were built almost entirely through an AI coding agent (Claude Code), with me providing direction, judgment calls, and the framing — not writing the implementation by hand. That's not incidental to the story. I spent most of my career as a professional programmer before later moving into a different role, so I know firsthand what building something like this used to take. Watching an agent take it from a brainstormed idea to a live, adversarially-tested, multi-service deployment in about two days was a genuinely visceral measure of how far coding agents have come in just the few years since I stopped writing code for a living — and, fittingly, a small live demonstration of this project's own thesis: someone without hands-on technical execution, directing an AI to get something built that they couldn't have built alone in the time available. Challenges we ran into A no-root dev sandbox with nothing pre-installed. Every piece of infrastructure — Node, Playwright's Chromium system libraries, fonts, ffmpeg, a TTS engine, even Docker itself (rootless) — had to be assembled by hand in user space, without interactive sudo access. Proving cross-origin trust convincingly, not just claiming it. It would have been easy to fake the multi-origin story with one app playing three roles. Getting a real browser agent to navigate real separate origins and call real WebMCP tools took real orchestration work. Bidirectional prompt injection. The first pass only screened the worker's submitted deliverable for injection attempts. It took a second look to realize the requester's own job description — text the judge also reads — is just as valid an attack surface, and needed equally explicit defense. Verification itself is an attack surface. Once a Broker is willing to run a sandboxed test and an LLM call on request, that's a cost someone could weaponize as a denial-of-service. Working out a fault-based bond mechanism for who pays for verification, and under what conditions, took more thought than the "happy path" demo did. Racing a hard deadline without cutting corners on hygiene. Keeping API keys and private planning notes out of a repository that had to go public fast, including rewriting git history safely when something slipped through, ate real time that would rather have gone to features. Realizing that verifying non-code deliverables — a professional's credential-backed judgment call, a claimed identity or demographic, a piece of physical-world photo evidence — is still an open trust-protocol problem, not something the current Tier 1 (sandbox) / Tier 2 (LLM judge) pipeline actually solves. The demo intentionally runs a code bugfix because it's the one task type that pipeline can verify end to end today; documented as a real gap in docs/PROTOCOL.md rather than glossed over. Accomplishments that we're proud of Genuine multi-origin WebMCP behavior, verified live rather than just claimed — real cross-origin document.modelContext calls driven by a real browser agent, not a single app simulating three roles. A prompt-injection defense that actually holds up in both directions, checked against real adversarial test cases, not just described. A trust-and-escrow design honest enough to explicitly separate what's live, what's designed but unimplemented, and what's an open problem — including an original piece of systems thinking (a fault-based Submission Bond) for a cost-based denial-of-service risk that isn't obvious until you think through who's paying for verification. Shipping to a real, live, three-service deployment rather than stopping at "works on my machine." What we learned The hard part of an open, permissionless task market was never discovery — it's trust, and specifically, defending the act of verifying trust from being gamed or exploited itself. That problem doesn't go away once you've built a matching engine; it's the actual product. I also came away more convinced of the personal thesis behind this project than I was going in: a huge amount of what AI-assisted tools like this make possible isn't about making already-capable people faster. It's about letting someone contribute a clear goal and good judgment, and have that be enough — whether that's a non-technical worker declaring a Skill in plain language, or, in this project's own making-of story, an ex-programmer-turned-analyst directing an AI a

Moxscore turns a Magic the Gathering Commander decklist into a clear health score, spotting weak mana, missing ramp, draw or interaction, so you and you agent can make smarter upgrades through webmcp

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Commander decklists can be hard to read at a glance. A list of 100 cards does not immediately reveal whether a deck has enough ramp, draw, interaction, lands, or a healthy mana curve. 

 I built Moxscore to turn a decklist into understandable signals and practical next steps, without handing players an unexplained, black-box verdict. My goal was to have a really useful tool that helps me tune my decks towards the bracket I aim for. 

 What it does 

 Moxscore is a browser-based Commander deck analyser. Paste a decklist, upload an export to receive: 

 
 A transparent deck health score 
 Role breakdowns for areas such as ramp, draw, interaction, lands, and mana 
 A mana-curve view 
 Combo signals and a beta Commander-bracket estimate 
 Deterministic category- and card-level tuning guidance 
 

 The core analysis runs locally in the browser, with no account required. WebMCP makes this analysis accessible to agents through clear, structured interactions as well as the normal player-facing interface. 

 How we built it 

 I designed Moxscore around a simple pipeline: ingest a Commander decklist, normalize the cards, classify cards into useful deck roles, calculate structural signals, and turn those signals into readable guidance. 

 The scoring system is heuristic and deterministic rather than AI-generated. That means players can understand what is being measured and why a recommendation appeared. I paired that analysis with a browser-first interface and WebMCP capabilities so both people and agents can work with the same deck-analysis flow. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making analysis useful without pretending it is absolute truth. Commander decks are highly contextual: a card that looks weak in isolation may be essential to a commander, theme, budget, or playgroup. 

 A real challenge was also had to handle varied decklist formats, incomplete exports, card-role ambiguity, and the challenge of translating many individual card signals into guidance that is concise and actionable. For WebMCP, we needed to make the important actions and outputs explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Moxscore provides a useful first read of a 100-card deck in seconds while keeping its reasoning grounded in visible deck structure. 

 We are especially happy with: 

 
 Local, account-free core analysis 
 Transparent deterministic scoring instead of a black-box verdict 
 A practical health score, role breakdown, and mana-curve view in one place 
 Guidance that points to categories and cards, not just a number 
 A WebMCP-enabled experience that lets agents participate in deck analysis meaningfully 
 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the best agent-facing website actions are not vague commands—they need clear inputs, predictable outputs, and useful boundaries. WebMCP encouraged us to think carefully about what “analyse this deck” should mean and what structured information should come back. 

 We also learned that transparency is a feature. For a hobby as nuanced as Commander, players need guidance they can inspect, challenge, and adapt to their own table. 

 What's next for Moxscore 

 Next, we want to improve card-role classification, expand import reliability, refine the bracket estimate, and add more context-aware tuning suggestions. 

 In the product roadmap there are accounts with bracket aimed AI enhanced suggestions, pod analytics to see how 4 decks could stack up against each other Discord bot extensions to make it even more accessible. 

 I also want to deepen the WebMCP experience so agents can help players explore specific questions e.g whether a deck needs more interaction, where its curve is crowded, or which structural changes are most likely to improve consistency, or go deeper in specific meta, all while keeping the final deckbuilding decisions with the player.

An agent-native AI tool scout that turns real business needs into transparent, budget-aware software recommendations for people and their agents.

 Plain Chrome without WebMCP: the form still works and the status panel says so. Chrome, we need to talk. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Clever AI Tool Scout: describe a task, add a budget, get three vetted tools. Humans and agents use the same engine.

 ChatGPT calls find_ai_tools via WebMCP. The result lands in the chat and on the page at the same time. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 cleverkitools.com started with a simple question: how far can a non-developer (me) get building a real product with ChatGPT alone? The answer became a curated catalog of 100 vetted AI tools for small and medium-sized businesses, with a KMU score, checked prices and honest caveats for every tool. When WebMCP (and the challenge) appeared, the next question was obvious. What if agents could use that catalog the same way people do? 

 What it does 

 Clever AI Tool Scout is a recommendation interface on top of the catalog. A person / human describes a business task, optionally adds a monthly budget in EUR, and gets up to three fitting tools with a reason, a caution and a link to the full review. An AI agent can do exactly the same through one WebMCP tool, find_ai_tools , with the same two inputs. People and agents share one recommendation engine. 

 Live: cleverkitools.com/webmcp-challenge 

 Why WebMCP is suited for this use case 

 A tool catalog is a structured question with a structured answer. Without WebMCP an agent has to scrape a hundred German profile pages, guess prices and infer categories. With WebMCP the site says exactly what it can do: give me a task and a budget, I return ranked tools, prices in EUR, cautions and profile URLs. The agent gets a deterministic contract instead of a DOM to navigate, and the site owner keeps control over how recommendations are made.
In addition, I just wanted to try WebMCP 🙂 

 How it improves the user experience (or AGENT exprience?). 

 
 For people: the same form, same results, nothing changes. No direct improvement. 
 For agents: one straight call instead of dozens of page loads. No open API neccessary. No running MCP server neccessary. 
 

 The Agent Flight Recorder shows every human and agent request of the session as a four-step trace (request received, intent matched, budget evaluated, result returned). Query text stays in the browser. I used it for debugging. 

 What people and agents can accomplish together that was not possible before 

 An agent can now answer "which AI tool should my small business use for X within Y euros" from a curated, price-checked source instead of from training data. It can hand the person a page that already shows the shortlist. The person can refine the task in the form, and the agent can pick that up again. 

 On the other hand, to be honest, well, it's more a tech demo atm and not a super use case, I must admit. I'm sure better use cases will follow. 

 How we built it (we = ChatGPT Codex and me) 

 
 One tool, find_ai_tools , registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Input schema: task (string, required) and max_monthly_budget (number, EUR, optional). 
 The execute handler runs the same recommend() engine as the HTML form, renders the cards into the page and returns structured JSON. 
 The handler respects the AbortSignal passed by the browser. 
 Search core: 13 intents with German and English terms, category weights, tool boosts and a relevance floor. Prices are normalized to EUR from a known regular entry price (checked 21 Aug 2026). 
 Catalog: 100 current tools, 15 new entries, 19 archived tools with replacements, loaded as static data. Everything runs in the browser, no server round-trip. 
 Progressive by design: without document.modelContext the page is a normal form, and the status panel says so. 
 Built with ChatGPT and Codex, deployed on cleverkitools.com. 
 

 What the agent receives: 
 {
 "request": { "task": "…", "max_monthly_budget": 30 },
 "visible_results_updated": true,
 "selection_status": "matched | fallback | archive_redirect | over_budget",
 "matched_intents": ["Video, audio & music"],
