 {
 "name": "OpusClip",
 "profile_url": "https://cleverkitools.com/ki-tools/opusclip/",
 "category": "Social Media & Ads",
 "why_fitting": "…",
 "caution": "…",
 "status": "current",
 "kmu_score": 86,
 "price": "Freemium · ab 15 USD/Monat (ca. 13,13 EUR/Monat)"
 }
 ],
 "archive_match": { "name": "Copy.ai", "status": "archived", "replacement": { "name": "Genspark" } }
}
 
 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is only available in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome with the flag enabled, so the page had to work as a normal form everywhere else and report its WebMCP state without pretending. The second challenge was keeping one engine for both audiences: the agent needs structured fields, the person needs readable cards, and both had to come from the same call. 

 What's next 

 Not 100% sure yet. Looking for your and other user's feedback.

title: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer
pitch: Human Focus in AI.
about_excerpt: Human Focus in AI. Like Comment Story Updates AI Usage Skill Visualizer — WebMCP Challenge Edition WebMCP E2E workflow completed with PDF generation and reverse handoff Evaluation result with 438/500 score, PDF generation, and successful reverse handoff Generated AI Usage Report with an overall score of 438/500 Chrome extension extracting the ChatGPT conversation log for evaluation Inspiration This project started with a question about my own use of AI. During a conversation with AI, it pointed out something about the way I was using it. That made me wonder: How well am I actually using AI? Then another question came to mind: Isn't everyone using AI in more or less the same way? And if not: What is the difference? That was the starting point for visualizing human AI usage skills. By that time, I had already been using AI for more than two years. Because of that experience, it felt natural to me that the final output alone could not tell you how well someone had used AI. If I wanted to understand how a person used AI, I also needed to look at the conversation process that led to the final result. So the idea was to evaluate the conversation log, the final output, and the relationship between them. That became the foundation of AI Usage Skill Visualizer. As I continued developing it, I noticed something else. Knowing whether someone uses AI, or how much they use it, is not the same as understanding how well they can actually use it. And knowing about AI is not the same as being able to use AI effectively in real work. AI Usage Tracking ≠ AI Usage Skill AI Knowledge ≠ Practical AI Capability From the beginning, the concept was also broader than just building a standalone evaluation application. I wanted to connect the whole process: Use AI → Capture the interaction process → Evaluate human AI usage → Visualize the result → Return the result to the AI workflow At the time, however, I did not have a practical way to directly connect the environment where people were actually using AI with the Visualizer. So I started with what I could actually implement at the time: a standalone application. The first approach was simple. Users manually entered their conversation logs and outputs, and the Visualizer evaluated them. But once I started using it myself, I realized that this manual input process was more cumbersome than I had expected. To reduce that friction, I built a Chrome extension that could bring ChatGPT conversations into the Visualizer. That made the process of importing conversation logs much simpler. There was still another gap between the AI workflow and the Visualizer. This is where WebMCP changed what was possible. Using WebMCP Site Tools, the AI workflow can directly use the Visualizer's capabilities to run the evaluation, generate a PDF report, and read the generated report back into the workflow. By combining that with the Chrome extension and reverse handoff, I was also able to return the evaluation result to the original ChatGPT conversation. The Challenge Edition demonstrates this flow: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer → Evaluation → PDF Report → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary WebMCP was not something I added afterward simply because this was a WebMCP Challenge. From the beginning of the idea, I wanted to connect everything from using AI, to evaluating how it was used, to returning the result back to the AI workflow. Using WebMCP finally allowed me to move closer to that original concept in a practical way. Human Focus in AI. What it does AI Usage Skill Visualizer — WebMCP Edition is a Challenge-specific implementation that demonstrates how WebMCP can connect an AI interaction directly to AI usage evaluation. The project combines: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer The Chrome extension can extract a ChatGPT conversation and provide a path for that conversation to become Visualizer input. For the public Challenge demo, the built-in public sample data is used so that the evaluation workflow can be reproduced consistently. The user starts the analysis from AI Usage Skill Visualizer. From there, Work uses WebMCP Site Tools to continue the workflow. The WebMCP workflow can: receive the conversation log and final output run the Challenge-specific evaluation return structured evaluation results generate a PDF report read the generated report back into the workflow After the evaluation and report workflow are complete, the result is prepared for reverse handoff. The Chrome extension then returns the evaluation prompt to the original Chrome ChatGPT conversation. The extension: identifies the target ChatGPT conversation receives the evaluation payload finds the ChatGPT composer inserts the evaluation prompt verifies the inserted text It deliberately does not click Send or simulate Enter. The final submission remains under human control. After the user manually sends the prompt, ChatGPT summarizes the evaluation inside the original conversation. The complete demonstration flow is: Chrome Extension → WebMCP → AI Usage Skill Visualizer → Evaluation → PDF Report → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary The Challenge Edition uses deterministic evaluation logic created specifically for this public demonstration. It is intentionally separate from the production AI Usage Skill Visualizer evaluation engine. The important part of this Challenge project is not the simplified score itself. The important part is that WebMCP turns the Visualizer from a separate destination into something that can participate directly in an AI workflow. How we built it I built the WebMCP Challenge Edition as a separate implementation from the production AI Usage Skill Visualizer. The Challenge application uses a lightweight web interface built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, together with a local backend for report generation and supporting the end-to-end workflow. The application exposes WebMCP Site Tools that can be discovered and called from Work. The main tools are: evaluate_ai_usage_demo This tool receives structured evaluation input including: conversation_log output It then: receives the submitted conversation log and output displays them in the Visualizer runs the Challenge-specific deterministic evaluation renders the evaluation result returns structured evaluation data through WebMCP create_ai_usage_report This tool receives the evaluation result and generates the PDF report used by the Challenge workflow. The generated PDF is not only a UI result. It becomes a real workflow artifact that can be passed to the next stage. read_generated_report This tool reads the generated report back into the workflow so that Work can verify the result and continue the process. Together, these Site Tools allow Work to move from structured input through evaluation and report generation without requiring the user to manually transfer intermediate results between each stage. The Challenge Edition also integrates with a Chrome extension. The extension plays two roles. First, it can extract a ChatGPT conversation and provide a path for that conversation to become Visualizer input. Second, it supports reverse handoff. After the WebMCP evaluation and report workflow are complete, the evaluation result can be returned to the original Chrome ChatGPT conversation. The extension inserts the evaluation prompt into the ChatGPT composer and verifies that the intended text was inserted correctly. It does not automatically submit the prompt. The user manually clicks Send. This creates an intentional boundary: WebMCP and the extension automate the workflow, while the human retains control of the final submission. For the public demo, the built-in public sample data is used as the evaluation input for reproducibility. The Challenge-specific scoring logic is deterministic and separate from the production evaluation system. No external AI API is required for Challenge scoring. The submitted conversation text is not persisted in a database, localStorage , sessionStorage , or cookies. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was understanding how to build around a new interaction model. I did not begin with the complete workflow. I started with the smallest possible WebMCP proof of concept. I first needed to confirm that: a web page could register a WebMCP tool the tool could be discovered the tool could be executed structured data could reach the application the application could update its UI the tool could return a structured response Once those pieces worked, I expanded the implementation step by step. The next challenge was moving from a single WebMCP call to a complete workflow. The final Challenge Edition does not stop after evaluation. It continues through: Evaluation → PDF Generation → Report Reading → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary That required the Visualizer, WebMCP Site Tools, the report backend, and the Chrome extension to work together. title: Lemma
pitch: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control
about_excerpt: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hi, my name is Bernabé, and this is my project, Lemma . Over the past year, I’ve heard stories and read news about researchers—and even students—using AI to discover new proofs or make progress on long-standing mathematical problems, including some of the famous Erdős problems. This is exciting and optimistic, but it also introduces a new challenge: as AI helps produce an increasing number of proofs, conjectures, and solutions, how will humans connect them into a coherent development of mathematics and science? And, perhaps more importantly, what role will researchers play in that process? Terence Tao recently published an insightful article exploring this topic , in case you want to go down that rabbit hole. This is a complex question that the scientific community will need to address together. I don’t pretend to have the answer, but as a software engineer, I wanted to contribute through something I know how to build. I had seen applications that use AI agents to solve mathematical problems and produce LaTeX documents. However, the result can quickly become a collection of messy, disconnected information—something similar to spaghetti code in software development. Mathematical reasoning rarely follows a single, linear path. Researchers explore different strategies, reconsider assumptions, return to earlier decisions, and abandon dead ends. In a traditional AI conversation, that structure is easily lost, especially as the context grows. That is why I created Lemma. What it does Lemma is an IDE-like collaborative workspace where humans and AI agents work on mathematical reasoning together. Engineers, mathematicians, physicists, students, and anyone working with mathematics can use Lemma to define objectives, provide context, explore strategies, and develop solutions as structured reasoning graphs. Instead of treating a solution as one long document or conversation, Lemma organizes it into objectives, strategies, branches, and individual reasoning steps. Users can interrupt the process at any moment, correct an agent, introduce a new idea, return to an earlier step, or create an alternative branch without overwriting the original path. The core workflow is interrupt, branch, continue : a human changes the direction of a solution, and the agent reads the updated state through WebMCP and continues from there. WebMCP is fundamental to this experience. Humans interact through a visual workspace, while agents can directly read and update the same structured reasoning graph. Both operate on the same source of truth, using the interface that works best for each of them. Ultimately, Lemma is my approach to keeping humans in the loop—combining human creativity, context, and judgment with the speed and capabilities of AI to pursue mathematical goals together. How we built it Lemma is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces . The frontend uses React 19, Vite, strict TypeScript, React Router, XYFlow, and Dagre . XYFlow and Dagre power the visual reasoning canvas, where strategies, branches, dependencies, and mathematical steps are displayed as an interactive graph. Mathematical content is written in Markdown with embedded TeX and rendered using react-markdown, remark-math, and KaTeX . The backend is built with Supabase , using: Supabase Auth for authentication. PostgreSQL for the persisted reasoning graph. Row Level Security to protect each workspace. Realtime to keep the interface synchronized after changes. Storage for context files and supporting material. Edge Functions for the authenticated API and embedding pipeline. pgvector and full-text search for semantic step retrieval. The reasoning graph is the source of truth. Entities such as workspaces, objectives, strategies, branches, steps, assumptions, sources, decisions, and results are stored as structured relational data instead of being inferred from a Markdown document. The frontend, API, and WebMCP layer share the same Zod schemas , helping ensure that humans and agents interact with the same validated contracts. At the top-level page, Lemma registers 22 WebMCP tools . These allow agents to inspect the workspace, create and update objectives, develop strategies, add steps and dependencies, create branches, mark assumptions or dead ends, compare branches, request human decisions, search previous reasoning, and generate a clean solution. All agent mutations use the same authenticated application services as the visual interface. When an agent changes the graph, the result is immediately reflected and highlighted in the workspace. The web client is hosted on Vercel , while Supabase provides the database and backend services. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was developing a clear mental model for structuring mathematical problems. Mathematical reasoning is not simply a document, a chat, or a linear list of steps. I had to think carefully about which entities should participate in the process, how they should relate to one another, and how to preserve alternative paths without losing the history of the original reasoning. Designing the interface was another major challenge. A reasoning graph can contain objectives, strategies, branches, steps, dependencies, assumptions, and results, so presenting all that information in a way that remains comfortable to navigate and understand was difficult. I am happy with the current direction, but the interface could still be improved significantly as the conceptual model evolves and more people test it. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of having built a working prototype in record time that already allows mathematical problems to be explored in a visual and organized way. There is still plenty of room to improve the problem-solving process, but one moment made me especially proud. A friend of mine who is studying mathematics tested Lemma and told me that he loved how easy it was to work with AI agents through the application. That feedback made the idea feel real. It showed me that Lemma was not only an interesting technical experiment, but that its visual and structured approach could genuinely make AI-assisted mathematical reasoning easier to follow. What we learned The most important thing I learned was how people mentally approach mathematical problems. Although I enjoy mathematics, it is still a hobby for me. Building an application intended to help people who are significantly better at mathematics than I am was challenging at first. It forced me to think beyond the final answer and focus on the actual reasoning process: how ideas are introduced, how assumptions affect later conclusions, how different strategies emerge, and why returning to an earlier decision is such an important part of solving difficult problems. I also learned that building effective tools for AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to make their work inspectable, editable, and easy for humans to redirect. What's next for Lemma The next step is to improve Lemma’s conceptual model and introduce additional entities that support other types of mathematical work. For example, Lemma could also be used as a learning environment, with dedicated explanation nodes that help users understand why a particular step works—not just what the next step is. There are many other possible workflows that could be built on top of the same reasoning graph. I would also like to integrate tools based on Lean , allowing agents and researchers to translate results into formal proofs and mechanically verify whether a conclusion is correct. This could create a valuable bridge between exploratory mathematical reasoning and formally verified results. Another feature I would love to create is a collaborative mode. Researchers could publish their work so that others could explore it, contribute new ideas or branches, and use previous research as a source of reference and context. In the long term, Lemma could become more than a workspace for solving individual problems: it could become a shared, connected environment for developing, verifying, and communicating mathematical knowledge alongside AI. title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Valence
pitch: Interactive chemical discovery.
about_excerpt: Interactive chemical discovery. Like Comment Story Updates Insipration Traditional online chemistry research can be a hassle, with multiple tabs and half an hour of searching just to look up a molecule. As an example, to find a non-toxic polymer precursor built from only period-2 elements, the typical routine is searching PubChem and noting down hazard classifications and cross-checking molecular weights, a tough ask if you want to do it in a single tab. What it does The interface is an interactive periodic table and chemistry bench. A user describes a research goal, and through WebMCP an agent runs the workflow. On the interface, there is a build panel that keeps the scientist(user or agent) in control; everything is audited(keystrokes, tool calls) and logged by the trace panel via a ghost cursor. Beginners/Non-experts can interactively play with the periodic table by combining elements. Full explanations for both successful molecules and rejected combinations. Across the app, 23 tools are registered on document.modelContext . Tools include Selection and bonding: for 2D/3D molecular visualization. ** PubChem lookup:** for data grounding via the public API. Molecular design and comparison: for similarity evaluation, comparative analysis, alternative search, hazard classification. All scored transparently. Constraint solving: Async routines for multivariable discovery jobs, status streaming, candidate ranking and task cancellation utilty and state: Full state serialisation. All numbers are sourced directly from PubChem live and PubChem cached. Honest degradation to an offline bundled set when the API is unreachable. How we built it Vite and TypeScript WebMCP. @mcp-b/global wraps a native document.modelContext when the browser has one; a small spec-shaped shim covers the rest. Tools register synchronously at module load, so an agent scanning on page load already sees them. The store is a tiny observable. Every UI handler and every tool mutates state through it. A built-in operator runs the same tool that an external agent calls, so the command bar and a real agent share one code path. That was also our test harness. Data comes from PubChem PUG REST and PUG View, called straight from the browser. Rendering. 3Dmol.js for the 3D viewer, lazy-loaded and smiles-drawer for 2D structures. Deployment: Vercel. Challenges we ran into PubChem rate-limiting Its public API throttles per client address and returns 503 under load, it was unreliable during quick iterations, so we bundled an offline compound set as fallback. Finding the right surface Our first version registered tools on navigator.modelContext . ChatGPT reported "no callable tools". Agents read document.modelContext . We moved there and added the shim. Async tool contracts The constraint solver could take fifteen seconds, and a timeout left half-built state on the canvas. We reworked it into a job that returns an id immediately, streams status, can be cancelled, and commits its result in a single step. The 3D viewer got stuck Two model loads racing in before the 3Dmol chunk finished each created their own viewer on the same element, and later updates landed on the orphan. We used a single-flight guard to resolve this. Trust in a science tool PubChem's aggregated GHS data includes minority-notifier misclassifications, so water in some examples was showing false hazards. We now read only the primary classification. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works in one turn. Ask for a molecule by constraints, get a ranked, hazard-checked answer with a 3D model on the canvas, then edit a constraint and re-run without re-prompting. The beauty of the shared canvas. The agent and the person operate one instrument exactly like we envisioned Every claim is checkable: source and fetch time on every number, evidence-based hazard language, per-candidate rejection reasons. Our bundled fallback held out when PubChem was unreachable. What we learned WebMCP's value is shared state on a live surface. A headless MCP server can answer questions. It cannot manipulate pixels or read back what you just did. Agent tools need async contracts. This is helpful for debugging. Test against the actual agent surface early. ChatGPT caught the registration bug in minutes. The built-in operator running the same tool path as an external agent was the best decision for development speed. What's next for Valence A richer chemistry surface with cross-references and deeper bioassay data. A shareable recipe-card permalink, so a build can be sent to someone. A multi-compound bench, so an agent can lay out a small reaction rather than one molecule at a time. A resilient data path for the PubChem rate limits, and more teach-mode content for beginners. title: Lumos: Human-First WebMCP for Transparent AI Collaboration
pitch: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Lumos lets people and AI agents collaborate through explicit consent, scoped tools, clear action previews, and user-controlled execution—built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates For WebMCP Challenge judges Live URL: https://welockai.com/panel/ Repository: https://github.com/candasoz01-cmd/lumos-core License: Apache-2.0 Open in: ChatGPT’s in-app browser, or Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext : lumos-list-tasks , lumos-propose-task , and lumos-complete-task . Reading requires explicit session-scoped sharing consent. Every write is previewed and confirmed inside Lumos. Declining writes nothing, and completing a task cannot be used to discover task existence without consent. The recorded native proof used Chrome 152. ChatGPT’s in-app browser was not used as the recorded native proof; the live Lumos panel is the judge-facing surface. Inspiration AI agents can move quickly through software, but speed without visible authority boundaries can undermine trust. Lumos already had a task board and a human approval flow. For the WebMCP Challenge, we explored a focused question: how can an agent use a real product surface without taking the final decision away from the person? What it does Lumos exposes three task-board tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : lumos-list-tasks reads the task board only after the user explicitly approves sharing it with agents. The permission is session-scoped, visible in the panel, and revocable. lumos-propose-task proposes a task but does not create it until the user approves the panel's own confirmation dialog. lumos-complete-task requires board-sharing consent first, then a separate approval before changing a task's status. The confirmation preview shows the exact fields involved, including title, priority, schedule, status, source, and status transition. Cancelling produces no write. If WebMCP is unavailable, Lumos fails closed, registers no tools, marks the surface unsupported, and continues as a normal panel without a shim or polyfill. How we built it The public Lumos panel is built with Astro and browser-native JavaScript. A narrow bridge in the existing panel runtime connects WebMCP tools to the established task workflow. The tools return MCP-compatible content payloads and reuse the same task persistence and confirmation paths as the human-facing interface. The implementation includes source-contract tests and a Playwright end-to-end harness that exercises tool registration, consent refusal, approval, cancellation, task creation, and completion. The harness simulates the browser's agent-side WebMCP host so it validates the page implementation without pretending to be native browser proof. The public panel is deployed on Vercel, and the source is available under the Apache-2.0 license. What changed during the challenge Lumos, its panel, task module, and approval flow existed before August 25, 2026. The WebMCP-specific layer was added during the challenge period. That work added the three tool registrations, session-scoped read consent, per-mutation approval, full-field action previews, fail-closed behavior, and automated verification. Security review also led to concrete fixes: task data is no longer returned without sharing consent; task-completion lookups cannot reveal whether a task exists before consent; and a stale dialog-close event can no longer cancel a later approval prompt. Challenges we faced The hardest part was treating privacy and consent as implementation details rather than slogans. A read-only task list can still contain sensitive personal or work information. A confirmation that hides priority or schedule is not meaningful consent. Different error responses can also leak whether a task exists. WebMCP is emerging, so we also had to keep three kinds of evidence separate: source behavior, harness-based end-to-end verification, and native browser-agent invocation. Lumos does not add a compatibility shim when the platform API is missing. What we learned Read-only does not automatically mean safe to share. Approval must show every field that will be written. Refusal and failure need different machine-readable results. Unsupported environments should fail closed without changing the ordinary product. Human control works best when it is part of the product flow, not an agent-side promise. What's next Next we will expand native live-origin verification as supporting browsers expose WebMCP, preserve raw evidence for agent discovery and invocation, and continue testing consent revocation and approval behavior across clients. The goal remains the same: useful agent collaboration with authority, privacy, and final control kept visibly in human hands.  1 2 3 



 
 PrintChum — Your Companion for Print-Ready Photos 

 

 1. Problem Statement 

 Creating standardized ID and document photo layouts is a daily necessity for photo studios, print shops, schools, and individuals. However, the existing workflow is plagued by significant friction: 

 
 Tedious Manual Workflows: Arranging multiple photo sizes (such as 2 × 2 in, 1 × 1 in, Passport, and Wallet sizes) in desktop software like Photoshop or MS Word requires manual cropping, repetitive copy-pasting, and tedious alignment calculations. 
 Physical Dimension Inaccuracies: Generic image editors often distort real-world physical dimensions during export or printing, leading to rejected government, passport, or school application photos due to incorrect millimeter specifications or DPI downsampling. 
 Severe Privacy Risks: Most online photo tools require users to upload sensitive portraits and identity documents to remote cloud storage, where images may be stored indefinitely, indexed, or exposed to data breaches. 
 Wasted Photo Paper: Without optimal 2D bin packing, manual sheet layouts result in low paper utilization and expensive photo paper waste. 
 

 

 2. Solution Overview 

 PrintChum eliminates manual layout preparation by delivering an automated, privacy-first, browser-local photo layout engine. 

 Users upload a photo once, adjust the crop framing, and select standard presets or custom packages. PrintChum’s deterministic layout algorithm instantly packs the required photo quantities onto the target paper sheet, overlays precision cutting guides and nameplates, and generates a print-ready PDF or triggers direct printing. 

 Privacy-by-Design Architecture 

 PrintChum processes images locally within browser memory : 

 
 Image cropping, color composition, nameplate rendering, layout packing, and vector PDF compilation occur entirely on the client side. 
 Customer photos are never stored in databases or permanent cloud storage . 
 External server communication is strictly limited to optional AI background removal, where images are processed in-memory and immediately returned to the client without persistence. 
 

 Mathematical Precision & Real-World Dimensions 

 PrintChum maps screen pixels to true physical print dimensions using exact unit conversion constants:
 1 in = 2.54 cm = 25.4 mm = 72 pt (PDF) = 300 px (at 300 DPI) 
The 2D shelf-packing engine optimizes the printable area after subtracting horizontal and vertical margins ($M_x$ and $M_y$):
 W printable = W paper − 2 ⋅ M x , H printable = H paper − 2 ⋅ M y 
Paper utilization efficiency is computed deterministically:
 Utilization Efficiency  ( % ) = ( ∑ i = 1 n w i ⋅ h i W printable ⋅ H printable ) × 100 % 

 

 3. Key Features 

 
 Single Crop, Multi-Size Distribution: Crop and position a portrait once; PrintChum automatically resizes, frames, and renders it across multiple target dimensions (2 × 2 in, 1 × 1 in, 1.5 × 1.5 in, Passport, 2R, Wallet, or Custom sizes). 
 Deterministic Layout & Multi-Page Pagination: Automatically arranges mixed photo sizes with customizable margins, horizontal/vertical spacing, and auto-rotation (0° or 90°), cleanly overflowing onto subsequent pages when needed. 
 Precision Cutting Guides & Annotations: Renders corner crop marks, dashed cutting lines, and dimensional labels for effortless trimming with rotary or guillotine paper cutters. 
 Dynamic Nameplates for IDs: Add customizable nameplates (inside or outside the photo frame) supporting Full Name, ID/Student Number, Department, Role, and custom styling (fonts, background colors, and borders). 
 Reusable Studio "Service Sets": Save and load recurring package presets (e.g., "Package A: 2 pcs 2x2 + 8 pcs 1x1 on 4R Paper" ). 
 Direct Vector PDF Export & 300 DPI Printing: Export vector-coordinate PDFs via pdf-lib at 72 points/inch with embedded 300 DPI image assets for crisp, uncompressed physical prints. 
 Agentic WebMCP Integration: Native browser-level Model Context Protocol (WebMCP via document.modelContext ) enabling browser AI assistants to configure layouts, apply presets, and control the editor programmatically. 
 

 

 4. Technologies Used 

 Frontend & Application 

 
 Framework: Next.js (App Router, React 19) 
 Language: TypeScript 
 Styling & UI Components: Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Radix UI, Lucide React 
 State Management: Zustand 
 Form Handling & Validation: React Hook Form, Zod 
 

 Graphics, Layout & Export 

 
 Image Framing & Cropping: react-easy-crop , HTML5 Canvas API 
 Layout Engine: Custom framework-independent 2D shelf-packing & pagination algorithm 
 PDF Compilation: pdf-lib (point-accurate physical coordinate rendering) 
 Printing Engine: Native Browser Print API & Print-Specific CSS ( @media print , @page ) 
 

 

 5. Target Users 

 
 Photo Studios & Freelance Photographers: Rapidly prepare standard client packages without opening complex desktop editing suites. 
 Print Shops & Internet / Computer Cafes: Serve walk-in customers seeking quick ID package prints with automated layout packing and zero paper waste. 
 Schools, Universities & HR Departments: Standardize ID badge photo formatting and student/employee nameplates at scale. 
 Individual Job Seekers & Travelers: Create exact-dimension passport, visa, resume, and government ID photos at home with guaranteed sizing compliance.

title: InclusivePatch
pitch: Repair accessibility barriers with an agent, approve every change, and prove the keyboard journey works.
about_excerpt: Repair accessibility barriers with an agent, approve every change, and prove the keyboard journey works. Like Comment Story Updates InclusivePatch Inspiration Accessibility testing often ends with a report. A scanner finds missing labels, broken keyboard navigation, poor contrast, or inaccessible form behavior. Then the real work begins: a developer must understand each issue, choose a fix, modify the interface, and test the entire journey again. I wanted to explore a different question: What if an AI agent could work directly with the developer on the live web experience, not just explain an accessibility report? That idea became InclusivePatch . InclusivePatch is a human-and-AI accessibility remediation workspace powered by WebMCP. Instead of giving ChatGPT screenshots or copying errors into a conversation, it exposes structured tools that let an agent understand and interact with the same live page the developer is reviewing. What it does InclusivePatch demonstrates the complete accessibility repair lifecycle: Scan → Review → Fix → Replay The demo contains a checkout with six intentionally planted accessibility issues, including missing form labels, incorrect focus order, a keyboard trap, validation messages that are not announced, low-contrast text, and an ambiguous accessible name. Using WebMCP, an AI agent can scan the checkout, inspect evidence, retrieve allowed remediation options, and stage bounded fixes. The agent never silently modifies the page. Every proposal is visible for human review, and the developer can approve it, reject it, or revise subjective wording before anything is applied. After approved fixes are applied, InclusivePatch replays an 11-step keyboard-only journey and deterministically verifies whether the experience is now usable. It also shows a before-and-after comparison and preserves a history of agent actions, human decisions, patches, and verification results. How we built it InclusivePatch is a React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite and deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. The visible interface and the WebMCP executors share one typed workspace engine, so both operate on exactly the same application state. The application exposes ten narrow, phase-aware tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Zod validates every tool input. The accessibility layer combines axe-core with deterministic fixture probes, while browser localStorage preserves the synthetic workspace state. JSON and Markdown remediation manifests are generated locally. There is no embedded chatbot, unrestricted selector input, arbitrary JavaScript execution, or generic DOM mutation tool. Available tools change with the workspace phase, and every mutation creates visible, version-bound evidence. How WebMCP is used InclusivePatch exposes structured tools to: Scan the current checkout Read the workspace state Inspect an accessibility issue Retrieve allowed remediation options Stage a fix Apply approved fixes Replay the keyboard journey Compare the original and repaired versions Undo a change Export the remediation manifest When the agent stages a fix, the developer sees it immediately in the UI. If the developer rejects a proposal, the agent can read the updated state and adapt. That shared live state makes WebMCP fundamental to the experience rather than an API added beside it. Challenges we ran into The hardest design question was how much authority the AI agent should have. A broad modify_page tool would be flexible but difficult to constrain, audit, or trust. InclusivePatch instead exposes small actions with predefined remediation options. Every write is validated, versioned, recorded, and—where judgment is involved—subject to explicit human approval. Another challenge was proving that a fix actually improved accessibility. InclusivePatch does not stop after changing the page. It executes the same deterministic keyboard journey before and after remediation, so improvement is verified rather than assumed. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human-in-the-loop remediation lifecycle in one shared interface Six deterministic accessibility findings backed by axe-supported and fixture-specific probes Ten strictly validated, phase-aware WebMCP tools Bounded and reversible proposals instead of arbitrary page mutation Human rejection and linked revision of subjective accessible wording An 11-step deterministic keyboard journey with before-and-after evidence An auditable activity history and portable remediation manifest 43 unit, integration, and contract tests plus five Chromium end-to-end tests A 20/20 Codex CLI first-tool-selection evaluation What we learned The most useful agent experience is not necessarily an autonomous agent that replaces the interface. A stronger pattern is: Human controls the intent. AI coordinates the work. Deterministic software verifies the result. WebMCP makes that collaboration possible inside the web application. We also learned that small tools with clear inputs, predictable side effects, and verifiable outputs are substantially more reliable than broad generic tools. What's next for InclusivePatch InclusivePatch currently focuses on one controlled checkout so the human-agent workflow can be demonstrated clearly and reliably. Future versions could scan larger applications, support multiple accessibility journeys, connect fixes to source components, generate implementation patches and pull requests, integrate with CI accessibility testing, and build remediation histories across releases. The larger vision is not another accessibility scanner. It is an accessibility engineering workflow in which an AI agent helps developers move from finding a problem to proving that the user experience has actually been repaired. Try it Live application: https://inclusivepatch.aiconic-innovations.workers.dev Source code: https://github.com/1aifanatic/inclusivepatch-webmcp-challenge Demo video: https://youtu.be/4kPJV9zc7Ps No account or credentials are required. The checkout and all entered data are synthetic. Built with WebMCP, React, TypeScript, Vite, Zod, axe-core, Playwright, Vitest, and Cloudflare Workers. title: Stack Underflow: your AI agent plays in the office
pitch: A 3D office comedy where your browser AI agent joins as a robot coworker - it walks, talks, waves, and writes its own lines. No API keys, no backend: WebMCP makes it a player, not a remote control.
about_excerpt: A 3D office comedy where your browser AI agent joins as a robot coworker - it walks, talks, waves, and writes its own lines. No API keys, no backend: WebMCP makes it a player, not a remote control. Like Comment Story Updates Hello, I'm your AI Companion in Stack Underflow! Conversation with a player - agent responding live! With options... AI agent relaxing in our conference room, among the trees... Making friends with our Junior Developer (npc) First day with AI Agent, next to our amazing reception Agent observes new colleagues - what they are talking about? Title screen listing 24 WebMCP tools (after compatibility verification) Inspiration Every agent demo we have seen does the same trick: screenshot the page, guess the pixels, click like a tourist. We asked a different question - what if the agent was not operating the game, but playing it with you as a character? So we built Stack Underflow: a 3D office comedy where you are an AI/IT trainer at a delightfully dysfunctional software company, and your browser's AI agent can join as a robot coworker . It has a desk. It walks to people, interacts, jokes. And when you talk to it, the agent writes the robot's lines - and the reply options it offers you - on the spot. The kicker: the game ships zero AI infrastructure . No API keys, no backend, no per-player cost. The model is already in your browser. WebMCP lets the page hand it tools; the player brings the intelligence. What it does A full 3D office sim: 14 coworkers with schedules, moods, gossip and speech bubbles, quests, a four-period day, an economy that can bankrupt you, and a coffee machine the whole company runs on. 24 WebMCP tools that turn your agent into a second player. It joins as a named character with a personality it keeps, looks around, walks to people and rooms by name , steps and turns like a human, plays gestures, and speaks in speech bubbles you can read across the office. Two-way conversations, live-authored. You can walk up and click the robot - or it walks over and starts talking to you . The agent writes every line, and the 1-4 replies you pick from, including which option ends the chat. Nobody has ever read this dialogue before. It was written seconds ago, for you. A wait_for_player_message long-poll that resolves the instant you click a reply - a push channel built on top of a pull-only protocol. Safety by design: the agent is a player, not an admin . It cannot touch your camera, answer your dialogue, or hand itself money (the tools for that were deleted on purpose). Destinations are names, never coordinates, so it cannot clip through the world. Its text is rendered, never executed. How we built it Three.js + TypeScript + Vite , no game engine. Every desk, wall, fridge and coffee machine is written in code - no downloaded assets. A thin WebMCP bridge probes the browser's model-context surface at load (the spec is still moving, so we detect rather than assume) and publishes all 24 tools with self-describing JSON Schemas, examples included. The robot is composed from the same pure functions the scheduled NPCs use - A* pathfinding, procedural walk cycles, furniture collision - so the agent obeys exactly the same physics you do. Because WebMCP calls are agent-initiated, the conversation handshake is a poll-and-supply state machine with a bounded wait: if the agent goes quiet, the robot shows an in-character "buffering..." line and the player is never blocked. A built-in setup guide hands every player a copy-paste prompt for their agent, delivered in-character by the receptionist. Deployed static on Vercel at play.devpowers.com, DNS through Cloudflare - the whole game is a static bundle, which is the point: no server means no AI backend to run. Challenges we ran into The protocol has no push. WebMCP is agent-initiated only, so "notify the agent the player replied" is impossible by design. Our first idea was polling every 5 seconds. The better answer: hold the tool call open and resolve it the instant the player clicks. Measured at 2.6 seconds against a 25-second ceiling - from the agent's side it feels like a notification. The spec is a moving target. Sources disagreed on the registration namespace, so the bridge probes document.modelContext , then navigator.modelContext , then the testing shim - a wrong guess would have been an invisible dead integration on the judge's machine. Keeping the agent honest. Early tool drafts included flag-setting and relationship editing. We deleted them: a player-agent that can grant itself reputation is not playing. Then we added a test that fails if that ever comes back. Unit tests could not see the real bugs. The dialogue panel did not exist until a player talked to a real NPC first, and the quest log silently swallowed clicks on the dialogue buttons. Both were found only by driving the full loop in a real browser through an injected WebMCP host - so that drive became a permanent end-to-end suite. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent stayed in character for 18 minutes unprompted — one continuous loop of tool calls: walking to the kitchen, "auditing" the coffee machine, confessing it had poured coffee into a maintenance port, and waiting for replies between each. Nobody scripted that. We only gave it a stage and a listener. The agent-authored dialogue renders in the game's own dialogue window, in the same font, in the same panel - indistinguishable from hand-written content until you realize you are reading something the game's author never wrote. It survived contact with its first players: played with own agent, laughed, and immediately filed bug reports (we are still in alpha version ;) 751 unit tests and a full browser e2e suite that plays the game entirely through WebMCP tool calls, exactly the way a judge would. Five days. First commit to submission, one solo developer , working with AI agents (ChatGPT/Codex, Google Antigravity, Claude, Zed) while building for them. What we learned WebMCP leverage is authoring, not clicking. Any agent can drive a UI through screenshots. Only a model resident in the browser can write a character into a game's dialogue system in real time. Design for what the API makes possible , not just faster. Design for the absent agent. The hardest work was every path where the agent is slow, silent, or gone: queued requests, bounded waits, in-character fallbacks. That is what makes it safe to ship the feature to real players. When a spec moves, probe. Ten lines of detection beat a wrong assumption you cannot patch after the deadline. What's next for Stack Underflow: your AI agent plays in the office This is day 5 of a longer story, and the current architecture is the foundation for it: Multiplayer offices - room codes for 5-10 players, humans and AI agents sharing one office. The agent companion was deliberately built outside the NPC scheduler: a remote player and a local agent are the same thing to the renderer, so so multiplayer is the next seat, not a rewrite - a room code maps cleanly onto a Cloudflare Durable Object (WIP). Agent-to-agent drama - your robot talking to someone else's robot while human players watch, interrupt, and take sides. Your personalized ChatGPT as your character - the agent who already knows your jokes joining the office as you . The quest engine, more in-game events, mini-games (to play together! Atari?), and more office disasters to survive. Built by a solo developer under Edukey (full-stack AI training company) and DevPowers (WebDev + AI powers for our clients to take control with WebMCP tools as well!) - this game is our showroom for what AI-augmented building feels like, and we practice what we teach. title: Hear My Site
pitch: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time.
about_excerpt: Give AI agents ears for the browser. Hear My Site exposes live page and meeting audio as WebMCP tools, so your local agent can understand what you hear and work with you in real time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI integrations treat the browser as a remote control: click this button, fill that form, or navigate to that page. We wanted to explore a more WebMCP-native question: What important context exists inside the browser that an agent cannot access just as effectively from a terminal or traditional MCP server? Live audio is one answer. Traditional browser automation surfaces such as the Chrome DevTools Protocol are excellent at exposing the DOM, network activity, screenshots, and input events, but live collaborative audio is not naturally represented as page state or a sequence of browser actions. Hear My Site turns that missing real-time modality into incremental semantic context that agents such as Codex can consume while the event is happening. While watching a tutorial, webinar, or online meeting, the human continuously receives information through the browser, but their agent hears nothing. Sharing that context usually requires recording the session, uploading audio, waiting for a transcript, or repeatedly copying captions into a chat. We wanted the browser to expose this transient, browser-native context directly, allowing the human and agent to attend to the same live event at the same time. The project began as Hear My Browser , an extension that works on websites we do not control. We then expanded the idea into Hear My Site : a headless package that lets websites provide the same capability natively, without requiring every visitor to install an extension. The result is not simply “MCP inside a browser.” The browser is part of the problem because it owns the live media streams, user permissions, page lifecycle, and shared experience that the agent needs to understand. What it does Hear My Site gives AI agents ears for browser applications. A website supplies its existing audio streams—such as local microphone audio and remote WebRTC tracks—and Hear My Site mixes and transcribes them using the provider configured for that experience. It currently ships with adapters for Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe while keeping the agent-facing interface independent of either provider. Across both integrations, Hear My Site exposes exactly three WebMCP roles: start listening, retrieve incremental context, and stop listening. Hear My Browser uses the default names: start_browser_transcription get_browser_transcript stop_browser_transcription Adopting sites can rename all three roles to match their product. Our meeting demo exposes them as join_meeting , follow_meeting , and leave_meeting . An agent can start listening, retrieve only the transcript segments it has not seen before, and stop when the task is complete. The incremental cursor-based interface is important for long sessions. Instead of repeatedly sending an entire meeting or lesson transcript into the agent's context window, the agent retains the latest cursor and requests only new segments. Our meeting demo shows the complete experience. Up to five people can join a lightweight WebRTC room, and each browser owns its own local transcription session. WebMCP joins through an explicit tool call, the room shows its presence and bounded live captions, and visitors never need to enter a transcription credential. This enables interactions such as: “Keep listening to this lesson and wait until I ask a question.” “What explanation did the speaker just give for event loops?” “Summarize the decisions made since the last time you checked.” “Which questions from this meeting have not been answered yet?” Hear My Browser provides the same tools for YouTube, webinars, and meeting websites that have not integrated Hear My Site themselves. How we built it We organized the project as a pnpm monorepo with three parts: A browser-only, framework-agnostic TypeScript package containing the shared transcription core. A WXT Manifest V3 extension that adapts Chrome tab capture to that core. A React and Vite meeting demo using WebRTC, a Cloudflare Worker, and Durable Objects for signaling and short-lived credential provisioning. The shared core separates browser audio capture, transcription transport, transcript storage, and WebMCP registration. Audio sources are dynamically connected through a Web Audio graph. An AudioWorklet converts the mixed signal into the format required by the selected transcription provider and emits small chunks suitable for low-latency streaming. Provider adapters handle Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and OpenAI GPT-Live-Transcribe. They normalize different authentication methods, session setup messages, audio formats, interim results, finalized utterances, errors, and connection lifecycles into one shared transcription state machine. Manual UI controls and WebMCP tool calls operate the same session and transcript store. The website can change providers without changing the three tools or the cursor format used by agents. Tools are registered with the current imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The extension keeps browser-specific responsibilities—tab capture, popup controls, Chrome storage, offscreen document lifecycle, and tab ownership—as adapters around the shared package. The meeting demo uses full-mesh WebRTC for up to five participants. Its Cloudflare Worker and Durable Object coordinate room membership, SDP, and ICE signaling, while the Worker also provisions constrained, single-use Gemini ephemeral tokens from a server-side secret. They never receive media or transcript text, and the long-lived key is never returned to the browser. Meeting media remains peer-to-peer, while transcription audio travels directly from each browser to Gemini. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was browser lifecycle management. Chrome requires a real user gesture before tab capture can begin, while an agent may invoke a WebMCP tool later. We designed the popup, background worker, offscreen audio document, and tool errors so this security boundary remains explicit instead of hiding it behind an unreliable fallback. Supporting multiple live transcription services required more than changing an endpoint. Providers differ in audio formats, authentication, session initialization, WebSocket events, connection limits, and how they represent interim and finalized text. We created a provider boundary that normalizes those differences without leaking provider-specific behavior into the WebMCP tools. This gives websites and agents one stable contract even as transcription services evolve. Long-running transcription introduced another challenge. Provider connections may expire or need rotation, but a lesson or meeting can continue much longer. The transport can reconnect while preserving the higher-level session, accumulated transcript, and agent cursor. Audio ownership was also subtle. Extension-captured tracks should stop when transcription ends, but WebRTC tracks borrowed from a meeting must continue carrying the call. The shared package therefore tracks ownership explicitly and cleans up only the resources it owns. Finally, WebMCP is still experimental. We deliberately target the current document.modelContext API and return a clear unsupported-browser error rather than shipping a deprecated alias, polyfill, or unverified fallback path. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Hear My Site is more than a browser automation demo. It brings a live, collaborative audio modality into agents such as Codex and gives them semantic access to transient browser-native context that would otherwise require a separate recording, upload, and backend transcription pipeline. We are also proud of keeping the agent interface intentionally small. Three tools express the complete lifecycle, while the cursor protocol makes continuous monitoring practical for real agent context windows. Hear My Site is not tied to one AI vendor. Gemini and OpenAI can both power the transcription layer, while websites and agents depend on one stable WebMCP contract. The provider is an implementation choice; the human-agent collaboration model remains the same. The extension, headless package, website UI, and WebMCP tools all operate the same live transcription state. In the product runtime, there is no second agent-only implementation that can drift from the user experience. Privacy is reflected in the architecture rather than only described in a policy. The meeting Worker never receives media or transcript text and never returns its long-lived Gemini key to the browser; the headless package does not persist credentials; and spoken content is identified as untrusted data rather than agent instruction. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the browser itself is part of the problem—not merely a convenient place to
