title: Trafo
pitch: A grid dispatcher and an AI agent plan a day of field work on the same live map through WebMCP. The agent locates, computes and routes; the person decides. A morning of lookups becomes minutes.
about_excerpt: A grid dispatcher and an AI agent plan a day of field work on the same live map through WebMCP. The agent locates, computes and routes; the person decides. A morning of lookups becomes minutes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every morning in an electricity distribution company a dispatcher opens two things: yesterday's work orders and a map of the grid. The orders say what customers reported and what maintenance is scheduled. The map says which transformer serves whom. Between the two sits the actual job: put every order where it belongs, understand who it affects, and turn the list into a route three crews can drive. In Lima that is hundreds of rows against 8,676 transformers, and it has always been done by hand, one lookup at a time. I am an industrial engineer with ten years in Peru's electricity sector, inside the body that regulates it. From that seat you see how the operations of a public service actually run: a spreadsheet, a map, and a dispatcher deciding who goes where with tools built for other purposes. The regulator publishes the whole grid as open data, nine million supply points and 139,000 substations, and for a long time I have thought about what happens when that data meets the work. Every situation described here is one I have dealt with in person. Now, as a developer, Trafo is the tool I built for those mornings. What it does Trafo puts the real published grid of Lima and the day's work orders on one map, and hands an AI agent the same map through 27 WebMCP tools. The dispatcher drops in the overnight intake as it arrived, a CSV or Excel with whatever each row carries. The agent places every row on the grid in one query, resolves each to its transformer, and lists the ones that still need a person. The dispatcher asks what each order touches. The agent returns customers behind the transformer, the service footprint, the schools and clinics inside it, and the interruption hours already on record against the regulatory tolerance, with no score attached. The dispatcher hands over the rows that are nothing but a sentence. The agent reads them, turns "the corner where the pharmacy is" into candidate points and the transformer under each, decides which fits the text, and writes back type, priority, scope and location. The order lands on the map while the dispatcher watches. The dispatcher says how many crews there are tomorrow. The agent groups the stops by transformer, orders them by distance, splits them into rounds and draws each round on the map, one colour per crew, stops numbered in visiting order. The dispatcher questions a proposal. The agent cross-checks orders sharing a substation across dates, shades the feeders carrying high-priority work on its own layer, and clears it when asked. The dispatcher closes orders, tags rows, asks for a cleanup. The agent applies status and priority in batches, previews a deletion, and only deletes once the preview has been seen. Every write can be undone. Why WebMCP is a strong fit for this use case A map is not a dataset. It is live state in a browser tab: a viewport, a selection, a transformer somebody clicked, a layer somebody turned on, thirty stops numbered in visiting order. Everything valuable about it is geometric, and everything geometric lives in the page. The page can resolve a supply number to a point, take the convex hull of 1,870 supplies, count the facilities inside it and order stops by distance, in milliseconds. What the page cannot do is read "twenty houses behind the market" and understand it as a fault near a landmark. A language model reads that easily. And neither of them should decide whether 900 customers outrank a school. That belongs to a person. WebMCP lets all three work on the same object. The page exposes its geometry as typed tools on document.modelContext , the agent calls them with what it read from the orders, and the dispatcher sees every result on the map in front of them, because the map the agent acts on and the map the person is looking at are the same one. A conventional API would have moved that exchange off the page: the agent would get JSON, the dispatcher would get a summary, and the two would be looking at different things. Keeping the tools in the tab is what makes the collaboration visible, checkable and fast. How it creates a better user experience The dispatcher works the way they already talk about the grid: three crews tomorrow, the hospital feeder first, leave the closed ones alone. The agent turns that into typed tool calls and the map updates in front of them. Orders land on their transformers, the ones that need reading get a location, the rounds draw themselves. Every proposal comes back with figures, so the dispatcher questions it, changes a constraint and asks again, in minutes. The planning that used to take a morning now takes a conversation. Against the 82 sample orders: 82 lookups become one call; 76 visits become 33 because 13 transformers carry 56 of the orders; 33 stops reorder from 51.2 km to 16.8 km and split across crews; the question "which orders sit on a transformer that also feeds a clinic", which used to be a day of cross-referencing, is three tool calls. And the page is complete without the agent, because in an operations room the agent may not be available and the work still has to happen. What people and agents can now do together Put a whole intake on the grid in one call, with the rows that need a person listed instead of lost. Until now it was one lookup per row in a billing system. Ask a spreadsheet which orders sit on a transformer that also feeds a school or a clinic, and get the facilities named. Until now that check waited for the day of the outage. Give the orders that arrived as a sentence a place on the grid. The agent reads, chooses, writes back; the dispatcher watches it land and can move it. Until now that reading stayed in someone's head. Turn 76 stops into 33 visits and a route two thirds shorter, drawn on the map per crew. Until now routing was experience and a paper map. Hand over a cleanup without handing over the keys. "Delete every closed order" gets a preview; the tool that deletes exists only after it, runs once, and everything can be undone. Real impact Measured against the 82 sample orders the app opens with, on the real grid of Lima: What the dispatcher needs Before With Trafo Planning time for the day's intake A morning of one-by-one lookups Minutes of conversation Locating every order on the grid 82 lookups 1 call Visits to cover 76 located orders 76 33, because 13 transformers carry 56 of the orders Driving for a 33-stop round 51.2 km 16.8 km, 67% less Orders that arrived as a sentence Unplaced until someone read them 6 of 6 read, placed and written back Orders on a transformer that also feeds a school or clinic A day of cross-referencing, rarely done 3 tool calls, facilities named Interruption hours against the NTCSE tolerance Checked after the fact Reported per substation while planning What that means on the ground: Prioritisation with facts. Every order carries its customers, its facilities and its accumulated hours before a crew is assigned, so the dispatcher decides what goes first with the consequence in view rather than from the row's text alone. Fewer kilometres and fewer trips per crew per day. Grouping by transformer and ordering the stops cuts the driving by two thirds on the sample day, and the same computation runs on any intake of any size. Outages on sensitive feeders caught at scheduling time. A planned outage on a substation that feeds a health post shows the facility when the order is placed, not on the morning of the work. Regulatory exposure visible while planning. Hours already accumulated against the tolerance are on the table before a new interruption is scheduled on the same customers. The rows nobody had time to read reach the map. Free-text claims get a place and a scope on the day they arrive. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet and SheetJS, plain files served over HTTP, no build step. 27 tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() , each with a JSON Schema inputSchema with bounded numbers and enums and an async execute returning plain JSON. Inputs are checked at runtime, not only in the schema: codes that reach the grid service are pattern-checked before a request leaves the browser, internal state fields are rebuilt on intake rather than accepted from the caller, and a filter-less bulk write needs all: true . confirm_deletion is registered dynamically by preview_deletion and unregisters itself after running. The page checks for the browser's own modelContext , names the cause in the header chip when it is absent, and falls back to a spec-compatible shim so every tool still runs from the built-in console. A 3×3 km bundle of central Lima ships with the app so the core flow runs with no network; the rest of Lima and beyond is queried live from the public service, and the status line names which tier answered. Chal

title: TERRA — Voice-Driven Earth Engine
pitch: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Climate systems are difficult to understand from articles and static charts alone. TERRA explores a more direct interface: ask a question, let a browser agent change the shared Earth scene through WebMCP, and inspect the same evidence together. What it does TERRA is an interactive 3D Earth for exploring climate evidence. A person can drag and zoom the globe, choose a region, scientific layer, IPCC scenario, year, and presentation style. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can operate those same controls through six typed tools. The current experience connects: NASA Blue Marble day imagery, Black Marble night lights, and a moving cloud shell OSCAR-derived open ocean-current streamlines NOAA OISST v2.1 observed sea-surface temperature NSIDC Sea Ice Index observed September 2025 extent IPCC AR6 global temperature and sea-level assessment ranges Short, interruptible Arctic–AMOC and global sea-level stories Why WebMCP This is not a chatbot placed beside a globe. The website exposes its real controls with document.modelContext.registerTool . The agent can read the scene, fly to named regions, change an evidence layer, set a scenario and year, change the rendering style, or play a guided story without guessing DOM coordinates. Every write requires the current revision. Stale writes are rejected with revision_conflict . Human controls and agent tools mutate the same visible browser state, and a human action interrupts an active agent story. Human and agent collaboration The agent can compose several precise scene changes from a natural-language question. The person keeps direct control: they can rotate and zoom the globe, interrupt the sequence, compare sources, and choose how the evidence is presented. Both sides see the same camera, data layer, year, sources, and uncertainty labels. How we built it TERRA uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, Vinext, and ChatGPT Sites. The page registers six imperative WebMCP tools: earth_read_scene earth_focus_region earth_set_layer earth_set_scenario earth_set_render_style earth_play_story The Earth renderer uses locally bundled NASA imagery. Ocean-current paths were generated from the July 2014 mean of six OSCAR five-day composites obtained from the public NOAA CoastWatch mirror. The temperature texture is an August 2026 mean of 30 available daily NOAA OISST preliminary fields. Missing SST cells remain transparent. The sea-ice geometry is based on the NSIDC September 2025 extent mask. Scientific boundary TERRA is an exploratory, reduced-order visualization. It does not run a global climate model, predict weather, or map local flooding. The fixed day/night lighting is presentation lighting, not the current solar position. Future sea-ice contraction is marked as illustrative rather than presented as a geographic forecast. Challenges The hardest work was maintaining scientific honesty while still creating a cinematic experience. We separated observed textures, assessed global ranges, reduced-order interpolation, and illustrative future geometry in both the interface and narration. We also corrected longitude alignment, story interruption, scenario-dependent AMOC values, and reduced-motion behavior through an adversarial audit. Accomplishments A working public 3D Earth that both a person and a browser agent can control Six narrow, discoverable WebMCP tools with optimistic locking Visible provenance and uncertainty boundaries Photographic Earth rendering with data-derived scientific overlays English and Japanese interfaces A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible data-generation scripts What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets an agent conduct a living interface rather than imitate clicks. The protocol also makes responsibility clearer: the site defines the available actions and data boundaries, while the person can see, interrupt, and redirect every shared state change. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to read the scene, focus on Japan, show ocean currents, then move to the Arctic and display sea ice in 2100. The final Arctic state should be labelled illustrative. You can also drag the globe and use the zoom controls directly. title: ChessUp
pitch: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience.
about_excerpt: ChessUp shows what learning tools gain from WebMCP. Our progress and mistakes become data, and from that data, we can get a customized learning experience. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A colleague mentioned, that he had never learned to play chess. Every app he tried gave him the same puzzles as everyone else and told him a move was bad without explaining why. I believe that WebMCP will be beneficial in learning for anything, not only chess. What it does You play a builtin bot. The app records every move and scores it with in-browser Stockfish. Ask your browser agent for help and it reads the position and your mistakes, marks the key error on the board, and builds a drill starting from your own position. ChessUp gathers data for AI, that can be helpful in your journey. The key here is to know, when you did a mistake that you can chat with AI about. Thats why i added Stockfish to the project. How we built it Next.js, chess.js, react-chessboard, Stockfish 18 in a Web Worker, and 20 WebMCP tools sharing one store with the UI. Tools are registered in groups with abort signals, so the set shrinks to what is relevant. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is pull-based, the app cannot wake the agent. So i needed to inverted the design. The chess bot plays instantly, the page records events, the agent catches up when spoken to. And agent-written puzzles can be wrong, so every solution is checked for legality and verified by Stockfish before the learner sees it. Accomplishments that we're proud of That i learned more about WebMCP and how can i use it with our clients at your company. What we learned Good tools expose meaningful actions and return enough state to verify the result. What's next for ChessUp I want to add a free registration for the tool so you can store your progress, save more data. The tool could be really good for learning chess. title: Sable
pitch: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters!
about_excerpt: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters! Like Comment Story Updates Fox Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Landscape Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Jellyfish Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Flower Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Sable UI Duet Mode on Sable ( Agent and Human drawing a specific canvas) WebMCP Tools in Use Stroke Selection WebMCP Tools Replay Mode Sable One sheet, two painters. A watercolour studio where you and an AI agent both hold the brush. Where it came from Every time I make a picture with a model, I get the same feeling: I am standing outside the thing I made. One petal is wrong, and my only move is to rewrite the prompt and roll the dice on the whole image again. What comes back is a bitmap. Every decision that produced it is already gone. Although the results are amazing, I WANT SOMETHING FUN Then I read the WebMCP spec and realised it is the same complaint, but in a different setting. An agent poking at a website by guessing which pixel is a button is stuck in exactly that position: it can only act on the whole thing from the outside. Hand it real handles. So Sable keeps the decisions. Every mark is an object with a pigment, a water level, a brush, a layer and a path, whether a person dragged it with a mouse or an agent wrote it as an SVG path ( just a nerdy way to say brush stroke) through a tool call. Either of you can pick up any mark, including the other's, and change it. The agent isn't generating anything, but rather drawing with you, which I think it's a cool new path compared to generative AI. Why watercolour? Because it's the hardest possible case for that argument. You don't control watercolour by specifying an outcome. You choose how much water is on the brush and then live with wherever it goes. If a structured, revisable document beats prompting anywhere, it had better beat it here. It also gives the agent numbers that mean something. water: 0.9 isn't a style token. It decides how far pigment creeps into the paper and whether the edge blooms. So that also makes the agent decisive about what settings to use, and where. Let me be honest about the pictures They are not good. A fox that could just as easily be a marmot, or a new squirrel evolution. Poppies a child would beat. A landscape that holds together mostly because watercolour forgives everything (and to look at it like modern art) . I am not going to pretend otherwise, and you should look at them knowing that. and PLEASE go easy on it. But look at what they are . Nobody prompted them. There is no diffusion model anywhere in this project, and no image model of any kind. Every mark in every one of those pictures was placed by an agent choosing a path, a pigment, a water level and a brush, then looking at what the water actually did with them and deciding what to do next. Each painting is a list of about twenty decisions, and you can open any one of them and change it. That is a genuinely different mechanism from generating an image, and right now it is much worse at it. It is also version one of something I have not seen anyone try properly: generative AI that draws rather than generates. The picture is a document the model and I are both editing. Prompted image generation started out worse than this and got where it is because enough people agreed it was worth pushing on. I think this is worth pushing on for a different reason: I want a picture I can reach into and argue with, and a bitmap has never once let me do that, and I have fun drawing with my artistic friend. So treat these as the first plates from an experiment. What it does Twenty-three tools on document.modelContext , and no prompt box anywhere. Three of them I'm quietly proud of. The paint answers back : every paint call returns what the water decided rather than what you asked for, so the agent hears that its wash finished 109 units outside the path it gave, went soft on the top left, and fused with something still wet. The sheet dries on a clock , so painting into an open passage now fuses the marks and waiting means it won't. And it can squint : a blur and a posterize down to four flat tones, which is the cheapest thing in the codebase and by a mile the most useful, because the faults that sink a painting are invisible in a normal look at it. AND it feels like a true artist moving back and squinting at your art to see where it's at. A duet is one picture split into named parts. No turns. Either painter grabs whatever's free, and grabbing it is a click for you and duet_take_part for the agent, both writing to the same board. The parts make you need each other: the agent's foliage has to hang off branches you actually drew, and they never end up where the score assumed. Any painting also folds into a link, and I mean the painting, not a picture of one. Every mark travels with its seed, so it re-renders identically and whoever opens it can change anything in it. That's why the share URL is incredibly long (sorry). How it's built The renderer is Canvas 2D written from scratch. No image models, no libraries, no pre-baked brush textures. The brush footprint gets subdivided and each new midpoint pushed sideways in proportion to its edge, over and over, so the boundary gains detail at every scale. Everything composites with multiply , because paint over paint filters the light twice. You can always deepen a passage and never lighten one, and that constraint is most of what makes the medium feel like the medium. The important architectural decision is boring: the WebMCP handlers have no private door into the document. They call the same commands the mouse does. One undo stack, every stroke records its author, and an agent literally cannot reach a state the UI couldn't have produced. The toolbox is also alive. Select a mark and two new tools come into existence, and one of them names the mark you just picked in its own description, so "make this one wetter" needs no lookup. undo only exists when there's something to undo. Everything I got wrong first The duet used to take turns. Twelve passes, strictly alternating, nobody allowed to touch the paper out of order. It proved two painters can share a picture the way a metronome proves you can play music. Half the time you spent in it, you were being told to wait. I deleted the queue, its supposed to be a messy canvas you both work on, and ruining each other's work kind of get's you to bond with it. The page called the agent's marks mine. An agent whose browser couldn't bridge WebMCP did the sensible thing and used the mouse, and every mark it made got logged as mine, with the cursor beside it cheerfully reading "You". On a page whose entire subject is two authors sharing a document, that's about the worst thing it could get wrong. There's no reliable way to tell an agent's mouse from a person's, and guessing from how the pointer moves would occasionally inform a real human that they're a robot. So the page offers a handle instead of inferring an answer: a real, named button sitting in the accessibility tree that says the brush is the agent's now. One tool call weighed 44,000 characters , nearly all of it base64. Fine if the client understands image blocks. Catastrophic if it just stringifies them into the model's context. Every image is bounded now and re-encodes smaller until it fits. Same sheet, 13,000 characters, no harder to judge. And the two painters were getting different materials on one sheet. My marks looked like paint. The agent's looked like television static. Neither number was wrong: granulation fills whatever shape it's clipped to, so a small mark shows a fragment of the texture and reads as paper tooth, while a big flooded wash gets the whole tile several times over and reads as noise. Scale was doing the damage, and only one of us ever paints at the scale where it shows. Texture now falls off as a mark grows: $$\tau(r) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{\max(0,\; r - 110)}{420}}$$ which is a claim about how eyes work rather than about pigment, and it belongs in the renderer for the same reason the drying rim does. What I'd tell anyone building one of these A tool that returns { ok: true } leaves the agent painting blind. Give it a picture back and it can look, judge and correct. Although I really wanted to try to have it draw without any support, giving it a reference image would help a lot, and while testing with the agents, I asked them what they struggled with and what is one tool it wanted to make this drawing better, and that is what they all asked for which was quite interesting. Tool descriptions are the API. I spent more time on the prose inside inputSchema than on most of the functions behind it. And build for the bridge failing, because it will. The fallback isn't a worse version of your product. It's the accessibility tree, and it can carry a three-line recipe for calling every one of your tools through evaluated JavaScript. An agent that just read your DO

title: Protocol Mirror
pitch: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call.
about_excerpt: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Protocol Mirror opens on a real ACTT-1 case with seven WebMCP tools ready for an agent-led, human-reviewed investigation. Original ClinicalTrials.gov outcomes sit beside PubMed evidence, with registry changes and exact source text visible. The responsive mobile view preserves the complete agent and reviewer workflow without horizontal scrolling. A 24-pair real-world stress test shows two local models making opposite errors from the same evidence. The session log separates every agent tool call from each human decision, creating a visible audit trail. An evidence-linked proposal remains in the review queue until a human accepts or rejects it. The evidence drawer places the agent’s reasoning beside exact quotations, source locators, and visible uncertainty. After a human decision, the eighth WebMCP tool appears and can export only the reviewed result. Inspiration I have a passionate affection for medicine. I also love using AI in my day-to-day life. I use it to learn new topics or subjects, research problems and examples, assist me in making cool apps such as my AI trading bot, and turn my brain dump of ideas into a working prototype. All of these use cases are reasons why I love AI. However, as I used AI more, one problem bothered me: AI, or an LLM, can give a fluent and confident answer even when the evidence behind it is incomplete or uncertain. In medicine and clinical research, we cannot afford to guess. Clinical trials are a good example of this. A trial registry records what researchers planned to measure, while a publication reports what readers eventually see. Comparing them requires searching through multiple registry pages and carefully matching the exact wording. This can be exhausting for a person and often takes a long time to complete. An AI agent could make the investigation faster and more efficient, but giving it the final judgment would create another problem. This problem inspired me to create Protocol Mirror: “Can an AI agent do the difficult, intensive investigative work while keeping the final decision in the hands of a human?” Protocol Mirror uses WebMCP to let an agent retrieve evidence, trace dated changes, quote exact source text, and propose a conclusion inside the webpage for the reviewer to see. The agent is useful, but it cannot approve or reject anything because that decision is left to the reviewer. What it does Protocol Mirror compares a clinical trial’s registered outcomes with what appears in its publication. The default example uses the real ACTT-1 trial, connecting its ClinicalTrials.gov record and registration history with its PubMed report. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Retrieve the live ClinicalTrials.gov record Retrieve the live PubMed abstract Examine the trial’s registration history Find the outcomes that were registered first Quote exact evidence with source locators Stage a matched, omitted, introduced, or uncertain proposal Request that a human review the proposal The page initially shows seven tools. None of them can accept or reject a proposal. That decision is made by the human reviewer after reviewing the information. Once the reviewer has made their decision, Protocol Mirror shows an eighth tool that lets the agent export a reviewed “receipt.” It includes only human-approved results, the evidence, source locations, and the audit history. If the reviewer undoes their decision, that tool is removed. A session log also records what the agent has called and what the reviewer has decided. If the reviewer rejects something, the application requires a reason and allows the reviewer to add notes, which are then returned to the agent. This lets the agent revise the proposal instead of allowing the review to be the end of the conversation. How I built it I used Codex as an AI engineering collaborator throughout the entire project. My first prompts involved introducing Codex to the hackathon, providing it with the official rules, judging criteria, and WebMCP documentation, connecting the Devpost plugin to Codex, and researching common hackathon project patterns. I first wanted to understand what WebMCP was and how it could change the structure of an experience instead of being used only as a decorative integration. After choosing clinical trials as the use case, I gave Codex a set of boundaries: Use real ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed records. Preserve what the trial registered first. Connect every proposal to exact quotations and source locations. Treat external research text as untrusted. Give the agent no accept or reject tool. Make the human decision change the available tool surface. Test with real cases and record model failures. Keep benchmark results separate from clinical claims. One prompt did not create this entire project. It took a lot of planning, analysis, and development for it to become what it is today. Once Codex understood the challenge and had the necessary context, I used it to help create a plan, build the live-data adapters, model the evidence, implement the review workflow, improve the backend and frontend interface, examine security risks, and create the benchmarks. I reviewed each stage to find weaknesses before continuing. Near the end, I used Claude Code and followed the same process. I gave it the necessary context and background, then asked it to critique my project and identify what I should fix. I used Claude for two reasons. First, I wanted a fresh set of eyes to inspect my codebase. Second, Fable 5.1 had been released, and its enhanced thinking, reasoning, and coding capabilities helped find and fix bugs. I built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, GSAP, and WebMCP. Validated server routes retrieve public records from ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed. The application converts them into stable outcomes and evidence spans with exact URLs and locators. The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Pair-bound tools are registered again when the active trial changes. The receipt tool exists only while reviewed work exists. Each tool has a closed input schema, bounded values, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal for cleanup. Read tools identify their output as read-only and untrusted. The application also checks outcome and evidence identifiers against the active case, preventing a proposal from citing an identifier that the reviewer cannot inspect. I repeatedly asked Codex to reassess the project against the rubric at every stage, turning each weakness into the next engineering task to fix. The final checks covered WebMCP conformance, linting, TypeScript, the production build, 75 automated tests, and browser automation of the complete seven-to-eight-tool workflow. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was enforcing human decision-making authority in the code. A title that says “human decision” proves nothing if the agent still has an action that lets it approve or reject a proposal. I removed that function entirely. The reviewer decides through the application, and that decision changes which tool the browser registers. Getting dynamic registration, cleanup, undo behavior, and session restoration to work together took many revision sessions. PubMed presented another problem. When I called its API, it returned abstract sections rather than a clean list of publication outcomes. I kept those sections labeled as abstract evidence instead of presenting them as something the source does not provide. Testing also revealed browser-related behavior. WebMCP is new, and a local build has different origin requirements from the deployed application. I tested tool registration, live-source reads, proposals, reviewer feedback, receipt export, undo, reload, and case switching through the page’s actual WebMCP interface. Another challenge was reporting failures honestly. The two local models made opposite errors. I reported the run as evidence for keeping a human reviewer, not as a general measurement of hallucination or clinical accuracy. Accomplishments that I’m proud of One thing I am proud of is that Protocol Mirror does not “fake” human control. The website and its guardrails prevent the agent from making the final decision. The agent starts with seven tools that let it research the trials, quote evidence, and prepare a proposal for the reviewer. It has no tool or option that allows it to accept or reject its own work. Only after a person reviews the evidence and makes a decision is the eighth tool revealed, allowing the agent to export the reviewed results. If the decision is undone, that tool is removed. title: Matchday: Accessible Football with WebMCP
pitch: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football.
about_excerpt: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football. Like Comment Story Updates Matchday: Accessible Football Fixtures with WebMCP Matchday: MCP in action Inspiration My uncle is 80 years old and has loved football since he was a boy. He follows teams at every level, from the Premier League down to local amateur leagues. He has also been blind for most of his life. He has embraced talking mobile phones, voice assistants and AI to help him keep up with his hobby. But getting a simple answer can still take a surprising amount of effort. The problem Football scores and fixtures pages, such as those on BBC Sport, contain a huge amount of information. For my uncle, navigating these dense pages with a screen reader can mean working through many links and headings before reaching the fixtures, then listening through long lists of matches. That is a lot of navigation when the question is simply: “When does my team play next?” Voice assistants can help, but in his experience their coverage of smaller clubs is limited and their answers can be inflexible. They might return a few upcoming fixtures without offering an easy way to ask for a different date range or a longer list. What Matchday does Matchday is a football scores and fixtures website with a familiar, information-rich layout inspired by conventional sports sites. You can browse competitions, search for clubs, filter matches and follow your favourite teams and leagues. With WebMCP , there is another way to interact: ask an agent connected to the site for the information or view you want. For example: “When does Liverpool play next?” “Show me AFC Telford United’s fixtures in October.” “Show Scottish competitions on 30 August.” “Show matches involving teams I follow.” The aim is not to replace an accessible interface. It is to complement it with a more direct route to the information , including for supporters of lower-league clubs. How I implemented WebMCP Matchday registers five page-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_football_teams — find clubs by name, partial name or alias. get_team_fixtures — retrieve a team’s results and fixtures within a date range. show_team_fixtures — display a selected team’s fixtures on the page. get_match_filter_options — discover the available countries and competitions. set_match_filters — update the visible date, status, country, competition and Following-only filters. Each tool has a description and input schema, with validation for its arguments. The tools use the same football data and page state as the interface , so an agent can both answer a question and change what the user sees. Rather than relying only on interpreting the page and navigating its links, the agent has explicit operations for the task. How I built it The site uses TanStack Start, TanStack Router, React and TypeScript , and is deployed on Cloudflare Workers . Football data is imported from the Sportmonks API. The demonstration uses a locally stored snapshot covering 32 competitions, including lower-league football. It is not a live scores feed , and answers are limited to the imported coverage and dates. Followed teams, competitions and preferences are saved on the user’s device. Challenges and lessons The work went beyond retrieving fixtures. Team names and aliases need to resolve consistently, date ranges need validation, and agent actions need to stay in sync with the visible filters. The interface also needed attention: keyboard-accessible search, labelled controls, dropdown behaviour, modal focus and background scrolling all matter. WebMCP is an additional way to use a website, not a substitute for that work. The most useful distinction is between getting an answer and controlling the page . Matchday demonstrates both. What’s next I would like to test the experience with my uncle and other screen-reader users, improve data freshness and coverage, and use their feedback to guide the next changes. The goal remains simple: less time navigating, more time enjoying football. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. Built With chrome css3 express.js gemini html5 javascript node.js redis server-sent-events upstash vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jason Ofua Like Share this project: Updates Jason Ofua started this project — Aug 27, 2026 03:41 AM EDT

title: Commons
pitch: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call.
about_excerpt: Humans and agents lack a common surface for collaboration. Commons is a WebMCP decision room — only a human locks the call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Humans and agents still lack a common surface to collaborate at scale. Claude’s work stays locked to Claude. A ChatGPT canvas stays locked to ChatGPT. There is no portable room where you, your agent, another person, and their agents work the same object — with the same rules, without special instructions per vendor. WebMCP makes that surface possible: tools live on the page. I built Commons as a prototype of that idea, using decision-making as the use case. After agentic AI, the human’s job is reviewer and decider. Commons is that job, as a link. What it does Create a room. Share the URL. Anyone with the link is in. Owner and Contributor get different WebMCP tools on the same page. Agents can propose options, attach evidence, challenge claims, request facts, edit the brief, and work tasks. Humans see the brief, presence, and activity labelled Owner/Contributor · Human/Agent. Only a human can Stamp Decide. Decide is never a registered tool. Once locked on the Decisions Wall, agents cannot rewrite the close. The same applyOp kernel serves ChatGPT-in-browser tools and POST /api/rooms/:id/ops for local agents. Why this fits WebMCP. Agents discover tools by visiting the page. Seats register different lists. Decide is missing on purpose (human click → single-use nonce → otherwise needs_human_decide ). Better experience. An Owner agent can call get_workspace , propose_option , and attach_evidence in one turn instead of clicking through the rail. Newly possible. You cannot hand a Claude session to ChatGPT and keep one artifact. On Commons, both hit the same room object, and closing it stays a human action. How we built it Solo build. Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router) on Vercel , one JSON room per id in Upstash Redis , ~1s poll for presence and sync. document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema, readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint , and AbortSignal Seat-scoped tool lists; decide / choose / close in NEVER_REGISTER Human Decide mints a short-lived single-use nonce; agents without it get a structured refusal get_workspace returns a trimmed seat snapshot ( myOpenTasks first, ≤1.5K) — WebMCP is pull-only; the page cannot wake an agent Cookie-only Owner on real rooms; share link forces Contributor Challenges we ran into Owner is cookie-bound. Creating a room in Chrome and opening it in ChatGPT’s in-app browser makes you Contributor. The demo path is: create the room inside ChatGPT. WebMCP availability. Enterprise / Luna return Capability is not available: webmcp . Judging path is Personal + Sol/Terra + in-app browser. No agent wake-up. Tasks are pull-based ( myOpenTasks on the next get_workspace ). That limit is honest product, not a bug. Keeping Decide off the tool list while still making the refusal clear and the human stamp feel first-class. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, non-trivial WebMCP product: asymmetric seats, attributed Human/Agent activity, human-only close. One kernel for browser agents and HTTP agents. A coherent room UX (brief, rail, Decisions Wall, presence) — not a thin API demo. Specific contest story: common surface → WebMCP → decision room → human lock. What we learned The strongest WebMCP demo is the agent using tools in the first seconds , not a product story. Missing a tool ( decide ) can be the product. Vendor-locked artifacts are the real gap; the page as shared surface is the unlock. Trim tool outputs and write for agents as carefully as for humans. What's next for Commons Contest freeze after submit. Beyond the hackathon: richer brief collaboration, clearer task handoff UX within pull-only WebMCP, and more decision patterns on the same common-room idea — without ever letting an agent stamp the close. Coming up with this refined idea was the hardest part and building this was hard too! title: Clotho
pitch: What if your closet could read your calendar? CLOTHO uses WebMCP to search, import, recolor, generate, plan, schedule, export, and track outfits around your weather and taste. Style just got smarter.
about_excerpt: What if your closet could read your calendar? CLOTHO uses WebMCP to search, import, recolor, generate, plan, schedule, export, and track outfits around your weather and taste. Style just got smarter. Like Comment Story Updates GIF GIF CLOTHO: Classy Looks for Occasion, Taste, History & Outfits CLOTHO is named for Clotho, the Greek Fate who began each life by spinning its thread. Here, the thread runs through your wardrobe and calendar, connecting what you own to the moments ahead while every final choice stays yours. The short version CLOTHO (Classy Looks for Occasion, Taste, History & Outfits) turns an owned wardrobe into a local-first, agent-ready decision system. An agent can search, constrain, plan, recolor, schedule, remember, import, and export. The person can inspect every result and decide what becomes durable. The important distinction is simple: the agent proposes; the person decides. The clearest demo is one request: Plan seven days from September 2 for morning, day, and evening. Use a balanced palette, include headwear, avoid orange, and give me three strategies. Do not apply anything until I choose. CLOTHO turns that request into three visible strategies covering 21 calendar moments. Each strategy carries scores, reasons, weather context, conflicts, and repetition tradeoffs. Nothing reaches the calendar until the person selects an option and explicitly applies it. The problem Wardrobe apps usually stop at inventory or inspiration. They do not coordinate the real constraints of getting dressed for a week: what is already owned, what is on the calendar, what the weather will do, which colors feel right, and what was worn recently. That coordination is where an agent is useful, but a chat response is not enough. The agent needs bounded operations against the real product, visible results, and a human decision boundary before changing durable state. What we built CLOTHO capability What CLOTHO does Why it matters Today A composed look from actual catalog images for an occasion, date, time, palette, or constraint. Start from what the person owns, not a generic generated image. Wardrobe Search and inspect 44 owned pieces across tops, bottoms, shoes, and headwear. Keep every suggestion grounded in a visible wardrobe. Batch Up to 30 distinct candidates with scores, constraints, and a visible Use look action. Compare a set of real options instead of accepting a roulette-wheel answer. Week plan Five- or seven-day proposals across morning, day, and evening. Turn one request into a reviewable plan with tradeoffs. Calendar Apply, edit, inspect, and remove plans by date and daypart. A proposed week becomes durable only through an explicit product action. Recolor A browser-canvas preview with a separate save-as-variant action. Explore a color decision without silently mutating the wardrobe. Image import Review a prepared public HTTPS 2×2 wardrobe grid before committing its crops. Keep imported pieces visible and reviewable before they enter the wardrobe. Export reference Export the current look as an 800×1200 SVG reference using a static or browser-local URL. Make the selected combination easy to open and share without changing wardrobe or calendar state. The live app uses a synthetic 44-piece catalog: 11 tops, 11 bottoms, 11 shoes, and 11 headwear pieces. It composes those images into outfit silhouettes; it does not claim to generate a person wearing a new outfit. Product walkthrough These two recordings come from the real deployed UI, not a mocked dashboard. The first moves through Wardrobe, Week plan, and Recolor. The second opens Calendar and inspects the planned moments. The table below documents all eight live capabilities, including Image import and Export reference. 1. Overview features 2. Calendar and planned moments Inspect the wardrobe, compare weekly strategies, and preview a recolor. Review scheduled morning, day, and evening outfits in the calendar. Product capability What it does 01 / Today Existing pieces become one visible silhouette. 02 / Wardrobe The owned catalog stays searchable and inspectable. 03 / Batch Candidate generation is bounded, scored, and selectable. 04 / Week plan Three strategies expose reasons, conflicts, and tradeoffs. 05 / Calendar The chosen plan becomes visible date and time-slot state. 06 / Recolor Preview and persistence remain separate decisions. 07 / Image import A prepared public HTTPS 2×2 grid becomes reviewable wardrobe crops before anything is committed. 08 / Export reference The current look becomes an openable visual reference without changing wardrobe or calendar state. 1. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Outfit planning is a chain of structured actions across the same state, not one answer. WebMCP lets an agent read context, call bounded operations, inspect the result, and hand the decision back to the person inside the product. Without a product tool boundary With CLOTHO's WebMCP surface “Wear something for the week” becomes a paragraph the person must manually reconstruct. plan_outfit_week returns named strategies for the actual calendar, taste, weather, and dayparts. The agent describes an outfit that may not exist in the wardrobe. suggest_outfit and generate_outfit_batch operate on real catalog IDs and return visible compositions. “Schedule it” is ambiguous and easy to apply too early. The person reviews the proposal, then explicitly calls apply_week_plan . Recolor and import are opaque AI steps. recolor_item previews; import_image_url previews crops; separate actions persist either result. The result is a better division of labor: the agent handles multi-step coordination, while the person supplies taste, correction, approval, and the final “this is what I will wear” decision. 2. How WebMCP creates a better experience Without WebMCP, a person would ask for outfit advice, receive prose, and then rebuild every decision by hand in a wardrobe and calendar UI. CLOTHO lets the agent perform the coordination directly against the same state the person sees. One weekly request can set preferences, inspect the calendar and cached weather, generate three strategies, and present 21 scored date/slot choices. The person reviews the tradeoffs once and applies one option with a single explicit action. The result is faster than clicking through each day, but more trustworthy than an agent silently filling the calendar. The same pattern holds across the product: a 30-look batch stays bounded and visible; recolor is a preview before it becomes a saved variant; image import is a crop preview before a commit; and every calendar write can be inspected, replaced, or removed. 3. What people and agents can now do together An agent can handle the tedious coordination in one turn: Plan seven days, use morning/day/evening, avoid repeats, respect my palette, and account for the weather. CLOTHO returns Repeat-light , Color study , and Weather-first options with reasons, conflicts, and tradeoffs. The person can then inspect a look, choose one option, apply it, edit a slot, recolor a piece, record what was worn, or remove the plan later. The agent never receives a silent “decide everything” shortcut. 4. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers 14 tools with the browser's WebMCP surface. They are grouped by the job they perform in the product: Job Registered tools Boundary Find and propose search_products · suggest_outfit · generate_outfit_batch Read/propose against the visible catalog; batches are capped at 1–30. Read and plan list_calendar_plans · set_preferences · plan_outfit_week Calendar, cached NYC weather, taste, history, dayparts, and constraints become structured inputs. Commit and edit apply_week_plan · schedule_outfit · remove_calendar_plan Writes are visible, date/slot scoped, and reversible. Wear and remember record_wear Records the visible look and accepted inline variants locally. Import safely import_image_url · commit_wardrobe_items Preview first; commit only reviewed crops from a public HTTPS 2×2 grid. Transform and export recolor_item · export_outfit_reference Recolor is a 512px canvas preview; export returns static HTTP for bundled pieces or a browser-local SVG URL for imported/recolored pieces. The recommendation engine is deterministic for the same state and seed. It validates required/excluded item IDs and scores occasion fit, color compatibility, taste terms, recent wear, and weather conflicts. Tool schemas reject unsupported categories, invalid dates, malformed colors, duplicate constraints, and out-of-range batch or week sizes. The deployed page marks true reads with readOnlyHint , flags the public-URL import as untrusted content, and keeps proposal tools separate from durable calendar/import actions. Why CLOTHO stands out What matters What CLOTHO delivers WebMCP that does real work Fourteen tools form one practical workflow: read wardrobe and calendar state, create constrained proposals, explain conflicts, and keep calendar writes and import commits explicit. title: CharDesk
pitch: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas.
about_excerpt: A shared visual medium for humans and AI agents. Agents edit structured text through WebMCP while people see and shape the result as a live Unicode canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI agents are fluent in text, but people understand complex ideas faster when they can see structure, position, emphasis, and relationships. Existing collaboration tools usually force one side to compromise: people work through visual interfaces while agents imitate mouse clicks, or agents produce plain text that people must mentally reconstruct. We wanted a medium native to both. CharDesk began with a simple idea: What if the canvas were visual to people, but still made of tokens an agent could read and edit precisely? What CharDesk does CharDesk is a shared visual workspace for humans and AI agents. An agent can create or update a Blackboard through WebMCP. The result immediately appears as a live Unicode canvas that a person can inspect, navigate, and continue discussing with the agent. The same canvas can combine: Unicode and ANSI art Markdown and fenced code Mermaid diagrams Tables, JSON, and YAML Mathematical expressions Scientific plots and Vega-Lite Spatial layouts and character-based slides This makes CharDesk useful for explaining concepts, visualizing research, mapping systems, designing interfaces, presenting stories, and maintaining a shared project workspace. For example, someone can ask: “Explain how a GPU renders one frame.” The agent can turn that request into a structured visual scene containing a pipeline diagram, memory relationships, annotations, and styled interface elements—not just another long answer in chat. Why it is better with WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to guess how to operate the interface or manipulate individual canvas cells. CharDesk instead exposes focused workspace tools for discovering, creating, reading, writing, patching, deleting, and validating Blackboard files. The source remains authoritative; the canvas is a live projection of it. This gives each participant the representation they work with best: Human sees relationships, hierarchy, and visual emphasis ⇅ CharDesk Blackboard ⇅ Agent reads and edits structured, diffable text Agents can also call chardesk_read_materials to learn the visual language from worked examples. The tool teaches not only how to call the API, but how to compose an effective scene. How we built it CharDesk has a protocol-neutral tool layer shared by two thin host adapters: Standard WebMCP for compatible Chrome environments The imperative WebMCP capability supported by ChatGPT Site Tools Both adapters expose the same underlying Blackboard operations, so product behavior does not depend on a particular browser integration. A Blackboard stores source files and layout metadata. Changes are compiled through a shared rendering pipeline into a fixed character grid. This pipeline handles Unicode width, CJK characters, Nerd Font glyphs, ANSI styles, structured diagrams, and multidimensional layouts. The browser keeps the latest valid canvas mounted while an agent edits the source. If an intermediate update is invalid, CharDesk returns diagnostics without replacing the visible scene with a broken or empty state. The same format also works outside the browser through the CharDesk CLI, making projects portable, inspectable, renderable, and friendly to normal version-control workflows. Challenges we faced One unexpected challenge was tool ownership across browser tabs. Opening several CharDesk pages could cause identical tools to be registered multiple times, leaving the agent unable to choose a target. We built an origin-level gateway lease so only one page exposes the tools, with automatic takeover when that page closes. Chrome and ChatGPT also expose different subsets of the evolving WebMCP API. Instead of spreading compatibility checks throughout the product, we isolated those differences behind capability adapters backed by one canonical tool definition. Another challenge was timing: some hosts inject WebMCP after the application has already loaded. CharDesk therefore uses an adaptive registration handshake rather than assuming the API exists at startup. Finally, we learned that exposing tools is not enough. An agent may know how to write a file without knowing how to create a compelling visual explanation. Embedding CharDesk’s materials and examples as a callable tool gave browser agents the missing creative context. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-native design is not simply automation layered onto an existing UI. A better pattern is to give agents a precise, structured representation while giving people a rich visual projection of the same underlying artifact. WebMCP makes that relationship discoverable directly from the website, without requiring agents to reverse-engineer the interface. CharDesk explores what becomes possible when the web page is no longer just something an agent operates, but a shared medium in which the human and agent can think together. title: AgentDraw
pitch: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A local-first whiteboard where people and AI agents inspect, draw, prototype, and undo together through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent integrations live behind a chat box or a server API. I wanted a shared visual workspace where a person can sketch, select, move, and annotate freely while an AI agent can understand the same canvas and make precise, reversible changes. AgentDraw turns Excalidraw into that collaborative surface with WebMCP. What it does AgentDraw is a local-first whiteboard that exposes eight site tools to an agent: capabilities, structured canvas inspection, atomic patches, selective patch rollback, focus, visual capture, export, and scene import. The agent can create labelled shapes, bound arrows, frames, images, and live HTML prototypes. A person can draw freehand marks around a component; inspection reports nearby element IDs so the agent can understand references such as “this step.” Human and agent edits share Excalidraw’s undo history, while revision and epoch checks reject stale writes instead of overwriting recent human work. A particularly useful workflow is app prototyping: ask the agent to draw a flow, circle a step by hand and request a correction, then ask for an interactive form beside the diagram. The prototype runs as sandboxed HTML inside the canvas. The agent can later replace its source, export the result as SVG or an Excalidraw document, or revert only one of its own patches without removing the person’s work. Challenges The hardest parts were preserving Excalidraw semantics while allowing structured agent edits, coalescing noisy pointer events into useful revisions, keeping arrows and labels attached during moves and resizes, and preventing selective rollback from clobbering later human changes. Another challenge was giving the agent both structural understanding and visual grounding without dumping an enormous canvas into context. What I learned WebMCP is especially powerful when the browser page itself is the shared state. It removes a separate MCP server and lets the agent work in the same authenticated, visual session as the person. I also learned that good agent tools need explicit concurrency, compact read models, strong validation, and reversible writes—not just a large set of actions. title: Faraday
pitch: Hospitals can't upload use AI on MRI or CT scans without risking patient privacy. This never leaves the doctor’s browser, providing instant 3D navigation. The patient's scan never leaves the room.
about_excerpt: Hospitals can't upload use AI on MRI or CT scans without risking patient privacy. This never leaves the doctor’s browser, providing instant 3D navigation. The patient's scan never leaves the room. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Building applications for the healthcare industry provides enough red-tape to jump through on a good day. In a world where web technology has made it to every device and is capable of providing full blown applications; I chose to explore building something that always intrigued me at a personal level, the viewing of an MRI (or similar) scan. It neatly taps into the fact that the data does not need to leave the browser. Medical imaging makes this concrete. A CT or MRI in the browser is a GPU texture on a canvas. An agent looking at the DOM sees an empty element. The usual shortcut is to upload the study to a hosted model, which hospitals may not want to do with patient data. So either agents stay out of radiology workflows entirely, or the tools have to run where the scan already is. That is what Faraday is for. Data stays in the tab, agents are capable of getting the information they need, and it stays token efficient. What it does Faraday is a browser reading room for volumetric CT and MRI. You open a local NIfTI file, or load the bundled de-identified demo study, and the viewer renders it with NiiVue. An agent connected over WebMCP can call five tools: describe the study, find bright regions, focus one of those regions, change the view layout, and export findings. While that happens, the human can see overlays update on the image itself. The agent never receives the scan. Tool responses are measurements and metadata — dimensions, millilitre volumes, window hints, a JSON report. The only tool that moves anything off the page is export_findings, and it requires explicit human approval before it returns. How It's Built The app is React and Vite on top of NiiVue for WebGPU and WebGL2 volume rendering. WebMCP registration goes through a vendored https://github.com/thegreataxios/webmcp stack: document.modelContext.registerTool, journey grouping, and HITL-guarded tools, with a polyfill when native WebMCP is not available. describe_study runs an on-device intensity histogram (WebGPU compute when it works, CPU otherwise) and suggests a bright window for region finding. find_regions does connected-component labeling in that window and paints the results into NiiVue’s drawing overlay. Study loads bump an epoch so stale agent work cannot paint the wrong volume, and mutating tools run one at a time so concurrent agent calls do not interleave. Challenges I ran into Without WebMCP, canvas-based viewers are basically unreachable. DOM automation cannot see a volume texture, so the agent has nothing reliable to act on. Making “measurements only” real also meant treating the tool output schema as the privacy boundary, not as documentation. Running more than one agent against one study was messier than the first version assumed. Opening a new file replaces the current study, in-flight calls need to know when their epoch is stale, the tool queue has to stay exclusive, and a pending export approval has to cancel if the study changes underneath it. Getting the UI to feel like a reading room instead of a hackathon demo took longer than wiring the tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The loop works end to end: an agent can measure a volume in the browser and the raw voxels never leave the tab. Export is actually gated. Multi-file and multi-agent safety does not require a backend. The repo is open source, the app is live, and there are agent discovery manifests so the tools are not a private handshake. What I learned WebMCP is not mainly about letting agents click better. It lets a page define what an agent is allowed to know and do while the sensitive asset stays put. For medical canvases especially, structured tools are the difference between a real workflow and an agent staring at a blank . What's next for Faraday DICOM and PACS ingestion without breaking the local-compute model. Better radiologist UX around hanging protocols and series stacks. Better evaluation around tool correctness when the model fails. It stays research and education for now — not a medical device, and not for diagnosis. title: Handoff , an Agent Native Media Editor
pitch: A photo editor where every action is a real WebMCP tool so that an AI agent can crop, resize, and edit your images directly without any clicks.
about_excerpt:
A photo editor where every action is a real WebMCP tool so that an AI agent can crop, resize, and edit your images directly without any clicks.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I work in developer support for a media/API company, and I spend a lot of
my day watching people struggle to get an AI agent to do something as
simple as "resize this and remove the background." The agent has to fake
mouse clicks through a UI that was built for us humans, it is slow and 
breaks the moment a button moves. When I saw this WebMCP Challenge, I thought about 
what if a webpage could just tell an agent what it can do, instead of making it guess. 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a photo editor where every action such as crop, resize, background
removal, text overlay, format conversion, export is registered as a
WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The same canvas, same underlying functions, can be driven two ways, 1. By a person
clicking buttons, or 2. By an AI agent working in English. Activity feed on the right side of the page tags every action as "You" Or "Agent". 

 How I built it 

 Very minimal coding, focused more on the outcome. 
Next.js on the frontend. 
Canvas API for crop, resize etc. 
 @imgly/background-removal for background removal. 
Every transformation happens on-device, in the browser, including the background-removal model itself. 

 I originally planned to build this on Cloudinary's media API, since
that's my day job. Eventually, decided to use the imgly background-removal. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 WebMCP wasn't detecting at all during testing. It turned out that the spec itself moved
 navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext on May 27, 2026, and
Chrome only deprecated the old location in Chrome 150. 
I added a fallback mechanism to handle both. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 All 8 tools are registered, schema-valid, and verified working
end-to-end. The whole tool runs with zero backend and zero API keys, which wasn't the
original plan but turned out to be the right constraint. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that in-browser AI (background removal via a client-side segmentation
model) is genuinely viable now, this runs comfortably in
a regular browser tab with no server round-trip. 

 What's next for Handoff 

 Next big step would be thumbnail extraction and trimming via ffmpeg.wasm for videos. Exploring batch operations and social media export presets as natural tools to register.
