title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? title: DuckStudio
pitch: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab.
about_excerpt: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab. Like Comment Story Updates DuckStudio idle state prior to dataset selection, displaying upload controls on the left and an empty workspace placeholder. Default workspace screen showing no active tasks and prompting dataset activation from available presets or CSV upload. DuckStudio SQL & Lineage tab displaying the generated aggregation query, execution metadata (92.5 ms over 250k rows). DuckStudio displaying a DATASET_UNAVAILABLE error notification after attempting analysis without an activated dataset. DuckStudio Charts dashboard displaying summary KPI cards and an "accounts by tickets" distribution scatter plot completed in 92.5 ms. DuckStudio Charts view showing re-run or alternate query execution completed in 127.4 ms across 250,000 scanned records. Inspiration Analysts in healthcare and finance face strict data protection agreements (DPAs) and egress bans: data cannot leave the tab, but cloud LLMs cannot query browser memory. WebMCP bridges this actuation gap by giving an agent browser-level tools. However, browser agents can observe both tool outputs and the rendered DOM. Sanitizing tool payloads is ineffective if the UI renders raw sensitive rows where the model can inspect them. DuckStudio solves this through custody with controlled release : the agent steers the analysis and inspects safe aggregates, but raw records never cross into tool envelopes or the rendered canvas. What it does DuckStudio is a privacy-first, agent native analytical app where a human and an AI agent operate the same local DuckDB-WASM engine. Data remains in the client tab. WebMCP registers four imperative tools: duckdb_get_context — Returns capabilities, revision, schema digests, budgets, and permitted next actions. duckdb_activate_dataset — Switches datasets using optimistic concurrency through expectedRevision and idempotency keys. duckdb_execute_sql_to_canvas — Validates read-only SQL before execution, runs it locally, creates an immutable artifact with lineage, infers an aggregate KPI or chart specification, and pins it to the canvas. It returns an artifact handle and safe summary—never raw rows. duckdb_verify_zero_egress — Returns scoped evidence covering uploads, release decisions, network interceptors, and artifact lineage. Core Invariants: › Policy follows the dataset. : saas_churn (250,000 synthetic rows) runs under public_synthetic permitting bounded row display. healthcare_pii (100,000 rows with MRN and diagnosis) runs under sensitive_aggregate_only , suppressing raw grids entirely and rejecting cohorts smaller than 10 patients ($k \ge 10$). SQL is gated before execution : Permits only single, parameterized SELECT or WITH queries. Blocks DDL, DML, ATTACH , COPY , remote URLs, and extensions before DuckDB receives them. Deterministic state : Monotonic revisions and idempotency keys prevent race conditions, stale writes, and hallucinated retries. How we built it Stack : Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, lazy-loaded ECharts, and self-hosted @duckdb/duckdb-wasm in a dedicated Web Worker. Edge deployment & isolation : Deployed statically to Cloudflare Pages with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp . DuckDB-WASM binaries ( eh bundle) and fonts are self-hosted in /public to avoid third-party CDN failure under strict COEP. One command path : Human controls, prompt chips, the built-in simulator, and the 4 WebMCP tools all dispatch the exact same 6 domain commands through revisioned-workspace . Honest metrics : The initial workspace is empty—there are no pre-baked artifacts. SaaS metrics such as 14.2% churn and $182,400 impacted MRR are computed live by DuckDB from in- memory row generators and verified by CI contract tests Challenges we ran into DOM as an exfiltration surface : Because agents can scrape rendered elements, we implemented a single custody boundary across tool payloads and React rendering. If a requested view violates policy, it is rejected outright ("deny-over-strip") rather than partially rendered. Eradicating ambient state : Agents fail when tracking implicit context like "the last query." We eliminated ambient state entirely: every canvas view and query refinement references an immutable artifact ID containing a cryptographic SQL hash and parent lineage. Wasm limits & worker lifecycles : Single-threaded DuckDB-WASM ( eh bundle) runs under a browser wasm memory ceiling, clamped to a 5,000 ms execution budget and a 10,000-row cursor. Query cancellation requires terminating and respawning the Web Worker to prevent memory corruption without leaving orphaned partial artifacts. Evidence must be scoped honestly : The custody badge reads 0 Bytes of Dataset Uploaded . Interceptors audit fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon , WebSocket , and WebTransport to separate analytical data from application bundle traffic, avoiding unsupported zero-knowledge claims. Accomplishments that we're proud of Sub-second analytical queries over 250,000 rows executed entirely in client wasm with 0 bytes of dataset egress. Agents receive compact envelopes containing KPIs, chart dimensions, and artifact handles instead of raw row dumps. Self-healing recovery: queries that fail validation or custody rules return structured error codes and actionable recovery steps, allowing models to self-correct autonomously. What we learned WebMCP is most reliable as an explicit, revisioned state machine. Providing schema digests and monotonic revisions prevents model hallucination far better than generic prompt engineering. Local execution is not sufficient for privacy. If an agent has DOM access, data custody must be enforced at the UI projection layer as strictly as the network layer. What's next for DuckStudio Interactive virtualized Data Grid : High-performance, keyboard-accessible table with range selection and clipboard support for public datasets. OPFS streaming export subsystem : Stream CSV/Parquet outputs directly to the Origin Private File System to bypass wasm memory ceilings during large exports. SQL editor deep links : URL-addressable analysis states to share reproducible artifact lineage graphs. * In-tab AI chat panel * : BYO-LLM and WebLLM support with explicit, user-gated PII consent boundaries. Multi-threaded execution : Transition to DuckDB-WASM's coi bundle once cross-browser WebAssembly threading ergonomics and worker isolation stabilize. title: Prove It — Verifiable AI for Screen Reader Users
pitch: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did.
about_excerpt: Every AI action gets a signed receipt with a deep link your screen reader can verify directly — so you never have to trust an agent's word for what it just did. Like Comment Story Updates The verification gap nobody talks about Blind and low-vision users already use AI agents to operate the web — filling forms, managing lists, navigating sites with dozens of menus. The part that still doesn't work is trust. A sighted user glances at the screen and knows instantly whether an action succeeded. A screen reader user has no equivalent glance. Today, verifying what an agent did means re-navigating the whole page by hand, which erases most of the time an agent was supposed to save. A study of 16 screen-reader-using programmers found that verifying AI output, not producing it, was consistently the most time-consuming part of their workflow. That's the problem Prove It is built to solve. What it does Prove It is a household task manager where every action an AI agent takes — adding a task, marking it done, changing its priority, deleting it — produces a structured, inspectable receipt : what changed, exactly where it lives in the page, and what to say if it failed. Every receipt includes a deep link . Clicking it moves real keyboard and screen-reader focus straight to the element that changed, so the person hears their own assistive technology confirm the action in its own words — not a paraphrase from the agent, and not a guess from re-navigating the page. Failures get the same treatment. If the agent tries something invalid — an unknown task, a bulk delete it isn't allowed to perform — that produces an error receipt too. Proving what an agent didn't do, and why, is as important as proving what it did. How I built it The whole app runs on one function, performTool(name, args) , which is the single source of truth for all seven tools ( list_tasks , add_task , set_task_status , update_task_priority , delete_task , focus_task , get_last_receipt ). That one function is wired to two transports: Native WebMCP. On load, the page feature-detects document.modelContext / navigator.modelContext and calls registerTool() for each tool with a strict JSON Schema. Any WebMCP-aware agent — Chrome's built-in agent with the WebMCP flag on, or ChatGPT's in-app browser — can discover and call these tools directly, no code changes required. In-page demo agent (fallback). If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the same seven tool schemas are sent to the Claude API as tools , so anyone can test the full loop — natural language in, tool call, receipt, verify — in an ordinary browser with no flags. Every write tool returns { tool, changeType, timestamp, target: {selector, description}, before, after, errors } . changeType is created , updated , deleted , verified , or error . Receipts render as a literal torn-paper "receipt tape" in the UI — a visual metaphor for the whole concept: a printed proof of exactly what happened. The negative test There is no delete_all_tasks or bulk-export tool, on purpose. The agent is instructed to delete tasks one at a time and to ask before any bulk action — so "prove it" also covers proving the agent can't do something irreversible, because the capability was never exposed as a tool in the first place, not because a prompt told it to behave. Challenges I ran into The trickiest part wasn't the receipts — it was making the deep link mechanism actually work for a screen reader, not just look like it does. Early on, clicking a receipt just scrolled to an element and added a CSS glow, which does nothing for someone who can't see the glow. The fix was making sure every deep-linked element is a real, focusable DOM node ( tabindex="-1" where it isn't natively focusable) with an aria-label that reflects its current state, and that the deep link calls .focus() on that exact node. The visual highlight is a bonus for sighted collaborators, not the verification mechanism itself. The other challenge was keeping one tool contract honest across two very different transports. Rather than writing tool logic twice, performTool() is called by both the native registerTool().execute() handlers and the in-page agent loop, so a receipt means the same thing regardless of which agent produced it. What I learned Verifiability isn't a feature you bolt onto an agent's output after the fact — it has to be a structural property of the tool contract itself: a real DOM target, a real before/after diff, a real focus event. WebMCP's tool registration model turns out to be a genuinely good fit for this, because the receipt an agent returns and the page's actual state can be forced to be the same object, not two things that merely claim to agree. What's next Extending the receipt/deep-link pattern beyond a single demo page — a small library other WebMCP sites could adopt so "verifiable receipts" becomes a convention across the ecosystem, not a one-off feature of this app. Built With accessibility aria css3 html5 javascript json-schema model-context-protocol screen-readers vanilla-js webmcp Try it out github.com proofit-phi.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Vijayalakshmi S Like Share this project: Updates Vijayalakshmi S started this project — Aug 31, 2026 12:44 PM EDT

title: Lingji
pitch: Turn structured data into an audible, editable score that humans direct and WebMCP agents inspect, refine, and verify.
about_excerpt: Turn structured data into an audible, editable score that humans direct and WebMCP agents inspect, refine, and verify. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Turning a CSV into meaningful sound normally requires both data-mapping and music/audio expertise. I built Lingji so a person can decide what the data should communicate while a browser agent handles precise mapping, arrangement, inspection, and verification inside the same live composition. The flagship demo uses 64 exoplanets. It lets people hear patterns across temperature, radius, orbital period, distance, and stellar temperature without hiding how the sound was produced. What it does Lingji is a browser-based data-sonification studio that works both manually and through WebMCP. A person can upload and inspect a CSV, map columns to musical properties, generate a deterministic score, play and edit it, and lock notes, tracks, or mappings. Clicking any note traces it back to its source row, raw value, normalization, rule, and musical result. A browser agent can use nine semantic WebMCP tools to inspect the same live project, explain a selected note, respect human locks, modify unlocked mappings and arrangements, render a playback plan, and validate the source-to-sound chain. How we built it Lingji is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vite. Sound is synthesized locally with the Web Audio API; there is no backend and no AI audio-generation service. The dataset, mapping, composition, and project-state engines are separate from the interface, so human controls and WebMCP tools call the same underlying functions. The page registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Mutations are revision-aware, protected changes are rejected, locks survive regeneration, and validation checks generated events against their source data and rules. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making collaboration safe without making it rigid. Regeneration must preserve deliberate human edits and locks while still giving the agent useful control over the remaining composition. Provenance was another core challenge. A note is not useful for data exploration when its origin is hidden, so Lingji carries source row, raw measurement, normalization, and mapping rule through every generated event. We also preserve scientific field identifiers for agents while showing readable labels and units to people. Accomplishments we're proud of Lingji remains fully usable without an agent. Nine working WebMCP tools expose non-trivial live project operations. Human creative constraints are enforceable locks, not suggestions. Every generated note is inspectable rather than an unexplained AI output. The 64-exoplanet demo runs entirely in the browser. Deterministic validation verifies the internal source-to-note chain after agent changes. Screenshots The 64-exoplanet composition Measurements become explicit sound rules A selected note explains itself The agent respects the human's locked choice Final validated score What we learned Human-agent collaboration needs more than giving an agent buttons to press. The agent needs semantic access to the artifact, and the human needs visible control over what may change. Sonification also becomes more trustworthy when every sound can answer, "Which data produced this, and by what rule?" Lingji intentionally does not claim that validation proves the dataset is true or that the composition sounds good. Validation checks mapping consistency; the person judges meaning and musical quality. What's next Next steps include side-by-side sonification comparisons, more musical scales and synthesis options, richer dataset navigation, and user testing with educators, researchers, data communicators, and accessibility practitioners. title: Givens
pitch: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it.
about_excerpt: Stuck on a sudoku? Point an agent to help you with it. Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of the 'Givens' website featuring a sudoku grid and other sections like shared logs and tools so your agent can help you with it The story of Givens Givens is a Sudoku studio where a person and an agent share one live grid. The agent names the next technique and highlights the cells. You decide whether to fill, lock, or take one safe step. What inspired this I am an avid sudoku solver and have had countless moments where I make good progress on the puzzle itself but then I've gotten stuck on some step. Now, there are online resources and guides and communties that can help out here, but I thought WebMCP was an interesting solution to this problem. A complete solution is a string of 81 digits. If the agent dumps it in chat, the page was pointless. If it clicks around the DOM, it will mis-click. The product I wanted is the thing in between: collaborative deduction. What I learned WebMCP is not MCP in the browser. MCP can live on a server with no page open. WebMCP tools exist only while a visible, origin-isolated document is connected. ChatGPT’s in-app browser also implements a subset: Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool works. Declarative HTML form tools do not show up as site tools. Tools inside iframes are invisible, even same-origin. So registration has to happen on the top-level page, after the board mounts, with feature detection: if (typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === "function") { await document.modelContext.registerTool({ /* ... */ }); } I also learned that Codex can solve Sudoku in its head. If the only write tool is set_cell , it will skip the tutor and emit 81 answers. Tool descriptions and every read_board snapshot have to say: do not dump the grid; change it only through tools; trust the snapshot, not memory. On the puzzle side, computed candidates are not enough for pairs. A naked pair does not fill a cell; it removes digits elsewhere. That elimination has to be stored, or the next hint never sees it. Bundled puzzles have to be uniquely solvable. One “evening” grid I wrote by hand had two solutions. The brute-force solver is a backtracking search over the cell with the fewest candidates; we keep going until we have 0, 1, or >1 completions, and we only ship grids with exactly one. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: OpenRoom
pitch: AI Room Planner & Furniture Shopping. WebMCP demo: furnish a real room photo with catalog products, by hand or through the AI app you already use.
about_excerpt: AI Room Planner & Furniture Shopping. WebMCP demo: furnish a real room photo with catalog products, by hand or through the AI app you already use. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI room planning and furniture shopping through WebMCP. Securely connect Claude Code or another desktop MCP client. Review the room and approve its products before Shopify checkout. A Japandi redesign created with coordinated catalog products. The original room, ready for human or AI-assisted redesign. Browse and place true-scale catalog furniture directly in the room. Inspiration Planning a room is still a fragmented experience. Inspiration may begin in an AI conversation, but the room layout, product catalog, and checkout usually live in separate tools. The AI can suggest what to buy, yet it cannot see the current room, understand which object is selected, or safely make changes alongside the user. We built OpenRoom around a simple question: what if the room itself could become a shared workspace for people and AI? WebMCP made it possible to treat the web page as more than something an AI can describe. OpenRoom exposes a small set of safe, structured actions that let an AI inspect and edit the same room the user is viewing. Our goal was not to add another chatbot to a shopping site, but to create a human-and-AI design surface where every action remains visible, reversible, and under the user’s control. What it does OpenRoom is a photo-based room planner connected to a furniture shopping experience. The current demo begins with a calibrated room photograph and a set of mismatched furniture. A person can select, move, rotate, replace, undo, and reset individual pieces. An AI app can work on the same live scene through six focused tools: get_scene get_selection search_products replace_object move_object add_scene_to_cart The catalog contains 43 products across eight furniture categories. Products are placed using real-world dimensions, constrained to the room’s usable floor, and rendered with perspective-aware scale, depth ordering, alternate photographed views, and contact shadows. OpenRoom can also represent relationships such as a table lamp standing on a table. WebMCP-capable browsers can call the tools directly. Desktop AI clients can reach the same tools through OpenRoom’s local MCP companion, which pairs with the active browser tab and executes every command against the same live scene. When the room is ready, OpenRoom prepares a local approval sheet. A person can continue through a Shopify cart permalink, while an AI agent can receive mapped cart lines and the store’s UCP MCP endpoint. OpenRoom stores no Shopify credentials and never performs an external cart write on the user’s behalf. How we built it OpenRoom is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Immer, and Zod. At its center is one validated Scene model measured in real-world meters. Human interactions, native WebMCP calls, and local MCP calls all go through the same revision-aware command and history layer. This prevents the UI and the AI from developing separate versions of the room. Instead of relying on a 3D renderer or generating a new image after every edit, we built a deterministic photo compositor with ordinary DOM layers. A calibrated projection maps room coordinates onto the photograph’s floor plane. Product dimensions determine visual size, registered anchors keep cutouts grounded, and separate layers handle rugs, shadows, furniture, selection, and controls. Furniture images and alternate views are produced offline and checked into the project, so the application makes no runtime image-model calls. For agent access, we created a transport-neutral manifest for the six tools. Native WebMCP registers that manifest through document.modelContext. The local MCP companion exposes the same manifest over MCP stdio and forwards calls through a paired, loopback-only browser relay. The companion stores no copy of the room. Commerce follows the same minimal approach. OpenRoom uses a public Shopify store domain, static product-to-variant mappings, cart permalinks, and the store’s own UCP MCP endpoint. The application remains a static deployment on Cloudflare Pages, with no application backend or commerce token. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was making a two-dimensional photograph behave like a spatial editor. The Scene needed to remain measured in meters while the image used perspective. We had to calibrate the visible floor, project rotated furniture footprints, keep every object on usable floor space, preserve realistic relative scale, and handle special cases such as rugs and furniture stacked on other furniture. The second challenge was safe co-editing. A person might change the selection or undo a command while an AI is preparing its next action. Every mutation therefore includes the expected scene revision and state version. Stale commands fail without changing the room, forcing the agent to read the latest state before continuing. Connecting desktop MCP clients to state held inside a browser tab was another difficult boundary. We built a local relay that listens only on 127.0.0.1, uses an expiring single-use pairing code, checks exact origins and manifest identity, and forwards only the six approved tools. We also explored a browser-side WebGPU image harmonizer. One candidate failed its licensing requirements, while another took a median of 86 seconds against an eight-second target and introduced visible artifacts without improving the composition. We decided not to ship it. That experiment led us back to a faster, more predictable photo compositor. Finally, commerce had to remain useful without quietly crossing the user’s trust boundary. We designed checkout so OpenRoom prepares the cart data and opens a visible approval step, while the person or their chosen AI client performs the final action. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that OpenRoom makes the same room genuinely co-editable by a person and an AI. There is no hidden agent-only state and no second implementation of the editing logic. We also built one consistent six-tool contract across native WebMCP and the local MCP companion. Both paths share the same schemas, validation, handlers, scene history, and approval flow. The finished experience combines true-scale photo placement, collision-aware movement, alternate furniture views, accessible pointer and keyboard controls, deterministic catalog search, and Shopify handoff without requiring an application backend, a commerce access token, or runtime image generation. Most importantly, OpenRoom remains useful without an AI connection. The human editor is the primary experience, and AI adds another way to operate it rather than replacing it. What we learned We learned that an agent-enabled interface is not simply a chatbot embedded in a web page. It is a stateful product with a small, explicit action surface, clear error recovery, and visible consequences. A single source of truth was essential. Once people and agents shared the same validated Scene and command history, actions became easier to test, explain, undo, and trust. We also learned that visual quality does not always require a generative model. Careful calibration, real dimensions, correct view selection, silhouettes, shadows, and layering produced a faster and more repeatable experience than the browser-side model we tested. Finally, approval is not just a security mechanism. In a shopping workflow, showing exactly what will happen before anything leaves the application is part of the product experience. What's next for OpenRoom The biggest next step is letting people bring their own room photographs. That will require room calibration, object and floor analysis, and a clear workflow for correcting uncertain measurements. We also have a deterministic natural-placement solver in the repository that is currently intentionally disconnected from the product. We want to reintroduce it through a transparent, reversible experience where users can preview an arrangement, understand what changed, and undo it in one step. Beyond that, we plan to expand room types and catalog coverage, add more photographed views, improve mobile editing, and deepen integration with Shopify and other stores that expose standard agent commerce tools. We also want to grow the evaluation suite around longer human-and-AI design journeys, especially interruptions, stale state, partial redesigns, and checkout handoffs. title: Seven Games to Show the Future of WebMCP
pitch: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts.
about_excerpt: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts. Like Comment Story Updates Seven kinds of website, one AI agent, ten minutes. The page hands your agent real WebMCP tools and shows what it does to each business. Every page was drawn for one human visitor. Agents are arriving far faster than any of it can be redrawn. Room 5: one canvas, two hands. Your click and the agent's tool call land in the same document in the same second — nobody takes turns. Room 6: tools whose authority lasts only while the tab is open. Close it and the capability is gone — no token to leak or replay. The ending closes every tool it opened, then shows every call the agent actually made — each one stamped real or ghost. Inspiration Most WebMCP demos answer the wrong question. They show a tool that works — and a remote MCP server plus a normal web app would have worked just as well. We wanted to build the thing that cannot be built that way, and to be honest about which parts of our own project fail that test. So we asked a harder question: if agents can use any website, which websites stop making money? Almost every business model on the web has a line item that depends on human friction: impatience, boredom, embarrassment, forgetting to untick the box, not reading the terms. An agent has none of that friction. That is not a bug in the agent. It is a hole in the business model. What it is Seven Rooms is an interactive explainer that uses WebMCP to make its own argument. Every website maximizes one of seven things — attention, funnels, lock-in, marketplaces, creation, verification, coordination — and you walk through all seven. In each room, your own agent calls the real WebMCP tools that room registered on the page, and you watch what happens to that kind of business. Then the site does what it predicts the web will do: it calls unregisterAll() , closes every tool it opened, locks your agent out, and shows a report card of every call your agent actually made — each one labelled real or simulated. No backend, no analytics, no tracking. All state in localStorage ; Start over erases it. Why WebMCP specifically — and where it isn't needed The honest test is falsification: could this be a remote MCP server plus a normal web app? For five of our seven rooms, the answer is yes, and we say so in the README. Those rooms are the argument , not the proof. Two rooms cannot be built that way. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Edit the same object in the same second. Room 5 ships a fourth tool, get_canvas , purely so the agent can look before it draws — which is what turns a race condition into a duet. Grant authority that expires when you look away. Room 6 puts presence-scoped consent next to a clause designed to exploit mere presence, then shows the bright version: the agent reads all six clauses in a second, flags §4, and declines on your behalf with the reason on the record. That is better consent than clickwrap has ever produced. Deliberate with labelled agent votes. Room 7 seeds sixty positions carrying human / agent / mixed receipts. Your agent votes beside you and may disagree. Flip "Count humans only" and the result flips — nothing deleted; the receipts were always there. Because the page authors the tool, the page can require the receipt: an agent vote arrives labelled by construction, instead of being guessed at by a fraud model afterwards. That is the difference between "detect the bots" and "give the bots a name badge". Ask for a thing instead of describing a path. Room 3's suggested prompt is "Export everything this site has about me as JSON" , and export_everything does it. No selector, no click sequence, no brittle scraper — and no vendor API either. The site published the capability itself. How it creates a better user experience The page hands the agent an honest, typed capability instead of making it guess at the DOM. Descriptions are written for the agent and are true; readOnlyHint is set only where a tool genuinely does not mutate state. The on-page tool list shows a one-line summary for the human while the agent receives the full description — two readers, two lengths, one truth. And the site never pretends. Feature-detecting document.modelContext proves only that tools are exposed, never that an agent is present — because we polyfill, so it exists everywhere. The only honest proof is an agent calling something, which is what handshake is for. Every call in the final report card is stamped real or ghost. Visitors with no WebMCP browser are not locked out: a built-in ghost agent runs the same execute functions through the same registry, so it lands in exactly the same state. How we implemented WebMCP Everything the site knows about the browser API lives in one file, src/webmcp/bridge.ts . Rooms call registerPageTool(tool) and get back an unregister() . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "export_everything", description: "Export everything this dashboard holds about the signed-in user as one portable bundle, in json or csv.", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); 24 tools. Five site tools registered once at boot ( handshake , describe_site , list_rooms , go_to_room , next_slide ), and nineteen room tools. Lifecycle. Room tools are registered when a room's options slide renders and unregistered by that slide's cleanup — by the prediction slide, the room has no tools left. The deck runs the outgoing cleanup before the incoming render, so two slides can never hold the same name. Every registration carries a fresh AbortController signal, because the spec has no unregisterTool() . pagehide closes everything: nothing outlives the document. Isolated worlds. An extension-based agent cannot see a page-set document.modelContext , so the bridge also publishes a DOM manifest and accepts calls through it. The isolated-world agent gets the same tools, the same titles, and the same annotations a native one does. Challenges The spec has no unregisterTool() . Removal is AbortController.abort() , which changed how the whole lifecycle had to be shaped. You cannot tell whether an agent is there. We wanted the status chip to be honest, so it has four states rather than a boolean, and only a real tool call moves it to connected . pagehide fires into the back/forward cache. The document is not destroyed — DOM and JS stay intact — so pressing Back can restore a live page with zero registered tools and no reload to fix it. We re-register on pageshow when persisted is true. That gap is worth flagging beyond this project: presence-scoped authority is only as scoped as the page author's discipline, because the platform gives you no signal for "the user stopped attending." title: Hopyard Designer — WebMCP for Hop Farms
pitch: A shared hopyard design workspace where farmers and AI agents plan poles, wire, cost, and structural load together — agents propose alternatives, farmers decide, powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A shared hopyard design workspace where farmers and AI agents plan poles, wire, cost, and structural load together — agents propose alternatives, farmers decide, powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Hopyard Designer with webMCP Inspiration Planning a hopyard is a connected design problem. Plant spacing affects the number of plants and the planting-stock cost. Pole spacing changes the structure and material quantities. Wire, anchors, wind loads, and labor all affect the final estimate. Hopyard Designer already helped growers and installers work through these decisions in a visual web app. The WebMCP Challenge gave us a chance to explore a harder question: can an AI agent help compare design alternatives without hiding changes from the farmer or taking control of the final decision? We wanted the farmer and the agent to work in the same design space. The agent should be able to read the current plan, prepare alternatives, and explain the differences. The farmer should be able to inspect each proposal in the existing 2D and 3D views before deciding what to keep. What it does Hopyard Designer calculates planting-stock cost, facility quantities, preliminary structural loads, and a live material estimate from a hopyard design. As the design changes, the app updates: pole and anchor quantities main wire, training wire, and twine lengths hop positions and planting-stock cost preliminary wind and crop-load checks a construction-oriented 2D plan an interactive 3D farm a downloadable estimate PDF For the challenge, we added a WebMCP workflow that lets an agent create alternatives without changing the original plan. In the demo, the agent compares a Korean I-shaped training layout with a North American 18-foot Y-shaped reference. Both options appear side by side with their plant counts, material requirements, estimated costs, and engineering status. The farmer chooses which option to preview. The selected candidate appears in the same 2D and 3D workspace, but it is not committed yet. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Zustand manages the active design and a separate candidate workspace. Konva renders the 2D construction plan, while Three.js renders the farm in 3D. We used BlenderMCP to create a reusable GLB asset kit containing pole variants, anchors, turnbuckles, wire hardware, and low-poly hop geometry. The web renderer places these assets procedurally instead of loading a fixed model of the whole farm. This keeps every candidate editable and allows the design to update immediately. Repeated components use instancing to keep the 3D view responsive, even when the farm contains hundreds of plants and many structural elements. How WebMCP works The design page initially registers five WebMCP tools: get_design_context list_regional_profiles simulate_design show_candidates preview_candidate The agent starts by reading the current design and its calculated results. It can then simulate alternatives and place up to three candidates in the shared comparison tray. When a candidate enters preview, the page dynamically registers two additional tools: apply_candidate discard_preview This changes the available tool set from five to seven. Apply and Discard only exist while a preview is active. After either action, the page returns to five tools. This creates a visible review step. The agent can prepare and preview options, while the farmer uses the shared interface to decide whether to apply or discard the active preview. The apply_candidate tool description explicitly directs the agent to use it only after user approval. WebMCP inputs use strict JSON Schema and are validated again with Zod at runtime. Candidate IDs are deterministic. Preview stores an exact copy of the active design, so Discard can restore it without relying on reverse calculations. The production site uses Chrome's WebMCP Origin Trial. We also built CDP-based checks that verify tool registration, tool invocation, the five-to-seven-to-five lifecycle, responsive layouts, and browser console errors against the live page. Existing product vs. challenge work Hopyard Designer existed before the challenge with: a human-operated design form planting-stock and material calculations preliminary structural-load calculations live Korean material estimates authentication and project saving 2D and 3D visualization estimate PDF export The following work was added for the WebMCP Challenge: seven WebMCP tools with runtime validation deterministic, non-destructive candidate simulation the agent design alternatives tray temporary candidate previews in the existing 2D/3D workspace dynamic Apply and Discard tool registration the five-to-seven-to-five tool lifecycle Korean and North American reference profiles the reusable BlenderMCP GLB asset kit the public /design/demo judge route browser-level WebMCP verification English and Korean UI, help, PDF, narration, and caption support The complete source repository is available under the MIT License. Challenges we ran into Keeping the workflow non-destructive An agent needs enough freedom to explore, but a design tool should not silently overwrite a farmer's work. We separated simulation, display, preview, and application into distinct states. A simulation creates a candidate without touching the active design. The candidate only changes the shared canvas when it enters preview. The original design remains available for exact restoration. Making browser support testable WebMCP availability depends on the browser runtime. A browser without the API can make a correct implementation look broken. We added an Origin Trial token for the production origin and built browser-level checks instead of relying only on mocked unit tests. These checks exercise the real tools through Chrome and verify the complete lifecycle. Rendering a full farm in 3D A detailed plant model looked good by itself but became too expensive when repeated hundreds of times. We replaced it with a low-poly procedural asset kit and used instancing for repeated components. The resulting farm can still be rotated and zoomed while remaining connected to the editable design. Comparing regions without inventing data The Korean profile can use the active HOPEDEN catalog. The North American profile is explicitly identified as a reference configuration. The app does not pretend to provide live US pricing or local engineering approval. Both the interface and the WebMCP results preserve that distinction. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working five-to-seven-to-five WebMCP tool lifecycle Deterministic alternatives that do not mutate the baseline design Exact restoration after Discard Human selection and review in the same 2D and 3D workspace Real WebMCP calls rather than simulated agent results Procedural Blender assets that respond to design changes A public demo that works without an account Protected authentication and project-saving routes for normal users English and Korean interfaces and estimate PDFs Automated tests for WebMCP contracts, candidate state, responsive layouts, accessibility, and deployment What we learned A useful agent interface is not the same as automating clicks. The agent works better when the page exposes clear operations with validated inputs, stable identifiers, and results that explain what changed. This is more reliable than asking an agent to infer the meaning of visual controls. We also learned that dynamic tool registration can communicate application state. In this project, the presence of Apply and Discard tells the agent that a candidate preview is active. The shared preview gives the farmer a practical way to verify an agent's proposal. The agent can explore alternatives quickly, but the farmer still sees the same plan, quantities, safety status, and estimate before making a decision. What's next for Hopyard Designer — WebMCP for Hop Farms We plan to add more regional construction profiles, supplier integrations, and project revision history. Future versions could allow growers to: compare contractor proposals save approved agent changes as project revisions review how each input affects materials and cost connect additional regional price catalogs export a complete design package for a local engineer keep an auditable record of human and agent decisions The goal is not to replace the farmer, installer, or engineer. It is to make the design process easier to inspect, compare, and communicate. title: Constraint Canvas
pitch: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again
about_excerpt: Every rejection becomes a rule the agent cannot break again Like Comment Story Updates Rejecting a table opens rule capture. The app turns that correction into a rule and applies it to future proposals. The agent replans around the new rule and finds 16 seats elsewhere. The layout reaches 144 seats with zero violations. Asked for 40 more seats, the agent proposes five tables through WebMCP. Nothing changes yet because proposals are previews until approved. Willowmere Hall on load. 96 seats, eight built-in rules, and three locked objects the agent cannot move. What it is ConstraintCanvas is a venue floor planner where a human and an agent work on the same canvas at the same time. You place the stage, lock anything that cannot move, and decide which sponsor gets the front booth. The agent handles the tedious parts, like fitting more seats without breaking egress, finding clearance violations, and explaining exactly which rule blocked a placement. The floor planner is only the demo. The real idea is what happens when the human says no. Inspiration Agent corrections are usually temporary. You tell the model not to do something, that instruction lives in context, and a few turns later you may have to repeat it. That felt like the wrong place to store human judgment. If I say seating must never block a door, that should not just be prompt context. It should become application state that is visible, editable, and enforced. In ConstraintCanvas, rejecting an agent proposal can create a named rule with provenance. That rule is added to a visible rulebook and enforced against every future proposal. The agent does not need to remember better. The application enforces the correction. Why this use case fits WebMCP The site owns the semantics. The application knows what counts as blocking an exit in metres. An agent using DOM automation would have to infer geometry from pixels. With WebMCP, the floor state and rules are exposed directly as structured data. State is shared. The human and agent both modify the same floor plan during the same session. Read, preview, and write are separated. Six of the nine tools use readOnlyHint . Tools that can affect the floor only generate previews, and the user approves changes before they are applied. That separation lives in the tool contract rather than in prompt instructions. Refusals are structured. A blocked proposal returns the rule ID, rule statement, offending item, and numeric shortfall. The agent can replan using actual constraint data instead of guessing why a call failed. What people and agents can do together The core use case is constrained spatial planning. The human defines the boundaries and important decisions. The agent optimises inside them. The application guarantees that those boundaries are respected. Without that enforcement, the human either does the optimisation manually or delegates it and rechecks every result. WebMCP enables a third model: delegate the arithmetic, keep the judgment, and turn corrections into persistent constraints. How WebMCP was implemented ConstraintCanvas registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , grouped into inspection, proposal, explanation, and constraint authoring. Two headers are required before document.modelContext is exposed: Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) Tools are defined as descriptors and registered through a shared bridge that wraps every execute call. This keeps logging and refusal handling at the tool boundary instead of duplicating it inside each implementation. Each tool has its own abort controller so the surface can be withdrawn and republished cleanly. Results are returned as JSON. The most interesting part is that the tool contract changes at runtime . When a user ratifies a new rule, the proposal tools are re-registered with the active constraints included in their description , then the surface emits toolchange . That means a correction changes what the agent is told it can do before the next call is created, not only what the application rejects afterwards. Validation runs in three passes: Check locks as hard boundaries. Compare rule violations before and after the proposal. Convert valid proposals into a preview for human approval. The differential check is important because an existing violation should not block a proposal that actually improves the layout. How I built it The app uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, SVG, and IBM Carbon design tokens. It is deployed on Vercel. There is no state library and no canvas library. The constraint engine is intentionally simple. Placement uses a greedy search with scoring rather than a general solver. The priority is not algorithmic complexity. It is producing layouts that remain valid and explainable. Eight built-in rules use the same evaluation engine as user-created rules. For egress, the app runs a flood fill outward from doors across the floor grid. Straight-line distance is not enough because an object can be physically close to an exit while still being blocked by surrounding furniture. Circulation also enforces a minimum free-area ratio: $$ \frac{A_{\text{floor}} - \sum_i w_i h_i}{A_{\text{floor}}} \ge 0.70 $$ This gives seat maximisation a hard upper bound. The app also includes a small agent panel that calls getTools and executeTool against the same surface, so the full interaction can be demonstrated without a separate agent browser. Challenges Different WebMCP implementations exposed different APIs. The spec describes ModelContext as an EventTarget , so I initially used addEventListener for toolchange . That worked in Chrome but failed in ChatGPT's implementation, causing React to unmount and render a blank page. Native calls are now feature detected against a minimum surface of registerTool , with regression tests for reduced implementations. Bad refusals waste agent turns. An early optimise_layout refusal only returned: Unknown objective. The agent had no way to discover valid inputs and spent several calls guessing. Refusals now require a next_step , and invalid values return the accepted alternatives. Thinking models preserve metadata across tool calls. Gemini 3 attaches a thought signature to function call parts. I initially rebuilt the response from extracted tool calls and dropped that metadata. The server route now forwards the original model turn unchanged. Valid layouts can still look wrong. Early plans passed every rule but broke the visual rhythm of existing seating. The optimiser now detects repeated furniture spacing and includes alignment in its scoring function. Model calls needed caching. One planning task could use five or six requests because the agent repeatedly inspected unchanged state. Inspection results are now cached per conversation and invalidated when a proposal changes the floor. What I learned A tool contract should be written as if it is the agent's only source of truth. A refusal should explain what failed and what the agent can do next. Otherwise it becomes a dead end that wastes tokens and tool calls. I also learned not to assume that one implementation of an emerging standard represents all of them. Most importantly, WebMCP is not only useful because a webpage can expose tools. The more interesting capability is that the tool surface itself can change at runtime. That allows a human correction to become part of the application's active contract, which is much stronger than asking the model to remember it. title: Arena
pitch: Behavioral release evidence for WebMCP tools. Arena proves that agent routes preserve the authorization, approval, and side-effect boundaries enforced by human interfaces.
about_excerpt: Behavioral release evidence for WebMCP tools. Arena proves that agent routes preserve the authorization, approval, and side-effect boundaries enforced by human interfaces. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives agents structured tools instead of forcing them to guess through a page. But discovery is not proof. A tool can claim to be read-only, return a successful preview, and still bypass a confirmation or create a delayed charge. Arena asks a narrower, testable question: does the agent route preserve the same protection outcome as the human route? What it does Arena runs a human route and a WebMCP agent route against the same reviewed contract. It records authoritative effects, waits for delayed writes to settle, compares the two outcomes, and issues a signed verdict. The included checkout demo makes the failure concrete. The vulnerable release returns a successful preview, then creates a hidden $149 charge. Arena observes that delayed effect and fails the release. The fixed release runs under the same commitments and passes with no charge. How humans and agents work together The deployed app registers two real tools through document.modelContext.registerTool: start_generated_release_audit prepares a server-owned audit and returns the exact commitments for review. get_generated_release_audit_status lets the agent poll the run without gaining approval authority. The human interface shows the release, agent, tool, arguments, target, nonce, browser session, invariants, and expiry. Approval creates a short-lived, single-use capability bound to that exact intent. Replay, expiry, argument changes, and release changes fail closed. After approval, Arena dynamically registers the reviewed candidate tool and joins its callback result to the terminal backend trace. How we built it Arena uses React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Cloudflare Workers, Node.js, and Playwright. Its evidence layer signs portable proofs with Ed25519. Verifiers resolve the signing key against Arena's published trust set instead of trusting a key embedded in the proof. The project includes a CLI, adapter SDK, GitHub Action, SARIF and JUnit output, reusable WebMCP eval fixtures, human documentation, llms.txt, a JSON documentation index, and proof schemas for agents. Challenges The hard part was separating three claims that are easy to mix together: static source hints, runtime tool registration, and observed behavior. Arena keeps those layers independent. A static match cannot become a behavioral pass, and an upstream eval score cannot replace signed effect evidence. Native WebMCP is also still experimental. The hosted app uses the real Promise-returning API in compatible browsers. Compatibility-browser tests are labelled as shims and never presented as native proof. What we learned Tool descriptions are useful for discovery, but security claims need measurement. Human and agent routes do not need identical clicks. They do need equivalent authorization, spending limits, ownership checks, confirmation, and visible side effects. What's next The next step is broader owned-target adapter coverage and vendor-backed agent identity. Arena deliberately does not claim to make arbitrary third-party sites safe. It proves one scoped release, records what happened, and gives teams evidence they can verify in CI. Challenge work disclosure Arena existed before the challenge as an agent-readiness CLI. The Human-vs-Agent Boundary Audit, real WebMCP registration, owned checkout target, exact-intent approval, terminal effect settlement, signed portable evidence, hosted workbench, and release gates were built during the challenge window. The dated comparison is linked in the public repository.
