video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: Ferrule
pitch: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports.
about_excerpt: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In August 2022 a third of Pakistan went under water. My family is from Sindh. My uncle spent that month running between four places. A food store with rice and oil in it. A school that had become a shelter because it had a roof and a gate. A group of men with pickup trucks who would drive anywhere if you called them early enough. And a cold room, in the back of a pharmacy, holding the insulin for a whole district. Four organisations. Four sets of records. None of them could see the others. He held the entire thing together with a phone and a notebook. He wrote down who had what, who had asked for what, and who he had already promised it to. And he got things wrong, because anyone would. A family got sent to a shelter that had filled up an hour earlier. Boxes were double promised. Insulin sat in a cold room for two days because the person who needed to know it was there was on a different page of the notebook. Nobody in that story needed better software for their own organisation. The pantry knew its own stock perfectly well. The shelter knew its own beds. What was missing was the seam. The part between them. The thing my uncle was doing by hand with a biro. When I read the WebMCP spec, that is the gap I saw. Not another site publishing tools for itself, but the layer that lets a person and an agent work across four sites that will never, ever hand each other their data. Every organisation in that network had a reason to keep their own records. None of those reasons went away just because a flood arrived. So Ferrule is the notebook, rebuilt as software, with the agent doing the running around and the human still holding the pen for anything that costs something real. What it does Ferrule is a dispatch desk. Open it and you are looking at one queue that reaches across five independent websites, each on its own origin, each with its own data in its own browser storage. The four partner sites are real, usable sites. A volunteer can open the pantry and reserve a food box with no agent anywhere near it. What each one adds is a small set of WebMCP tools. Nineteen across the four of them. The Desk publishes seven verbs of its own and nothing else. intake_request , find_capacity , draft_plan , commit_plan , open_lease , close_lease , read_ledger . That is the whole surface any agent gets. No partner tool is ever callable directly, and there is no second path for a privileged caller, because there is no privileged caller. Here is what actually happens when the queue moves. A lease opens. Time boxed, scoped to a purpose, and it names exactly which partner tools it permits. Only once that lease is granted does the partner's own site mount into the Desk as a frame. It was not on the page a second earlier. When the lease closes, expires, or is revoked, the frame comes down and the tools it carried leave with it. The policy engine decides. Every hop is checked against a scope map before it travels. A refusal is a value with a sentence in it, never a thrown exception, so an agent reading the answer knows what happened and why. The run stops for a person. commit_plan is the one verb in the system that succeeds and goes nowhere. It answers with a status of awaiting_human_approval , an approval id, and a line telling the caller outright that none of its verbs continues from here. So a model reads that, reports the plan as raised, and stops, instead of looping or treating it as an error. What the human sees is the target origin, the tool, the arguments, the required scope, and a digest taken over the substance of the plan. Rename the plan and the digest holds. Change the origin, the tool, the arguments, or the order, and the approval is void. Then the write lands , and the partner's own page updates itself. Nothing is suggested for you to go and do by hand. Anything coming back is fenced. A value from a tool that declares untrusted content gets wrapped in a quarantine region, labelled as text written outside the Desk, and rendered as inert text. Data, never instruction. Every hop is recorded. Seventeen pinned fields per row, tab separated, byte stable, and it round trips: export the ledger and reimport it and you get the same bytes back. Who asked whom for what, the policy decision, the duration, and whether the approval came from the scripted run or from a model. There are three ways to drive it, and a judge needs nothing for any of them. Press Run the relief scenario . No key, no sign in, nothing to configure. A declared step list drives all seven verbs, crosses two origins, and stops at the approval. Open the agent controls and press Use the hosted endpoint, no key needed . Now a model picks the verbs and the order, and nobody wrote that order down. It opens its own lease, reads capacity, drafts a plan, and hits the same halt in front of the same person. Point a WebMCP extension or the Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel at the Desk. Seven declarations with schemas, read only hints, and a stated return shape on each one. There is also a topology view that draws the session as it happened, and an evidence page that lists sixteen security claims with a label on each saying what actually backs it. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript end to end, deployed as six static sites plus one small endpoint. Front end. React 19 and Vite for all five product apps. Tailwind CSS 4 on the partner sites, because a partner site should look like a small charity built it. The Desk runs its own design system instead: a fixed eight by four grid that closes at 1280 by 800 with no page scroll, a four tier elevation ladder, and a set of pinned design tokens with a build check that fails if a value drifts off the four pixel base unit. The topology view is three.js through React Three Fiber. WebMCP. A platform wrapper sits over document.modelContext and is the only module in the entire repository allowed to name it. A syntax tree gate enforces that, rather than a code review convention. Under the wrapper is the vendored polyfill, pinned byte for byte, so the Desk behaves the same in a browser with native WebMCP and in one without. The broker. @ferrule/broker holds the frame host, the lease manager, the policy engine, the approval gate, the quarantine wrapper, and the ledger. It contains no React at all, which is deliberate: the lease state machine, the policy table, the digest, and the serialiser all run in a node test project against fakes, with no DOM anywhere near them. Origins. Every origin value lives once, in an origin registry. A build gate fails on a raw origin string literal anywhere else in apps/ or packages/ . All five product origins serve Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 on every path, and a gate fails the build if a site configuration drops the rule. The keyless agent. gateway/ is an OpenAI compatible endpoint on its own separate Netlify site, deployed outside the workspace and outside the root TypeScript project. It holds a model key so a reader does not have to, and it bounds what it will spend: one model, a token ceiling written over rather than trusted, a message count, a body size checked before parsing, and a daily request allowance kept in Netlify Blobs. Refusals answer 200 with an assistant message, because an agent reading a 4xx learns less than an agent reading a sentence. Hosting. Netlify, seven sites. Five product origins, one deliberately unkeyed probe origin that carries no product code and exists only to be measured, and the gateway Challenges we ran into The one that nearly sank the whole thing. A judge is most likely to arrive with a browser extension. An extension's content script runs in an isolated world: it shares the page's DOM and it does not share the page's JavaScript globals, because the user agent hands each world its own wrapper for the same node. document.modelContext is a property on document whenever it arrives from a polyfill, and a polyfill is what runs in every browser that does not implement WebMCP natively, which today is most of them. So I measured it, on the deployed Desk, in plain Chrome with no flags, reading the same expression in both worlds through the DevTools Protocol. In the page's own world the surface was present with all three of its members. In an isolated world it was absent entirely. An extension pointed at that page reads nothing at all. The tools are there. The extension cannot reach them. The answer is a cross world bridge. The Desk publishes its seven declarations as JSON inside a script element, because the DOM is shared across worlds, and it accepts invocations by window.postMessage , because that channel crosses the boundary too. Every invocation goes through the same wrapped verb body the platform registered, so a hop arriving over the bridge lands on the ledger exactly like any other. Two

title: Job Scout: WebMCP Career OS
pitch: A WebMCP-powered career OS for job discovery, fit scoring, resume tailoring, application capture, CRM, and interview tracking—with human approval before any submission.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered career OS for job discovery, fit scoring, resume tailoring, application capture, CRM, and interview tracking—with human approval before any submission.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Job searching is fragmented across job boards, spreadsheets, resumes, recruiter messages, application portals, and interview notes. I originally built Job Scout to solve that problem for myself: find relevant jobs, understand why they fit, and keep the entire application lifecycle in one place. 

 It evolved into something much bigger: a multi-user Career OS designed for both humans and AI agents. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, the goal is to make those workflows agent-accessible without giving an AI uncontrolled authority over a user's career. The system can help discover, analyze, organize, and prepare — but consequential actions such as submitting an application remain behind explicit human approval. 

 What it does 

 Job Scout: WebMCP Career OS brings the job-search lifecycle into one product: 

 
 Job discovery and searchable market browsing 
 Personalized job-fit scoring and explanations 
 Saved, dismissed, applied, and application-stage tracking 
 Resume building, versioning, ATS analysis, and job-specific tailoring 
 Cover-letter generation 
 Reusable application-answer generation 
 Application capture and career CRM workflows 
 Interview-management workflows 
 Anonymous demo access with isolated temporary state 
 Durable multi-user accounts and preserved career history 
 Agent-accessible workflows designed around WebMCP 
 Human confirmation before any application submission 
 

 The underlying philosophy is simple: AI should reduce the mechanical work of a job search without taking control away from the job seeker. 

 How we built it 

 Job Scout uses a split-plane architecture. 

 The job market is represented as an immutable, versioned snapshot rather than repeatedly loading the global job corpus into each user's database. Each user's mutable state — preferences, sessions, saved jobs, applications, resume evidence, and lifecycle history — stays in a much smaller PostgreSQL-backed state plane. 

 The backend is built primarily with Python and FastAPI , with PostgreSQL/asyncpg for durable state. The product includes server-side sessions, role and lifecycle separation, anonymous demo identities, telemetry, health receipts, rate limiting, and account-upgrade paths. 

 The browser experience is built as a responsive product UI with desktop and mobile acceptance testing. Automated tests cover backend contracts, database behavior, cross-user isolation, lifecycle safety, accessibility, keyboard behavior, reduced motion, and end-to-end browser flows. 

 WebMCP provides the bridge between the web application and agent-driven interaction: rather than depending on brittle visual automation, the product is being shaped around explicit, bounded capabilities that an AI agent can understand and invoke. 

 Challenges 

 One of the hardest problems was separating identity, authorization, and lifecycle correctly. 

 Anonymous users need to explore the product without creating an account, but if they later sign in, their saved jobs and application state should survive. At the same time, cleanup of expired demo accounts must never be capable of deleting an account that has become durable. 

 That led to explicit lifecycle classification, atomic demo-to-durable conversion, revocable sessions, race-condition testing, and a strict rule that user IDs are opaque identifiers rather than sources of authorization truth. 

 Another challenge was making agentic behavior useful without making it reckless. Job applications affect real people and real opportunities, so Job Scout intentionally stops short of autonomous submission. The agent can prepare the work; the human remains the final decision-maker. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent-ready software benefits from the same things that make distributed systems reliable: explicit contracts, narrow capabilities, deterministic state transitions, provenance, and fail-closed boundaries. 

 WebMCP is especially interesting because it creates an opportunity to design web applications that are understandable to both people and agents instead of forcing agents to reverse-engineer interfaces intended only for humans. 

 What's next 

 The remaining work is focused on deeper WebMCP convergence, end-to-end acceptance, additional workflow polish, named-account authentication, and demonstrating the complete career journey: 

 discover → evaluate → save → tailor → prepare → track → interview 

 The end goal is a Career OS where an AI agent can do dramatically more of the busywork while the user keeps control of every consequential career decision.

title: ToolForge
pitch: A human-in-the-loop WebMCP readiness inspector that turns existing website interactions into reviewable, testable agent tools.
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop WebMCP readiness inspector that turns existing website interactions into reviewable, testable agent tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a structured language for working with agents, replacing fragile visual guesswork with explicit tools. But the adoption challenge extends far beyond any single website or industry: every developer must still inspect their interface, identify meaningful actions, define schemas, make authorization decisions, and connect custom controls to real application behavior. ToolForge addresses that broader infrastructure gap. Rather than building another WebMCP-enabled storefront, we created a reusable, cross-functional developer tool that can audit many kinds of websites ranging from ecommerce and marketplaces to games, productivity tools and financial applications. It recognizes semantic forms, custom actions, composite workflows and uncertain elements, then converts them into evidence-backed candidates for developer review. ToolForge does not blindly expose everything clickable or pretend that business intent can be inferred from the DOM. It accelerates the repeatable parts of WebMCP adoption while preserving human control over meaning, safety and execution. The storefront is simply our end-to-end proof; the product itself is a general bridge between today’s websites and an agent-ready open web. What it does ToolForge is an injectable, development-mode readiness inspector for existing websites. It scans the live DOM including open Shadow DOM roots and accessible same-origin frames and organizes interactions into five groups: Declarative-ready native forms Form-like interactions Composite workflows High-confidence imperative actions Ignored or low-confidence elements For native forms, ToolForge drafts toolname , tooldescription , and toolparamdescription attributes from the page's existing labels and structure. The developer reviews every value, decides whether to enable toolautosubmit , applies the attributes to the live DOM for immediate testing, and can copy a minimal stable-ID attribute diff back to source. For custom JavaScript controls, ToolForge drafts metadata and a JSON schema but refuses to present the tool as complete until the developer provides a real function reference or execute body. Related controls such as separate price chips, region controls, and an “All filters” button can be grouped into one composite workflow instead of becoming dozens of tiny tools. Low-confidence elements are not silently discarded. Developers can search the ignored queue, inspect structural evidence, highlight the real page element, keep it ignored, promote it for review, or re-evaluate it after the page changes. Manual decisions persist across rescans for the current session. The repository includes a complete storefront that proves the result end to end. It exposes: search_products through the imperative WebMCP API add_to_cart through a declarative form with developer-approved autosubmit checkout through a declarative form without autosubmit, preserving human confirmation How we built it ToolForge is a static, dependency-free application built with semantic HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. It has no backend, framework, build step, runtime model call, or page-data upload. The finished storefront and the unannotated demo target share the same product rendering, cart state, and human interface logic. This creates an honest before-and-after comparison: demo-target.html contains no WebMCP surface, while index.html contains the reviewed declarative attributes and loads the imperative implementation from webmcp.js . The declarative tools reuse the forms' existing submit handlers. The imperative search_products tool uses document.modelContext.registerTool() and calls the same search function as the human interface. ToolForge's panel is isolated in Shadow DOM, observes dynamic page changes with a MutationObserver , records evidence for each classification, and gates every imperative export on a real developer-supplied handler. Automated Chrome DevTools Protocol tests cover tool discovery, execution policy, native forms, form-like controls, composite workflows, ignored-element review, dynamic content, open Shadow DOM, same-origin frames, duplicate collapsing, stable rescans, and the imperative export gate. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was staying honest about what the DOM can and cannot reveal. HTML can provide parameter structure, but it cannot reliably reveal private JavaScript behavior, business meaning, or authorization policy. ToolForge therefore does not invent handlers or automatically decide which actions are safe. Modern commerce pages presented another challenge because filters are often implemented as many independent buttons rather than native forms. Treating every chip as its own tool created noisy and misleading results. We added structural composite-workflow detection so related price and region controls become a single filter_listings candidate while product-card actions remain separate. We also had to balance filtering with developer control. A large ignored count was technically accurate but difficult to audit, so the ignored set became a searchable review queue with evidence, highlighting, promotion, persistent decisions, and re-evaluation. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working, polished storefront with three real WebMCP tools across both declarative and imperative APIs A clear safety demonstration: reversible add-to-cart can autosubmit, while checkout requires human confirmation A deterministic readiness inspector that works without AI inference or a backend Five evidence-backed readiness categories instead of an inflated list of clickable elements Composite workflow detection that groups related filters into a usable schema A fully reviewable ignored queue instead of silently discarding uncertain controls Automated browser regression coverage for the scanner and WebMCP execution policy Mobile Lighthouse scores of 100 for Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO What we learned Semantic HTML is already a strong bridge to agent-ready interfaces: a real form provides useful parameter structure and an existing execution path. The harder problems are meaning, authorization, and developer intent. Those cannot be responsibly inferred from labels alone. We also learned that WebMCP adoption tools should optimize for inspectability rather than maximum candidate counts. A smaller set of coherent, evidence-backed workflows is more useful than dozens of technically clickable but context-free actions. What's next for ToolForge Next steps include packaging the inspector as a browser extension, adding source-aware adapters that can produce framework-specific patches, supporting richer developer-defined workflow grouping. title: OpenFinance: Agentic B2B Supplier Portal
pitch: OpenFinance lets AI agents work directly with supplier portals using WebMCP, automating B2B finance workflows at scale, boosting team productivity, and eliminating costly, complex integrations.
about_excerpt: OpenFinance lets AI agents work directly with supplier portals using WebMCP, automating B2B finance workflows at scale, boosting team productivity, and eliminating costly, complex integrations. Like Comment Story Updates Human approval for submitting a document AP portal overview Inspiration In my experience working in the B2B payment and commerce space I’ve seen many buyer portals and frustrated suppliers spending valuable time on repetitive manual work just to get paid. The obvious way to automate that is to connect the systems directly, but that creates another problem: those integrations are costly to build, hard to maintain, and often only make sense for the largest suppliers. They also tend to break when portals change. The moment I heard about WebMCP, this was the first problem that came to mind. It felt like a natural fit for something that had always been painful to solve. It also felt like a strong fit for human-agent collaboration. This is financial data moving between businesses, so the agent can handle the repetitive work while people stay involved where review, approval, or judgment is needed. What it does OpenFinance is a B2B supplier portal with WebMCP built in. It lets a supplier’s AI agents work directly with the portal through 12 governed WebMCP tools, handling tasks like submitting invoices, resolving exceptions, providing evidence, opening cases, tracking payments, keeping finance systems up to date, and more. The goal is to remove repetitive portal work, save finance teams time, and keep the human operator in the loop, with a human-in-the-loop approach wherever review or judgment is needed. How I built it I used Codex to do the coding, infrastructure decisions, technology choices, testing, and documentation. OpenFinance was built as a working authenticated supplier portal. I suggested Vercel and Supabase, and Codex helped choose the rest of the stack: Next.js and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel, with Supabase for authentication and PostgreSQL for persistence. The portal exposes 12 WebMCP tools covering invoice submission, validation, exceptions, evidence, cases, status, and payments. The tools use the supplier’s existing signed-in browser session and call secure backend routes. The frontend shows information and collects human decisions, while the important financial rules, permissions, supplier isolation, validation, and state changes are enforced on the backend. For sensitive actions like submitting invoices or evidence, the operator gets a clear approval screen before anything is sent. I also built a separate supplier-side reference app for the demo so I could show the full workflow across two independent systems, with the agent acting as the bridge between them. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making the app work like a real finance workflow rather than a basic tool in short time. These portals are full of follow-up steps. Submitting an invoice alone was not enough. I also wanted to make the difference between WebMCP and browser automation very clear - The agent is using structured tools exposed by the portal, not just clicking through pages. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I don't come from a coding background, so getting this working end to end is something I'm especially proud of. I built a real workflow across two separate systems without creating integration between them which is really cool. The same agent can submit work into the buyer portal, understand what comes back, take follow-up actions, and keep the supplier's system updated. What I learned It is not enough for an agent to take an action. It also needs to bring the right information back to the human, present it clearly, and keep the company’s systems up to date. I also saw how WebMCP could help with a much broader B2B problems: getting different systems to work together without building and maintaining another custom integration. What's next for OpenFinance The long-term goal is bigger than one portal. OpenFinance can be a supplier portal of its own, but also act as a WebMCP bridge to other buyer portals that do not support WebMCP yet. That would let suppliers use the same agent across both WebMCP-enabled portals and legacy portals, while giving older portals a more generic path to become agent-ready without each supplier building another custom integration. Over time, that could grow into a network where agents can work across many buyer portals through one common model. About the demo - how it was made The agent panel is a visualization. I created it this way because I felt it made the flow much easier and faster for a new viewer to understand what was happening behind the scenes across two separate systems. Every WebMCP tool call, argument, result, approval, and application state shown was captured from a live execution against the deployed portal. All demonstrated tools and workflows are fully functional in the live application. And I also preferred the AI voice over mine :) Contest note The contest submission is the Acme AP supplier portal. The supplier invoice system shown in the demo and repo is a separate reference application used to demonstrate the full workflow. title: Tail Risk
pitch: Tail Risk tells an organ-transport coordinator when a commercial flight that looks available on the timetable is no longer operationally safe to rely on.
about_excerpt: Tail Risk tells an organ-transport coordinator when a commercial flight that looks available on the timetable is no longer operationally safe to rely on. Like Comment Story Updates TAIL RISK TAIL RISK is one web page that tells an organ-transport coordinator whether a commercial flight is still operationally safe to rely on, and that takes the recommendation away from the assistant acting on it the moment the evidence behind it stops being true. A donated kidney is available in Chicago at 19:45 and has to be in a Boston theatre by 04:15. Four commercial flights connect ORD to BOS inside that window. An assistant asks the page which one to use. The earliest, UA 417 , is the obvious pick on a timetable and the wrong one. Its aircraft is over Colorado, 87 minutes late into O'Hare, and 76 of those minutes cannot be absorbed by the scheduled turn: UA 417 BROKEN −76 min binding: AIRCRAFT_ROTATION cargo acceptance +20 · aircraft rotation −76 · destination delivery −18 UA 623 works, at +33 minutes . The assistant commits, and what comes back is not a message. It is a certificate: the margin, the binding constraint, the tail number, the inbound sector, a validity horizon, and a fingerprint over all of it. Five minutes later the carrier swaps the aircraft. N24211 becomes N77518, which is still inbound from Houston. Nothing about the timetable moves. The mission margin goes from +33 to −11 . And this is the part the project exists for: PLAN_SELECTED PLAN_INVALIDATED select_transport_plan withdrawn select_transport_plan withdrawn get_selected_plan registered get_selected_plan withdrawn revalidate_plan registered revalidate_plan withdrawn explain_invalidation withdrawn explain_invalidation registered replan_mission withdrawn replan_mission registered get_selected_plan and revalidate_plan are not disabled and they do not return an error. They are unregistered . toolchange fires. The assistant holding that plan discovers the world moved because its own tool list changed under it, and the only route forward is replan_mission , which re-evaluates against current evidence and lands on UA 1051 at +15 minutes, TIGHT . An agent's previous decision had a validity condition, reality broke it, and the web application withdrew the capability before the agent could act on stale information. The problem is real, and it is not a data problem The FAA notes that organs and biological material travel on commercial airlines virtually every day. UNOS documents cargo acceptance cutoffs of 60 to 120 minutes and cargo offices that are not open around the clock. A coordinator choosing between two flights is reading a timetable. A timetable does not say which aircraft is assigned to a flight, and it does not say that the aircraft is currently in the air somewhere else. That single fact is what turns a comfortable +58 minutes into −76, and no amount of delay-probability modelling recovers it, because it is not uncertainty. It is arithmetic that nobody did. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP surfaces are a menu: the same tools, always present, and an agent picks one. This one is a statement about the present. Which tools exist encodes what is currently true. That matters here more than it would in a shop. Time-critical transport is a domain where the expensive failure is not a bad decision, it is a decision that was good and quietly stopped being. There is no channel for pushing that fact to a host agent mid-conversation, and a page that only answered questions could not raise it. Removing the capability is the push. registerTool 's AbortSignal plus toolchange is the only mechanism on the web today that lets a site interrupt an agent's plan without being asked, and it is the whole reason this product is a page with tools rather than a report. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Hold a plan whose validity the page keeps checking, and be interrupted by the page when it stops holding. A coordinator with a phone can refresh a flight tracker. An agent in a chat window cannot be interrupted: between the moment a plan is chosen and the moment the shipment reaches the counter, nothing reaches it. TAIL RISK re-evaluates every option on every evidence change, rechecks the certificate's basis against the new world, and when the fingerprint no longer matches it withdraws the capabilities whose existence implied the plan was still good. The agent then has a structured explain_invalidation giving the field-by-field difference, and exactly one way forward. The division of labour is the point. The person is the one who knows the deadline and who will call the airline. The agent is the one who can hold four candidate flights, three constraints and a validity horizon in mind at once and act at the moment something changes. Neither is doing the other's job. How I implemented WebMCP Twelve tools, and the set of them is a pure function of mission state. surfaceFor(state, hasInvalidation) in packages/domain/src/machine.ts is the whole rule. ToolLifecycle owns one AbortController per registered tool, so unregistering is aborting a signal and the tool surface is derived state rather than something maintained by hand. Reconciliation is driven by state transitions, never from inside a handler. reconcile() throws if called during a tool execution. A transition that lands mid-call is deferred and applied the moment the handler returns, so the surface never silently stops tracking the machine exactly when an agent is the one driving it. One measured platform behaviour that cost a working build. When a handler's own state change unregisters that handler's tool, aborting the registration inside a finally lands in a microtask that is still within Chrome's await on the handler's promise. The agent then receives UnknownError: The operation failed for an unknown transient reason for a call that in fact succeeded. guard() therefore schedules the reconcile with setTimeout(0) , the next macrotask, so the result reaches the caller before its tool stops existing. Measured in Chrome 152 by driving the deployed page with Playwright and calling every tool through document.modelContext.executeTool , which is how the failure was found at all. Every direct document.modelContext call lives in one package. @tr/webmcp is the only code that touches the platform. It also enforces Chrome's documented budgets at registration time (30 characters of name, 500 of description, 150 per parameter description, roughly 1.5 KB of output) and records overruns rather than leaving them to surface as unexplained tool-selection drift. No free-text field anywhere in the surface. Every string an agent can send is an enum, a three-letter airport code, a flight number under ^[A-Z0-9]{2,3} ?[0-9]{1,4}$ , an option id under ^O[0-9]{1,2}$ , or a bounded ISO instant. Every string an agent receives is an identifier, an enum, an ISO instant or a number. untrustedContentHint: false is a claim this build can make honestly, because no external prose enters the system in the first place. The decision is arithmetic, and it names its own bottleneck No language model decides whether a mission works. An agent chooses which flights to ask about and explains the answer to a person; the answer is computed: acceptance_margin = latest_acceptance − package_at_cargo rotation_margin = sched_departure − (projected_inbound_arrival + turnaround) propagated_delay_floor = max(0, inbound_delay − max(0, scheduled_turn − turnaround)) delivery_margin = deliver_by − (projected_arrival + release + ground) mission_margin = min(acceptance, rotation, delivery) The engine always returns which constraint bound. Collapsing that to a score is the failure this product exists to avoid: a coordinator told the binding constraint is aircraft rotation calls the airline, and one told the risk is 74% calls nobody. Empirical P50/P80/P95 margins sit beside the deterministic figure and never override it. UA 623 is VIABLE +33 and simultaneously TIGHT AT P95 , because 41 minutes of historical additional delay over 126 observations takes it to −8. Where history is thin the answer is INSUFFICIENT_HISTORY ; where no aircraft is published the verdict is UNKNOWN rather than a number. Missing evidence never becomes operational confidence. TAIL RISK. A schedule tells you when a flight should leave. This tells an agent whether the mission still works. video_title: TAIL RISK
video_transcript_excerpt: Tail risk tells an organ transplant coordinator whether a commercial flight is still safe to rely on. A kidney keeps about a day on ice. Most of them fly as cargo on ordinary passenger flights, where hours of delay cost the organ. A donated kidney has a flight. The flight is on time. The aircraft is not. And when a recommendation stops being true, this page takes it away from the assistant that was acting on it. A kidney is available in Chicago at a quarter to 8:00 in the evening. It has to be in a Boston theater by a quarter past 4:00. For commercial flights connect to here to Logan inside that window. And a timetable says nothing about which aircraft will fly it. UA 417 is the earliest, and on the timetable, the obvious choice. Its aircraft is over Colorado, 87 minutes late into a here. 76 of those minutes cannot be absorbed by the schedule turn. Mission margin minus 76. The published departure time never moved. Every figure is arithmetic. Cargo acceptance, aircraft rotation, destination delivery. The mission margin is the smallest of the three, and the page always names which one it was. UA 623 works at plus 33 minutes. So, the assistant commits, and what comes back is not a message. It is a certificate, the margin, the tail number, the inbound sector, and a fingerprint over all of it. That fingerprint is what makes Taylor definition rather than a judgment call. Then the carrier swaps the aircraft. November 24211 becomes November 77518, still inbound from Houston. The timetable does not move. The mission margin goes from plus 33 to minus 11. And this is the whole project. Get selected plan and revalidate plan are not disabled, and they do not return an error. They are unregistered. Tool change fires. The assistant holding that plan finds out because its own tool list changed under it. Replan mission is the only route forward, and it reevaluates against current evidence. UA1051 hold at +15 minutes. Tight. And the page says tight rather than good. 12 web MCP tools and which of them exist is a pure function of mission state. Register tool with an abort signal is the mechanism. The state machine is the authority. A schedule tells you when a flight should leave. Tail risk tells an agent whether the mission still works.

title: TAAMs Import Sourcing Desk
pitch: A web page where a person and an AI agent source verified food imports together - the agent operates the same screen the buyer is looking at, and cannot send anything without the buyer's approval.
about_excerpt: A web page where a person and an AI agent source verified food imports together - the agent operates the same screen the buyer is looking at, and cannot send anything without the buyer's approval. Like Comment Story Updates main image(pinned-and-highlighted) product load approval Inspiration Importing food into a country starts with two questions that have nothing to do with software: is this a real supplier, and is this a real price? Buyers answer them by hand today — reading government customs portals, cold-calling trading companies, guessing whether a quoted price is normal. All of that happens before a single quote is ever sent. We had already built a remote MCP server for this data, and we watched what people actually did with it. The agent gives you a good summary. Then you open the real tool and redo the comparison yourself, because sourcing decisions are made by looking at things side by side . The summary is not the work. That is the gap WebMCP closes. The comparison the agent builds is the comparison you are looking at. We wanted to find out whether that changes the workflow or just moves the JSON, so we built the same sourcing problem as a page an agent can operate. What it does A sourcing desk for food imported into Korea, backed by TAAMs — a B2B marketplace where verified, officially imported products are traded directly with the importers who cleared them through customs. You search a product and get real customs clearance records: the monthly import unit price in USD/kg broken down by exporting country, the overseas suppliers actually shipping it, and the Korean companies already buying it. You pin origins side by side, filter to one supplying country, and draft a sourcing enquiry to a named supplier. Every one of those actions is a button a person can click. Seven of them are also registered as WebMCP tools, so an agent can reach for the same buttons. The seven tools, in three tiers Tier A — lookup (4 tools). search_import_products resolves free text in English or Korean to the exact name used in clearance records; get_import_price_trend , get_top_exporters and get_active_importers fetch and render. The agent does the tedious part — name resolution, twelve months of history, nine countries — and the human keeps the judgement. Tier B — screen control (2 tools), zero network requests. pin_to_comparison_board and highlight_supplier_country fetch nothing at all. They rearrange what is already in front of the human. Open the network tab while they run and nothing fires; that is asserted in the test suite, not just claimed. This is the tier that only exists inside the page. A remote MCP server can return better JSON. It cannot know that a table is on your screen, let alone which row deserves attention. Tier C — action, gated by a human (1 tool). draft_sourcing_request fills in a real enquiry to a real supplier and then stops. An approval dialog shows exactly what is about to leave — product, supplier, quantity, notes. Only on approval does a pre-filled email open from the user's own mail client, and the person still presses send. Cancel, and the draft stays on screen to edit by hand. Its most important behaviour is what it refuses to do. The agent has authority to prepare and no authority to send. What it looks like with real data Ask "Thai mango or Brazilian? Put both on the board and tell me who I should buy from." and the agent pins two cards from the same product: Thailand Brazil Import price $6.47/kg $5.16/kg Clearances (2025) 3,310 651 Named suppliers 42 5 Thailand is 25% more expensive with five times the shipment history and eight times the supplier base. That is a sourcing decision, on screen, from 4,368 customs records for one fruit. It works with no agent at all Search, pin, highlight and RFQ are all clickable. Someone who has never heard of WebMCP gets a complete tool; an agent makes it faster. Each tool handler is a one-liner delegating to the same function the page's own button calls, so there is no agent-only code path and no human-only one — checkable from the source. How we built it Deliberately minimal: zero dependencies, no build step, one static page, no backend of its own. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool() at load, and the page calls the public TAAMs read API directly from the browser. Three findings about the gap between the published spec and the shipping browser, because that gap was part of the work: 1. The API is on document.modelContext , not navigator.modelContext . Much published material still shows navigator . We feature-detect both so the page survives the object moving again. 2. requestUserInteraction() does not exist in Chrome 151. The approval gate was designed around it. The object only carries ontoolchange , executeTool , getTools and registerTool , so we built the gate ourselves as an in-page modal. That turned out better: the human sees the actual draft rather than a generic system prompt. 3. executeTool takes a tool object and a JSON string . Not a name, not an arguments object — both are rejected. This is documented nowhere we could find; we established it by enumerating the object in a live browser and trying each candidate convention until one returned a result. That third finding is what made the whole thing testable. getTools() and executeTool() are exposed to the page, so a test can drive the tools exactly as an agent drives them — no ChatGPT needed in the loop. Every claim in the README is checked that way, in a real Chrome, against the live API. Challenges we ran into The schema could not express the demo's own question. pin_to_comparison_board originally took a product name and nothing else. But the question a buyer actually asks is "this origin or that one?" — same product, two countries — and a board keyed on product alone cannot hold that. You would be pinning the same product twice. No wording fixed it; the argument list had to change. We found this by rehearsing tool selection rather than tool execution: handing a model only the registered tool definitions and the demo's question, and asking what it would call. It never reached for the screen-control tier at all. Both screen-control tools were written as if the user would name them. "Call this when the user says 'compare'." A question that never uses the word never reaches the tool. Nothing told the agent it could reach for them on its own judgement. Adding that one clause is what makes the agent, in the demo video, say "I'll pin both options first, then highlight the stronger sourcing lane" — unprompted. A filtered fetch got stored as the whole truth. Narrowing the supplier list to one country overwrote the session's list, so a card for any other country counted zero suppliers in it. Brazil showed "0 suppliers" when it has five. The API had been right the whole time; the number on screen was wrong. The tests were passing through all of it. 22 of 22 green while the supplier column read "Unknown supplier" on every row, while a month-less price call returned a 500, while Brazil showed zero. Each assertion was true and each missed the point. What caught them: looking at the screen, and running the thing in a real agent browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Tier B genuinely makes zero network requests, and you can check it. Not a design intention — an assertion in the test suite that counts requests during those calls and fails if any fire. It failed once, honestly, when a name-resolution call snuck in. That is fixed and guarded. The action tool refuses, visibly, every time. The agent in our demo says it itself: "Review it in the approval dialog and click Approve to open the pre-filled email — nothing has been sent yet." We put that instruction in the tool's return value and the model honoured it. An agent that does not overclaim is worth more here than one more feature. It runs in ChatGPT's actual in-app browser. Not only behind a Chrome flag. ChatGPT opened the page, found all seven tools, pinned two origins, highlighted Thailand, drafted an RFQ to a named Thai exporter, and stopped for approval. That run is the demo video. The data is real, public, and government-sourced. 1,318,602 customs clearance transactions since 2023, 169,089 registered overseas manufacturers across 202 countries, built on records published by Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and Korea Customs Service. Not scraped listings, not self-reported catalogues. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product surface, not documentation. Every behaviour we wanted came from a sentence in a description, and every behaviour we did not get was a sentence we had not written. The gap between "the agent could do this" and "the agent does this" was one clause about when to act on its own judgement. Testing execution is not testing selection. executeTool bypasses the model's decision entirely, so a suite can be fully green while the agent never picks the tools at all. title: Storyforge
pitch: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests.
about_excerpt: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most game companions feel like scripted followers, while AI assistants usually live in a separate chat window. We wanted to explore what happens when an agent becomes a genuine party member—one that understands the battlefield, remembers the journey, offers useful advice, and acts through the same rules as the player. Storyforge grew from the idea that AI should not replace the player or secretly rewrite the game. It should make the adventure feel more social, strategic, and alive. What it does Storyforge is a fantasy action RPG in which the player becomes the Last Heir and travels across five corrupted realms to recover the Eclipse Seals. The player fights enemies, completes realm-specific objectives, collects weapons, recruits companions, and confronts multi-phase bosses. Each companion has a distinct personality, ability, tactical role, trust level, and independent motivation. Through WebMCP, an external agent can: Inspect the live battlefield and fellowship state Understand health, enemies, inventory, objectives, pressure mechanics, and boss phases Explain the next valid quest action Recommend companion abilities and battle strategies Issue reversible tactical commands Propose coordinated party plans for the player to approve Agent actions appear in a visible activity feed, keeping the collaboration understandable and accountable. How we built it We built Storyforge with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and a deterministic TypeScript game engine. The WorldEngine is the canonical source of truth for combat, quests, inventory, companions, relationships, and campaign progression. Both the React interface and WebMCP tools operate on this same state. The game registers typed, JSON-schema-based WebMCP tools through document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . Read tools expose purpose-built views of the battlefield and fellowship. Action tools pass validated commands into the engine rather than manipulating the interface or inventing results. Consequential agent actions create visible proposals that the player can accept or reject. Activity is persisted locally, and the project includes automated tests for combat, quest progression, companion behavior, and WebMCP integration. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agents useful without allowing them to bypass the game. Early versions made companions feel cosmetic because the player could complete most objectives alone. We redesigned the campaign around companion-specific abilities, recruitment trials, trust, pressure mechanics, coordinated attacks, and independent initiatives. We also had to keep agent reasoning grounded. Instead of asking an agent to interpret pixels, we exposed structured battlefield state and enforced every action through the game engine. Another challenge was browser compatibility. WebMCP, browser speech synthesis, microphone access, and deployment environments expose different capabilities. We added feature detection, captions, typed-command fallbacks, visible status indicators, and a Chrome Origin Trial token. Finally, presenting a large game world alongside combat information, party controls, dialogue, recommendations, and agent activity required several UI redesigns to prevent overlapping panels. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is part of the actual gameplay rather than a decorative chatbot. The agent sees the same canonical state that drives combat and can affect the encounter through real, constrained tools. At the same time, the player retains authority over movement, major plans, and consequential changes. We are also proud of the fellowship system. Companions persist across realms, fight alongside the player, develop trust, unlock combinations, offer contextual advice, and sometimes leave to pursue opportunities based on their own priorities. The result is a complete five-stage campaign with distinct environments, collectible equipment, recruitment challenges, escalating realm mechanics, multi-phase bosses, persistent progression, remappable controls, and a visible human-agent collaboration history. What we learned We learned that believable agentic gameplay depends more on constraints and consequences than unlimited freedom. Agents feel intelligent when they receive accurate context, understand what is currently possible, and make decisions that visibly affect the world. Giving an agent unrestricted control would have made the game less coherent and less enjoyable. We also learned that transparency improves trust. Showing tool calls, recommendations, proposals, and outcomes makes the agent feel like a teammate whose reasoning can be understood—not an invisible system changing the game behind the scenes. Most importantly, AI companions become compelling when they have specialized capabilities, incomplete information, relationships, and motivations of their own. What's next for Storyforge Next, we want to deepen the social and strategic side of the fellowship: Dynamic voice generation with a distinct voice for every companion and boss Longer companion memory and relationships shaped by player decisions Procedurally generated quests grounded in persistent world rules More companion disagreements, personal missions, and conflicting priorities Drop-in cooperative play between human and agent-controlled party members Additional realms, weapons, enemies, and branching endings Improved tactical planning with environmental interactions and party formations Shareable campaign histories that preserve every important human-agent decision Our long-term goal is for every Storyforge adventure to feel like playing with a group of friends who understand the world, surprise you, and help create a story none of you could have produced alone. title: Chapa - engineering impact you and your agent shape together
pitch: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you.
about_excerpt: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you. Like 4 Comment 2 Story Updates Chapa meets WebMCP: the live developer-impact site becomes agent-operable. 19 tool registrations, reads open, writes human-approved. 18 distinct tools across 4 surfaces: discovery, profiles, verification, and the badge studio; all callable from the page itself. Agents propose, humans approve: simulate and preview freely, but nothing persists without explicit human confirmation. Try it live at chapa.thecreativetoken.com. Point any WebMCP-capable agent at the site or scan the QR. Inspiration Your repos show what you shipped. They do not show the engineer behind them. A CV can say "reliable," "consistent," or "quality-focused," but those are claims. Chapa tries to turn the work itself into evidence. Chapa analyzes 12 months of engineering activity and builds an Impact Profile across four core dimensions: Delivery, Quality, Consistency, and Breadth. An optional fifth dimension, Craft, appears when a developer provides a report from an AI coding tool. The profile includes a developer archetype, composite score, and trend over time. An internal confidence score adjusts the composite when data is incomplete. GitHub can be the starting point, but the profile is not limited to GitHub. Chapa can combine activity from GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg, and enterprise-managed GitHub accounts uploaded through the Chapa CLI. The result is a live SVG badge that can sit in a README and evolve as the developer's work evolves. Badges marked Verified metrics carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature, so their verification records can be authenticated and tampering detected. But there was a problem. The badge could show your engineering impact, but it could not explain it. Why is Quality 62? What caused the score to fall this month? What would happen if Delivery improved by ten points? How does this profile compare with another developer's? A static badge cannot answer those questions. An agent can. Why WebMCP WebMCP changes Chapa from something an agent can merely look at into something an agent can understand. Behind the badge is structured state: dimension scores, normalized submetrics, archetype, confidence, trend history, verification data, and badge configuration. Trying to infer that state from the DOM would be fragile and incomplete. With WebMCP, Chapa exposes the underlying model directly. An agent can call explain_dimension and receive the score, formula, normalized submetrics, and an improvement tip. It can call get_impact_history to reason about changes over time, or compare_profiles to compare two developers dimension by dimension. The agent is no longer interpreting pixels. It is working with the same engineering model that produced them. Creator Studio made the fit even stronger. Studio was already terminal-first: users type commands such as /set colorPalette indigo or /preset holographic . That command registry already defined Chapa's mutation vocabulary. WebMCP became another interface to the same system rather than a separate agent API. Human clicks, terminal commands, and agent tool calls all converge on the same underlying actions. What people and agents can do together Understand the profile Instead of searching through panels, you can ask: "Why did my score drop this month?" The agent can inspect the impact history, explain the affected dimensions, and answer using the same numbers Chapa displays. suggest_improvements runs Chapa's existing insight engine against the real profile, so recommendations come from the developer's own activity rather than generic advice. Explore what could change simulate_score lets an agent change hypothetical dimension values and calculate the resulting composite score, tier, and delta. Nothing is persisted. That means the agent can answer questions like: "What happens if I improve Quality to 80?" before anything changes. Compare engineering profiles compare_profiles validates another public handle, loads both profiles, and returns the delta for every dimension. What previously required opening two profiles and comparing them manually becomes a structured question an agent can answer. Understand verification explain_verification explains what a Chapa signature proves, what it does not prove, when the verification record expires, and whether it uses the current or legacy format. Verification becomes something a person can actually understand rather than just a cryptographic status indicator. Shape the badge Creator Studio contains seven visual style categories. Instead of navigating controls, a developer can describe what they want: "Make it minimal, remove the glow, and use the terminal preset." The agent translates that intent into the same /preset and /set commands a person would type. Those commands appear in the Studio transcript as they execute. The agent does not get a secret mutation path. It uses the same one the human does. Human control stays at the boundary The most important design decision was deciding what the agent should not control. Agents can inspect, explain, compare, simulate, preview, and restyle freely. Persistence is different. save_badge_config creates a proposal in the UI and waits for the developer to approve it. The agent can help shape the result; the human decides when it becomes real. In production, confirmation persists the configuration, invalidates the badge cache, and updates the public share page and live SVG. In judge demo mode, confirmed saves remain local. How I implemented WebMCP Chapa registers 19 WebMCP tool registrations across four surfaces, using 18 distinct tool names because Creator Studio and public profiles both register explain_dimension . Landing page ( / ) get_site_capabilities , find_profile Creator Studio ( /studio and /studio?demo=1 ) list_style_options , apply_badge_style , apply_preset , preview_badge , reset_badge_config , save_badge_config , simulate_score , suggest_improvements , explain_dimension Public profile ( /u/{handle} ) get_impact_profile , get_impact_history , verify_badge , compare_profiles , explain_dimension , get_embed_snippet Verification page ( /verify/{hash} ) get_verification_record , explain_verification A shared useModelContextTools hook registers each catalog on document.modelContext . A catalog signature keys registration so updated definitions register cleanly, and an AbortController removes tools when the component unmounts. In Creator Studio, Quick Controls, terminal commands, and WebMCP calls all resolve to command text and pass through the same executeCommand registry. This keeps the terminal transcript, React state, live preview, and pending save configuration on one shared mutation path. Trust and safety Public profile and verification tools are read-only. Any tool that may return user-controlled text, such as a display name from a source platform, sets untrustedContentHint to true . Free-text values are length-bounded and control characters are removed at the tool boundary. The server also removes private data before it reaches the browser. For example, a profile's confidence value and penalty reasons never enter the React Server Component payload for a visitor viewing another developer's profile. verify_badge strips confidence again at the client boundary as defense in depth. A feature flag named webmcp_enabled controls the entire WebMCP surface. A database value can override the environment configuration, allowing the tools to be disabled without a deployment. Challenges One of the most useful bugs I found was not in a tool. It was in the trust model around one. explain_dimension is used in two contexts. In Creator Studio, the data belongs to the developer viewing it. On a public profile, some of that data originates from another developer. The original tool factory hardcoded the trusted annotation. Nothing exploitable was exposed because no user-controlled text was present in the current submetrics. But the next field containing something like a repository name could have crossed the boundary incorrectly. I changed the factory so trust context is a required parameter. Each caller now has to declare what it knows. The second challenge appeared in badge caching. Because badge content can be localized, it was possible for the rendered locale and cache key locale to disagree. An English badge could therefore end up in a Spanish cache slot. I replaced those independent decisions with a single resolveBadgeLocale entry point that returns both the localized strings and the corresponding cache key. The caller can no longer accidentally pair one locale with another locale's cache entry. What I am proud of WebMCP did not become a parallel control plane bolted onto Chapa. The agent uses the same domain model and, in Creator Studio, the same command registry as the person using the interface. That gives Chapa a clear collaboration bounda

title: SurveyGuard
pitch: SurveyGuard helps people and AI agents collaboratively detect, explain, and fix survey quality, privacy, and bias issues before publication using structured WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
SurveyGuard helps people and AI agents collaboratively detect, explain, and fix survey quality, privacy, and bias issues before publication using structured WebMCP tools.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Creating a good survey is harder than it appears. A survey can look complete while still containing leading language, double-barrelled questions, unclear timeframes, sensitive questions without an opt-out, conflicting response options, or unnecessary requests for personal information. 

 These issues are often identified through manual reviews, long checklists, and repeated back-and-forth between researchers, product teams, and stakeholders. The process takes time, depends heavily on reviewer experience, and can still produce inconsistent results. 

 SurveyGuard was inspired by a simple question: 

 What if a person and an AI agent could review and improve a survey together inside the same live workspace? 

 Instead of requiring an agent to interpret buttons, scrape page content, or guess how the survey application works, SurveyGuard exposes clearly defined survey actions through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the survey, identify risks, explain findings, and perform approved actions while the person remains in control. 

 What SurveyGuard does
SurveyGuard is a WebMCP-enabled survey quality workspace that helps people and AI agents collaboratively review surveys before publication. 

 The current MVP allows users to: 

 Create, edit, and delete survey questions
Configure question types and response options
Validate survey questions against defined quality checks
Identify personally identifiable information
Detect leading or loaded wording
Flag potentially double-barrelled questions
Identify sensitive questions that may need a “Prefer not to answer” option
Detect unclear reference periods
Flag exclusive options such as “None of these” in multi-select questions
Review findings by severity
Apply recommended corrections
Monitor a dynamic survey-readiness score
Generate a concise survey-readiness report
Findings are organized into three levels: 

 Blocking: A high-risk issue that should be addressed before publication
Needs review: An issue requiring human judgment or revision
Suggestion: A non-blocking quality improvement
SurveyGuard uses fictional survey content in the demonstration and does not depend on private company data, confidential research, or customer information. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit
Survey review is not just a question-and-answer experience. It requires an agent to inspect structured survey content, understand validation results, modify specific questions, add response options, and confirm how those actions changed the survey. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent may have to infer this structure from the visual interface and navigate the application indirectly. That approach can be slow, fragile, and difficult to verify. 

 With WebMCP, SurveyGuard exposes narrow and intentional tools that describe exactly what an agent can do. The agent works with the same survey and application state that the user sees. 

 The MVP includes the following site tools: 

 get_survey_summary
list_questions
validate_survey
rewrite_question
add_prefer_not_to_answer
generate_readiness_report
For example, a user can ask an agent to: 

 Validate this survey, explain the highest-risk issue, and help me fix it. 

 The agent can call the validation tool, return structured findings, explain the most important issue, and then use an appropriate write tool after the user approves the change. 

 This creates a more reliable experience than asking the agent to guess how to manipulate the interface. 

 Human-agent collaboration
SurveyGuard is designed around human review rather than unattended automation. 

 The application separates inspection from modification: 

 The agent retrieves the current survey structure.
The agent runs structured validation.
The agent explains the identified issues.
The user reviews the recommendation.
An approved change is applied through a specific WebMCP tool.
The interface updates so the user can verify the result.
SurveyGuard recalculates the readiness score and remaining findings.
The agent provides speed and consistency, while the user maintains responsibility for context, judgment, and final approval. 

 This is particularly important in survey design because whether a question is appropriate can depend on the research objective, intended audience, jurisdiction, and sensitivity of the subject. 

 How I built it
SurveyGuard was built as a React-based web application with a responsive three-panel review experience: 

 A question list for navigating the survey
An editor for reviewing wording, question type, and response options
A validation panel for displaying findings and recommended actions
The validation engine evaluates each question using transparent, deterministic rules. Each finding includes: 

 A unique issue code
A severity level
A short title
An explanation
A recommended correction or action when appropriate
The interface calculates a survey-readiness score based on the number and severity of unresolved findings. The score updates as users edit questions or apply corrections. 

 WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool defines: 

 A specific name
A focused description
A narrow input schema
Required parameters
Read-only annotations where applicable
An execution handler connected to the survey’s existing application logic
The tools return structured results so an agent can understand what happened and communicate the result to the user. 

 The application also preserves a normal visual workflow for people and can display a preview state when WebMCP is not available in the current browser environment. 

 Challenges I faced
Designing useful tool boundaries
One challenge was deciding how much authority each tool should have. A single broad tool that could change the entire survey would be flexible, but it would also be harder to control and verify. 

 I chose narrower tools such as rewrite_question and add_prefer_not_to_answer. This makes each action easier for the agent to select, easier for the user to understand, and easier to test. 

 Separating blocking issues from recommendations
Not every survey-quality concern should prevent publication. Treating every finding as equally severe would create unnecessary friction and reduce trust in the validator. 

 To address this, SurveyGuard separates blocking issues, review items, and optional suggestions. 

 Keeping the human in control
A technically successful agent action is not necessarily the right research decision. SurveyGuard therefore treats agent recommendations as reviewable actions and clearly communicates that human approval is recommended before publication. 

 Managing shared application state
WebMCP tools and the visible interface need to operate on the same current survey. Tool outputs, question edits, validation results, and readiness scoring must remain consistent after every action. 

 The MVP connects tool execution to the same underlying state used by the visual interface so changes can be seen and verified immediately. 

 Working within a short build window
The challenge required prioritizing a focused, demonstrable workflow. Instead of attempting to build a complete survey-authoring platform, I concentrated on the core WebMCP experience: inspect, validate, explain, improve, and verify. 

 What I learned
Building SurveyGuard reinforced several important lessons: 

 Agent-native applications need explicit actions, not just an AI chat box.

title: AlphaX
pitch: Universal mediation layer that turns any website into an agent-native surface using WebMCP — with full human supervision.

Universal mediation layer that turns any website into an agent-native surface using WebMCP — with full human supervision.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 The biggest barrier to the agent-native web is adoption. Most websites will not implement WebMCP themselves anytime soon. AlphaX was born from a simple question: what if I could turn any existing website into a reliable, agent-ready surface — while keeping the human firmly in control? 

 Instead of waiting for every site to add tools, AlphaX acts as a universal mediation layer. It analyzes a page, synthesizes high-quality WebMCP tools, registers them live, and lets agents use them under strict human supervision. 

 What it does 

 AlphaX lets you: 

 
 Paste any URL 
 Automatically generate structured WebMCP tools from the page 
 Review and approve those tools 
 Register them via document.modelContext.registerTool 
 Let agents call the tools while you supervise every sensitive action 
 Maintain full provenance and audit logs 
 

 It supports three supervision modes (Strict, Supervised, Autonomous) so the human always remains sovereign. 

 How I built it 

 AlphaX is a full-stack system: 

 
 Frontend : React + TypeScript + Zustand + Tailwind 
 Backend : Express + Playwright (controlled browser) 
 Tool Synthesis : Groq + Gemini + a strong heuristic fallback 
 Persistence : Supabase 
 WebMCP : Full imperative registration with polyfill support 
 

 The system extracts page structure, generates tools, registers them dynamically, translates tool calls into Playwright actions, and streams live feedback and provenance to the operator. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 
 Making tool generation reliable across very different websites 
 Keeping Playwright stable in a production environment 
 Designing a supervision model that feels safe without becoming annoying 
 Balancing power-user features with first-time clarity for judges 
 Deploying a Playwright-heavy backend alongside a Vite frontend 
 

 What I learnt 

 Building a meta-layer on top of WebMCP taught us how important human-in-the-loop design is. Agents become far more useful when they operate on real websites through clean, schema-validated tools — but only when the human retains clear control and visibility. 

 What's next 

 
 Better multi-step goal planning 
 Improved tool quality through learning from successful runs 
 Chrome extension for deeper same-origin mediation 
 Support for authenticated sessions and multi-site orchestration

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.
