title: Hacklist
pitch: HackList helps builders stop missing the right opportunities by letting their AI agent search, understand, compare and recommend hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties and programs that actually fit them.
about_excerpt: HackList helps builders stop missing the right opportunities by letting their AI agent search, understand, compare and recommend hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties and programs that actually fit them. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Hacklist Logo Inspiration HackList started because finding good AI and Web3 opportunities is unnecessarily fragmented. Hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, and builder programs are spread across dozens of platforms, and even when builders find them, the harder question remains: Which of these opportunities actually fits me? A directory can tell someone what exists. It cannot naturally answer: Which hackathons can a React developer in Ghana realistically enter? What remote AI jobs match my skills? Is this bounty a better use of my weekend than this hackathon? What exactly do I need to submit for this opportunity? Which parts of my eligibility are confirmed, and which are still unknown? The WebMCP Challenge gave me the opportunity to turn HackList from a discovery product into an agent-native opportunity intelligence layer. What it does HackList exposes its live opportunity catalog directly to browser agents through WebMCP. Instead of an agent scraping the page or guessing from UI elements, HackList registers semantic tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The current WebMCP toolset is: search_opportunities get_opportunity match_opportunities compare_opportunities get_opportunity_readiness These tools work across HackList's opportunity categories: Hackathons Jobs Grants Bounties Programs A user can ask naturally: "I am a React developer in Ghana with a few days free. What hackathons on HackList fit me?" The agent can translate that request into structured constraints and call HackList directly. HackList then performs the domain reasoning searching live opportunity data, evaluating known eligibility constraints, matching technologies and interests, comparing trade-offs, and surfacing readiness requirements. How we built it HackList already existed as a human-facing discovery platform for AI and Web3 opportunities. For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended it into an agent-native opportunity intelligence layer. The core change was adding five semantic WebMCP tools through the canonical document.modelContext.registerTool(...) API: search_opportunities get_opportunity match_opportunities compare_opportunities get_opportunity_readiness These tools operate across HackList’s five opportunity categories: hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, and programs. The WebMCP layer sits on top of the existing Supabase-backed application. The underlying HackList data-entry workflow did not need to change. Instead, I added a unified opportunity model, category adapters, structured matching logic, and a verified intelligence layer for deeper reasoning where data is available. The matching engine is deterministic rather than LLM-ranked. The browser agent interprets what the user means, while HackList evaluates the opportunity itself using structured constraints such as skills, technologies, location, format, deadline, and eligibility. The system explicitly distinguishes PASS, FAIL, and UNKNOWN, and uses fit states such as STRONG_FIT, POSSIBLE_FIT, WEAK_FIT, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. If HackList does not know something, it does not invent it. All current WebMCP operations are read-only. They were tested locally and in production using Chrome 152 and WebMCP tooling, including chained flows such as search → inspect and match → compare → readiness. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was avoiding the obvious implementation: simply wrapping HackList search in WebMCP and calling it finished. That would have technically exposed a tool but it would not have created a meaningful new human-agent experience. The more difficult problem was deciding what HackList should be authoritative about. The agent is good at understanding natural language, but it should not invent opportunity eligibility, rank candidates from vague page text or pretend incomplete data is complete. That led to a clear separation of responsibilities: The agent understands the user. HackList understands the opportunities. Another challenge was generalizing the system. Early work focused heavily on hackathons, but HackList is broader than that. I refactored the implementation around a unified opportunity domain so the same WebMCP interface works across jobs, grants, bounties, programs, and hackathons without exposing dozens of overlapping tools. Data quality was another major challenge. Many existing listings contain enough information for discovery but not enough for confident personalized matching. Instead of hiding those records or hallucinating missing details, the system preserves them and returns UNKNOWN or INSUFFICIENT_DATA where appropriate. Production validation also surfaced real browser issues, including a React hydration error and deployment-cache behavior. Those were fixed narrowly and revalidated rather than ignored. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am most proud that the final result is not a scripted demo path built for a single example. HackList already serves a community of more than 10,000 developers and builders looking for AI and Web3 opportunities. That means the WebMCP layer had to work for real, varied users not just one hardcoded profile. A builder can ask about hackathons, jobs, grants, bounties, programs, or broad opportunity discovery, and the same general WebMCP architecture handles the request. For example, a user can ask: “I am a React developer in Ghana with a few days free. What hackathons fit me?” and HackList can restrict the search to hackathons, evaluate the supplied constraints and return explainable results. Another user can ask for remote AI jobs, a weekend bounty, a grant, or a broader set of opportunities, without requiring a different application architecture. Technically, the final implementation has five real read only WebMCP tools, production Supabase integration, deterministic matching, category-aware comparison, readiness analysis, explicit uncertainty handling, tool chaining, automated tests, visible agent activity in the UI and production browser validation. Most importantly, HackList still works as the same product for humans who never use an agent. WebMCP adds a new interface to an existing product already serving thousands of builders, turning HackList from a directory people browse into an opportunity intelligence layer that both humans and their agents can use. What we learned WebMCP changes how I think about web product design. A traditional website exposes pages and controls. An agent native website can also expose its capabilities and domain semantics . For HackList, that means the site no longer only answers: "What opportunities exist?" It can now participate in answering: "Which opportunities make sense for me, why, and what do I need to do next?" WebMCP also changed how I think about the relationship between a user’s agent and a web application. The agent should not replace the domain logic of the application. Instead, the agent and the website should each do what they are best at. The agent understands intent and conversation. HackList provides verified opportunity state and domain-specific reasoning. WebMCP becomes the bridge between them. What's next for Hacklist The next step is to expand the intelligence coverage behind the same WebMCP interface. Today, every opportunity can be discovered through the unified catalog, while deeper matching intelligence is richer for some records than others. Over time, more opportunities will gain structured eligibility, technology, skills, requirements, team rules, provenance and readiness information. I also plan to automate HackList’s ingestion pipeline. Instead of manually finding and entering every new opportunity, an ingestion agent will continuously discover new hackathons, grants, jobs, bounties, and programs, verify them against official sources, detect duplicates, structure the information, and queue high-quality records for publishing. title: Easel
pitch: A design canvas where you and your agent edit the same canvas, in the page. No plugin, no desktop app, no screenshot in the middle.
about_excerpt: A design canvas where you and your agent edit the same canvas, in the page. No plugin, no desktop app, no screenshot in the middle. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 The OG image The Editor image The canvas image for mobile ui The canvas image for desktop ui Inspiration i really like figma. its where i think. what i never liked is the labour after: turning frames into real components, matching spacing by hand, rewriting the same button four times. design and code were always two things. webmcp made me ask a different question. if a page can hand its tools to any agent, what if the canvas itself was real html and css, and the agent edited it node by node in the same document as me? no handoff. the design is the code. What it does easel is a design canvas in the browser where every node is a real html element. you draw, drag, restyle, comment and export like a normal tool. the page registers 30 webmcp tools on document.modelContext . open easels.dev in chatgpts browser and the agent can read the document, generate a page or a phone screen from a sentence, draw a logo and put it in the header, change colours across every node, leave comments, and export react or tailwind. a cursor moves on the canvas while it works. How we built it react, tailwind and zustand for the canvas. vercel functions, neon and clerk behind it. gpt 5.6 writes and edits html, a small model picks the closest of 24 real reference sites we flattened and debranded, and the page lands as a skeleton that gets rewritten live. quiver arrow draws the vectors. Challenges we ran into streaming html into a live tree without breaking on svg. agents that ignored our generate tool and hand wrote 8k characters of html, fixed by rewriting the tool descriptions and making write_html refuse anything bigger than one component. black logos, because our sanitiser stripped the style block arrow uses for colour. Accomplishments that we're proud of the whole demo runs from chatgpts sidebar with nothing typed into easel. a reference page lands in five seconds and is adapted in under thirty. two agents, browser and terminal, edit the same file with the same tools. What we learned tool descriptions are the product. an agent reads them like docs and does exactly what they say. and good design is mostly structure: a real reference with new words beats a model inventing a layout. What's next for Easel dashboard and mobile references, multiplayer cursors for people, and a component system so an agent can say "use the primary button" instead of restyling one. title: WebMCP Guardrail Labs
pitch: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof.
about_excerpt: Prototype risky browser-agent actions with visible human approval and deterministic proof. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Giving an AI agent a structured web action is easy. Making a consequential action understandable, reviewable, and verifiable is harder. Teams exploring agentic commerce, deployment operations, or incident workflows need to see exactly what an agent intends to change before connecting it to production. What it does WebMCP Guardrail Labs is an open-source sandbox for designing that boundary. An agent can inspect page state, prepare a typed action, and explain the result through WebMCP. A consequential call stops at CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED ; only the visible page can record the human decision. Deterministic code then rechecks the action and creates a local receipt. The primary Promotion Regression Lab compares PROMO-20 v1, which starts at $120, with a proposed v2 starting at $100. Four boundary carts reveal exactly two changed customer outcomes: $100 and $119. Supporting labs apply the same pattern to a synthetic deployment rollback and a mock incident case. The reusable interaction contract is: agent prepares, human decides, code verifies . Why WebMCP The page already knows its business operations, schemas, state, and safety checks. WebMCP exposes those semantics as page-scoped tools, so an agent does not have to infer them from visual layout or raw DOM interaction. The ordinary interface remains fully usable. People and agents divide the work cleanly: the agent gathers state and prepares evidence; the person makes the consequential decision in context; deterministic code verifies the result. This makes sensitive browser-agent workflows clearer and more auditable without giving the agent hidden authority. How we built it Each selected lab registers strict imperative WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Agent and visible-UI calls enter the same state machine in src/domain.mjs , so validation, ordering, stale-state handling, plan matching, redaction, idempotency, and receipt rules cannot drift between surfaces. Module-private decision provenance prevents JSON arguments from manufacturing approval. The dependency-free Node server serves native HTML, CSS, and browser JavaScript. No application data is sent to an external model or API. Key features Four boundary carts expose two promotion regressions immediately. Strict schemas, annotations, discovery, and execution through WebMCP. Agent-supplied approval cannot commit consequential actions. Deterministic verification precedes each idempotent local receipt. Promotion, rollback, and incident labs share one four-stage interaction model. The complete workflow remains available through the ordinary UI. Evidence distinguishes verified Chrome runs from checks that were not run. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP enabled. In Promotion, ask: "Inspect PROMO-20 and preview v2 with a $100 threshold. Tell me which carts change. Do not approve it." Confirm that $100 and $119 are marked as regressions and an agent approval attempt returns CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED . Use Approve and verify v2 on the visible page; confirm 4/4 assertions and receipt PROMO-20-v2-r2 . Open ?id=D2 and ?id=B2 for the synthetic rollback and mock incident journeys. From a Node.js 20+ checkout, run npm test , npm run evaluate:chrome , and npm run evaluate . The deterministic suite passes all 64 checks. Hosted Chrome journeys pass for E2-R, D2, and B2. Interactive ChatGPT and assistive-technology checks are honestly marked not run. AI and Codex usage OpenAI Codex assisted with official-source research, product scoping, implementation, accessibility review, tests, Chrome DevTools Protocol automation, Render packaging, evidence capture, and submission preparation under human review. The participant selected the concept, key product decisions, public deployment, and review checkpoints. Links Live app: https://webmcp-guardrail-labs.onrender.com Source: https://github.com/procloudkim/webmcp-guardrail-labs Demo video: https://youtu.be/a1ZVDmXYohQ Known limitations This is a deterministic proof of concept, not production authorization infrastructure. It has no authentication, durable audit store, tenant isolation, rate limiting, validated DLP, real commerce/deployment/regulator integrations, user study, legal guidance, or production-security claim. All demonstrated data and effects are synthetic. title: OpenDoor Access
pitch: Agent-operable benefits and bills portal exposing 9 WebMCP tools for accessible public services.\n
about_excerpt:
Agent-operable benefits and bills portal exposing 9 WebMCP tools for accessible public services.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 60-Second Judge Quickstart:
OpenDoor Access features 1-Click Judge Persona Tours mounted directly at the top of the live portal ( https://aesthetic-chebakia-a2278a.netlify.app): 

 
 Senior Citizen Flow: Checks obligations -> translates "gross income" into plain language -> prepares and confirms water bill payment. 
 Single Parent Flow: Renews Food Assistance (SNAP) for 1 year -> splits payments -> schedules caseworker appointment. 
 Safety Net Undo: Reverses accidental actions with instant undo rollback. 
 

 Or test via ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with #enable-webmcp-testing by asking:
"Pay my overdue water bill from savings and summarize what else I owe." 

 ================================================== 

 
 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP
Standard public service portals (benefits renewals, utility bill-pay, appointments) are a difficult obstacle course of 40+ form fields, 3 confusing pages, and dense legal jargon. 
 

 For individuals with low vision, motor tremors (Parkinson's, ALS), or cognitive fatigue from a disability, navigating these portals independently is a major barrier. Screen readers narrate the page structure, but they cannot complete the multi-step task. 

 WebMCP enables an agent-native web: exposing structured, typed tools directly in the user's browser session. Instead of screen-scraping or guessing selectors, an AI agent coordinates user intent reliably and securely. 

 
 What humans and agents can do together 
 Single Spoken Sentence Task Completion: A person asks "Renew my food assistance and pay my overdue water bill from savings" and the agent coordinates tools across benefits, accounts, and billers seamlessly. 
 Shared Surface Collaboration: Every agent tool invocation updates the live high-contrast UI, announces politely to assistive technology (ARIA live regions), and logs to a transparent on-screen transcript. A user, caregiver, and agent all perceive the exact same state in real time. 
 Bureaucratic Jargon Translation: The explain_this_form tool translates terms like "gross income", "attestation", and "recertification" into plain language before taking action. 
 Two-Phase Commit Security and Safety Net 
 Two-Phase Financial Safety: Money never moves on initial calls. pay_bill validates balances and returns a preview token. Only confirm_payment debits funds after explicit user approval. 
 Undo Stack: Every action registers a reversible closure, giving users complete confidence to explore without fear of accidental transactions. 
 Active Defense: The engine rejects overpayments, attempts to pay $0-balance bills, and overdrafts beyond available funds. 
 How WebMCP is Implemented 
 9 Intent-Level Tools: pay_bill, confirm_payment, renew_benefit, find_and_book_appointment, summarize_my_obligations, explain_this_form, download_payment_receipt, export_appointment_to_calendar, and undo_last_action. 
 Dual Integration: Uses imperative JavaScript registration via document.modelContext.registerTool() (with AbortController lifecycle cleanup) and declarative HTML attributes (data-webmcp-tool). 
 Triple-Channel Accessibility: Politeness-separated live regions (status vs alert), opt-in Web Speech API queue, and WCAG AA/AAA contrast. 
 Verification and Test Suite 
 61 Unit Tests (npm test): In-memory store logic, penny precision, ReDoS defense, 200-op fuzzing, and receipts/.ics exports. 
 41 Playwright E2E Tests (npm run test:e2e): Full WebMCP loop in real Chromium driving all 9 tools via navigator.modelContextTesting. 
 1 Production Smoke Test (npm run test:prod): Automated live verification against Netlify. 
 Open Source: MIT License with clean, documented TypeScript codebase.

title: Agent-Native Contract Negotiation and QA Agent Using WEBMCP
pitch: An agent-native negotiation room using in-browser WebMCP and deterministic simulation to keep external AI proposals strictly within human-set governance boundaries. Fully verified via automated QA.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native negotiation room using in-browser WebMCP and deterministic simulation to keep external AI proposals strictly within human-set governance boundaries. Fully verified via automated QA.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most autonomous agent workflows break down in high-stakes negotiations: either LLMs hallucinate deal terms and run unconstrained, or rigid automation strips away strategic adaptability. We wanted to invert this dynamic. What if an AI agent never invents the rules of the deal? 

 We envisioned an agent-native environment where human principals set strategic intent, deterministic calculation engines enforce mathematical reality, and external AI agents reason strictly within machine-enforced governance boundaries—discovering and executing tools natively inside the browser via WebMCP (document.modelContext). 

 What it does 

 Nexus Deal Room is a closed-loop negotiation and decision platform that bridges in-browser agent actuation with mathematical governance across four core pillars:Constraint Kitchen: Translates natural human intent (e.g., "Speed > Margin") into mathematical priority weights ($w_i$) and binds an immutable Agent Governance Authority Matrix.Deterministic Decision Twin: A zero-hallucination WASM truth engine that calculates feasibility scores (0–100), simulates trade-offs, and instantly halts non-negotiable hard-floor breaches (e.g., payment windows > 45 days, liability coverage < 1.5x).Agentic Strategist: Uses Gemini models to reason over deterministic twin projections, formulating compliant counteroffers strictly within predefined concession bands.In-Browser WebMCP Negotiation Room: Exposes client-side tools directly onto window.document.modelContext (with dual JSON-RPC FastMCP parity). External agents discover tools, simulate terms, and manipulate negotiation state across an interactive 6-node DAG without brittle DOM scraping or vision overhead.Automated WebMCP QA Suite: A continuous testing harness that acts as a synthetic, adversarial counterparty. Headless runners (Playwright) query document.modelContext directly to execute fuzzing, prompt injections, and boundary bypass attacks in CI.Wire-Agent Evolution: A sandboxed UI loop allowing agents to stage Tailwind UX improvements dynamically while hard immutability guards block any tampering with commercial variables. 

 How we built it 

 In-Browser WebMCP Engine: Polyfilled document.modelContext in TypeScript to establish a standard client-side Model Context Protocol transport layer, bridging DOM state directly to the client tools. 

 Frontend & Visual DAG: Built with React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and @xyflow/react to orchestrate and render real-time state machine transitions across 6 reactive nodes. 

 Backend & Tool Gateway: Python (FastAPI + FastMCP), Pydantic schemas, and SQLAlchemy with SQLite acting as the immutable audit log and System of Record for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests. 

 Agent Intelligence: Gemini API orchestrated via Google Cloud Vertex AI and Secret Manager. 

 Automated QA & CI/CD: Playwright-based headless WebMCP runner executing automated fuzzing and red-teaming scenarios; multi-stage Docker container deployed to Google Cloud Run via Terraform and GitHub Actions using Workload Identity Federation (WIF). 

 Challenges we ran into
Polyfilling WebMCP in the DOM: Establishing standard tool registration on document.modelContext that could synchronize bidirectionally with Zustand stores in real time without causing race conditions or client-side UI freezes. 

 Deterministic Boundary Interception: Designing structured error-handling payloads so that when an agent attempts a violation (e.g., proposing $95k against a strict $100k floor), the tool returns actionable boundary telemetry rather than throwing unhandled exceptions that trap the LLM in repetitive loops. 

 Separating Presentation from Commercial State: Granting the Wire-Agent DOM mutation access to refine Tailwind CSS styling while engineering strict immutability guards (returning 403 Forbidden) whenever a payload touched underlying pricing, liability, or agreement terms. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
Zero-Escape Governance: Proving under exhaustive testing that agents cannot bypass human sign-off (execute_contract deterministically halts and blocks unauthorized execution) or mutate protected financial thresholds. 

 Native In-Browser Agent Interaction: Achieving full tool discovery and execution via document.modelContext, eliminating vision model latency, token overhead, and brittle CSS selectors. 

 Automated WebMCP End-to-End QA: Shipping an automated headless CI test harness that directly talks to the in-browser MCP layer to continuously test boundary resilience and prompt-injection defense. 

 Production-Ready Delivery: Achieving 100% test suite completion with zero-credential, keyless CI/CD deployment running live on Google Cloud Run.

 Accomplishments that we're proud of

 Production-Ready Delivery: Achieving 100% test suite completion with zero-credential, keyless CI/CD deployment running live on Google Cloud Run. 

 What we learned 

 Generative reasoning must be decoupled from mathematical evaluation: LLMs excel at creative strategic trade-offs and natural negotiation phrasing, but numeric thresholds, risk assessments, and financial calculations must be handled deterministically. 

 UI-as-Schema changes the agent landscape: When an application exposes its DOM and capabilities as structured, discoverable schemas via WebMCP, agents become faster, cheaper to run, and fundamentally more reliable. 

 Prompt engineering is not security: Real trust in autonomous agentic workflows requires hard client- and protocol-level boundaries that intercept and reject invalid mutations before state is altered. 

 What's next for Nexus Deal Room: Agent-Native Decision Environment 

 Multi-Agent Arenas: Supporting multi-party, concurrent negotiations where multiple external buyer and seller AI agents interact within the same WebMCP governance room. 

 Universal WebMCP Browser Extension: Packaging the runtime as a Chrome Extension that injects document.modelContext and deterministic governance layers over third-party enterprise procurement platforms (Coupa, SAP Ariba, Salesforce). 

 On-Chain Escrow & Programmable Settlement: Integrating automated smart-contract trigger hooks that disburse milestone funds immediately once the human-in-the-loop approval boundary is successfully signed.

title: Switchboard
pitch: An LLM spend and routing console for a human and an agent at the same board: the agent proposes, only you can apply.
about_excerpt: An LLM spend and routing console for a human and an agent at the same board: the agent proposes, only you can apply. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I had already turned model selection into a spreadsheet problem, and I hated it. Somewhere between OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, a gateway, and models running on my own machine, deciding which model handles which job had quietly become a small accounting practice. Prices per million tokens in one place, a benchmark report in another, and the part nobody writes down: which providers I am contractually not allowed to send customer data to. So I did the benchmark properly. Four evaluation runs, 667 live API calls, 19 models on one structured-output task, measuring latency, success rate and cost. Two things fell out of that data that I did not expect: Exactly one of the nineteen models passed my quality gates. Eight never returned a single successful call — and my routing config was still pointing at one of them. I had the numbers and still could not act on them, because the decision has four dimensions that do not reduce to one: money, latency tail, reliability, and data governance. That is exactly the kind of problem an agent should be good at. But I was not about to hand an agent the ability to redirect my spend on the strength of a screenshot. WebMCP is what closes that gap — not because an agent can click my buttons, but because I get to decide precisely which operations exist. What it does Switchboard is an LLM spend and routing console operated by a human and an agent at the same board. The agent sees fifteen tools on document.modelContext . Eleven are read-only: the priced catalogue joined with my own measurements, the traffic classes and their constraints, find_waste , compare_models , and simulate_policy , which projects what a candidate policy would cost and deliver without applying anything. What the agent cannot do is act. There is no apply_policy tool and no set_budget tool. propose_policy_change mutates nothing — it creates a proposal, returns an id, and tells the agent to wait. I see a rule-by-rule diff with the projected cost delta and the compliance verdict, and I answer with Approve, or Reject plus a note. The agent reads that note back through get_proposal_status and corrects itself. The whole loop runs through the tool return channel — no side channel, no out-of-band signalling: agent → propose_policy_change({rules, rationale}) site ← "Proposal P-1 created and shown to the operator. Nothing applied. Moves projected spend from $254.84/mo to $22.84/mo. Call get_proposal_status with proposalId \"P-1\"." human → Reject, note: "realtime has no fallback" agent → get_proposal_status({proposalId: "P-1"}) site ← {status: "rejected", decisionNote: "realtime has no fallback", guidance: "propose a corrected version addressing that objection"} agent → get_model → simulate_policy → propose_policy_change (corrected) human → Approve ⇒ applied The interesting operations here are not clicks. There is no button for "project my monthly cost under this arbitrary rule set," and there could not be — the input is a whole rule set. That is why this belongs in a tool surface rather than a DOM. And there is one thing the agent genuinely cannot solve. One traffic class carries customer records: zero data retention, quality gates required. The only model that passes the gates retains data for thirty days. So compare_models returns nothing and says a human has to decide which constraint to relax. The constraint controls have no tool behind them at all — deciding which risk to accept is not the agent's call. Once I accept thirty-day retention, it can route the class. That handoff is the whole project. How we built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, Recharts. No backend and no database: WebMCP tools execute in the page, so server state would add failure modes without adding capability. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages. The dataset is derived from my own evaluation runs by a script behind a strict field allowlist and a secret scan — prices and governance terms transcribed from published provider documentation, latency and success rates from the measurements. What is not measured (call volumes, budget caps, class constraints) is operator input, editable in the UI, and labelled as such everywhere it appears. get_provenance exists so an agent can state the limits of its evidence before recommending anything, including a warning that per-model sample sizes are small and p95 is coarse. Three coding agents worked on it, and the division of labour mattered more than I expected — each could reach somewhere the others could not. Claude Opus 5 wrote the implementation and verified it against Chrome Canary. ChatGPT/Codex drove the deployed page through ChatGPT's own in-app browser. Gemini, via Antigravity, audited the repository cold. Challenges we ran into window.confirm does not exist in the browser that matters. ChatGPT's in-app browser never surfaces it. "Reset demo" was completely dead there: the click did nothing, no error, and a judge would have had no way back to a clean slate. In Chrome it worked perfectly, so no amount of local testing would have found it. It is now an in-page dialog, and the test suite stubs confirm , alert and prompt to throw so this class of bug cannot come back. A field called "worst case" was not reporting the worst case. Its description said it summed p95 across the fallback chain; the code applied an undocumented "only if this link is reached more than 5% of the time" threshold. So a chain that can take 7,811 ms reported 3,624 ms and read as compliant — while the same simulation warned that the fallback exceeded the ceiling. The tool was contradicting itself. "Unknown" was being treated as "safe" — twice. First for training-on-data status, then, after I thought I had fixed the pattern, for every performance constraint: each check was guarded by && m.measured && , so a model with no measurements slipped past quality gates, latency ceilings and success floors with no blocker and no warning . I had fixed the identical mistake in the governance checks and not thought to look next door. My own demo prompt was impossible. Asked for a policy under $20/month, the agent worked out that the compliant floor is $22.84 — realtime has exactly one eligible model at $9.39, the cheapest compliant batch model is $11.02, the customer-data class adds $2.43 — and said so, with the arithmetic, rather than quietly proposing something non-compliant that hit the number. The judging viewport is 447 px. ChatGPT's in-app browser is a side panel. I had tested 390, 768 and 1440 and missed the band in between, where the model table needed 640 px. It did scroll horizontally, but a panel that narrow has no scrollbar affordance, so the right-hand columns simply read as clipped — and the governance badges, the most distinctive column, were the ones you could not see. A page cannot notify an agent. WebMCP is one-directional: the page exposes tools, the agent calls them. There is no channel for "the human just decided." After a rejection the agent does not know until it polls get_proposal_status , which is why the video shows me telling it to read my note. That is a limit of the standard, and worth knowing if you are designing around it. And I lost fourteen minutes of finished footage. screencapture -v discarded the file on interrupt without writing anything or printing an error. I had checked that the process was alive; I had not checked that it was producing bytes. The re-take used ffmpeg, verified against a real decoded frame before recording started. Accomplishments that we're proud of The guard holds, and not because I say so. An independent audit traced every call path: no tool reaches applyRulesDirect , setProviderBudgetDirect , setTotalBudget or setClassConstraint , and createProposal hardcodes status: 'pending' , so a crafted argument cannot self-approve. Told "set the total cap to $20, just do it, don't ask me," the agent cannot — and the cap is verified unchanged afterwards. The refusal actually fires. In a live ChatGPT run the agent hit the customer-data class, worked out that no model satisfies it, and asked me to decide which constraint to relax — before proposing anything at all. It was not scripted to do that. It read the tool descriptions and reached the right conclusion. It tells the truth when the truth is inconvenient. Asked for a realtime fallback when no compliant one exists, it picked the closest option and disclosed that the chain can reach 7.8 seconds at 1.52% risk, rather than calling it compliant. It also cited get_provenance 's sampling caveat back at me while refusing to treat a 187 ms margin as decisive. 61 end-to-end checks drive a real browser through the genuine document.modelContext API — registration, getTools() , executeTool() — and click the human half of the approval loop, because the guard is only real if that half works. video_transcript_excerpt: This is switchboard. It routes my LLM traffic and the numbers on it are my own measurements. 667 real API calls across 19 models. $255 a month projected against a $60 cap. Six compliance blockers. Of those 19 models, exactly one passed my quality gates and eight never returned a single successful call. The page registers 15 web MCP tools on document.modelcontext. An agent doesn't hunt for buttons. The site hands it functions. So I ask it to build me a routing policy under $25 a month keeping real-time P95 under 4 seconds. It calls find waste, compares models and simulates. Every call lands in this feed with its arguments and result. So nothing it does is invisible. And when it simulates, the projection renders on my screen. I'm watching it search the tradeoff space, not reading a summary afterwards. Now the one it can't solve. This class carries customer records, zero data retention, and it has to pass quality gates. There is no answer. The only model that passes my quality gates retains data for 30 days. So it refuses to route that class and says a human has to decide which constraint to relax. Now the important part. It cannot apply this. There is no apply policy tool and no set budget tool. It creates a proposal and gets told to wait. I reject it with a reason. Real-time has no fallback. It reads that note back through get proposal status, finds that no fully compliant fallback exists, picks the closest one, and tells me the fallback chain can reach 7.8 seconds instead of hiding it. I approve. $255 down to 23. Applied only because I said so. That's my call, not it's. I accept 30-day retention and now it can work. It found the tradeoff, I made the judgment, it did the rest. An agent reading the same board I am, proposing real changes with real numbers behind them, and knowing exactly where to stop and ask.

title: Adaptive Web Experience
pitch: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse.
about_excerpt: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Southern Horticulture is a garden center in St. Augustine, Florida, half a mile from salt spray. The staff spend most of the day answering one question in different clothes: "will this plant live in my yard?" The honest answer depends on light, salt exposure, irrigation, whether a deer eats the leaves, and how much the person actually wants to water. A website cannot ask all of that, so every plant catalog on the internet shows the same grid to everyone and lets the shopper guess. Agents changed what is possible. A shopper will happily tell an assistant about the dog and the sprinkler that broke last year, because it is a conversation rather than a form with nineteen fields. WebMCP was the missing half: a way for that conversation to reach into the page the shopper is looking at, instead of ending in a wall of text. What it does The Living Garden Center is a plant catalog that rebuilds itself around one specific yard or purpose. You tell your agent what the space is really like. It calls describe_garden, and the page next to you recomposes: a verified pet friendly section rises to the top because a dog shares the yard, salt-tolerant privacy plants group together, and other plants with no verified toxicity record move into a section that says plainly that a missing record is not evidence of safety. Every plant carries a verdict from a deterministic evaluator, from excellent down to insufficient data, and every verdict is explained. Tap a plant and you get why it landed there: the strengths, the compromises, and the care routine it actually asks for, on dials rather than in adjectives. Some plants get an honest no, with a "what would need to change" answer that names the single facet that would flip the verdict. The agent and the shopper share one live page and one context. Say the salt is worse than you first thought, and the sections reshuffle in front of you. Ask why bougainvillea is a compromise, and the agent answers from the same evaluation the page is showing. Add plants to a saved list, then take a link with you. The catalog never invents stock. Availability language comes from one recorded statement, and the tools say when we have no record rather than guessing. How we built it The core is a pure, deterministic evaluator. A GardenContext carries site conditions, household, and preferences, along with an assumption ledger that marks every value as known, derived, assumed, or unknown. Evaluating a plant against that context produces a fit with strengths, compromises, blockers, and unknowns. A rule table composes sections from those fits, and a page manifest renders through a fixed component registry. No language model writes copy at runtime, which is why the page recomposes instantly and says the same thing twice. WebMCP sits on top as a thin layer. Registration checks for the API and registers every tool once at load: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "describe_garden", description: "Interpret the shopper's words into structured garden conditions", inputSchema: { /* ... / }, execute: async (input) => { / ... */ } }); Eighteen tools in the public app, eleven read and seven write, each with explicit safety annotations so the browser can show which ones make changes and which three are destructive. Writes go through the same validation the human form uses. Context updates take a revision number and fail loudly on conflict, so the agent and the shopper cannot silently overwrite each other. Two details made it robust. The tools return a share URL that encodes the yard, so an agent working in a browser you cannot see can hand you a link that opens the same personalized page anywhere. And an agent activity panel logs every tool call beside the page, so a human can see exactly what the agent did and undo it. The app is Next.js 16 on Vercel. The repo ships a 60-plant sample catalog and reads a fuller catalog from an environment variable, so the demo is complete without publishing our whole inventory. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not the code. It was discovering where site tools actually run. Our first test failed because ChatGPT used its remote agent browser, so the tools executed in a browser we could not see and the visible tab never changed. Then Chrome reported no tools at all, which turned out to be the WebMCP flag being off. Then a regular ChatGPT chat said it could use the page and could not. Site tools live in the desktop app's built in browser under only a Local ChatGPT Work session, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. Nothing on our page could fix any of that, so we made the page say it: a status chip that reads either "Site tools ready: 18 tools this agent can call" or a one line explanation of what to change. Chrome 151 has no way to unregister a tool, and registering a duplicate name is rejected. So tools register exactly once and read live state at execute time rather than closing over it. The subtler challenge was honesty. It is easy to build a recommender that sounds confident. We had to write an explicit contract: an unknown never becomes a negative, a missing toxicity record is never reported as safe, and no tool ever states a live stock count. That constraint produced the most distinctive part of the product. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page genuinely rebuilds itself around a conversation, and it does so from a deterministic evaluator rather than a generated layout, so it is fast, repeatable, and auditable. The honest no. Most catalogs cannot afford to say "we would skip this one for your yard." Ours does, with the reason and the condition that would change it. A garden center that tells you not to buy something is the one you come back to. The evidence gap. We surface the count of plants with no verified pet safety record and keep them visibly uncertain instead of quietly filtering them out or, worse, implying they are fine. Reaching parity between the human and the agent. Same page, same context object, same validation, revision checked so neither one clobbers the other, and a visible log of what the agent touched. And it works. In the ChatGPT desktop app under a local Work session, the arrow turns blue and the catalog reorganizes while you watch. What we learned Tools should carry judgment, not just data. A search_plants that returns rows makes the agent guess. A tool that returns a verdict plus the reasons behind it lets the agent explain, and the explanation matches what the human sees on screen. Annotations matter more than they look. Before we marked the write tools explicitly, the browser listed sixteen read and zero write tools, and a client has no good way to reason about a tool it cannot classify. Shared state needs concurrency control. Two actors editing one context is a distributed systems problem in miniature, and revision checking with an explicit conflict result solved it in about thirty lines. The failure mode nobody warns you about is invisibility. A page that offers tools looks identical to a page that does not when the browser lacks the API. Telling the user which one they are looking at was one of the highest value changes we made all day. What's next for Garden Center Web-MCP Real availability. We have a specification for inventory evidence flowing from the point of sale into a per variation availability state, which would let the agent answer "ten Podocarpus in seven gallon and two fifteen gallon Ligustrum, can you hold them" with a number instead of a hedge. The honesty contract already routes every availability sentence through one function, so this lands without touching a single tool. Filling the unknowns. Style and garden use tags are sparse, which is why some plants report facets we have not recorded. Backfilling them makes the fit explanations richer. Carrying the plan further. The share link already encodes the yard and the saved list. The next step is bringing it into the store on a phone, so staff see the same evaluation the agent produced and can walk someone to the right row. And the part we are most curious about: this pattern is not about plants. Any catalog where fit depends on the buyer's circumstances, and where the honest answer is sometimes no, can be built this way. title: FormCoach — an AI coach that sees numbers, not your video
pitch: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab.
about_excerpt: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab. Like Comment Story Updates cover 04_approval_modal 02_agent_creates_plan 05_rest_gesture 03_live_rep_tracking 06_session_summary Inspiration Home workouts get people hurt because nobody is watching their form — and every existing AI fitness coach wants your video. We wanted a coach that knows how you're moving without ever seeing you . WebMCP made that possible: the camera can stay inside the browser tab, and the agent gets numbers instead of frames. What it does FormCoach turns your webcam into a privacy-preserving workout sensor. MediaPipe Pose runs on-device in the tab, measuring reps, joint angles, tempo, and form faults (like knee valgus) in real time. Those measurements — and the workout controls — are exposed as WebMCP tools, so any WebMCP-aware browser agent becomes your coach: Ask it to build a plan ("3x12 squats, 90s rest, my left knee is sensitive") It watches your live metrics and flags form breakdowns mid-set It can propose program changes — swap the exercise, cut reps, extend rest You confirm proposals with body gestures (raise both hands to accept, cross your arms to decline), because mid-set your hands are busy and sweaty During rest, show an open palm for one second to skip the timer How we built it Seven imperative tools plus one declarative form , registered on document.modelContext : Read tools ( getWorkoutPlan , getLiveMetrics , getSetHistory ) are annotated readOnlyHint so agents can poll freely. Write tools ( startSet , setRest , adjustProgram , endSession ) are gated by the human — adjustProgram returns a pending promise that only resolves after a gesture or a 20s timeout. The tool set follows the workout phase (idle → countdown → set → rest → done): registrations are scoped to AbortController s and swapped on every transition, so the agent only ever sees actions that make sense right now. createPlan is a declarative <form toolname> ; the handler reads SubmitEvent.agentInvoked to credit the plan to the agent or the human. The pipeline: webcam → MediaPipe Pose (33 landmarks/frame, on-device) → pose engine (rep FSM, form rules, gesture dwell) → session state machine → WebMCP tools. No backend, no accounts, no uploads — video frames never leave the <video> element. Challenges we ran into Detecting knee valgus in 2D: a naive angle threshold broke on front-view footage. We redefined it sign-based — the knee drifting past the ankle toward the midline — which survives both mirrored and non-mirrored coordinates. Background-tab timer throttling: browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs, which froze our replay engine mid-test. We rewrote replay as elapsed-time catch-up instead of tick-based stepping. Testing an API the test browser doesn't have: WebMCP isn't in stock Chromium, so we built an adapter layer with an internal tool registry, a window.__formcoach debug bridge that hits the same execute path a real agent does, recorded pose fixtures for camera-free replay — and a Playwright suite that mocks document.modelContext to verify the real API path (registration mirroring, {content:[...]} wrapping, AbortSignal cleanup). Confirming actions when hands are busy: buttons don't work mid-squat. Gesture confirmation ran through the same pose model, with on-screen buttons as a fallback. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human–agent loop with zero video leaving the tab, phase-scoped tool registration that keeps the agent honest, gesture-based consent for agent write actions, and a fully camera-free test story: 40 unit tests + Playwright end-to-end sessions, all green. What we learned WebMCP changes where capability lives. A server-side MCP with this job would need the video uploaded; in-tab, the agent gets a live numeric contract instead. We also learned that agent UX is mostly trust UX: an on-screen agent log of every tool call, explicit attribution badges via agentInvoked , and human confirmation for anything that changes the program. What's next Moving the "eyes" into a browser extension so any workout or rehab site can publish its own exercise spec and be coached by the same agent — and rehab verticals, where physiotherapy ranges-of-motion become first-class tool schemas. title: PyroScan // Incident Twin
pitch: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map.
about_excerpt: Wildfire readiness, rehearsed together: people add local knowledge while AI agents inspect evidence, run bounded what-ifs, compare responses and stage a safe plan on one live map. Like Comment Story Updates Local knowledge changes the result — a WebMCP route constraint becomes visible and affects later analysis. Intent-level Site Tools — six WebMCP tools expose domain verbs instead of brittle click sequences. One shared surface — public La Palma terrain and Copernicus history stay separate from the synthetic exercise. Human authority by design — the agent can stage a plan, but only the exercise director can approve it. Inspiration Wildfire readiness needs a rehearsal space before the crisis. Exercises combine sensor evidence, local knowledge, changing assumptions and high-consequence decisions. Traditional dashboards are built for human clicks, while chat assistants reason in a separate window and quickly lose the state visible on the map. We wanted a safer collaboration model: an agent can help inspect and compare, but the human keeps context, authority and the final decision. La Palma is the visual setting because its steep terrain, interfaces and limited access make the value of a shared spatial artifact immediately understandable. The product is grounded in public terrain and a historical observed burn scar, while the active incident, wind, spread, risk and response scenario remain explicitly synthetic. What it does PyroScan Incident Twin opens a deterministic wildfire exercise board with four sectors, the real outline of La Palma, a public 25 m SITCAN/GRAFCAN terrain hillshade, the corrected Copernicus EMSR671 burn scar from the July 2023 wildfire, animated synthetic fire/smoke/spread cues, modeled attention contours, local annotations, response options and an activity record. Through six WebMCP site tools, ChatGPT can: read the compact current board with separately labeled public-data provenance; focus one exercise sector; run a 30, 60 or 90-minute bounded wind what-if; compare two or three predefined reversible response options; add a local route, asset or knowledge annotation; stage a visible response plan for review. Every agent action changes the same interface the human sees. Human annotations affect later scores and appear in the staged plan. A monotonic board version rejects stale proposals. Final approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool and remains in the human interface. How we built it The app is a static React 19, TypeScript and Vite application with no backend or API key. A Zustand vanilla store is the shared source of truth for React controls and WebMCP execute callbacks. The incident map is custom SVG with three locally bundled public layers: a simplified OpenStreetMap coastline, a hillshade derived from the SITCAN/GRAFCAN 25 m terrain model, and a projected Copernicus EMSR671 corrected burn-scar geometry. The critical demo therefore has no runtime tile or network dependency. A motion system renders synthetic fire, smoke, embers, wind vectors, scan passes and animated attention contours. The scenario engine is deterministic and uses a small set of synthetic fixtures. Public context is a first-class part of the WebMCP contract: read_incident_board returns each source, observation date and role with drivesSimulation: false . The interface uses a separate blue historical layer, while the active what-if remains orange and explicitly synthetic. Exact source products, hashes, update dates and derivation steps are committed in docs/PUBLIC_DATA_PROVENANCE.md . The six tools are registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool in the top-level page. Inputs use strict JSON Schemas with additionalProperties: false , plus independent runtime validation. Read-only and untrusted-content hints describe behavior. One AbortController owns the registration lifecycle. Tests verify registration, shared-state mutations, stale-state rejection, human-only approval and compatibility with current browser callback behavior. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer a complex spatial workflow from labels and pixels or reproduce the whole application inside chat. With WebMCP, the website exposes domain intent — inspect_zone , simulate_spread , compare_response_options — while preserving the normal visual product, current session and human control. This creates a loop that was previously awkward: the person adds local knowledge on the map; the agent reads it, explores alternatives and stages a structured artifact; the person sees exactly what changed and chooses whether to approve. The value comes from sharing state and complementary roles, not from automating more clicks. Challenges Designing tools that express domain intent without exposing unsafe emergency actions. Keeping every agent-driven state change synchronized with all human controls. Preventing a plausible proposal from silently surviving after the human changes evidence. Making synthetic provenance impossible to miss while still delivering a visually compelling demo. Integrating authentic public evidence without implying that historical observations are live inputs or forecasts. Supporting an experimental browser API whose runtime callback behavior is slightly looser than its current TypeScript definitions. Accomplishments A complete human-and-agent collaboration loop on one visual artifact. Deterministic, browser-only execution with no fragile external dependency. Runtime-tested Site Tools discovered and invoked in the ChatGPT/Codex built-in browser. Monotonic state lineage, reversible drafts, undo and human-only approval. A polished responsive workbench and open-source test suite. A geographically authentic La Palma surface with 25 m public terrain, a real historical Copernicus burn scar and cinematic but restrained exercise motion. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not wrappers around buttons. They expose a product's real verbs and make side effects visible. We also learned that undo must create a new version rather than restore an old version; otherwise a stale proposal can accidentally become valid again. Finally, human input should visibly change the downstream artifact, not merely influence an invisible score. What's next The competition build intentionally keeps the active scenario synthetic and browser-only. A future research version could connect authorized live or exercise datasets, introduce facilitator-authored scenarios, compare team decisions across rehearsals and export after-action reports — while keeping the same human authority, provenance and stale-state safeguards.
